0.title: Revelation: The Unveiling of the Victorious Lamb
0.overview:
Revelation is the most debated book in the Bible. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria questioned whether the apostle John wrote it — not because he rejected the book, but because he found it so unlike the Gospel. In the centuries since, the book has generated more controversy, more speculation, more bad charts, and more genuine spiritual comfort than any other portion of Scripture. Before we open a single seal, we need to understand what kind of book we are reading.

The word that opens the book — apokalypsis — means “unveiling.” Revelation does not conceal the future in cryptic code to be cracked by clever scholars in the final generation. It unveils a reality that was always there but hidden from ordinary sight: the reign of the slaughtered Lamb over all of history. The book was written to be read aloud in congregations (1:3), probably by a lector standing in a first-century house church. Its images were designed to be heard, felt, and worshipped — not diagrammed. If your primary response to Revelation is to reach for a chart, you are already in danger of missing the point.

Revelation belongs to three overlapping literary genres simultaneously. As an apocalypse, it uses symbolic visions, cosmic imagery, and heavenly perspectives to reinterpret earthly events — a thoroughly Jewish genre with deep roots in Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, and the rich inter-testamental literature (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch). As prophecy, it speaks the word of God into a specific historical crisis, calling the church to faithfulness and warning the world of judgment. As a letter (1:4; 22:21), it is addressed to real congregations facing real pressure, and it carries all the pastoral weight of Paul’s epistles. Missing any one of these three dimensions distorts the whole.

The author is John, exiled to the island of Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9). Early Christian testimony overwhelmingly identified him with John the Apostle, the beloved disciple. The book was most likely written during the reign of Domitian (c. AD 95–96), when the imperial cult was being aggressively promoted in the province of Asia and Christians were being pressed to acknowledge “Caesar as Lord.” Seven actual churches — in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea — received this letter. They were living under the crushing weight of Rome’s total-sovereignty claim. Revelation is the pastoral response of an exiled pastor to congregations in crisis.

Four Frameworks for Reading Revelation

Faithful, Bible-believing, Christ-loving readers have understood the overall structure of Revelation in four main ways. The reading followed here is the amillennial/idealist position — the historic Reformed mainstream — with the other frameworks noted at every major structural decision point. All four frameworks agree on the non-negotiables: Christ has decisively won. The church will endure to the end. History is moving toward a fixed and glorious goal. Jesus returns in visible, bodily glory. The wicked face final judgment. The righteous receive a new creation. Where they differ is in the timing, sequencing, and nature of the visions.

The Preterist framework holds that most — or all — of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century. The great tribulation is the Roman-Jewish War of AD 66–70, culminating in Jerusalem’s destruction. The beasts represent Nero and the Roman imperial system. “The things that must soon take place” (1:1) and “the time is near” (1:3) are taken with strict literalness: the book addresses events imminent to its first readers. The partial-preterist position (R.C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton) holds that chapters 1–19 are largely fulfilled while chapters 20–22 remain future. Preterism’s great strength is its seriousness about the book’s own time-markers. Its challenge is explaining how a largely-fulfilled Revelation speaks with permanent power to the church in every age.

The Historicist framework reads Revelation as a symbolic map of the entire sweep of church history from Pentecost to the Second Coming, with the seals, trumpets, and bowls charting the rise and fall of empires. The Reformers broadly held this view, identifying the papacy with the beast. Though now a minority position, historicism produced generations of courageous preaching by men who believed they were living inside the very story Revelation was telling.

The Idealist (Amillennial) framework — the reading followed here — reads Revelation as a profound symbolic portrayal of the cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan, the church and the world, that characterizes the entire period between the first and second comings. The visions do not map a sequence of datable historical events; they depict recurring spiritual realities — the pressure of empire, the suffering of the saints, the apparent triumph of evil, and the certain victory of God — that are enacted in every age. The seals, trumpets, and bowls are best understood as parallel series (recapitulation), each sweeping from the cross to the Second Coming with increasing intensity. This reading takes seriously both the first-century occasion and the book’s permanent relevance. Its advocates include Augustine (City of God), B.B. Warfield, Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen, G.K. Beale (whose commentary is the fullest scholarly treatment available), Dennis Johnson, and Michael Wilcock.

The Premillennial/Futurist framework holds that most of Revelation (especially chapters 4–22) describes events still future, culminating in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. Two major streams: Historic Premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) teaches that the church goes through the tribulation before Christ returns to establish his kingdom on earth, followed by the final judgment. Dispensational Premillennialism (John MacArthur, Charles Swindoll, J. Vernon McGee, John Walvoord, Charles Ryrie) adds the distinctive of a pre-tribulation Rapture — the church is caught up before a seven-year tribulation falls on an unbelieving world, with that period constituting God’s final dealings with national Israel. Shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and widely popularized through the Scofield Reference Bible, this is the dominant eschatological framework in much of evangelical America. It deserves full respect as the honest, Scripture-rooted reading of millions of sincere believers, and its specific interpretations are noted at every key junction.

How to Read Revelation

Three principles will guide us. First, let the book’s own genre shape how you read it. Apocalyptic literature communicates through symbols, not newspaper reporting. When you read of a dragon with seven heads and ten horns, you are not meant to visualize a literal creature — you are meant to feel the horror of satanic power in all its many-headed, grasping form. Second, hear the book through first-century ears. Most of Revelation’s images come from the Old Testament — Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus — and from the Roman world of the first century. When John’s original hearers heard “the great city,” they heard “Rome.” Third, read for comfort and courage, not for curiosity. Revelation was written to sustain the church’s witness under pressure. It was written to answer one question above all others: Is Jesus really Lord, or is Caesar? The answer, given in vision after dazzling vision, is: the Lamb who was slain is Lord of lords and King of kings. Everything else is footnote.

When was it written, and by whom? Most early writers place it near the end of Domitian’s reign, around AD 95; Irenaeus, who knew men who had known John, says the vision was seen near the end of Domitian’s reign, almost within his own generation. Some argue for a date before AD 70, under Nero, pointing to the temple in 11:1–2 and the seven kings of 17:10. The later date is more likely: the churches have had time to decline (2:4; 3:15–17), and Smyrna’s church seems to be well established. The author calls himself simply John, a servant who needs no introduction (1:1, 9). Dionysius of Alexandria doubted that he was the apostle, because the Greek is so different from the Gospel’s. But Justin and Irenaeus, the earliest witnesses, say it was the apostle, and the difference in style suits a different kind of book written in exile. The more likely conclusion is that the apostle John wrote it.

How should the thousand years of chapter 20 be read? Premillennial Christians hold that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Postmillennial Christians hold that the gospel will so prevail that a long age of peace will come before he returns. Amillennial Christians hold that the thousand years is the present age, from Christ’s first coming to his second, in which Satan is bound so that the gospel goes to the nations and the saints reign with Christ, followed by one return, one resurrection and judgment, and the new creation. This commentary takes the amillennial view, because Revelation repeatedly tells the same story from different angles, because the rest of the New Testament speaks of one return with resurrection and judgment together (John 5:28–29; 2 Pet 3:10–13), and because the binding of Satan matches Jesus’ words about binding the strong man (Matt 12:29).

1.title: The Son of Man Among the Lampstands
1.overview:
The book opens with a triple identification of its nature: a revelation, a prophecy, and a letter. All three genres are in play simultaneously, and the reader who forgets any one of them will misread the whole. John does not ease us in gradually. Within three verses we have God the Father, Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit (the seven spirits), angels, and the entire church across time — the whole cosmic cast assembled on the opening page.

The chapter moves in three great waves. The Prologue (vv. 1–3) establishes the book’s source, content, and urgency. The Greeting (vv. 4–8) is a full trinitarian doxology that would have been recognized immediately as a counter-imperial manifesto — titles of the kind Caesar claimed for himself (“faithful,” “firstborn,” “ruler of kings”) are given to Jesus. Then the Vision of the Son of Man (vv. 9–20) is the pivot of the entire book: before any seal is opened, any trumpet blown, or any bowl poured, John sees who stands at the center of history. Everything that follows is commentary on this one vision.

The vision of the glorified Christ is drawn almost entirely from Daniel 7 and 10. John’s first readers — Jews and Gentile God-fearers schooled in the Hebrew scriptures — would have felt the weight of every image. The white hair of the Ancient of Days, the eyes like flame, the feet like burnished bronze, the voice like many waters, the two-edged sword from his mouth: this is not a gentle Jesus meek and mild. This is the eternal Son in his glory, the conqueror of death, the sovereign over all history. The seven lampstands among which he walks are the seven churches — and the first thing any congregation needs to know about itself is that the glorified Christ walks among them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three verses, and the whole book is already positioned. Verses 1–2 give the chain: God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ, to show his servants what must soon take place; Christ made it known by sending his angel to his servant John; John bore witness to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, to everything he saw. Nothing here originates with the writer. Verse 3 then pronounces the first of the book’s seven beatitudes, and it falls on three groups at once: the one who reads the words aloud, those who hear them, and those who keep what is written — because the time is near.

The word apokalypsis means an unveiling, a covering taken off something that was there already. That single word rules out the most popular use of this book. Revelation is not a code hiding the future from ordinary readers until a clever generation cracks it; it is the cloth coming off the throne, so that a church which can see only the magistrate and the temple of the emperor may also see who has been governing the world the whole time.

“Soon” (v. 1) and “the time is near” (v. 3) are the book’s first difficulty and are addressed at the verses themselves. In short: the Greek en tachei speaks of speed rather than of the calendar; the New Testament dates nearness from the cross, so that every generation since Pentecost has lived in the last days; and in any case a great deal of what this book describes fell on these very congregations within a few years.

The beatitude of v. 3 is the sentence that should govern how the book is used. The blessing is not attached to understanding it but to keeping it. And the picture behind the verse is a room, not a desk: one reader, many listeners, a scroll that had to be carried by hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Book to Be Kept

The revelation comes from God through Christ, his angel and John, to the churches. It is an unveiling, not a code, and its blessing falls on those who hear it and keep it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: One reader stood before a listening house church.

Now: After any chapter of this book, ask whether it left you with an opinion or a resolve.

verseByVerse.quote: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.

Meaning first. Revelation 1 introduces the whole book and the Christ who stands at its centre. The book is an unveiling that God gave to Jesus Christ, passed through an angel to John, and sent to the churches, and a blessing rests on all who read it aloud, hear it and keep it (vv. 1–3). John greets seven churches in Asia with grace and peace from the eternal God, from the sevenfold Spirit before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of earth’s kings (vv. 4–5a). Then he breaks into praise to the Christ who loves us, has set us free from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom of priests (vv. 5b–6). He announces Christ’s coming on the clouds, seen by every eye (v. 7), and God declares himself the Alpha and the Omega, the Almighty (v. 8). John explains where he was: exiled on Patmos for the gospel, in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, when a trumpet-like voice told him to write to seven named churches (vv. 9–11). Turning, he saw seven golden lampstands and, among them, one like a son of man, robed as a priest, with white hair, blazing eyes, bronze feet, a voice like many waters, seven stars in his hand, a sword from his mouth and a face like the sun (vv. 12–16). John fell as though dead, but Christ laid his hand on him: do not be afraid, I am the first and the last, the living one who died and lives for ever, holding the keys of Death and Hades (vv. 17–18). He commissions John to write, and explains that the stars are the angels of the churches and the lampstands are the churches themselves (vv. 19–20). The chapter’s message to a small, persecuted church is simple and immense: the risen Christ is alive, he rules, and he walks among his churches.

Setting and background. John was exiled to Patmos, a small island off the coast of modern Turkey, most probably near the end of the emperor Domitian’s reign (about AD 95), as the early church writer Irenaeus reports; some date the book earlier, in the late 60s under Nero. The author calls himself simply John, a servant and brother, and the church from the second century identified him as the apostle John, son of Zebedee. The churches of Asia faced pressure from three sides: the imperial cult, which expected citizens to honour the emperor as lord; trade guilds whose feasts involved idols; and hostile local synagogues. Some Christians were compromising, some were growing cold, and at least one had already died (2:13). Revelation is written to them, and to the whole church after them, to show who really rules.

What kind of book this is. Revelation combines three kinds of writing. It is an apocalypse, a genre full of symbolic visions, numbers and heavenly scenes, like Daniel and Zechariah. It is a prophecy (v. 3), a word from God calling for response. And it is a letter (v. 4), sent to real congregations with real problems. Each shapes how it is read. Its images are symbols, not photographs: Christ is not literally a lamb with seven eyes (5:6), and the sword from his mouth is his word. Its message calls for faithfulness, not speculation. And whatever it meant must first have meant something to those seven churches.

The revelation of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Revelation” (apokalypsis, an uncovering, an unveiling). The book’s title tells us God is not hiding things but showing them. “Of Jesus Christ” means both the revelation that comes from Jesus, who gives it, and the revelation about Jesus, who is its subject. Both are true. Above all, the book unveils Christ.

Which God gave him to show to his servants. Key words. The chain of revelation: God gives it to Christ; Christ sends it by his angel; the angel shows it to John; John writes it to the churches. Every link guarantees the message is from God himself. “Servants” (doulois, slaves): all believers, not a spiritual elite.

The things that must soon take place. Key words. “Must” (dei, it is necessary): the events follow God’s sure plan. The phrase echoes Daniel 2:28, where Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Daniel saw it far off; John says it must happen soon. “Soon” (en tachei, quickly, without delay). Since the resurrection, the last days have already begun (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). Many of the book’s events started happening at once in the persecution of these churches, and the rest are near in God’s timing (2 Peter 3:8–9).

He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John. Key words. “Made it known” (esēmanen, signified, showed by signs). The verb is related to the word for a sign, a hint at the symbolic form of what follows. God communicates in pictures here.

Who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Bore witness” (emartyrēsen, testified). Witness is a key theme of the book: Christ is the faithful witness (v. 5), and believers suffer for their testimony (6:9; 12:11). The word for witness later became the word for martyr.

Even to all that he saw. John is a faithful reporter: he writes what he saw, no more and no less.

Where Christians differ: how to read Revelation. Preterists see most of the book fulfilled in the first century, in the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70) or the Roman Empire. Historicists read it as a timeline of church history, often identifying the papacy with the beast. Futurists, including dispensationalists, place most of chapters 4–22 in a seven-year tribulation at the end of history, after a secret rapture of the church. Idealists see it as timeless symbols of the conflict between good and evil. Verdict: the best reading combines the strengths of several. The book spoke first to first-century churches about their real enemies. Its visions then show, in a series of repeated cycles, the conflict between Christ and Satan through the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings. And it ends with a real, future, visible return of Christ, a final judgement and a new creation. This is often called the modified idealist or eclectic approach, and it fits the amillennial reading this app follows. It keeps the book relevant to every generation without losing its historical roots or its real future.

What it does not mean. “Soon” does not mean John was wrong because nearly two thousand years have passed. In Scripture, the end has been near since the resurrection, and God’s patience is not slowness (2 Peter 3:8–9). Nor does “revelation” mean a puzzle for experts. It was sent to ordinary believers to be read aloud and obeyed.

In a sentence. This book is the unveiling God gave to Jesus Christ, to show his servants what must happen soon; Christ sent it through his angel to John, who has faithfully reported everything he saw as God’s word and Jesus’ testimony.

On a Tuesday. Revelation is not a book for curiosity about the future but for courage in the present. Read it asking: what does this show me about Jesus, and how should I live because of it?
verseByVerse.note: John wrote on Patmos, probably in the mid 90s AD under the emperor Domitian, though some date it to the late 60s under Nero. “Revelation” translates apokalypsis, an unveiling. The book is full of Old Testament imagery, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah and Zechariah.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.

Setting and background. Most early Christians could not read and did not own books. Scripture was read aloud in the gathered church, as in the synagogue (Luke 4:16; Colossians 4:16; 1 Timothy 4:13). Revelation expects to be read aloud, from start to finish, to a listening congregation. Heard this way, its patterns, repetitions and climaxes work like music.

Blessed is the one who reads aloud. Key words. “Blessed” (makarios, truly happy, favoured by God). This is the first of seven beatitudes in Revelation (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). The number seven, the number of completeness, runs through the book. “Reads aloud” (anaginōskōn): the public reader in the church service.

The words of this prophecy. Key words. “Prophecy” (prophēteia). Revelation calls itself prophecy, God’s word through a prophet, carrying the authority of the Old Testament prophets. It is not only prediction; prophecy calls people to repent and be faithful.

And blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it. Key words. “Keep” (tērountes, observe, obey, hold fast). The blessing is not for those who decode the book, but for those who obey it. Revelation is to be kept, like a command, not solved, like a riddle. The book ends with the same blessing (22:7).

For the time is near. Key words. “Time” (kairos, the decisive moment, the appointed season). “Near” (engys). Because the end is near, the response cannot be postponed.

What it does not mean. This blessing does not promise special favour for those who build timelines. It promises blessing to those who listen and obey. A church that knows every theory about the beast but does not keep itself from idols has missed the blessing.

In a sentence. God blesses the one who reads this prophecy aloud to the church, and blesses all who hear it and hold fast to what it says, because the decisive time is close.

For worship. Read Revelation aloud in church, in whole sections, as it was meant to be heard. The book is a promise of blessing to listeners who obey.
verseByVerse.note: The first of seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Greeting to the Seven Churches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What looks like a routine letter-opening is a declaration of allegiance. Verse 4 names the sender and the seven churches of Asia, and sends grace and peace from “him who is and who was and who is to come” and from “the seven spirits who are before his throne” — the Father in his eternal self-existence, and the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness. Verse 5a completes the trinitarian greeting with three titles for Jesus Christ: the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, the ruler of kings on earth. Prophet, priest and king — and titles of exactly the kind the Roman emperor claimed for himself.

At verse 5b the greeting breaks off into praise before it is finished: to him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. The tenses carry the doctrine. He loves — present, continuous, written to people who may not survive the year. He freed — past, completed, at the cost of blood. He made us a kingdom and priests — past, already done, so that the church’s royal and priestly standing is a present possession and not a future promotion (Ex. 19:6). Verse 6 closes the doxology with glory and dominion forever and ever, and the word for dominion, kratos, is an imperial word being handed to a crucified man.

Verse 7 is the announcement the book exists to make: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10 fused into one sentence — the same fusion Jesus made at his trial (Matt. 26:64). The coming is public, universal, and unmissable, and the wailing may be repentance or terror; the text leaves both standing, and the same sight will produce both.

Verse 8 gives God the Father the last word of the section in his own voice, which happens only twice in the book: I am the Alpha and the Omega… who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty. Pantokratōr — ruler of all — occurs nine times in Revelation and once in the rest of the New Testament (2 Cor 6:18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Loved, Freed, Made Priests

Grace comes from the eternal God, the sevenfold Spirit and Jesus Christ — faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, ruler of kings. He loves us, has freed us by his blood, and has made us a kingdom and priests.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Churches under pressure heard Caesar’s kind of titles given to a crucified man.

Now: Endurance grows from hearing that he loves us now.

verseByVerse.quote: John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.

Setting and background. Asia here means the Roman province in the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus its leading city. The seven churches (named in v. 11) lay roughly in a circle along a Roman road, in the order a messenger would travel: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea. There were other churches in Asia (Colossae, Hierapolis, Troas), so seven were chosen as a complete set, representing the whole church. Each letter in chapters 2–3 was meant to be heard by all (2:7: what the Spirit says to the churches).

John to the seven churches that are in Asia. Key words. “Seven” (hepta). In Revelation, seven signals completeness. The seven churches are real congregations, and at the same time stand for the whole church in every age.

Grace to you and peace. Key words. “Grace” (charis), God’s undeserved favour, and “peace” (eirēnē), the wholeness and reconciliation it brings. The standard Christian greeting, as in Paul’s letters. Revelation is a letter.

From him who is and who was and who is to come. Key words. This is God the Father, described with an expansion of the divine name revealed to Moses, I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14). He exists in the present, has always existed, and is coming. The Greek is deliberately unusual: John keeps the name unchanged after the preposition “from”, which would normally change its form, as if God’s name cannot be bent by grammar. The emperor’s power was passing; God’s is eternal. Note “is to come” rather than “will be”: God’s future is his coming to judge and renew (11:17).

And from the seven spirits who are before his throne. Key words. “Seven spirits” (hepta pneumatōn). Placed between the Father and the Son as a source of grace and peace, they must be the Holy Spirit himself, described in his fullness and his complete activity. The imagery comes from Zechariah 4, where seven lamps are the eyes of the Lord, and from the sevenfold description of the Spirit resting on the Messiah in Isaiah 11:2. Later, the seven spirits are the seven eyes of the Lamb sent out into all the earth (5:6). The greeting is Trinitarian: Father, Spirit and Son.

Where Christians differ: who are the seven spirits? Some take them as seven angels, the highest angels standing before God (compare 8:2). Others take them as the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness. Verdict: the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace come only from God, never from angels, and the seven spirits stand within a divine greeting from Father and Son. Revelation’s symbolic numbers make sevenfold a natural way of picturing the one Spirit, perfect and active everywhere (5:6).

And from Jesus Christ the faithful witness. Key words. Christ’s three titles echo Psalm 89, the psalm of God’s covenant with David. “The faithful witness” (ho martys ho pistos): Christ told the truth about God, and held to it before Pilate unto death (John 18:37; 1 Timothy 6:13). The persecuted churches are to be faithful witnesses like him (2:13, where Antipas is called by the same title).

The firstborn of the dead. Key words. “Firstborn” (prōtotokos). Christ is the first to rise from the dead into resurrection life, never to die again, and his resurrection is the beginning and guarantee of ours (Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstborn also carries the sense of rank: the heir with supreme status (Psalm 89:27).

And the ruler of kings on earth. Key words. “Ruler” (archōn). Psalm 89:27 promises that David’s son will be the highest of the kings of the earth. Jesus already is. The emperor in Rome, who seemed to rule the world, is under the authority of the crucified Jew whose followers he persecuted. The book will show the kings of the earth in rebellion (17:2), defeated (19:19), and finally bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (21:24).

What it does not mean. The seven spirits do not mean seven Holy Spirits, or that the Spirit is divided. Seven is the number of fullness. Nor does “ruler of kings” mean Christ’s reign is only future. He rules now, though his reign is not yet seen by all.

In a sentence. John writes to the seven churches of Asia, wishing them grace and peace from the eternal God who is, was and is coming, from the Spirit in all his fullness before the throne, and from Jesus Christ, who witnessed faithfully, rose first from the dead and rules every king on earth.

On a Tuesday. Whoever holds power over you, an employer, a government, a culture, is under the rule of Jesus Christ. Faithful witness is worth it, because the faithful witness rose again.
verseByVerse.note: The seven churches lay on a circular road in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). “Seven spirits” probably stands for the Holy Spirit in his fullness.

verseByVerse.quote: To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

Setting and background. As soon as John names Christ, he breaks into a doxology. The wording draws on the exodus: at Sinai, God told Israel, redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the Passover lamb, that they would be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). Christ has done a greater exodus for his people.

To him who loves us. Key words. “Loves” (agapōnti, present tense: who keeps on loving us). Christ’s love did not end at the cross; he loves his suffering church now. Before Revelation shows a single judgement, it tells the church it is loved.

And has freed us from our sins by his blood. Key words. “Freed” (lysanti, loosed, released, past tense: a finished act). Sin is pictured as a chain, and Christ’s death is the price that broke it. “By his blood” (en tō haimati autou): by his sacrificial death in our place. Penal substitution is assumed here: Christ’s blood frees us because he bore the penalty our sins deserved (5:9).

And made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. Key words. “Kingdom” (basileian) and “priests” (hiereis). Echoing Exodus 19:6, the church, Jew and Gentile together, is now the people God promised Israel would be. We are a kingdom: the people over whom Christ reigns, who share his reign (5:10; 20:6). We are priests: every believer has direct access to God and offers spiritual sacrifices of praise and service (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Hebrews 13:15). Note the tense: he has made us. This is present reality, not only future hope.

To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Key words. “Glory” (doxa), the honour and splendour due to him; “dominion” (kratos), might, ruling power. Glory and power belong to Christ, not to Caesar. Ascribing such a doxology to Jesus, which Jews reserved for God alone, shows that John worships Jesus as God.

Amen. Key words. “Amen” (amēn, so it is, so let it be). The hearers in the church were meant to say it with him.

Textual note. Older manuscripts read “loosed” (lysanti); later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “washed” (lousanti), a difference of one letter in Greek. The older reading is stronger. Both are true in Scripture (7:14 speaks of robes washed in the blood of the Lamb). Similarly, older manuscripts read “a kingdom, priests” and later ones “kings and priests”; the meaning is close. They also read “loves” (present) where later ones read “loved” (past).

Where Christians differ: the priesthood of all believers. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that, alongside the shared priesthood of the baptized, there is an ordained ministerial priesthood that offers the sacrifice of the Mass. Verdict: the New Testament never calls church leaders priests in a sacrificial sense. Christ is the one high priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27; 10:12–14), and every believer is a priest with direct access to God through him. Elders and deacons are servants who teach and care, not priests who offer sacrifices.

What it does not mean. Being a kingdom and priests does not mean Christians rule now by political force, or that the church should take over the state. Our reign is shared with the slain Lamb, and it now looks like faithful witness and suffering (v. 9). It will be fully seen in the new creation (22:5).

In a sentence. To Jesus, who goes on loving us, who has set us free from our sins at the cost of his own blood, and who has made us a kingdom of priests serving his God and Father, belong glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Use this verse as a doxology in prayer and in song. Every believer can come straight to God as a priest, because the blood of Christ has opened the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.

Setting and background. This verse combines two Old Testament prophecies, as Jesus himself did (Matthew 24:30). Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, to receive an everlasting kingdom. Zechariah 12:10 shows Jerusalem looking on the one they pierced and mourning for him as for an only son. John applied the Zechariah text to the crucifixion in his Gospel (John 19:37).

Behold, he is coming with the clouds. Key words. “Behold” (idou, look!). “Is coming” (erchetai, present tense: his coming is so certain it is already under way). “Clouds” in Scripture often signal God’s own presence (Exodus 13:21; 19:9; Acts 1:9–11). Christ will come as he left, personally and visibly, in divine glory.

And every eye will see him. Key words. “Every eye” (pas ophthalmos). His return will be public, universal and unmistakable. No one will need to be told about it (Matthew 24:26–27).

Even those who pierced him. Key words. “Pierced” (exekentēsan), as in John 19:34–37. Those directly responsible, and all who share their rejection of him, will see the one they wounded, now as their judge.

And all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Key words. “Wail” (kopsontai, beat the breast in mourning). In Zechariah 12, the mourning is repentance, as the Spirit of grace is poured out. Here it seems to be mainly the grief of the unrepentant facing judgement, though the book also hopes for the nations’ conversion (11:13; 15:4). For believers, the same coming is the day of joy (22:20).

Even so. Amen. Key words. “Even so” (nai, yes) is Greek; “Amen” is Hebrew. A double affirmation in two languages: it will certainly happen.

Where Christians differ: one coming or two? Dispensationalists distinguish a secret rapture, when Christ comes for his church before a seven-year tribulation, from his later visible coming with his church to judge and reign on earth for a thousand years. Verdict: Scripture teaches one visible return of Christ. Every eye will see him; there is no secret coming. The gathering of believers to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17) happens at that same public, trumpet-sounding return, which brings the resurrection, the final judgement and the new creation together (Matthew 24:29–31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Revelation itself shows the church on earth through the tribulation, protected but not removed (7:3; 11:1–2; 12:6).

What it does not mean. This is not a spiritual coming in someone’s heart, nor Christ’s coming in judgement on Jerusalem in AD 70 alone. Every eye and all tribes of the earth points to the universal, final return.

In a sentence. Look: Jesus is coming with the clouds, and everyone will see him, including those who pierced him, and every people on earth will mourn because of him; yes, it will happen. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Live as someone who will see him. The one who was pierced for you is coming back; the question is whether you will meet him with joy or with grief.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, "who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”

Setting and background. This is one of only two places in Revelation where God the Father speaks directly (the other is 21:5–8). He sets his signature on the introduction. The same titles are given to Christ later in the book (22:13), showing that the Son shares the Father’s identity.

I am the Alpha and the Omega. Key words. Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω) are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. God is the source and the goal of everything, and everything between. He began history and he will bring it to its end. Compare Isaiah 44:6, where the Lord says he is the first and the last, and besides him there is no god.

Says the Lord God. Key words. “Lord God” (kyrios ho theos), the Greek form of the Old Testament “the LORD God”. Israel’s covenant God speaks.

Who is and who was and who is to come. As in v. 4: the eternal God, present, past and coming.

The Almighty. Key words. “Almighty” (pantokratōr, ruler of all, all-powerful). The word appears nine times in Revelation and only once elsewhere in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 6:18). It translates the Old Testament title “LORD of hosts”, the God of armies. To persecuted believers watching Rome’s power, this is the point: God, not Caesar, holds all power.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “the beginning and the ending” after Alpha and Omega, borrowed from 21:6 and 22:13. The older manuscripts do not have it. The meaning is unchanged.

What it does not mean. God’s rule does not make evil less real or suffering painless. Revelation is honest about both. But it means that evil will not have the last word, because God is the Omega.

In a sentence. The Lord God declares that he is the first and the last, the eternal one who is, who was and who is coming, the ruler of all.

For worship. Begin prayer with who God is. When life feels out of control, confess that the Almighty is the Alpha and the Omega of your story too.
verseByVerse.note: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.

parallels.desc: I am the first and I am the last

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — The Vision of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before a seal is opened or a trumpet blown, John is shown a Person, and everything in the remaining twenty-one chapters happens under the authority of the one he sees here. Verses 9–11 set the scene: John, calling himself brother and partner rather than apostle, exiled on Patmos for the word of God, in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, hears a voice like a trumpet commanding him to write and to send the book to seven named churches. The three things he shares with his readers — the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance — are bound together in the Greek by a single article. They arrive as one package.

Verses 12–13 give the setting of the vision: seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of them one like a son of man in a high priest’s long robe with a golden sash across his chest. The temple’s single seven-branched lampstand (Zech. 4:2–6) has become seven separate stands scattered along a Roman postal road, and Christ is not above them or outside them but among them, doing the priest’s daily work of keeping the lamps burning.

Verses 14–16 describe him feature by feature, and every feature is quarried from the Old Testament: white hair (Dan. 7:9 — the hair of the Ancient of Days, given here to the Son of Man), eyes like flame (Dan. 10:6), feet like burnished bronze from the furnace, a voice like many waters (Ezek. 43:2), seven stars in the right hand, a sharp two-edged sword from the mouth (Isa. 11:4; 49:2), and a face like the sun at full strength (cf. Matt. 17:2).

Verses 17–18 give John’s collapse and Christ’s answer. He falls as though dead; the right hand that holds the stars is laid on him without letting them go; and he hears Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades. Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-identification (Isa. 44:6) is claimed by a man who died.

Verses 19–20 close with the commission — write what you have seen, what is, and what is to take place after this — and with Christ explaining his own symbols: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, the seven lampstands are the churches. The identity of the angels is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse; what is not disputed is where they are. In his hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man Among the Lampstands

John sees the glorified Christ, clothed as a priest, walking among the churches, holding their stars in his hand, and holding the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exile kept the Lord’s day alone on Patmos, and heaven opened.

Now: The one too glorious to look at is the one who says, “Fear not.”

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying, "Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying, “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”

Setting and background. Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southwest of Miletus and some 60 miles from Ephesus. Romans used such islands as places of banishment. Early church writers (Irenaeus, Eusebius) say John was exiled there under Domitian and released after Domitian’s death in AD 96. The seven churches are named in the order of a circular postal route, beginning from Ephesus, the nearest port to Patmos.

I, John, your brother and partner. Key words. “Brother” (adelphos); “partner” (synkoinōnos, fellow sharer). John does not stand above the churches as a distant authority; he suffers with them. Like Paul, he writes from the same trouble his readers face.

In the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus. Key words. “Tribulation” (thlipsis, pressure, affliction, persecution). “Kingdom” (basileia). “Patient endurance” (hypomonē, steadfastness, staying under the load). These three belong together, governed by a single article in Greek. To be in Jesus is already to share in his kingdom, and it is also to share in suffering, and the way through is endurance. Tribulation here is not a future seven-year period only; John and his readers are already in it. The kingdom is not only future; they are already in it.

Was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. Key words. “On account of” (dia, because of). He was there as a penalty for preaching the gospel, not as a missionary or tourist.

I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day. Key words. “In the Spirit” (en pneumati): a state in which the Holy Spirit gave him prophetic vision, as with Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:12–14; 11:1). The phrase marks major sections of the book (4:2; 17:3; 21:10). “The Lord’s day” (tē kyriakē hēmera): the first day of the week, Sunday, when Christians met to worship because Christ rose on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). This is the first time the expression appears; early writings such as the Didache use the same term for Sunday. The adjective “lord’s” was also used of things belonging to the emperor; Christians claimed the day for their true Lord.

And I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet. Key words. “Trumpet” (salpingos). The trumpet recalls Sinai, where God spoke with a trumpet blast (Exodus 19:16–19). A voice behind (Ezekiel 3:12) that will turn out to be Christ’s own.

Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches. Key words. “Book” (biblion, scroll). One scroll to be sent to all seven. Each church would hear not only its own letter but all seven, and the whole book.

Where Christians differ: is “the Lord’s day” Sunday or the day of the Lord? Some have taken it to mean that John was transported in vision to the future Day of the Lord, the day of judgement. Others hold that Christians should keep Saturday as the Sabbath, and that the Lord’s day is the Jewish Sabbath. Verdict: the Lord’s day is Sunday. The Old Testament Day of the Lord is always expressed differently (hēmera kyriou), and early Christian usage of John’s phrase clearly means the first day of the week. This app’s view is that the Sabbath command is fulfilled in Christ, who is our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), and that the Lord’s day is not a burden of rules but the privilege of gathering on the day of resurrection to worship, rest and hear God’s word.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add in v. 11 the words “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last” and “which are in Asia”. They are absent from the older manuscripts.

What it does not mean. Being in the Spirit is not a technique for producing visions that Christians should seek today. John’s experience was a unique prophetic revelation, given to write Scripture. Now that the canon is closed, we meet the Spirit’s voice in what he wrote (22:18–19).

In a sentence. I, John, who share with you the suffering, the kingdom and the patient endurance that belong to those in Jesus, had been banished to Patmos for preaching God’s word and Jesus’ testimony; on Sunday, the Lord’s day, the Spirit took hold of me, and behind me a voice as loud as a trumpet told me to write down what I saw and send it to the seven churches, from Ephesus round to Laodicea.

On a Tuesday. Suffering for Christ, the kingdom of Christ and endurance in Christ come together. If you are under pressure for your faith, you are not off course; you are a partner with John.
verseByVerse.note: Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean, about 40 miles off the coast of Asia. “The Lord’s day” is Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.

Setting and background. In the tabernacle and temple, a golden lampstand with seven lamps burned in the Holy Place, tended by priests (Exodus 25:31–40). Zechariah saw a golden lampstand, which spoke of God’s people shining by the Spirit (Zechariah 4:2–6). Here John sees seven separate lampstands, which v. 20 explains are the seven churches.

Then I turned to see the voice. A vivid way of saying he turned to see who was speaking.

I saw seven golden lampstands. Key words. “Lampstands” (lychnias, stands that hold lamps). The church is not the light itself; it holds up the light of Christ to the world (Matthew 5:14–16). “Golden”: precious to God. Small, struggling congregations in pagan cities are, in God’s sight, gold.

And in the midst of the lampstands. Key words. “In the midst” (en mesō). Christ is not far away in heaven, out of reach. He walks among his churches (2:1), seeing all, tending the lamps, as the priest tended the lampstand. This is both comfort and warning: he is present to strengthen and to correct.

One like a son of man. Key words. “Son of man” (huion anthrōpou), from Daniel 7:13, the heavenly human figure who receives the everlasting kingdom. Jesus’ favourite title for himself in the Gospels. He is truly human, and more than human.

Clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest. Key words. “Long robe” (podērē, reaching to the feet), the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:4). A golden sash was also part of the priestly dress. The figure in Daniel 10:5 is dressed in linen with a golden belt. Christ appears as the great high priest, ministering among the lampstands, and also as a king, since such robes signified dignity. Sashes were normally worn at the waist for work; a sash high on the chest suggests dignity and rest, a task completed.

What it does not mean. The details are not a physical portrait to be painted. They are symbols, each drawn from the Old Testament, to show who Christ is. Asking what he looked like misses the point; ask what each feature tells you about him.

In a sentence. When I turned to see who was speaking, I saw seven golden lampstands, and among them a figure like a son of man, dressed in a full-length priestly robe with a golden sash around his chest.

For worship. When the church gathers, Christ is present among his people. Worship as those whose high priest is in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.

Setting and background. Every feature here comes from the Old Testament, mostly from Daniel 7 and 10 and Ezekiel 1 and 43. The startling thing is that features belonging to the Ancient of Days, God himself, are now given to the Son of Man. John is showing, in pictures, that Jesus is God.

The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. Key words. In Daniel 7:9, the Ancient of Days, God on his throne, has hair like pure wool and clothing white as snow. White hair speaks of eternity, wisdom and dignity, and white of purity. Christ shares the eternal majesty of God.

His eyes were like a flame of fire. Key words. “Flame of fire” (phlox pyros), as in Daniel 10:6. Eyes that see through everything, pierce every disguise and burn in judgement. To Thyatira he will introduce himself this way, as the one who searches minds and hearts (2:18, 23).

His feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace. Key words. “Burnished bronze” (chalkolibanō, a rare word for a fine, glowing metal alloy), as in Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:7. Feet glowing like metal in a furnace suggest strength, stability and the power to trample enemies. They contrast with the feet of iron and clay of the statue of earthly empires in Daniel 2.

And his voice was like the roar of many waters. Key words. In Ezekiel 43:2, the voice of the God of Israel is like the sound of many waters. For John on an island, the image is the endless crash of the sea. Overwhelming, irresistible, drowning every other voice.

In his right hand he held seven stars. Key words. “Right hand”, the hand of power and authority. The stars are the angels of the churches (v. 20). The churches are held in his hand: they are in his power, and they are safe (John 10:28). Roman coins of the period could show the emperor’s infant son among stars, as a symbol of world rule; Christ holds the true stars.

From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword. Key words. “Sword” (rhomphaia, a long sword). Not held in the hand, but coming from his mouth: it is his word (Isaiah 11:4; 49:2; Hebrews 4:12). His word judges and conquers. At the end, he defeats his enemies with this sword alone (19:15, 21). The Roman governor had the right of the sword, the power of execution; Christ’s word is greater.

And his face was like the sun shining in full strength. Key words. As at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:2), and like the righteous in Judges 5:31. Unbearable glory.

What it does not mean. This is not a description of a monster. Every image says something good and true about Christ: eternal, all-seeing, strong, authoritative, protective, powerful in word, glorious. The gentle Jesus of the Gospels is also this Jesus. Both are the same person.

In a sentence. His head and hair were white as wool and snow, his eyes blazed like fire, his feet glowed like fine bronze fresh from the furnace, his voice thundered like a great waterfall, he held seven stars in his right hand, a sharp double-edged sword came out of his mouth, and his face shone like the sun at noon.

For worship. Let this vision correct small thoughts of Jesus. The friend of sinners is the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.

Setting and background. In Scripture, those who see God’s glory fall down overwhelmed: Isaiah (Isaiah 6:5), Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:28), Daniel (Daniel 10:8–10), and the disciples at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:6–7). John, who had leaned on Jesus’ chest at the Last Supper (John 13:23), now falls down as though dead at the sight of him.

When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. Key words. The right response to seeing Christ in his glory. Holy fear is not a lack of faith; it is a true sight of who he is.

But he laid his right hand on me. Key words. The same right hand that holds the stars. It is a hand of power, and a hand of tenderness. As in Daniel 10:10, and as Jesus touched the frightened disciples on the mountain (Matthew 17:7).

Saying, Fear not. Key words. “Fear not” (mē phobou, stop being afraid). The most frequent command in Scripture. The awe remains, but the terror is removed. The glorious Christ does not destroy his own servant.

I am the first and the last. Key words. In Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12, the Lord says he is the first and the last. Christ claims the same divine title the Father used in v. 8 (Alpha and Omega). Jesus is not a lesser god; he is the one God, with the Father.

And the living one. Key words. “The living one” (ho zōn). God is the living God, in contrast to dead idols. Christ has life in himself (John 5:26).

I died, and behold I am alive forevermore. Key words. “I died” (egenomēn nekros, I became dead): a real death, in history. “Alive forevermore” (zōn eimi eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn, living for ever and ever): his resurrection is not a return to ordinary life but entry into endless life. Death can never touch him again (Romans 6:9).

And I have the keys of Death and Hades. Key words. “Keys” (kleis), authority to open and shut. “Death and Hades”: death, and the realm of the dead (hadēs, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Sheol). Jewish tradition said that only God holds the keys of death. Christ has taken them. He decides who goes in and who comes out. For a church facing martyrdom, nothing could be more comforting: death has no power over those whose Lord holds its keys. He will open the graves at the resurrection (20:13). Death and Hades will finally be thrown into the lake of fire (20:14).

What it does not mean. The keys of Hades do not mean Christ went to hell to suffer further after his death. His suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). The keys mean authority over death, won by his death and resurrection. Nor does this support the idea of a second chance after death; the Bible gives none (Hebrews 9:27).

In a sentence. When I saw him I collapsed at his feet like a dead man, but he put his right hand on me and said, Do not be afraid: I am the first and the last and the one who lives; I was dead, but look, I am alive for ever and ever, and I hold the keys of death and of the grave.

On a Tuesday. Face death, your own and that of those you love, with this sentence: Jesus holds the keys. The grave is not locked against him, and he will open it.

verseByVerse.quote: Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”

Setting and background. Christ repeats the command to write (v. 11) and explains two of the symbols. This shows how Revelation works: symbols stand for realities, and sometimes the book itself tells us what they mean. Where it does, we must follow it; where it does not, we look to the Old Testament, from which nearly every image comes.

Write therefore the things that you have seen. Key words. “Therefore” (oun): because Christ has conquered death, John is to write without fear.

Those that are and those that are to take place after this. Key words. “After this” (meta tauta), echoing Daniel 2:29, 45. The book concerns both present realities and future events, and both are mixed throughout. Many read this as a three-part outline: what John has seen (chapter 1), what is (chapters 2–3) and what will be after this (chapters 4–22).

Where Christians differ: is this verse an outline of the book? Dispensationalists often take it as a strict outline, with chapters 4–22 entirely future, after the church is raptured at 4:1. Verdict: the phrase is better read as describing the whole book: what John saw includes things that are and things still to come, all mixed together. Chapter 12, for example, goes back to Christ’s birth and ascension. The book is not a strict timeline but a series of visions, each showing the same age between Christ’s comings from a different angle, and each ending at or near the final judgement.

As for the mystery. Key words. “Mystery” (mystērion): in the New Testament, not a puzzle but something hidden that God now reveals.

The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. Key words. “Angels” (angeloi, messengers). Each of the seven letters is addressed to the angel of that church (2:1 and the others).

Where Christians differ: who are the angels of the churches? Some say they are human messengers carrying the letters, or the pastor of each church. Others say they are guardian angels assigned to the churches. Others suggest they personify the spiritual life or heavenly counterpart of each church. Verdict: they are most likely heavenly angels connected with each church, since every other use of “angel” in Revelation (over sixty) means a heavenly being, and Scripture speaks of angels watching over God’s people (Daniel 10:20–21; Matthew 18:10). Yet the letters are clearly aimed at the congregations themselves, who are rebuked and called to repent. The angel represents the church before God, so to address it is to address the church. In practice, the messages are for every believer (2:7).

And the seven lampstands are the seven churches. Key words. Christ calls the church to shine for him in the darkness. In 2:5 he warns Ephesus that he could remove its lampstand: a church can lose its place as a witness if it will not repent.

What it does not mean. The seven churches are not seven ages of church history, as some have taught (Ephesus the apostolic age, Laodicea the last days). Nothing in the text suggests it, and every church in every age needs all seven letters.

In a sentence. So write what you have seen, both the present and what is to come; and here is the meaning of the seven stars in my right hand and the seven golden lampstands: the stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the lampstands are the churches themselves.

On a Tuesday. Your local church, however small, is a golden lampstand that Christ holds and walks among. Love it, serve it and help it shine.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place.<sup>2</sup>He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.<sup>3</sup>Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.<sup>4</sup>John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,<sup>5</sup>and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood<sup>6</sup>and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>7</sup>Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.<sup>8</sup>“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”<sup>9</sup>I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.<sup>10</sup>I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet<sup>11</sup>saying, “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”<sup>12</sup>Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands,<sup>13</sup>and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.<sup>14</sup>The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire,<sup>15</sup>his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters.<sup>16</sup>In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.<sup>17</sup>When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last,<sup>18</sup>and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.<sup>19</sup>Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this.<sup>20</sup>As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”

2.title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
2.overview:
The seven letters of chapters 2–3 are the most immediately practical section of Revelation. Before the cosmic drama unfolds, the risen Christ pauses to speak personally to each congregation — by name, with specific knowledge, with diagnostic precision. These are not generic pastoral encouragements. They are surgical letters, each one calibrated to the exact spiritual condition of a real church in a real city.

Every letter follows a recognizable pattern: (1) a self-identification of Christ drawn from the vision of chapter 1; (2) “I know” — a statement of Christ’s comprehensive knowledge of the congregation’s situation; (3) commendation or absence thereof; (4) rebuke or absence thereof; (5) a call to repentance or endurance; (6) “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches”; and (7) a promise to “the one who conquers.” The word nikōn (conqueror/overcomer) is the key word of the seven letters. Every letter ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, and the nature of overcoming is not occasional spiritual performance but faithful endurance to the end.

The seven churches were not chosen arbitrarily. They formed a postal circuit in the Roman province of Asia, moving roughly in a clockwise direction from Ephesus. Any one of them could be a “hub” for distributing the letter to surrounding congregations. But the number seven also signals completeness — these seven represent the whole church of every age. Every congregation since the first century has found itself somewhere in these seven letters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — To the Church in Ephesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ephesus was the first stop on the courier’s road: a harbour city of some quarter of a million people, home to the temple of Artemis, and the congregation Paul had spent three years building (Acts 20:31). Verse 1 addresses its angel and identifies the sender as the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the seven lampstands — both images sharpened from 1:13 and 1:16. He grips, and he is moving through the room.

Verses 2–3 are two full verses of commendation before a word of criticism, and it is genuine: works, toil to exhaustion (kopos), patient endurance, an unwillingness to bear with evil, false apostles tested and exposed, weight carried for his name’s sake, and no weariness after forty years. Paul had warned this very church that wolves would come (Acts 20:29–30) and they had acted on it.

Verse 4 turns: you have abandoned the love you had at first. The verb is not cooling but putting down and walking on. Everything in vv. 2–3 is visible from outside; what is missing can be seen only by the eyes of fire. Verse 5 gives the remedy in three ordered verbs — remember where you have fallen from, repent, and do the works you did at first — and then the threat: the lampstand removed from its place. Not salvation withdrawn; a congregation ceasing to give light. There is no church in Ephesus today.

Verse 6 returns to commendation before the letter ends: they hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which Christ also hates. Verse 7 sounds the refrain — he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches — and promises the conqueror the tree of life in the paradise of God: the tree guarded since Genesis 3:24 and standing open in the street of the city at 22:2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Orthodox but Loveless

Ephesus had sound doctrine, hard work and endurance, but had abandoned its first love. The cure is to remember, repent and do the works it did at first.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A second-generation church kept the truth and lost the warmth.

Now: Ask what would remain of your faith if the things others can see were taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: "To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: 'The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.

Meaning first. Revelation 2 contains the first four of Christ’s seven letters to the churches of Asia. Each follows a pattern: Christ introduces himself with a feature from the vision of chapter 1; he says, I know your works; he praises what is good and rebukes what is wrong; he calls for repentance or endurance; he says, let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches; and he makes a promise to the one who conquers. Ephesus is sound in doctrine and tireless in work, but has abandoned its first love, and must repent or lose its lampstand; the one who conquers will eat from the tree of life (vv. 1–7). Smyrna is poor, slandered and about to be imprisoned, yet Christ has no rebuke for it, only the call to be faithful unto death and the promise of the crown of life (vv. 8–11). Pergamum lives where Satan’s throne is and has held fast even when Antipas was killed, but tolerates the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, which permits idolatry and immorality; Christ will fight them with the sword of his mouth, and promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name (vv. 12–17). Thyatira is growing in love, faith and service, but tolerates a false prophetess, Jezebel, who leads believers into immorality and idol feasts; Christ, whose eyes are like fire, will judge her, and promises the faithful authority over the nations and the morning star (vv. 18–29). Together the letters show a Christ who knows his churches completely, loves them enough to rebuke them, and calls every believer to conquer by staying faithful.

Setting and background. Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, a great port and commercial centre with perhaps 200,000 to 250,000 people. It was famous for the temple of Artemis (Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and also had temples to the emperors. Paul spent nearly three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a riot broke out when the gospel threatened the trade in silver shrines of Artemis (Acts 19:23–41). Paul warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in and false teachers arise from among them (Acts 20:29–30), and Timothy was left there to oppose false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3). Early tradition says John himself later lived and ministered in Ephesus. By the time of Revelation, the church was perhaps forty years old, into its second generation.

To the angel of the church in Ephesus write. Key words. “Angel” (angelos, messenger). As explained at 1:20, the angel probably represents the church before God, but the message is for the whole congregation and, beyond it, for all churches (v. 7).

The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand. Key words. “The words of” (tade legei, thus says). This is the formula the Old Testament prophets used for the LORD’s own speech, “Thus says the LORD”. Christ speaks with the authority of God. “Holds” (kratōn, grips firmly). Each letter begins with a feature from the vision of chapter 1 (1:16) that suits the church’s situation. To a church that may lose its lampstand, he presents himself as the one who holds the churches in his power.

Who walks among the seven golden lampstands. Key words. “Walks” (peripatōn). Christ is present and active, inspecting his churches as the priest tended the temple lamps. He knows what goes on inside every congregation.

The pattern of the seven letters. Seven letters, each with seven parts: address, title of Christ, I know, praise, rebuke, command, promise. Two churches (Smyrna and Philadelphia) receive no rebuke. Two (Sardis and Laodicea) receive almost no praise. The rest are mixed. In every church, Christ’s knowledge is complete and his promises are rich.

What it does not mean. The seven letters are not a forecast of seven eras of church history. They are messages to seven real congregations, and all seven speak to every church in every age.

In a sentence. Write this to the angel of the church in Ephesus: These are the words of the one who grips the seven stars in his right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands.

On a Tuesday. Christ walks among the churches today. Think of your church as he sees it, not as its reputation or its programme describes it.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the greatest city of Asia and home to the vast temple of Artemis. Paul had spent nearly three years there.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name's sake, and you have not grown weary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.

Setting and background. Ephesus had been warned by Paul about false teachers (Acts 20:29–30), and by the time of Revelation it had faced them and won. Travelling preachers moved from church to church, and some claimed apostolic authority they did not have (2 Corinthians 11:13). Churches had to test them (1 John 4:1; Didache 11).

I know your works. Key words. “I know” (oida): the fiery-eyed Christ knows everything, the good and the bad. Every letter begins this way. Nothing is hidden from him: comfort for the faithful, warning for the compromising.

Your toil and your patient endurance. Key words. “Toil” (kopon, labour to the point of exhaustion). “Patient endurance” (hypomonēn, staying power under pressure). Ephesus was a hard-working, persevering church.

And how you cannot bear with those who are evil. Key words. “Cannot bear” (ou dynē bastasai, are unable to tolerate). They practised church discipline and did not tolerate evil in their midst, as Pergamum and Thyatira did.

But have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. Key words. “Tested” (epeirasas, examined, put to the proof). “False” (pseudeis, liars). They measured the claims of teachers against the apostolic gospel and exposed the frauds. This is exactly what Paul had asked of them.

I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary. Key words. “Bearing up” (ebastasas, carried a load). A play on words: they cannot bear evil people, but they have borne hardship for Christ’s name. “Not grown weary” (ou kekopiakes): they laboured (kopos) without growing tired (kopiaō), another play on words.

What it does not mean. Christ’s praise shows that sound doctrine and discipline matter. The rebuke that follows does not mean Ephesus should have been less careful about truth. Christ commends their orthodoxy before he calls them back to love.

In a sentence. I know what you have done: how hard you have worked, how you have persevered, how you refuse to put up with wicked people, and how you have examined those who claimed to be apostles and exposed them as liars; I know you have endured and carried burdens for my name, and have not given up.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear, even from popular teachers, by Scripture. Christ praises a church that checks the claims of those who speak in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.

Setting and background. Paul had praised the Ephesians for their love toward all the saints (Ephesians 1:15) and ended his letter to them with grace for all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love (Ephesians 6:24). Now, a generation later, that love has cooled. Jesus had warned that because lawlessness would increase, the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:12).

But I have this against you. Key words. The praise is real, but so is the charge.

That you have abandoned the love you had at first. Key words. “Abandoned” (aphēkes, left, let go). Not lost by accident, but left. “The love you had at first” (tēn agapēn sou tēn prōtēn, your first love). This probably includes love for Christ and love for one another, which in Scripture go together (1 John 4:20–21).
