The church kept doing the right things, and kept believing the right things, but the warmth of devotion that once drove it had gone. Its battles against false teachers may have left it suspicious and hard, defending the truth without the love that the truth produces.

Remember therefore from where you have fallen. Key words. “Remember” (mnēmoneue, keep remembering). Recall what you once were. “Fallen” (peptōkes): losing first love is a fall, not a small matter.

Repent, and do the works you did at first. Key words. “Repent” (metanoēson, change your mind and direction). The cure has three steps: remember, repent, return. “The works you did at first”: love is shown in actions. The way back to warm devotion is not waiting for feelings, but turning back to Christ and doing again the deeds of love.

If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent. Key words. “Come” (erchomai): not the final return, but a coming in judgement on this church in history. “Remove your lampstand”: the church would cease to be a witness and finally cease to exist as a church. Orthodoxy without love is not enough to keep a church alive. Historically, the church at Ephesus did continue for centuries, which suggests it heeded the warning; but the city itself is now ruins, and Christianity there long ago disappeared.

What it does not mean. Losing the lampstand does not mean true believers lose their salvation. Christ is speaking about the church as a community and its witness. True believers persevere because God keeps them (John 10:28–29); and one way he keeps them is by warnings like this one, which they heed.

In a sentence. But this is my complaint against you: you have walked away from the love you had at the beginning; so remember how far you have fallen, turn back, and do again what you did at first, or else I will come and take your lampstand out of its place, if you will not repent.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether your faith has become correct but cold. Remember what Christ’s love once meant to you, confess the drift, and do something today that love for him and for his people would do.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’

Setting and background. The Nicolaitans are mentioned only here and in v. 15, where they are linked with the teaching of Balaam: eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality (v. 14). Early writers (Irenaeus) connected them with Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but this is uncertain. They seem to have taught that Christians could join in pagan feasts and the trade guilds’ idolatrous life, perhaps claiming that what is done in the body does not matter. In Ephesus they were rejected; in Pergamum they were tolerated.

Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. Key words. “Hate” (miseis). Christ hates the works, not the people. Some things are right to hate: whatever destroys his people. Love does not mean approving everything.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Key words. Jesus often said, He who has ears, let him hear (Matthew 13:9). The words are Christ’s, yet they are what the Spirit says: Christ speaks by his Spirit. And it is “churches”, plural. Every letter is for every church.

To the one who conquers. Key words. “Conquers” (nikōnti, overcomes, wins the victory; from nikē, victory). Every letter ends with a promise to the conqueror. In Revelation, believers conquer the way Christ did: by faithful witness, even unto death (12:11). The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5–6). To conquer is not to win battles by force but to stay faithful to Christ to the end. And the conquerors are not an elite class of super-Christians: 1 John 5:4–5 says that everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith. Every true believer conquers.

I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God. Key words. “Tree of life” (xylou tēs zōēs): in Eden, the tree that gave life (Genesis 2:9). After the fall, the way to it was barred (Genesis 3:22–24). Christ promises to restore what Adam lost. “Paradise” (paradeisos, a Persian word for a garden or park), used of Eden in the Greek Old Testament. The tree of life reappears in the new Jerusalem (22:2, 14). Eternal life in the restored creation, in God’s presence. The goddess Artemis had a sacred tree at her temple, a place of asylum; Christ offers the true tree, and the true refuge.

What it does not mean. The promise is not a reward for a few especially victorious Christians, while others miss out. All who belong to Christ and persevere in faith will eat from the tree of life. The promise is meant to motivate perseverance, not to divide believers into ranks.

In a sentence. Still, this is to your credit: you hate what the Nicolaitans do, as I do; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches; and the one who conquers I will allow to eat from the tree of life in God’s paradise.

For worship. Thank Christ that what Adam lost, he restores. The tree of life is waiting for every believer who holds on to the end.
verseByVerse.note: The Nicolaitans are unknown outside Revelation; they seem to have taught that believers could take part in pagan feasts and immorality.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — To the Church in Smyrna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Smyrna, thirty-five miles north, was the most beautiful and most loyal city on the coast — a temple to the goddess Roma from 195 BC and a temple to Tiberius won in competition against ten rival cities in AD 26. Verse 8 introduces Christ to this church as the first and the last, who died and came to life: of all the images in chapter 1, the two about death are handed to the congregation that is about to face it.

Verse 9 names three things he knows. Their tribulation. Their poverty — ptōcheia, the destitution of a beggar, in a wealthy city, and the invoice for their faith. And the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts three words: (but you are rich). Laodicea will receive the exact reverse (3:17).

Verse 10 forbids fear without denying the suffering. The devil is about to throw some of them into prison — and the purpose clause that follows, that you may be tested, does not belong to the devil. The word is the one used of assaying metal; the striking hand is his, the assaying is not (cf. Job 1:12; 1 Pet. 1:6–7). The ten days are a bounded stretch, and the boundary was not set by the persecutor. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life — stephanos, the victor’s wreath, in a city whose own skyline was called the crown of Smyrna.

Verse 11 closes with the refrain and a promise stated negatively: the conqueror will not be hurt by the second death, defined at 20:14 as the lake of fire. Everything Smyrna’s enemies can do to it falls inside the smaller of the two categories.
verseByVerse.theology:
Poor, and Rich

Christ, who died and came to life, knows Smyrna’s tribulation and poverty — and says they are rich. Suffering is coming, bounded and purposeful; the faithful will not be hurt by the second death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Polycarp, bishop of this church some sixty years later, served Christ to the fire.

Now: Grace for a trial is given on the day of the trial, not in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: 'The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. "'I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. ‘I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

Setting and background. Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port about 35 miles (56 kilometres) north of Ephesus, a beautiful city that called itself the first of Asia. It was fiercely loyal to Rome: it built one of the first temples to the goddess Roma (195 BC) and won the honour of a temple to the emperor Tiberius (AD 26). Emperor worship was intense, and refusing it was seen as disloyalty. The city had a large and influential Jewish community. The city had been destroyed around 600 BC and refounded three centuries later, so it was said to have died and come back to life. Around AD 155, Polycarp, the elderly bishop of Smyrna, was burned alive for refusing to call Caesar lord; asked to curse Christ, he said that he had served him eighty-six years and Christ had done him no wrong, so how could he blaspheme his King who saved him?

The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. Key words. From 1:17–18. To a church facing death, Christ presents himself as the eternal God who has been through death and out the other side. As the city had, in a sense, died and lived again, the true Lord has truly died and risen.

I know your tribulation and your poverty. Key words. “Tribulation” (thlipsin, pressure, persecution). “Poverty” (ptōcheian, destitution, the poverty of a beggar, not merely being poor). In a wealthy city, Christians were destitute, perhaps because they lost jobs and trade by refusing guild idolatry, or had their goods seized (Hebrews 10:34).

(But you are rich). Key words. Rich in the things that matter: in faith, and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). The opposite of Laodicea, rich in its own eyes but actually poor (3:17).

And the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not. Key words. “Slander” (blasphēmian, abusive speech, blasphemy). Local Jews apparently denounced Christians to the authorities. Jews had legal tolerance in the empire and were excused from emperor worship; once they disowned the Christians as not Jews, Christians were exposed. In Polycarp’s martyrdom, Smyrna’s Jews were said to have joined eagerly in gathering wood for the fire.

But are a synagogue of Satan. Key words. “Synagogue” (synagōgē, assembly, gathering). “Satan” (the accuser, adversary). By accusing God’s people, they were doing Satan’s work, for Satan is the accuser of the brothers (12:10). Christ says they are Jews in name but not in reality. As Paul says, the true Jew is one inwardly, by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29); and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29).

What it does not mean. This is not antisemitism, and must never be used to justify it. Christ, John and the first church were Jews. The words are aimed at a particular community that persecuted Christians, and the charge is spiritual, not ethnic: rejecting the Messiah and accusing his people. Scripture holds out hope for Israel’s salvation (Romans 11:25–29), and Christians are called to love their Jewish neighbours and pray for them.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the first and the last, who was dead and came back to life: I know what you are suffering and how poor you are, though in truth you are rich, and I know the slander of those who claim to be Jews but are not; they are a gathering that serves Satan.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ costs you money or reputation, he knows. In his account you are rich.
verseByVerse.note: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port, loyal to Rome, with a large Jewish community, some of whom were slandering the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.

Setting and background. In the Roman world, prison was not usually a punishment in itself; it was a place to hold people before trial or execution. To be thrown into prison often meant death was coming. Smyrna was famous for its athletic games, where winners received a crown (a wreath), and the city’s ring of buildings on its hill was called the crown of Smyrna.

Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Key words. “Do not fear” (mēden phobou, fear nothing). Christ does not promise to stop the suffering; he tells them not to be afraid of it. As he told John (1:17).

Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison. Key words. “Devil” (diabolos, slanderer). Behind the Jewish slanderers and the Roman courts stands the devil. Persecution has a spiritual source. Yet even the devil can act only within the limits God allows (as in Job 1–2).

That you may be tested. Key words. “Tested” (peirasthēte, tried, proved). The devil intends it to destroy their faith; God intends it to prove and refine their faith (1 Peter 1:6–7). The same event has two purposes.

And for ten days you will have tribulation. Key words. “Ten days”: probably a short, limited period, as in Daniel 1:12–14, where Daniel and his friends are tested for ten days. The suffering is real but has an end set by God. It is not endless.

Be faithful unto death. Key words. “Faithful” (pistos, loyal, trustworthy). “Unto death” (achri thanatou, even to the point of death). Not just until you die naturally, but even if faithfulness costs your life.

And I will give you the crown of life. Key words. “Crown” (stephanon, a victor’s wreath, not a royal crown). The crown consists of life: eternal life (James 1:12). They may lose their earthly lives, but they will receive life that cannot end. The prize of the games was a wreath that withered; this one never does (1 Corinthians 9:25).

What it does not mean. Faithfulness unto death is not a work that earns salvation. It is the fruit and evidence of true faith, which God himself sustains. The crown is a gift (I will give).

In a sentence. Do not be afraid of what you are going to suffer: the devil will throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will be afflicted for a short time; stay faithful even if it costs your life, and I will give you life as your victor’s crown.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for believers in prison for Christ. And ask him for the courage to be faithful in the smaller costs you face, so that you are ready if greater ones come.
verseByVerse.note: “Ten days” probably means a short, limited time.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.’

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. As in v. 7. Smyrna’s letter, too, is for every church.

The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death. Key words. “Will not be hurt” (ou mē adikēthē, the strongest form of denial in Greek: will certainly never be harmed). “The second death”: Revelation explains this as the lake of fire, final and eternal punishment after the resurrection and judgement (20:6, 14; 21:8). The first death is physical death; the second is eternal separation from God under his judgement. Smyrna’s believers may suffer the first death, but they will never suffer the second. Jesus said, do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28).

Where Christians differ: is the second death the end of existence? Annihilationists hold that the second death means the wicked cease to exist after judgement. Verdict: Revelation describes the lake of fire as torment day and night for ever and ever (20:10; 14:11), and Jesus spoke of eternal punishment alongside eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The second death is called death because it is the final loss of all that makes life life: God’s presence and favour. It is conscious, eternal punishment, which is exactly why the promise here is so precious.

What it does not mean. The promise does not imply that some true believers may be hurt by the second death. All who are in Christ are safe from condemnation (Romans 8:1).

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches: the one who conquers will never be harmed by the second death.

For worship. Thank God that for believers, death is only the first death, and the second has no power over us (20:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — To the Church in Pergamum
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Pergamum, inland on a cone of rock a thousand feet high, was the administrative capital of the province and the seat of the governor — the place where the right of the sword actually resided. Verse 12 accordingly introduces Christ as him who has the sharp two-edged sword. Verse 13 says I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is: the Great Altar of Zeus on its terrace, the serpent-emblemed healing shrine of Asklepios whose god was titled Saviour, and the province’s first temple to a living emperor, all on the same hill. In that city they held fast his name and did not deny the faith even when Antipas — given Christ’s own title from 1:5, my faithful witness — was killed among them.

Verses 14–15 bring the charge. Some there hold the teaching of Balaam, who could not curse Israel and so taught Balak to seduce it instead (Num. 22–24; 25:1–9; 31:16): eating food sacrificed to idols and practising sexual immorality, which in a guild town arrived in the same evening. Verse 15 adds the Nicolaitans — the very group Ephesus was commended for hating in v. 6. The accusation is not that the whole church holds this, but that the church has some there who hold it, unchallenged.

Verse 16 commands the whole congregation to repent, and the pronouns then separate ominously: I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth. A church that will not act against error is not exempted from the action; the action is simply taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly.

Verse 17 sounds the refrain and gives three promises, each the reverse of what the compromisers wanted: hidden manna instead of guild meat (Ex. 16:33–34; cf. John 6:35), a white stone — a juror’s acquittal pebble, a victor’s banquet token, a guest’s ticket, the readings differ — and a new name known only to the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Strategy

Pergamum held fast under the sword but tolerated the teaching of Balaam — the invitation to compromise at the idol-feast. The whole church is called to repent of its silence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Guild banquets tied a man’s livelihood to idol meat.

Now: The argument for compromise is always reasonable. Christ offers hidden manna and a new name instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: 'The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. "'I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. ‘I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.

Setting and background. Pergamum, about 65 miles (105 kilometres) north of Smyrna, was the old capital of the province and probably still the seat of the Roman governor, who had the right of the sword: the power to execute. It stood on a huge hill crowned with temples. There was a great altar of Zeus, shaped like a throne, on the acropolis; a famous healing shrine of Asclepius, whose symbol was a serpent; and, above all, the first temple in Asia to the emperor Augustus and the goddess Roma (29 BC), making it the centre of emperor worship in the province. Its library was second only to Alexandria’s, and parchment (pergamēnē) is named after it.

The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. Key words. From 1:16. The governor has the sword of Rome, but Christ has the sword that really decides life and death: his word. And he will use it against the false teachers in the church (v. 16).

I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Key words. “Dwell” (katoikeis, live permanently). They did not choose the place; Christ knows how hard it is. “Satan’s throne” (ho thronos tou Satana). The throne-shaped altar of Zeus, the serpent of Asclepius and the governor’s seat of judgement have all been suggested, but the best explanation is the city’s leadership in emperor worship, combined with the governor’s power to condemn Christians. Satan’s power was concentrated there.

Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith. Key words. “Hold fast” (krateis, grip firmly). “Deny” (ērnēsō, disown). Christians were asked to say Caesar is Lord, and to curse Christ. They refused. “My faith” (tēn pistin mou): faith in me, or the faithfulness owed to me.

Even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells. Key words. “Faithful witness” (ho martys mou ho pistos mou), the title Christ bears himself (1:5). Nothing is known of Antipas except this verse; later tradition says he was roasted in a bronze bull. He is known to Christ by name, honoured with Christ’s own title. “Killed” (apektanthē). Martyrdom had already begun.

What it does not mean. Satan’s throne does not mean Satan rules there in place of God. Christ holds the sword, and Satan’s power is borrowed and limited. Nor does living where Satan dwells excuse compromise; it calls for greater faithfulness.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of the one who holds the sharp double-edged sword: I know where you live, in the place where Satan has his throne, and yet you keep a firm grip on my name and did not disown your faith in me, even when Antipas, my faithful witness, was put to death among you in the city where Satan lives.

On a Tuesday. You may live and work where unbelief seems to sit on a throne. Christ knows where you dwell. Hold fast his name there.
verseByVerse.note: Pergamum was a centre of emperor worship and home to a great altar of Zeus — perhaps why it is called the place “where Satan’s throne is.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

Setting and background. Balak, king of Moab, hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, but God turned the curse to blessing (Numbers 22–24). Balaam then found another way: Israel was seduced by Moabite women into sexual immorality and the worship of Baal of Peor, and God’s judgement followed (Numbers 25:1–3). Numbers 31:16 reveals that this was Balaam’s advice. Balaam became the classic example of a prophet who leads God’s people into sin for profit (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11). In Pergamum, trade guilds held feasts in honour of their patron gods, with meat offered to idols, and these often included sexual immorality. To refuse could cost a craftsman his livelihood.

But I have a few things against you. A faithful church can still have serious faults.

You have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam. Key words. “Teaching” (didachēn). Not merely bad behaviour but a doctrine that justified it, taught within the church. What Satan could not do by persecution (killing Antipas), he tried to do by compromise.

Who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel. Key words. “Stumbling block” (skandalon, a trap, a bait stick, something that makes people fall).

So that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. Key words. “Food sacrificed to idols” (eidōlothyta). Eating meat that had once been offered to an idol was not wrong in itself, if bought in the market or eaten at a private meal (1 Corinthians 10:25–27). But eating it in the idol’s temple, as part of a feast in the god’s honour, was participating in idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:19–22). The Jerusalem council had asked Gentile believers to abstain from both (Acts 15:29). “Sexual immorality” (porneusai): any sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman. Possibly also spiritual unfaithfulness, as the Old Testament often calls idolatry adultery, but in context the literal sense is clear.

So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Key words. “So also” (houtōs, in the same way): the Nicolaitans’ teaching is the same as Balaam’s, or very like it. In Ephesus they were hated (v. 6); in Pergamum they were tolerated.

What it does not mean. The problem was not that the church contained sinners; every church does. It was that the church tolerated teachers who taught that sin was acceptable, and did not discipline them. Pergamum had the opposite fault from Ephesus: love without truth, where Ephesus had truth without love.

In a sentence. But I have some things against you: some among you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who showed Balak how to trap Israel into eating food offered to idols and committing sexual immorality; and in the same way, some of you hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

On a Tuesday. Watch for teaching that makes compromise with the culture seem wise and safe, especially where your job or income is at stake. The pressure to fit in is often more dangerous than open hostility.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.

Setting and background. Balaam himself was confronted by the angel of the Lord with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:23, 31), and was later killed with the sword (Numbers 31:8).

Therefore repent. Key words. “Repent” (metanoēson). Addressed to the whole church, not just the false teachers. The church must repent of tolerating them, and the false teachers must repent of their teaching.

If not, I will come to you soon. Key words. “Come” (erchomai): a coming in judgement on this church in history, not only the final return.

And war against them with the sword of my mouth. Key words. “War” (polemēsō, make war). “Against them”: notice, against the false teachers. He comes to the church, but fights against those who lead it astray. “Sword of my mouth”: his word of judgement (1:16; 19:15). Christ judges by his word, exposing and condemning the false teaching. The faithful do not need to fear his sword.

What it does not mean. This does not authorise Christians to fight false teachers with physical weapons or violence. Christ’s sword is his word. The church’s weapons are the truth, and church discipline (Matthew 18:15–20; 2 Corinthians 10:3–5).

In a sentence. So repent; otherwise I will come to you without delay and fight against those people with the sword that comes out of my mouth.

On a Tuesday. If you are tolerating a sin because confronting it would be uncomfortable, Christ calls you to repent. It is better to be corrected by his word now than fought by it later.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’

Setting and background. Manna was the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and a jar of it was kept in the ark of the covenant (Exodus 16:33–34; Hebrews 9:4). Jewish tradition said that when the temple was destroyed, the ark and its manna were hidden by Jeremiah, and the Messiah would bring them out again. Jesus called himself the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35). In the ancient world, white stones had several uses: jurors voted to acquit with a white stone; white stones served as tickets of admission to banquets and festivals; and stones inscribed with names were used as amulets.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. As in vv. 7 and 11.

To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna. Key words. “Hidden manna” (tou manna tou kekrymmenou). Those who refuse to eat food offered to idols will eat the bread of heaven: Christ himself, and the feast of eternal life with him, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9). What they give up is nothing compared with what they will receive.

And I will give him a white stone. Key words. “White stone” (psēphon leukēn). Given the banquet in this verse, the most likely meaning is a ticket of admission to the messianic feast, combined with the sense of acquittal: the white stone of the verdict not guilty. Those rejected by the guilds’ feasts are admitted to Christ’s.

With a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it. Key words. “New name” (onoma kainon). In Scripture, a new name marks a new identity and relationship: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel. Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15 promise God’s people a new name. Whose name is it? Possibly the believer’s new name, given by Christ, a personal and intimate sign of belonging; or Christ’s own name, which only those who know him truly understand (3:12; 19:12). Either way, it speaks of personal, private intimacy with Christ, known only between him and the believer.

What it does not mean. Nothing here supports secret knowledge for spiritual elites, as later Gnostic groups taught. The new name is known by the one who receives it, and every conquering believer receives one.

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches: to the one who conquers I will give a share of the hidden manna, and a white stone with a new name written on it that only the person who receives it knows.

For worship. Christ knows you by name, personally, and has a place for you at his table. No feast the world offers can compare.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the white stone is uncertain; white stones were used as tokens of acquittal and as tickets of admission to feasts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — To the Church in Thyatira
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Thyatira was the smallest and least distinguished of the seven towns — no great temple, no governor, a valley with no defences, and more trade-guild inscriptions than any of the other six. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, dealt in its purple cloth (Acts 16:14). It receives the longest of the seven letters.

Verse 18 introduces Christ as the Son of God — the only use of that title in Revelation — with eyes like a flame of fire and feet like burnished bronze, in a town of metalworkers. Verse 19 gives the warmest commendation of the seven: love, faith, service and patient endurance, and latter works exceeding the first. Where Ephesus had gone backwards, Thyatira is growing, and love heads the list.

Verses 20–21 bring the charge: they tolerate a woman Christ calls Jezebel — a type, not a name (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 21:1–16) — who calls herself a prophetess and teaches Balaam’s programme over again. Nobody is accused of believing her; they are accused of letting her continue. Verse 21 adds that Christ gave her time to repent and she goes on refusing.

Verses 22–23 pronounce judgment, and every clause carries a distinction. The couch of the banquet becomes the sickbed. Those who commit adultery with her are threatened unless they repent — the door still open inside the sentence. Her children, in the Old Testament idiom, are those who have made her teaching their own. And all the churches will learn that he searches kidneys and hearts (Jer. 17:10) and repays each according to his works.

Verses 24–25 turn to the faithful remnant who never learned what some call the deep things of Satan — almost certainly the faction’s own boast about the deep things of God, with one noun replaced. To them: I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.

Verses 26–29 give the promise: authority over the nations, in the words of Psalm 2:8–9, handed on from the Son who received it from his Father; and then the morning star, which the book identifies as Christ himself (22:16; cf. Num. 24:17). Verse 29 closes with the refrain — and from this letter onward the refrain comes after the promise rather than before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Warm but Undiscerning

Thyatira grew in love, faith, service and endurance, yet tolerated a self-appointed prophetess teaching compromise. Christ gave her time to repent; to the faithful he lays no other burden than to hold fast until he comes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a guild town, her teaching offered relief with a spiritual justification.

Now: The faithful in a compromised church are not asked to fix it, only to hold on — and they are promised the morning star.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: 'The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. "'I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. ‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.

Setting and background. Thyatira, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Pergamum, was the smallest and least important of the seven cities, but the longest letter goes to it. It was a centre of manufacturing and trade, with more trade guilds than any other city in Asia: wool, linen, dyeing, leather, pottery, slave trading and, especially, bronze-working. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met in Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). Each guild had a patron god and held feasts in the god’s honour, and membership was almost necessary for anyone who wanted to work. The city’s chief god was Apollo, worshipped as son of Zeus, and the emperor was honoured as son of god too.

The words of the Son of God. Key words. “Son of God” (ho huios tou theou): the only time this title appears in Revelation. In a city that honoured Apollo and the emperor as sons of Zeus, Christ declares himself the true Son of God. The title echoes Psalm 2, which is quoted in vv. 26–27: the LORD’s anointed, his Son, will rule the nations.

Who has eyes like a flame of fire. Key words. From 1:14. Eyes that see through every disguise. He will search minds and hearts (v. 23).

And whose feet are like burnished bronze. Key words. From 1:15. Thyatira’s bronze workers would recognise the image of shining metal. Feet that stand firm and trample evil.

I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance. Key words. “Love” (agapēn), “faith” (pistin, or faithfulness), “service” (diakonian, practical ministry to others), “patient endurance” (hypomonēn). The very things Ephesus lacked, Thyatira had in abundance: love and service. Love produces service; faith produces endurance.

And that your latter works exceed the first. Key words. Unlike Ephesus, which had declined from its first love, Thyatira was growing. A church that was getting better, not worse.

What it does not mean. Growth in love and service does not mean all is well. Thyatira’s strength would also prove to be its weakness: a love that would not confront error.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Thyatira write: These are the words of the Son of God, whose eyes blaze like fire and whose feet shine like fine bronze: I know your works, your love, your faithfulness, your service and your perseverance, and I know that you are doing more now than you did at first.

On a Tuesday. Christ sees and values your quiet acts of service and faithfulness. Keep growing in them.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira was a town of trade guilds, whose feasts honoured pagan gods. Lydia came from there.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.

Setting and background. Jezebel was the Phoenician wife of King Ahab of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). She promoted the worship of Baal, killed the LORD’s prophets, supported hundreds of prophets of Baal, and led Israel into idolatry, which Scripture calls whoredom and sorcery (2 Kings 9:22). She was the Old Testament’s great example of a powerful person leading God’s people into false worship.

But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel. Key words. “Tolerate” (apheis, let alone, permit). The church’s failure was not that she existed, but that it allowed her to go on teaching. “Jezebel”: almost certainly a symbolic name, comparing this woman to Ahab’s queen. She was a real person in the church at Thyatira, possibly an influential and well-connected woman, and her teaching was having the same effect as the old Jezebel’s.

Who calls herself a prophetess. Key words. “Calls herself” (hē legousa heautēn). Self-appointed. She claimed to speak for God, which gave her teaching authority and made it hard to challenge.

And is teaching and seducing my servants. Key words. “Teaching” (didaskei) and “seducing” (plana, leading astray, deceiving). The same word is used of Satan, who deceives the whole world (12:9). False teaching misleads people who think they are being led to deeper truth. “My servants”: Christ’s own people.

To practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. Key words. The same two sins as at Pergamum (v. 14). Probably she taught that Christians could join in the guild feasts with their idolatry and immorality, perhaps claiming that God had revealed this freedom to her, or that experiencing the deep things of Satan could not harm a truly spiritual person (v. 24). It offered a way to keep one’s job and status without suffering.

I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality. Key words. “Time” (chronon). Christ had been patient, perhaps through warnings from the church or by his own patience (Romans 2:4). “Refuses” (ou thelei, does not want to). Her problem was not ignorance but an unwilling heart.

Where Christians differ: does this passage forbid women from teaching? Some use it to argue against women preaching; others say it shows women prophesied and taught in the church, and the problem was only false teaching. Verdict: Jezebel is rebuked for false teaching and immorality, not for being a woman who spoke. Scripture recognises women who prophesied (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5). This passage does not settle questions of church office; those are taught elsewhere. This app holds the complementarian view that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women serve in many vital ministries. The lesson here is for every church and every teacher, male or female: no claim to speak for God gives anyone the right to teach what contradicts his word.

What it does not mean. Tolerance is not always a virtue. A church that loves its people will not let them be led into sin by any teacher, however gifted or powerful. Loving people sometimes means saying no.

In a sentence. But this is my complaint against you: you put up with that woman Jezebel, who claims to be a prophet and who is teaching my servants and leading them astray into sexual immorality and eating food offered to idols; I gave her time to repent, but she does not want to turn from her immorality.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone who claims a special word from God that makes sin acceptable. And if you lead in your church, love your people enough to protect them from such teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

Setting and background. The old Jezebel’s end was terrible (2 Kings 9:30–37), and her family was destroyed (2 Kings 10). Christ’s judgement here is proportionate and fitting.

Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed. Key words. “Bed” (klinēn, couch, bed). A play on words. The bed of immorality and the couches of the idol feasts (where people reclined to eat) will become a bed of sickness. Judgement fits the sin. Compare 1 Corinthians 11:30, where abuse of the Lord’s Supper brought sickness and death.

And those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works. Key words. “Commit adultery” (moicheuontas): those who follow her teaching, whether literally sleeping with her or joining in her spiritual unfaithfulness. “Unless they repent”: there is still time. Christ’s warnings are meant to bring people back.

And I will strike her children dead. Key words. “Her children” (ta tekna autēs): her followers, those who have fully adopted her teaching, rather than her literal children. “Strike dead” (apoktenō en thanatō, kill with death, a Hebrew way of saying kill with pestilence or plague). A severe judgement on those who refuse to turn.

And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart. Key words. “Searches” (eraunōn, examines, investigates). “Mind and heart” (nephrous kai kardias, literally kidneys and hearts). In Hebrew thinking, the kidneys were the seat of emotions and the heart the seat of thought and will. Jeremiah 17:10 says that the LORD searches the heart and tests the mind, to give everyone according to their ways. Christ takes the LORD’s own role. Nothing is hidden from him, whatever outward show of spirituality people make.

And I will give to each of you according to your works. Key words. “According to your works” (kata ta erga hymōn). A principle of judgement throughout Scripture (Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Works are the evidence of what is in the heart.

What it does not mean. Judgement according to works does not mean salvation by works. We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). But true faith always produces works, and the works reveal whether faith is real. On the last day, the works will show the truth about the heart (Matthew 25:31–46). Nor does this mean every illness is God’s judgement on a particular sin; Scripture warns against that conclusion (John 9:1–3). Here Christ announces a specific judgement.

In a sentence. So I will throw her onto a bed of sickness, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into terrible suffering, unless they turn away from what she does, and I will put her children to death; then all the churches will know that I am the one who examines people’s deepest thoughts and desires, and I will repay each of you as your works deserve.

On a Tuesday. Christ searches your mind and heart. Live before him without pretence, and turn quickly from anything you would not want him to find.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.

Setting and background. Gnostic groups in the second century boasted of knowing the deep things, secret spiritual knowledge reserved for the initiated. Some taught that the truly spiritual person could indulge the body without harm, or even should experience evil in order to master it. Jezebel’s teaching seems to have been an early form of this.

But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching. Key words. Christ distinguishes the faithful from the followers of Jezebel. He knows exactly who belongs to which group.

Who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan. Key words. “Deep things” (ta bathea). Jezebel’s followers probably claimed to know the deep things of God (1 Corinthians 2:10). Christ calls them by their real name: the deep things of Satan. Alternatively, they claimed that to know Satan’s depths, to explore sin from inside, was a mark of spiritual maturity. Either way, the supposed higher knowledge was demonic.

To you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Key words. “Burden” (baros, weight). This echoes the Jerusalem council’s letter, which said it laid no greater burden on Gentile believers than to abstain from idol food and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29). Christ adds no new requirements, no secret knowledge, no heavy rules. Avoiding idolatry and immorality is enough.

Only hold fast what you have until I come. Key words. “Hold fast” (kratēsate, grip firmly). Hold on to what you already have: the apostolic gospel, faithfulness to Christ. Nothing new is needed. “Until I come” (achris hou an hēxō): until his return. Faithfulness is for the whole of life, until Christ comes.

What it does not mean. Deep knowledge of God is not wrong; Paul prays for it (Ephesians 3:18–19). What is wrong is a claim to a secret deeper knowledge that goes beyond, or contradicts, the plain gospel. Maturity is growing deeper into what was taught from the beginning, not moving beyond it.

In a sentence. But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who have not taken up this teaching and have not learned what they call the deep secrets, which are really Satan’s, I say this: I will not put any further burden on you; just hold firmly to what you have until I come.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a new revelation or a secret key to the Christian life. Hold on to the gospel you have, and keep holding until Christ comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

Setting and background. Psalm 2 describes the nations raging against the LORD and his anointed king, his Son. God says he will give the nations to his Son, who will break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel (Psalm 2:8–9). Christ now applies this promise to himself, and shares it with his faithful people.

The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end. Key words. “Keeps my works” (ho tērōn achri telous ta erga mou): unlike Jezebel’s works (v. 22), these are the works Christ commands and produces. “Until the end”: perseverance to the last.

To him I will give authority over the nations. Key words. “Authority” (exousian). Christians in Thyatira had no power at all; they could not even get a job without compromising. Christ promises that they will share his rule over the nations. Believers will reign with Christ (3:21; 20:4–6; 22:5; 1 Corinthians 6:2–3).

And he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces. Key words. “Rule” (poimanei, shepherd). The Greek Old Testament translated Psalm 2:9 with a word that means to shepherd, though in this context the shepherd’s rod is used in judgement. “Rod of iron”: unbreakable authority. “Earthen pots”: Thyatira’s potters would understand: clay pots, smashed in pieces, cannot be repaired. Opposition to Christ will be utterly broken.

Even as I myself have received authority from my Father. Key words. Christ received this authority from the Father (Matthew 28:18). He shares it with his people, as the Son of God shares his inheritance with the sons of God.

And I will give him the morning star. Key words. “Morning star” (ton astera ton prōinon): the planet Venus, which shines brightly before dawn, announcing the coming day. In 22:16 Christ calls himself the bright morning star. The promise is Christ himself. The conqueror will have Christ, and share his royal glory. Numbers 24:17 had prophesied a star coming out of Jacob and a sceptre rising out of Israel; Christ is that royal star. Roman generals honoured Venus as the star of victory, but Christ is the true sign of triumph.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. In the last four letters, this call comes after the promise rather than before it. Still for every church.

Where Christians differ: when do believers rule the nations? Premillennialists see this fulfilled in a future thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns. Verdict: believers already share Christ’s reign in a hidden way, as a kingdom of priests (1:6), and those who die in Christ reign with him now in heaven (20:4–6), which this app reads as the present age between Christ’s comings. The rule over the nations is completed at Christ’s return, when his enemies are judged (19:15) and his people reign with him for ever in the new creation (22:5). There is no separate future millennium on earth.

What it does not mean. Ruling with a rod of iron does not mean Christians now seek political power to impose the faith. Christ breaks his enemies by his word and at his coming. Our part now is faithful witness.

In a sentence. To the one who conquers and keeps doing my works to the end, I will give authority over the nations, to shepherd them with an iron rod and shatter them like clay pots, just as I have received authority from my Father; and I will give him the morning star; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

For worship. Thank Christ that the weak and powerless who belong to him will share his reign, and that the reward he promises is himself, the bright morning star.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.<sup>2</sup>”‘I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false.<sup>3</sup>I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.<sup>4</sup>But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.<sup>5</sup>Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.<sup>6</sup>Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.<sup>7</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’<sup>8</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life.<sup>9</sup>”‘I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.<sup>10</sup>Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.<sup>11</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.’<sup>12</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword.<sup>13</sup>”‘I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.<sup>14</sup>But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality.<sup>15</sup>So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.<sup>16</sup>Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’<sup>18</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze.<sup>19</sup>”‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.<sup>20</sup>But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.<sup>21</sup>I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works,<sup>23</sup>and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.<sup>24</sup>But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden.<sup>25</sup>Only hold fast what you have until I come.<sup>26</sup>The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations,<sup>27</sup>and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father.<sup>28</sup>And I will give him the morning star.<sup>29</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

3.title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
3.overview:
The final three letters of the seven complete the range of pastoral diagnosis the risen Christ brings to his churches. Sardis has a reputation for life but is spiritually dead. Philadelphia is small and weak but receives no rebuke and the most lavish promises. Laodicea is wealthy and self-satisfied and receives the most devastating rebuke of all.

Together the seven letters form a kind of mirror in which every church and every believer can find themselves. There is no congregation in history that does not exist somewhere on the spectrum these letters describe. The genius of John’s use of seven churches is that seven is the number of completeness: these seven letters are the full portrait of the church in every age, not just the church of Asia Minor in the first century.

The chapter ends with Christ standing at the door and knocking. The cosmic drama of the throne room is inseparable from the intimate pastoral reality of the local congregation. The one who will come with the clouds of heaven (1:7) is the same one who stands at the door of Laodicea and knocks (3:20). The book does not let us choose between the cosmic and the personal, the eschatological and the pastoral. Both are always in play.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — To the Church in Sardis
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Sardis had been the capital of Lydia and the seat of Croesus, and the first coins ever struck were minted there. By John’s day it was a comfortable provincial town with a magnificent past and no importance. Verse 1 introduces Christ as the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars — the Spirit and the messengers both in his hand — and then delivers the shortest, harshest assessment in the seven letters: you have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead. The word for reputation is onoma, a name. No heresy is named here and no persecution; Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned at all.

Verse 2 issues the remedy: wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. The works are not wrong but unfinished — finished enough for the province, not for God. Verse 3 adds three more commands, remember what you received and heard, keep it, repent, and then the threat: I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you. Sardis stood on a spur thought impregnable and fell twice, in 546 and 214 BC, both times to a night climber up the cliff while the garrison slept.

Verse 4 turns: you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments. The word is names again — the church has a name and is dead; these have no name and are alive. Verse 5 gives them three promises: white garments, a name never blotted out of the book of life (a city kept a citizen register and struck names from it at death or conviction), and confession of that name before the Father and the angels (cf. Matt. 10:32). Verse 6 sounds the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Name for Being Alive

Sardis had a reputation for life and was dead. Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember and repent, and he counts the few who have not soiled their garments.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The city had twice fallen to a night climb while the guards slept.

Now: Ask whether the reasons you would give for your church’s health are reasons Sardis could have given.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: 'The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: ‘The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. ‘I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.

Meaning first. Revelation 3 contains the last three of Christ’s seven letters. Sardis has a reputation for life but is dead; Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember the gospel and repent, or he will come like a thief; yet a few have kept their clothes clean, and the conqueror will walk with him in white, never be blotted out of the book of life, and be acknowledged before the Father (vv. 1–6). Philadelphia has little strength but has kept Christ’s word; he who holds the key of David has set before it an open door no one can shut, will make its persecutors acknowledge his love for it, and will keep it in the hour of trial; the conqueror will be a pillar in God’s temple, bearing God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem and Christ’s new name (vv. 7–13). Laodicea is lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, and Christ is about to spit it out; it thinks itself rich but is wretched, poor, blind and naked, so Christ counsels it to buy from him refined gold, white clothes and eye salve; he disciplines those he loves, stands at the door knocking, and will eat with anyone who opens; the conqueror will sit with him on his throne (vv. 14–22). The chapter shows that Christ’s verdict on a church can be the opposite of its reputation: the dead church looked alive, the weak church was strong in faithfulness, and the rich church was poor.

Setting and background. Sardis, about 30 miles (50 kilometres) southeast of Thyatira, had once been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for his wealth. Its acropolis stood on a steep hill, thought impregnable, yet it was captured twice by surprise: by Cyrus of Persia in 546 BC and by Antiochus III in 214 BC, both times when soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and found the walls unguarded. The city was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 17 and rebuilt with help from the emperor Tiberius. By John’s day it was prosperous but living on its past glory. It had a large and wealthy Jewish community, and a great temple of Artemis.

The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. Key words. “Seven spirits” (from 1:4): the Holy Spirit in his fullness, who gives life. A dead church needs the life-giving Spirit, and Christ has him to give. “Seven stars” (from 1:16, 20): Christ holds the churches in his hand; this church is still his.

I know your works. Christ knows more than the reputation; he knows the reality.

You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead. Key words. “Reputation” (onoma, name). Sardis had a name for being alive: perhaps busy, respected and well regarded by other churches. “Dead” (nekros). Spiritually lifeless. Interestingly, Sardis faced no recorded persecution and no false teachers; there was nothing worth attacking. It was comfortable, conformed and asleep. Paul describes people who have the appearance of godliness but deny its power (2 Timothy 3:5).

What it does not mean. Dead does not mean every member was unconverted; there were a faithful few (v. 4). It means the church as a whole had lost spiritual life: going through the motions, without the power of the Spirit, the reality of repentance or the warmth of love. Nor is a church alive just because it is busy, large or popular.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Sardis write: These are the words of the one who has the sevenfold Spirit of God and the seven stars: I know your works; you have a name for being alive, but you are dead.

On a Tuesday. A reputation is not a life. Ask Christ to show you whether your faith is living or only looks it, and ask for his Spirit to bring life.
verseByVerse.note: Sardis had been a great royal city. Its seemingly impregnable citadel was taken by surprise more than once in its history.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.

Setting and background. Twice in its history, Sardis fell because its watchmen were asleep. Everyone in the city would have known the story. Jesus had warned his disciples to stay awake because the thief comes when no one expects him (Matthew 24:42–44), and Paul used the same image (1 Thessalonians 5:2–6).

Wake up. Key words. “Wake up” (ginou grēgorōn, become watchful, keep on being alert). A present imperative: start being watchful and keep at it. Spiritual sleep is the condition of a church that is not watching for Christ, not praying, not on guard against sin.

And strengthen what remains and is about to die. Key words. “Strengthen” (stērison, make firm, support). “What remains” (ta loipa, the things that are left). Not everything is dead yet. There are embers that can be fanned into flame: some faith, some truth, some faithful people. Strengthen them before they too go out.

For I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Key words. “Complete” (peplērōmena, filled up, fulfilled). Their works looked impressive to people, but in God’s sight they were unfinished, hollow, lacking the reality of faith and love. Started but not carried through; outwardly correct but inwardly empty.

Remember, then, what you received and heard. Key words. “Received” (eilēphas) and “heard” (ēkousas): the gospel they were first taught, and the grace they were given. The cure for a dead church is not a new technique but the old gospel.

Keep it, and repent. Key words. “Keep” (tērei, hold on to, obey, keep on keeping). “Repent” (metanoēson, a decisive turning). First a decisive break with their sleep, and then a lasting faithfulness.

If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you. Key words. “Like a thief” (hōs kleptēs): unexpectedly, without warning. This may refer to a judgement on Sardis in history, or to Christ’s final return, which will be a disaster for those found asleep (16:15). For the watchful, the thief image is no threat (1 Thessalonians 5:4).

What it does not mean. Coming like a thief does not mean Christ’s return will be secret or invisible. It means unexpected. Every eye will see him (1:7); but those who are not watching will be caught unprepared, as Sardis was by its enemies.

In a sentence. Wake up, and shore up what is left before it dies too, for I have not found your works complete in my God’s eyes; so remember what you received and heard, hold on to it and turn back; if you do not wake up, I will come on you like a thief, at an hour you do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual sleep begins with neglecting prayer and Scripture, and with comfort. Go back today to the gospel you first received, and strengthen whatever in your life with God is weak.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

Setting and background. Sardis was famous for its wool and dyeing industry. White garments were worn at festivals, at victories and by citizens on special occasions. Ancient cities kept registers of citizens, and a name was erased when a citizen died or was disgraced. The idea of God’s book goes back to Exodus 32:32–33, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1, where those whose names are written in the book will be delivered.

Yet you have still a few names in Sardis. Key words. “Names” (onomata, persons). A play on v. 1: the church had a name for life, but only a few names were truly alive. Christ knows each one.

People who have not soiled their garments. Key words. “Soiled” (emolynan, stained, defiled). Clothing in Scripture often pictures a person’s life and conduct (Jude 23; Zechariah 3:3–5). These few had not been stained by compromise with the culture’s sin and idolatry.

And they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. Key words. “Walk with me”: fellowship with Christ. “White”: purity, victory and festival joy. “Worthy” (axioi): not that they have earned it, but that their lives fit the gift, as the robes made white in the Lamb’s blood (7:14) are given, not earned (19:8).

The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments. The robe of righteousness, given by Christ (Isaiah 61:10), and the purity of a life washed in his blood.

And I will never blot his name out of the book of life. Key words. “Never” (ou mē, the strongest negative: certainly not). “Book of life” (biblou tēs zōēs): God’s register of those who belong to him and will have eternal life. Revelation says these names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). The promise is a strong assurance, stated negatively: I will certainly not erase it.

I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. Key words. “Confess” (homologēsō, acknowledge, declare openly). Jesus promised that whoever acknowledges him before others, he will acknowledge before his Father (Matthew 10:32; Luke 12:8). Those who confess Christ on earth, at great cost, will be confessed by Christ in heaven.

Where Christians differ: can a name be blotted out of the book of life? Arminian Christians read this verse as implying that believers who fail to persevere can have their names erased and lose their salvation. Verdict: the verse is a promise, not a threat. Christ never says he blots anyone out; he says he will never do it. Names in the Lamb’s book were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8), so those who belong to Christ cannot be removed. Those who never persevere show that they were never truly written (1 John 2:19). The warnings in these letters are the means God uses to keep his people persevering; the promises assure them that he will.

What it does not mean. Worthy does not mean that some believers are good enough to deserve heaven. All are saved by grace. Their worthiness is the fitness of a life that has received and lived by that grace.

In a sentence. Even so, there are a few people in Sardis who have not stained their clothes, and they will walk with me dressed in white, because they are fit to do so; the one who conquers will be clothed in white like them, I will certainly not erase his name from the book of life, and I will acknowledge him by name before my Father and his angels; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

For worship. Thank God that your name is written in the Lamb’s book of life and will never be erased. Let that assurance make you bold to confess him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — To the Church in Philadelphia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Philadelphia was the youngest of the seven cities, founded as a missionary outpost of Greek culture on the edge of the uplands, and it sat on a fault line. The earthquake of AD 17 destroyed it, aftershocks went on for years, and people camped outside the walls rather than sleep under a roof. Twice the city took a new name to thank an emperor who paid for its rebuilding.

Verse 7 introduces Christ with four descriptions, none of them drawn from the vision of chapter 1: the holy one, the true one (alēthinos, the genuine article as against the counterfeit), and the holder of the key of David who opens and no one shuts — quoted from Isaiah 22:22, where the key of the royal house is laid on the shoulder of a new steward. Verse 8 sets before them an open door no one can shut, and gives the most encouraging assessment in the seven letters: I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

Verse 9 promises that the accusers who deny them a share in the promises will come and bow before them — and the sentence ends not with humiliation but with they will learn that I have loved you. Verse 10 is the disputed one: I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, where both the hour of trial and keep from are argued over, and the readings are set out at the verse. Verse 11 gives the instruction: I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.

Verse 12 answers the city’s history point by point: a pillar in the temple of God, never to go out of it, for people who had lived in tents outside their own walls; and three names written on him — God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ’s own new name (cf. 19:12) — for a town that had twice taken a new name and twice seen it fade. Verse 13 closes with the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Little Power, No Rebuke

Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before a weak church that has kept his word. Its accusers will learn that he has loved it; the faithful will be pillars in the temple of God and bear his names.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A small congregation in an earthquake town had been told it had no share in the promises.

Now: Christ measures a church by faithfulness, not size.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. "I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: ‘The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. ‘I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

Setting and background. Philadelphia, about 28 miles (45 kilometres) southeast of Sardis, was the youngest of the seven cities, founded in the second century BC by Attalus II, whose love for his brother earned him the nickname Philadelphus, brother-lover. It stood at the gateway to the high plateau of Phrygia, on an important road, and was founded to spread Greek culture into the east: a city with an open door. It was badly damaged in the earthquake of AD 17, and aftershocks went on for years; many residents lived outside the city for fear of falling buildings. After Tiberius helped rebuild it, it was renamed Neocaesarea, New Caesar. Like Smyrna, the church faced hostility from the local synagogue. In Isaiah 22:20–22, the LORD gives Eliakim, the new steward of King Hezekiah’s palace, the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts and what he shuts no one opens.

The words of the holy one, the true one. Key words. “The holy one” (ho hagios): in the Old Testament, the Holy One is God (Isaiah 40:25). “The true one” (ho alēthinos, genuine, real, faithful). Christ is the true Messiah, whatever the synagogue says.

Who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. Key words. “Key of David” (from Isaiah 22:22): authority over the house and kingdom of David. Christ, David’s greater son, decides who enters the kingdom. If the synagogue shuts out the Christians, saying they are not God’s people, Christ opens the door to them, and no one can shut it.

Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. Key words. “Open door” (thyran ēneōgmenēn). Two meanings fit. First, the door into the kingdom, guaranteed by Christ, which no one can shut against them. Second, a door of opportunity for the gospel, as Paul used the phrase (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3). As the city was a gateway for Greek culture, the church would be a gateway for the gospel.

I know that you have but little power. Key words. “Little power” (mikran dynamin). Small in numbers, influence and resources. Christ does not rebuke them for this. Weakness is not failure.

And yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name. Key words. “Kept my word” (etērēsas mou ton logon). Faithful in what matters. They held on to the truth and did not disown Christ under pressure. What Christ values is not size or power but faithfulness.

What it does not mean. The open door does not mean that weak churches will automatically grow, or that faithfulness guarantees success by the world’s measures. It means Christ has opened the way, and no opposition can close it.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the Holy One, the True One, who holds the key of David, so that what he opens no one can shut and what he shuts no one can open: I know your works; look, I have put in front of you an open door that no one can close; I know you have little strength, yet you have kept my word and have not disowned my name.

On a Tuesday. You may feel small and weak. Christ asks for faithfulness, not strength. Look for the door he has opened for you to speak of him, and walk through it.
verseByVerse.note: Philadelphia was a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

parallels.desc: he shall open, and none shall shut

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
