Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.

Setting and background. Isaiah prophesied that the nations who had oppressed Israel would come and bow down at Israel’s feet, acknowledging that the LORD had loved his people (Isaiah 45:14; 49:23; 60:14). Here the roles are startlingly reversed: Jewish persecutors will bow before a mostly Gentile church, acknowledging that Christ has loved it.

Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie. Key words. As at Smyrna (2:9). By rejecting the Messiah and persecuting his people, they had forfeited the right to the name of God’s people. “Lie” (pseudontai): their claim is false.

Behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet. Key words. “Bow down” (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves). Not worship of the church, but acknowledgement that the church is God’s true people. This may happen through their conversion (as Paul hoped, Romans 11:11–14) or at the final judgement, when every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11).

And they will learn that I have loved you. Key words. “Loved” (ēgapēsa). Echoing Isaiah 43:4, where the LORD says to Israel that they are precious in his eyes and he loves them. The love once claimed exclusively by the synagogue belongs to the despised church.

Because you have kept my word about patient endurance. Key words. “My word about patient endurance” (ton logon tēs hypomonēs mou): the command to endure as Christ endured, or the message of his endurance.

I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world. Key words. “Keep from” (tērēsō ek, keep out of, guard from). A play on words: because you have kept my word, I will keep you. “The hour of trial” (tēs hōras tou peirasmou): a time of testing coming on the whole world, which the rest of Revelation describes in the seals, trumpets and bowls.

To try those who dwell on the earth. Key words. “Those who dwell on the earth” (tous katoikountas epi tēs gēs): throughout Revelation this phrase means unbelievers, the world in rebellion against God (6:10; 13:8; 17:8). The trial is aimed at them, not at the church.

Where Christians differ: is this a promise of a pre-tribulation rapture? Dispensationalists read “keep you from the hour of trial” as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth before a final seven-year tribulation. Verdict: the same words appear in John 17:15, where Jesus prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one. To keep from is to protect within, not to remove from. Revelation consistently shows God’s people sealed and protected in the midst of the judgements (7:3; 9:4; 12:6, 14), while they still suffer at the hands of the beast. The promise was made to a church in the first century, which was never raptured; it was preserved. God protects his people from his wrath and from losing their faith, not from all suffering. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

I am coming soon. Key words. “Soon” (tachy, quickly). The promise that sustains endurance (22:7, 12, 20).

Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown. Key words. “Hold fast” (kratei, grip). “Seize” (labē, take). “Crown” (stephanon, victor’s wreath). Not that someone could steal their salvation, but that they must persevere to receive the prize. The warning is one of the means by which Christ keeps them.

What it does not mean. This passage does not support replacing love for Jewish people with contempt. The point is the vindication of a persecuted church, and the hope is that its persecutors will learn Christ’s love. Many in Philadelphia’s synagogue may have come to faith.

In a sentence. Look, I will make those in Satan’s synagogue, who claim to be Jews but are lying, come and bow at your feet and recognise that I have loved you; because you have kept my command to endure, I will keep you safe through the hour of testing that is coming on the whole world to test the earth’s inhabitants; I am coming soon; hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your crown.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith, Christ will vindicate you. Do not strike back. Hold fast, and trust him to show your opponents that he loves you.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

Setting and background. In a city shaken by earthquakes, where buildings collapsed and people fled outside the walls, a pillar was the part of a building that stood firm. Columns often remained standing in ruined temples. Cities sometimes honoured a distinguished citizen or priest by setting up a pillar inscribed with his name in a temple. And Philadelphia had twice been renamed after emperors (Neocaesarea and Flavia); Christ gives a greater name.

The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Key words. “Pillar” (stylon, column). Permanence, stability and honour. Those with little power and shut out of the synagogue will be pillars in God’s own temple. In the new Jerusalem, there is no temple building, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22); to be a pillar there is to belong permanently in God’s presence. Paul called church leaders pillars (Galatians 2:9).

Never shall he go out of it. Key words. “Never” (ou mē … eti, certainly never again). In an earthquake city, people had to flee again and again. In God’s temple, no one will ever have to leave. Eternal security and permanent belonging.

And I will write on him the name of my God. Key words. A name marks ownership. The high priest wore the name of the LORD on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38). Believers bear God’s name, as his servants (14:1; 22:4), in contrast to those who bear the beast’s mark (13:16–17).

And the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven. Key words. “New Jerusalem”: the city of God, the bride of the Lamb, coming down from heaven in the new creation (21:2, 10). Believers are citizens of that city (Philippians 3:20; Hebrews 12:22), whatever earthly citizenship they lose.

And my own new name. Key words. Christ’s new name (19:12, 16), expressing his full revelation and victory at his return. Believers will share in his glory.

What it does not mean. The three names are not literal tattoos, any more than believers will be literal pillars of stone. They are pictures of belonging to God, his city and his Son, for ever.

In a sentence. The one who conquers I will make a pillar in my God’s temple, and he will never have to leave it; I will write on him my God’s name, the name of my God’s city, the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

For worship. In a shaking world, thank God that you have a permanent place in his presence, and that you bear his name, his city’s name and Christ’s name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — To the Church in Laodicea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Laodicea sat at the junction of three trade roads and made its money three ways: banking, a glossy black wool exported across the empire, and a medical school producing a famous eye ointment. When an earthquake levelled it in AD 60 it refused imperial relief and rebuilt at its own expense — Tacitus records it, and the city was proud of it. Every line of this letter is written against that fact.

Verse 14 gives three titles, each a rebuke before any criticism: the Amen (the God of Amen, Isa. 65:16; cf. 2 Cor. 1:20), the faithful and true witness, and the beginning of God’s creation — archē, origin and source, not first creature.

Verses 15–16 turn on local geography. Hierapolis six miles north had hot healing springs; Colossae ten miles east had cold mountain water; Laodicea had to pipe water in and it arrived tepid and unpleasant. So cold is not indifference on a scale. Cold water is good and hot water is good; the charge is uselessness. I will spit you out of my mouth renders emeō, to vomit — the involuntary reaction to a cup of Laodicean tap water.

Verse 17 quotes the church’s own words, the only congregation permitted to speak in these letters: I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing — not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. The last three answer the three industries exactly. Verse 18 responds with an offer rather than a command — I counsel you to buy from me — gold refined by fire for the bank, white garments for the wool town, eye salve for the medical school (cf. Isa. 55:1).

Verse 19 reframes everything: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Prov. 3:12; Heb. 12:5–11), using phileō, the warmer word. Verse 20 has Christ knocking outside his own church, offering the evening meal to whoever opens — and the invitation narrows to the singular, if anyone. Verse 21 gives the last and largest promise of the seven, a seat on his own throne, grounded on a conquest already finished. Verse 22 closes the letters with the refrain for the seventh time.
verseByVerse.theology:
Useless, Not Merely Lukewarm

Laodicea’s water was neither hot nor cold and good for nothing, and so was its church. Rich and self-sufficient, it did not know it was poor, blind and naked. Christ counsels it to buy from him, disciplines because he loves, and knocks at the door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A city that refused imperial relief produced a church that said, “I need nothing.”

Now: Ask who in your town is helped because your church exists — and open the door to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: 'The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: ‘The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation.

Setting and background. Laodicea, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Philadelphia, stood in the Lycus valley, about 10 miles (16 kilometres) from Colossae and 6 miles (10 kilometres) from Hierapolis. It was rich: a banking centre, famous for a glossy black wool, and home to a medical school known for an eye salve made from a local powder. When an earthquake devastated it in AD 60, it refused help from Rome and rebuilt itself from its own wealth, as the historian Tacitus records. Its weakness was water: it had no good supply of its own and piped water in through an aqueduct. Paul mentions the church at Laodicea in Colossians 2:1, 4:13–16, and asked the Colossians to share letters with it. The church was probably founded by Epaphras.

The words of the Amen. Key words. “Amen” (ho Amēn): Hebrew for firm, sure, so be it. Isaiah 65:16 speaks of the God of truth, literally the God of Amen. Christ is God’s Amen, the one in whom all God’s promises are yes (2 Corinthians 1:20). In contrast to a church that was neither one thing nor the other, Christ is utterly reliable.

The faithful and true witness. Key words. From 1:5. He tells the truth, even when it hurts. Laodicea needs to hear the truth about itself, and this witness will tell it.

The beginning of God’s creation. Key words. “Beginning” (hē archē): the source, origin, ruler of God’s creation. Colossians, a letter Laodicea had heard read, says that by Christ all things were created, and he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:15–18). Christ is the origin and ruler of everything God made, including Laodicea’s wealth.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ was created? The ancient Arians, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, read “the beginning of God’s creation” as meaning that Christ was the first being God created. Verdict: the word archē can mean the beginning in the sense of the source or ruler, and that is its meaning here. Revelation gives Christ the titles of God: the first and the last (1:17), the Alpha and the Omega (22:13), worshipped with the Father (5:13). John’s Gospel says all things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3); so he cannot himself be a made thing. Christ is the uncreated source of creation, not its first product.

What it does not mean. The Amen is not just a word to close prayers. As a title for Christ, it means that he is God’s final, unshakeable yes.

In a sentence. To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the source and ruler of God’s creation.

For worship. Say Amen with understanding: Christ is God’s Amen, and every promise is sure in him.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea, about ten miles from Colossae, was a wealthy banking and textile city. Rebuilt without imperial aid after an earthquake in AD 60, it prided itself on needing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.

Setting and background. Nearby Hierapolis had famous hot springs, used for healing. Colossae had cold, pure, refreshing water. Laodicea’s water was piped in from a distance, arriving tepid and full of minerals; the remains of its pipes show thick deposits of calcium carbonate. The water was notoriously nauseating, the kind of water that makes people want to spit it out.

I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Key words. “Cold” (psychros) and “hot” (zestos, boiling). The image comes from the local water, not from spiritual temperature. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes; both are useful. Lukewarm water is useless.

Would that you were either cold or hot! Key words. Christ is not saying that it would be better to be against him (cold) than half-hearted. In the light of the water image, both cold and hot are good: either healing like Hierapolis or refreshing like Colossae. The problem is that Laodicea is neither; its works do nothing for anyone.

So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth. Key words. “Lukewarm” (chliaros, tepid). “Spit” (emesai, vomit, spew). A violent, disgusted image. Christ finds this church nauseating. Yet the tense (literally, I am about to spit) leaves time for repentance (v. 19).

Where Christians differ: what do hot and cold mean? The common reading takes hot as spiritually zealous, cold as openly hostile, and lukewarm as half-hearted; on that reading Christ would prefer open hostility to half-heartedness. Verdict: the local water explains the image better. Both hot and cold water are good; lukewarm water is useless and sickening. Christ does not want anyone to be cold toward him. He wants his church to be useful, either healing or refreshing, by real faith and love. Laodicea’s self-satisfied religion did no good to anyone.

What it does not mean. Being spat out does not mean that true believers lose their salvation. Christ is warning a church as a whole, much of which, like Sardis, may never have been truly converted. The response he wants is repentance (v. 19).

In a sentence. I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot, and I wish you were one or the other; but since you are tepid, neither hot nor cold, I am about to spit you out of my mouth.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether your faith does anyone any good, bringing healing or refreshment to others. Comfortable religion that serves no one is what Christ finds hardest to stomach.
verseByVerse.note: Often explained from local water: hot springs at nearby Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, while Laodicea’s piped-in water arrived tepid. Both hot and cold are useful; lukewarm is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,’ not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.

Setting and background. Each part of Christ’s counsel aims at one of Laodicea’s sources of pride: its banks and gold, its famous black wool, and its eye medicine. The proud city that refused Rome’s help after the earthquake had a church with the same attitude toward God.

For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing. Key words. Echoing Hosea 12:8, where Ephraim boasts that it is rich and has found wealth, and no one can find sin in it. Self-sufficiency is the root problem. The church thought it needed nothing, so it did not need Christ.

Not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. Key words. “Not realizing” (ouk oidas, you do not know). Christ says, I know your works (v. 15); they do not know their own condition. “Wretched” (talaipōros, miserable, as in Romans 7:24). “Pitiable” (eleeinos, deserving pity). “Poor” (ptōchos, a beggar). “Blind” (typhlos). “Naked” (gymnos, shamefully exposed). The richest church was spiritually a naked blind beggar. The poorest church, Smyrna, was rich (2:9).

I counsel you to buy from me. Key words. “Counsel” (symbouleuō, advise). Christ does not command but advises, as a friend. “Buy from me”: echoing Isaiah 55:1, where the LORD invites those who have no money to come, buy and eat, without price. They must come to Christ for what they need, admitting they have nothing to pay with.

Gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich. Key words. “Refined by fire” (pepyrōmenon ek pyros): purified gold, the true riches of faith tested by trials (1 Peter 1:7), and the treasure of Christ himself.

And white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen. Key words. “White garments”: the righteousness Christ gives (3:4–5; 19:8), in contrast to the city’s black wool. In Scripture, nakedness is a picture of shame and judgement (Ezekiel 16:37). Only Christ can cover our shame (Genesis 3:7, 21).

And salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see. Key words. “Salve” (kollourion, eye ointment). Laodicea’s medical school was famous for its Phrygian powder for the eyes. They need spiritual sight, which only Christ’s Spirit can give, to see their real condition and his glory (Ephesians 1:18).

What it does not mean. Wealth is not itself the sin. The sin is trusting in it, and thinking that prosperity proves God’s favour. A church can be well-funded and spiritually bankrupt. Nor does buying from Christ mean earning salvation; it is the kind of buying Isaiah describes, without money and without price.

In a sentence. You say, I am rich, I have done well and I need nothing, without seeing that you are miserable and pitiful, poor, blind and naked; so I advise you to buy from me gold purified in the fire, to make you truly rich, white clothes to put on and cover your shameful nakedness, and ointment for your eyes, so that you can see.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the thought that you need nothing. Comfort can make you blind. Come to Christ as a beggar, every day.

verseByVerse.quote: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.

Setting and background. Proverbs 3:12 says that the LORD reproves the one he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights, a verse also quoted in Hebrews 12:5–6. In the Song of Songs 5:2, the beloved knocks at the door, saying, open to me. In the ancient world, eating together was a sign of friendship and acceptance.

Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline. Key words. “Love” (philō, love as a friend, tender affection). “Reprove” (elenchō, expose, convict). “Discipline” (paideuō, train, correct, as a parent trains a child). Even this sickening church is loved. The rebuke of vv. 15–18 is not rejection but love. Christ’s harsh words are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

So be zealous and repent. Key words. “Be zealous” (zēleue, be earnest, burn with zeal; related to the word for hot, zestos, in v. 15). Lukewarmness is cured by zeal. “Repent” (metanoēson): a decisive turn.

Behold, I stand at the door and knock. Key words. “Stand” (hestēka, have taken my stand, and remain standing). “Knock” (krouō, keep knocking). A striking picture: Christ is outside his own church, and asks to be let in. The church had gone on with its life without him.

If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me. Key words. “If anyone” (ean tis): an individual appeal. Even if the church as a whole does not respond, any one person can. “Eat” (deipnēsō, share the main evening meal). Fellowship, friendship, communion with Christ, and a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9). Jesus ate with sinners (Luke 15:2) and shared meals with his disciples (Luke 24:30; John 21:12).

Where Christians differ: an invitation to unbelievers? This verse is often used in evangelism, as Christ knocking at the door of an unbeliever’s heart, waiting to be invited in. Verdict: in context it is addressed to a church, calling professing believers to repent and restore fellowship with Christ. It can rightly be applied to unbelievers, since the gospel calls everyone to turn to Christ, and many professing members of Laodicea were probably not truly converted. But the verse does not mean that Christ is helpless until a sinner decides to let him in. Scripture teaches that the dead sinner can respond only because God first gives new life (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:1–5). When Christ knocks, his voice is powerful: it opens deaf ears, and his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). The free invitation and God’s sovereign grace stand together.

What it does not mean. Christ’s discipline is not anger at people he has rejected. It is the opposite: the discipline of a father who loves. Nor is this verse about a once-for-all decision only; it calls for ongoing, renewed fellowship with Christ.

In a sentence. I correct and discipline everyone I love, so be earnest and turn back; look, I am standing at the door knocking, and if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and share a meal with him, and he with me.

For worship. At the Lord’s Supper, remember that Christ invites himself to eat with his people. Open to him, and enjoy his company.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’”

Setting and background. The final promise of the seven letters is the highest of all. It leads directly into chapters 4–5, where John sees God’s throne and the Lamb who conquered.

The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne. Key words. “Grant” (dōsō, give). A gift, not an earned right. “Sit with me on my throne”: sharing Christ’s royal rule. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28). Believers will reign with Christ (2:26–27; 20:4; 22:5; 2 Timothy 2:12). The church that thought it was rich, and was offered the riches of Christ, is promised more than it ever imagined: a share in his throne.

As I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. Key words. “Conquered” (enikēsa, past tense: a finished victory). Christ conquered by his death and resurrection (5:5–6). Then he sat down at the Father’s right hand (Hebrews 1:3; 12:2). The pattern for believers is the same: victory through faithful suffering, then glory. Christ’s throne and the Father’s throne are one (22:1, 3).

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The final call. All seven letters are for all the churches, and for every church today.

What it does not mean. Sharing Christ’s throne does not mean believers become gods or share his divine nature. It means they share in his reign as redeemed human beings, kings and priests under him (1:6; 5:10).

In a sentence. To the one who conquers I will give a seat with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne; whoever can hear should listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your church is like, these letters are for you. Find yourself in them, hear the rebuke, take the promise, and conquer by staying faithful to Christ.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: ‘The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. “I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.<sup>2</sup>Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God.<sup>3</sup>Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.<sup>4</sup>Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.<sup>5</sup>The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.<sup>6</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’<sup>7</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: ‘The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.<sup>8</sup>“I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.<sup>9</sup>Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you.<sup>10</sup>Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.<sup>12</sup>The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name.<sup>13</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’<sup>14</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: ‘The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation.<sup>15</sup>“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot!<sup>16</sup>So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>For you say, “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,” not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.<sup>18</sup>I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.<sup>19</sup>Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent.<sup>20</sup>Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.<sup>21</sup>The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.<sup>22</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.‘”

4.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Throne Room of Heaven
4.overview:
After the letters to the seven churches, the scene shifts dramatically. John is drawn up through an open door in heaven and finds himself standing before the throne of God. Everything changes. The pastoral specificity of the seven letters gives way to cosmic, overwhelming, dazzling vision. Before any seal is opened, before any trumpet sounds, before any judgment falls, John must see — and the church must see with him — what actually governs history. The answer is: this throne. This worship. This God.

Chapters 4 and 5 together form the interpretive center of the entire book. Chapter 4 answers the question: Who is God? Chapter 5 answers the question: How has God chosen to rule? The answer to the first is: the Creator of all things, infinitely holy, eternally worshipped, Almighty. The answer to the second is: through the slaughtered Lamb who has conquered. Everything that follows in Revelation — every seal, every trumpet, every bowl, every beast, every judgment, every promise — flows from these two chapters as from a spring.

Interpretive flag — “Come up here” (v. 1): Dispensational premillennialists have often read “Come up here” as a prophetic picture of the Rapture — the moment at which the church is caught up to heaven before the tribulation begins. The supporting observation is that the word “church” (ekklēsia) does not appear again in Revelation after chapter 3 until 22:16, suggesting the church has been removed from the scene. The amillennial/idealist reading understands “Come up here” as the commission given specifically to John for his visionary experience — John, not the church, is called up to receive the vision. The church’s absence from the term ekklēsia in chapters 4–22 is explained by the fact that the church is addressed throughout these chapters under other designations: the 144,000, the two witnesses, the great multitude, the bride, the new Jerusalem. The amillennial reading is followed here, with genuine respect for the dispensational position.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Throne Room of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 open the vision: a door standing open in heaven, the trumpet voice of 1:10 calling come up here, John at once in the Spirit, and then the sentence the whole book turns on — a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne. The word throne occurs some forty-seven times in Revelation and about fifteen times in the whole of the rest of the New Testament. Nothing else in the room is described first.

Verse 3 describes the one seated with three colours and nothing else: jasper (clear as crystal, 21:11), carnelian (blood-red), and around the throne a rainbow like an emerald. Carnelian was the first stone of the high priest’s breastpiece and jasper the last (Ex. 28:17–20). The rainbow is the sign given after the flood, a warrior’s bow hung up and pointed away (Gen. 9:13–16). No face is described, and the restraint is the point.

Verse 4 sets twenty-four elders on twenty-four thrones around it, in white garments with golden crowns — every reward promised to the seven churches, already being worn. Verse 5 fills the room with Sinai: lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder out of the throne itself (Ex. 19:16–19), and seven burning torches which John identifies as the seven spirits of God.

Verse 6 gives the floor — a sea of glass, like crystal, chaos frozen solid in front of the throne (cf. Ex. 24:10; 21:1) — and introduces four living creatures, nearer than the elders, covered in eyes. Verse 7 names them: lion, ox, the face of a man, and an eagle in flight, drawn from Ezekiel’s cherubim (Ezek. 1:5–11).

Verse 8 gives them Isaiah’s six wings and Isaiah’s song — Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come (Isa. 6:2–3) — sung without ceasing, day and night. Verses 9–11 close the chapter with a repeated movement: whenever the creatures give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and say Worthy are you, our Lord and God… for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Throne Comes First

Before any seal is opened, John is shown an occupied throne, ringed by a rainbow and surrounded by unceasing worship: holy, holy, holy. The Creator of all things is worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Domitian liked to be called “our Lord and God”; the elders give those words to the true throne.

Now: Lay down every crown you were given before the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this." At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.” At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.

Meaning first. Revelation 4 takes John, and the reader, into the throne room of heaven, before any judgement or beast appears. John sees a door open in heaven and is called up to see what must happen (v. 1). At the centre is a throne, and one seated on it, shining like precious stones and surrounded by an emerald rainbow (vv. 2–3). Around it are twenty-four elders on thrones, in white with golden crowns; from the throne come lightning and thunder; before it burn seven torches, the Spirit of God, and spreads a sea like crystal (vv. 4–6a). Four living creatures, full of eyes, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, never stop crying, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty (vv. 6b–8). Whenever they give glory to God, the elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne and praise him as worthy because he created all things (vv. 9–11). Before John sees anything of the world’s chaos, he sees that the universe has a centre, and it is a throne that is occupied. Everything that follows in the book flows from this throne.

Setting and background. The vision draws on the great throne visions of the Old Testament: Isaiah 6, where the Lord sits on a high throne and the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel 1, with its four living creatures, wheels, rainbow and crystal expanse; Daniel 7, where thrones are set and the Ancient of Days sits in judgement; and 1 Kings 22:19, where Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven. For readers living under the emperor, whose court ceremonies were grand and whose subjects were expected to hail him as lord and god, this chapter declares who truly sits on the throne of the universe.

After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! Key words. “After this” (meta tauta): after the seven letters, a new vision. It marks the order of John’s seeing, not necessarily the order of events. “Door standing open” (thyra ēneōgmenē, a door that has been opened). Heaven is not closed; God opens it to reveal himself.

And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet. The voice of Christ from 1:10.

Said, Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this. Key words. “Come up here” (anaba hōde). John is summoned, in vision, into heaven, to see earth’s history from heaven’s point of view. “Must” (dei): God’s sure plan, as in 1:1.

At once I was in the Spirit. Key words. As in 1:10. A new level of prophetic vision.

And behold, a throne stood in heaven. Key words. “Throne” (thronos). The word appears seventeen times in chapters 4–5 and over forty times in Revelation. This is the book’s central symbol: God rules. Rome’s throne, and Satan’s throne (2:13), are rivals that will fall.

With one seated on the throne. Key words. “Seated” (kathēmenos). God is not anxious or pacing; he sits, at rest, in sovereign control. John does not describe God himself in human form, only his radiance (v. 3), in reverent restraint. He is called, throughout the book, the one seated on the throne.

Where Christians differ: is John’s ascent the rapture of the church? Dispensationalists often read “Come up here” as a picture of the church raptured before the tribulation, noting that the word “church” does not appear on earth from chapter 4 to chapter 22. Verdict: the call is to John alone, to receive a vision; nothing suggests the whole church is taken up. The church appears throughout chapters 4–22 under other names: servants of God (7:3), saints (13:7), those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (12:17), the bride (19:7). The word church is absent because the visions use symbolic language, not because the church has gone. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

What it does not mean. Heaven is not described here in a way that can be mapped or measured. The vision uses symbols to communicate God’s majesty and rule, not the floor plan of heaven.

In a sentence. After that I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven, and the trumpet-like voice I had heard before said, Come up here, and I will show you what has to happen next; immediately the Spirit took hold of me, and I saw a throne in heaven, and someone sitting on it.

On a Tuesday. When the news is frightening and your own life feels chaotic, remember that before John saw any of the troubles, he saw the throne. Begin there.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.

Setting and background. Ezekiel saw a rainbow-like brightness around the throne of God (Ezekiel 1:28). The rainbow first appeared after the flood, as the sign of God’s covenant never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:12–17). Jasper is the first stone and carnelian (sardius) the sixth on the high priest’s breastplate (Exodus 28:17–20); the new Jerusalem has the glory of God, its radiance like jasper, clear as crystal (21:11).

And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian. Key words. “Appearance” (horasei, look, aspect). John describes God only by comparison with dazzling light through gems. “Jasper” (iaspidi): in the ancient world, a name for various precious stones, here probably a clear, brilliant stone like a diamond, since in 21:11 it is clear as crystal. Purity and brilliant glory. “Carnelian” (sardiō): a fiery red stone, named after Sardis. Perhaps God’s blazing holiness, even his wrath. John does not describe a face or form. God is light, and no one can see him and live (1 Timothy 6:16).

And around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald. Key words. “Rainbow” (iris, a halo, rainbow). “Emerald” (smaragdinō), green. Around the blinding, fiery majesty of God is a sign of his covenant mercy. The throne of judgement is surrounded by grace. Everything that follows, including the terrible judgements, happens within the circle of God’s faithfulness to his promises.

What it does not mean. The stones do not give God a physical form; God is spirit (John 4:24). The point is overwhelming, beautiful glory that words can only point to.

In a sentence. The one seated there shone like brilliant jasper and red carnelian, and a rainbow glowing like an emerald encircled the throne.

For worship. Worship the God whose glory is beyond description, and whose throne is surrounded by covenant mercy. His majesty and his faithfulness belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,

Setting and background. King David divided the temple priests into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24:3–19), and the temple musicians into twenty-four groups (1 Chronicles 25). At Sinai, God’s presence came with thunder, lightning and a thick cloud (Exodus 19:16). Daniel saw thrones set in place around the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9).

Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders. Key words. “Elders” (presbyterous). They sit on thrones, so they share in God’s rule. They wear white, so they are pure. They wear golden crowns (stephanous, victors’ wreaths), so they have conquered. These are exactly the promises made to the conquerors in the seven letters (2:10; 3:4–5, 21).

Where Christians differ: who are the twenty-four elders? Some see them as an order of angels, a heavenly council around God (Psalm 89:7). Others see them as representing the whole people of God, Old Testament and New: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. Verdict: the second view is the most likely. The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations (21:12–14), a clear twelve plus twelve. The elders receive what the seven letters promise to conquering believers: white robes, crowns and thrones. They represent the one people of God, redeemed from both covenants, already worshipping in heaven. The church on earth is represented before the throne.

Clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. Key words. White: purity and victory. Gold crowns: the victor’s reward.

From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder. Key words. As at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). God’s awesome majesty and coming judgement. The same sequence of lightning, rumblings and thunder appears at the climax of each series of judgements (8:5; 11:19; 16:18), each time intensified, linking them to this throne.

And before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God. Key words. “Torches” (lampades). As in 1:4 and Zechariah 4:2–6: the Holy Spirit in his fullness. The Spirit is before the throne, ready to be sent out into all the earth (5:6). Fire speaks of holiness, light and purifying power.

What it does not mean. The elders on thrones do not mean that believers share God’s divine authority. They reign under him, as the next verses show when they cast their crowns before his throne (v. 10).

In a sentence. Around the throne were twenty-four other thrones, with twenty-four elders seated on them, dressed in white and wearing golden crowns; from the throne came lightning, rumbling and thunder, and in front of it seven torches blazed, which are the sevenfold Spirit of God.

For worship. The whole people of God, from every age, is already represented before God’s throne. When you worship, you join them.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty-four may combine the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles — the whole people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 1:5–22, four living creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox and eagle), carry God’s throne-chariot, with wheels full of eyes, beneath an expanse like awesome crystal. In Isaiah 6:2, seraphim with six wings stand above God’s throne. In Solomon’s temple, a huge bronze basin called the sea stood in the court (1 Kings 7:23). In the ancient Near East, the sea was a symbol of chaos and evil; in Revelation, the beast rises from the sea (13:1), and in the new creation there is no more sea (21:1).

And before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. Key words. “Sea of glass” (thalassa hyalinē). Ancient glass was usually cloudy, so glass as clear as crystal was rare and precious. Possibly the sea speaks of God’s transcendence, the vast distance between his throne and creation (Exodus 24:10). Or, given the sea’s meaning in Revelation, the forces of chaos and evil lie calm and still before God’s throne: no storm reaches him. In 15:2, the conquerors stand beside the sea of glass mingled with fire, like Israel beside the Red Sea after the exodus.

And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures. Key words. “Living creatures” (zōa, living beings; not beasts, which is a different word, thēria, used for the evil beasts of chapter 13). They are high angelic beings, combining features of Ezekiel’s cherubim and Isaiah’s seraphim. “Four”: the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, 7:1). They represent the whole of creation, worshipping its Creator.

Full of eyes in front and behind. Key words. Eyes speak of ceaseless watchfulness and knowledge. Nothing escapes their sight, nor God’s.

The first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight. Key words. Each represents the highest of a kind of creature: the lion, the noblest of wild animals; the ox, the strongest of domestic animals; man, the wisest of all; the eagle, the swiftest of birds. Ancient rabbis said the same. Together they show all creation, at its best, worshipping God. In Ezekiel each creature had all four faces; here each has one.

What it does not mean. The four creatures were later linked by church tradition with the four Gospels (Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle). This is an ancient and memorable devotional association, but it is not what the text means. The creatures represent creation worshipping God.

In a sentence. In front of the throne was something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal, and around the throne, on every side, were four living beings covered with eyes in front and behind: the first was like a lion, the second like an ox, the third had a human face, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight.

For worship. All creation exists to worship God. When you see a lion, an ox, a soaring eagle or a human face, remember that their highest purpose is to praise him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

Setting and background. In Isaiah 6:2–3, the seraphim, each with six wings, cover their faces and feet and call to one another: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. Isaiah, seeing it, cried out, Woe is me, for I am lost.

And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings. Key words. Six wings, like the seraphim: two to cover their faces, in reverence; two to cover their feet, in humility; two to fly, in service (Isaiah 6:2).

Are full of eyes all around and within. Ceaseless awareness of God, and of all his works.

And day and night they never cease to say. Key words. “Never cease” (anapausin ouk echousin, they have no rest). Not a burden but a joy. Their worship is ceaseless because God’s holiness is inexhaustible. In contrast, those who worship the beast have no rest day or night in torment (14:11).

Holy, holy, holy. Key words. “Holy” (hagios; in Hebrew, qadosh, set apart, utterly other, pure). In Hebrew, repetition expresses the superlative. To say it three times is to say God is the holiest possible, holy beyond all measure. Holiness is the only attribute of God repeated three times in Scripture. Christians have long seen in the threefold Holy a hint of the Trinity, Father, Son and Spirit, though the main point is God’s infinite holiness.

Is the Lord God Almighty. Key words. “Almighty” (pantokratōr, ruler of all), as in 1:8.

Who was and is and is to come! Key words. As in 1:4, 8, with the order changed: past first. God’s eternity, and his coming to judge and renew.

What it does not mean. Holiness is not only moral purity, though it includes that. It means God is utterly distinct from everything he has made, in a class of his own. It does not make him distant and uncaring; the holy God comes near in Christ, so that sinners can stand before him.

In a sentence. Each of the four living beings had six wings and was covered with eyes, all round and even under the wings, and day and night they never stop saying, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was, who is and who is coming.

For worship. Sing Holy, holy, holy with understanding. You join the worship that has never stopped around God’s throne.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

Setting and background. When a king was defeated, he might lay his crown before the conqueror as a sign of submission. Client kings of Rome did so before the emperor. And the emperor Domitian liked to be addressed as our lord and god (dominus et deus noster), as the Roman historian Suetonius reports. The elders give this very title to the only one who deserves it.

And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne. Key words. “Glory” (doxan), “honor” (timēn), “thanks” (eucharistian). Creation praises God for who he is and gives thanks for what he has done.

Who lives forever and ever. In contrast to emperors who live and die.

The twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him. Key words. “Fall down” (pesountai) and “worship” (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves). Worship involves the body: they lie face down before God.

They cast their crowns before the throne. Key words. “Cast” (balousin, throw). Their victors’ crowns, received from God, are laid down before him. Whatever honour God gives his people, they give back to him. Their victory was his.

Saying, Worthy are you, our Lord and God. Key words. “Worthy” (axios, deserving, of equal weight). The word was used in acclaiming the emperor at his arrival. Only God is worthy. “Our Lord and God” (ho kyrios kai ho theos hēmōn): the title Domitian claimed belongs to God alone.

To receive glory and honor and power. Key words. God does not need these from us; he is worthy of them, and to give them is right.

For you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created. Key words. “Created” (ektisas). “By your will” (dia to thelēma sou, because of your will). God is worthy of worship because he is the Creator. Everything exists because he willed it; nothing exists by chance or of necessity. “They existed and were created”: perhaps they existed in his purpose and then came into being; or they exist now because they were created. The Creator has the right to rule, judge and redeem his creation, which is what the rest of the book shows.

What it does not mean. Casting crowns does not mean believers’ rewards are worthless. It means that their highest joy is to give all glory to God. Nor does creation by God’s will mean God needed to create. He created freely, out of love and for his glory.

In a sentence. Whenever the living beings give glory, honour and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him and worship the eternal one, and lay their crowns in front of the throne, saying, You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory, honour and power, because you created everything, and it is by your will that everything came to be and exists.

For worship. Lay down whatever crowns you have, your achievements, gifts and successes, before God. He made you, and everything you have came from his will.
