5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is perhaps the most emotionally dramatic chapter in the entire Bible. It begins with a crisis — a sealed scroll that no one can open — passes through grief — John weeps uncontrollably — and arrives at an explosion of worship that fills all of heaven and earth. The transition from weeping to worship is accomplished by a single announcement: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and he can open the scroll. And when John looks for the conquering Lion, he sees — a Lamb, standing as though slaughtered.

The scroll sealed with seven seals is the interpretive key to the chapter. A scroll sealed with seven seals in the ancient world was typically a legal document of great importance: a will, a deed of purchase, or a covenant document. Most scholars understand it as the scroll of history — God’s redemptive plan for the world, the title deed to creation, the covenant document of the new age. Seven seals indicates absolute sealing: only the one who is truly worthy can break them and open what they guard. The entire drama of Revelation — the seals, the trumpets, the bowls — is the Lamb opening this scroll.

The Lion who is the Lamb — the great reversal at the heart of chapter 5 — is the christological center of Revelation and, in a sense, of the entire New Testament. John is told to look for a conquering Lion. He looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. The conquest was accomplished through the cross. The power that governs history is the power of self-giving love. The one who has the authority to open the seals of history is the one who was willing to be the sacrifice that history required. This is the theological answer to every form of worldly power: the crucified one reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 put a scroll in the right hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Writing on both sides meant the contents were complete; seven seals was the number required for a Roman will, openable only by the rightful heir. A mighty angel heralds one question across creation — not who is strong enough but who is worthy?

Verses 3–4 answer it: nobody, in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Not the elders, not the living creatures, not Abraham or Moses or David. And John breaks down — I began to weep loudly — the only tears anyone sheds in the throne room of this book, and they are not rebuked. An unopened scroll means a world with no resolution: the martyrs never answered, Rome for ever, history running down like a clock nobody winds.

Verse 5 stops the weeping with an announcement rather than an argument: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Gen. 49:9–10; Isa. 11:1–10). The verb is the past tense of the word that ends every one of the seven letters. Whatever the churches are being asked to do, he has already done.

Verses 6–7 are the hinge of the book. John is told a Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — arnion, the diminutive, a lambkin, which becomes John’s main name for Christ twenty-eight times over. The participle is perfect: a past slaughter whose marks are still present. Seven horns are complete power, seven eyes complete knowledge (Zech. 4:10). Then, without ceremony, he went and took the scroll.

Verses 8–10: the creatures and elders fall before the Lamb — worship no creature in this book may receive (19:10; 22:8–9) — holding harps and golden bowls of incense which are the prayers of the saints (cf. Ps. 141:2). The new song grounds his worthiness in his death: you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made them a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.

Verses 11–12 widen the circle to myriads of myriads of angels (cf. Dan. 7:10) with a sevenfold ascription: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Verses 13–14 widen it to every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, addressing one doxology to the throne and the Lamb together; the living creatures say Amen, and the elders fall down and worship in silence.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced — and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”

Meaning first. Revelation 5 continues the throne-room vision and introduces the Lamb. In God’s right hand is a scroll sealed with seven seals, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it (vv. 1–2). No one in all creation is able, and John weeps (vv. 3–4). An elder tells him to stop: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open it (v. 5). John looks and sees, not a lion, but a Lamb standing as though it had been slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, the Spirit sent into all the earth, and the Lamb takes the scroll (vv. 6–7). Then heaven erupts in worship. The living creatures and elders, holding harps and bowls of incense, which are the saints’ prayers, sing a new song: the Lamb is worthy, because he was slain and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe, language, people and nation, and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth (vv. 8–10). Countless angels join in: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (vv. 11–12). Finally every creature everywhere praises the one on the throne and the Lamb together, and the elders fall down and worship (vv. 13–14). The chapter answers the question behind the whole book: who can carry God’s plan for history through to its end? Only the crucified and risen Christ, who conquered by dying.

Setting and background. In the ancient world, important documents such as wills, contracts and title deeds were written on scrolls, rolled up and sealed, sometimes with seven seals by seven witnesses. Only the person with the right could break the seals. Ezekiel was given a scroll written on the front and back, full of lamentation, mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Daniel was told to seal up his vision until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9).

Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll. Key words. “Right hand”: the hand of power and authority. “Scroll” (biblion). The scroll is in God’s hand: his plan for history, his purpose of judgement and redemption.

Written within and on the back. Key words. Scrolls were usually written only on the inside. Writing on both sides means it is full: God’s plan is complete; nothing needs to be added.

Sealed with seven seals. Key words. “Sealed” (katesphragismenon, sealed up tight). Seven: complete sealing. No one can know or carry out God’s plan without the right to open it.

And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals? Key words. “Worthy” (axios, deserving, qualified). The question is not who is strong enough, but who has the right and the character.

What is the scroll? Many suggestions have been made: the Old Testament, the book of life, a title deed to the world, a last will and testament. The best answer is that it contains God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation, his purpose for history from the cross to the new creation. Opening it means not only revealing that plan but carrying it out. As the seals are broken in chapter 6, events happen on earth.

What it does not mean. The sealed scroll does not mean God’s plan is uncertain or that God is unable to act. The question is who among creatures can carry it out on God’s behalf. The answer will be one who is both creature and more than creature.

In a sentence. Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the one seated on the throne, with writing on both sides, sealed with seven seals, and I saw a powerful angel calling out in a loud voice, Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?

On a Tuesday. History is not random. It is written in a scroll held in God’s right hand. Whatever happens this week is within his plan.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Key words. The whole universe, in ancient terms: heaven (angels), earth (living humans), under the earth (the dead). A complete search.

Was able to open the scroll or to look into it. Key words. “Able” (edynato, had the power). No angel, no king, no prophet, no saint. No creature has the worthiness to bring history to God’s good end, to defeat evil and redeem the world.

And I began to weep loudly. Key words. “Weep” (eklaion, kept on weeping, sobbing aloud). John grasps what is at stake. If no one can open the scroll, then evil will never be judged, suffering never ended, God’s promises never fulfilled, and the persecuted church never vindicated. His tears are the right response to a world without a redeemer.

Because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. Key words. “Found worthy” (axios heurethē). The problem is not power but worthiness. All have sinned (Romans 3:23). No sinner can redeem sinners.

What it does not mean. John’s tears are not a lack of faith. They show how great the need is. He has not yet seen the answer. Christians, too, can weep over the brokenness of the world, while knowing the answer.

In a sentence. No one anywhere, in heaven, on earth or under the earth, could open the scroll or even look inside it, and I wept and wept because no one was found who was worthy to open it or look into it.

On a Tuesday. Let John’s tears teach you how hopeless the world would be without Christ. No politician, movement or reform can bring history to its good end.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

Setting and background. Two great messianic titles from the Old Testament. In Genesis 49:9–10, dying Jacob calls Judah a lion’s cub and says the sceptre shall not depart from Judah until he comes to whom it belongs. In Isaiah 11:1, 10, a shoot will come from the stump of Jesse, David’s father, and the root of Jesse will stand as a banner to the nations. Jewish writings of the time used both images for a warrior Messiah who would destroy Israel’s enemies.

And one of the elders said to me, Weep no more. Key words. “Weep no more” (mē klaie, stop weeping). There is an answer.

Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Key words. “Lion” (leōn): royal, powerful, conquering. Jesus was born of the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14). He is the King promised to Judah.

The Root of David. Key words. “Root” (rhiza). Not only David’s descendant but David’s root, his source (22:16). As Jesus asked, if David calls the Messiah Lord, how is he his son (Matthew 22:41–45)? He is both David’s offspring and David’s Lord.

Has conquered. Key words. “Conquered” (enikēsen, past tense: a completed victory). The victory has already been won. The same verb the seven letters use for the believer’s victory (2:7). Christ conquered first, and his people conquer through him (3:21).

So that he can open the scroll and its seven seals. His victory gives him the right to carry out God’s plan.

What it does not mean. The Lion’s conquest is not the military victory many expected the Messiah to win. John is about to see how he won it (v. 6). Revelation never pictures the Messiah’s victory as violence against his enemies on the way to his throne; he conquered by being slain.

In a sentence. Then one of the elders said to me, Stop weeping; look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has won the victory, so he is able to open the scroll and break its seven seals.

For worship. Thank Christ that the victory is already won. Weep over the world, but not without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.

Setting and background. The Passover lamb was killed and its blood put on the doorposts, so that the LORD passed over Israel when he judged Egypt (Exodus 12). Isaiah 53:7 describes the Servant of the LORD led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing the sins of many. John the Baptist pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). In Jewish apocalyptic writing, a horned ram sometimes represented a conquering leader (Daniel 8:3; 1 Enoch 90). Zechariah 4:10 speaks of seven eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth.

And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb. Key words. John heard “Lion” (v. 5); he turned and saw a Lamb. This is the heart of Revelation, and of the gospel. The Lion conquered by becoming the Lamb. Power was redefined by sacrifice. “Lamb” (arnion, a little lamb). Christ is called the Lamb twenty-eight times in Revelation. “Between the throne and …”: at the very centre of heaven, sharing God’s throne (7:17; 22:1).

Standing, as though it had been slain. Key words. “Standing” (hestēkos): alive, risen. “As though it had been slain” (hōs esphagmenon, slaughtered, with its throat cut, perfect tense: having been slain and still bearing the marks). The risen Christ still bears the wounds of the cross (John 20:27). His death is not a past event he has moved beyond; it is the permanent ground of his authority and of our salvation.

With seven horns. Key words. “Horns” (kerata): in Scripture, a symbol of strength and power (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 18:2). Seven: complete power. The Lamb is not weak. He is all-powerful (Matthew 28:18).

And with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. Key words. Seven eyes: complete knowledge, seeing everything. The seven spirits: the Holy Spirit in his fullness (1:4). The Spirit is the Spirit of the Lamb, sent out by him into all the earth (John 15:26; 16:7; Acts 2:33). The Lamb is all-powerful, all-knowing, and present everywhere by his Spirit: fully God.

And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne. Key words. “Took” (eilēphen, perfect tense, a decisive act with lasting result). Echoing Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory and a kingdom. The Lamb receives authority to carry out God’s whole plan for history.

What it does not mean. The Lamb is not a sign of weakness. He has seven horns. Nor does his gentleness cancel his justice; the same book speaks of the wrath of the Lamb (6:16). Revelation’s Christ is the slain Lamb who conquers, and the conquering Lamb who was slain.

In a sentence. Then I saw a Lamb, standing at the centre, between the throne with its four living beings and the circle of elders; it looked as though it had been slaughtered, and it had seven horns and seven eyes, which are the sevenfold Spirit of God sent out into the whole world; and the Lamb came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

On a Tuesday. When you think of power, think of the Lamb. Christ’s way of victory, through sacrifice, self-giving and faithful suffering, is the way he calls you to walk too.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”

Setting and background. Harps (lyres) were used in temple worship (1 Chronicles 25:1; Psalm 33:2). Incense was burned on the golden altar before the Holy of Holies, and its smoke was a picture of prayer rising to God (Psalm 141:2). The Psalms often call for a new song, celebrating a new act of salvation (Psalm 96:1; 98:1; Isaiah 42:10).

And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Key words. They give the Lamb the same worship they gave the one on the throne (4:10). Since worship belongs to God alone (19:10; 22:8–9), this is a clear statement that Jesus is God.

Each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Key words. “Saints” (hagiōn, holy ones): all believers. The prayers of God’s people on earth are precious to God, kept in golden bowls in his presence. In 8:3–5, these prayers are answered by judgement on the earth. The persecuted church’s cries for justice (6:10) are heard.

And they sang a new song. Key words. “New” (kainēn, new in kind, not just recent). A new act of redemption, greater than the exodus, calls for a new song.

Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals. Key words. The question of v. 2 is answered: the Lamb is worthy.

For you were slain. Key words. “Slain” (esphagēs). The basis of his worthiness is his sacrificial death.

And by your blood you ransomed people for God. Key words. “Ransomed” (ēgorasas, bought, purchased, as in the slave market). His blood was the price. The people bought belong to God. This is substitutionary atonement: Christ paid the price that set us free (1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:18–19).

From every tribe and language and people and nation. Key words. Four terms, the number of the whole earth. The redeemed come from every ethnic and linguistic group. The church is gloriously multinational. This fulfils God’s promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3).

And you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God. As in 1:6 and Exodus 19:6.

And they shall reign on the earth. Key words. “Reign” (basileusousin). The redeemed share in Christ’s rule, and their rule is on the earth: the renewed earth of the new creation (21:1; 22:5). Salvation is not escape from the material world but the renewal of it.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every person, or for his people? Many Christians hold that Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all, so that it becomes actual when people believe. Verdict: the song says that Christ’s blood actually ransomed people for God, not that it made a ransom possible. And it ransomed people from every tribe, language, people and nation, not every person in every nation. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention of actually saving those the Father gave him (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25), and his death secures their salvation. Its value is infinite, sufficient for all, and the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone. But its design is to save a people chosen from every nation, and it does not fail.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “redeemed us” and “made us kings and priests, and we shall reign”, making the elders sing about themselves. The best manuscripts read “ransomed people” (or simply “ransomed for God from every tribe”) and “made them … they shall reign”. Some manuscripts also read “they reign” (present tense) rather than “they shall reign”. Both are true: believers reign now with Christ in a hidden way (1:6), and will reign fully in the new creation.

What it does not mean. Reigning on the earth does not mean a future thousand-year political reign before the final state. The promise is fulfilled in the new heaven and new earth, where God’s servants will reign for ever and ever (22:5).

In a sentence. When he had taken the scroll, the four living beings and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each with a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of God’s people, and they sang a new song: You are worthy to take the scroll and break its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you bought for God people from every tribe, language, people and nation, and made them a kingdom of priests to serve our God, and they will reign on the earth.

For worship. Sing to Christ for what he has done. Your prayers are kept in golden bowls before God. And look around your church: people from every nation are part of what he bought.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”

Setting and background. Daniel 7:10 describes the Ancient of Days with a thousand thousands serving him and ten thousand times ten thousand standing before him. At Jesus’ birth, a multitude of the heavenly host praised God (Luke 2:13–14).

Then I looked, and I heard around the throne … the voice of many angels. Key words. The circle of worship widens: first the living creatures and elders, now countless angels.

Numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands. Key words. “Myriads” (myriades, ten thousands). Ten thousand times ten thousand is a hundred million, but the point is a number beyond counting.

Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain. Key words. The angels speak of the Lamb rather than to him, perhaps because he did not die for them, but they join in praising what he did.

To receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing! Key words. Seven qualities, complete praise. “Power” (dynamin), “wealth” (plouton), “wisdom” (sophian), “might” (ischyn), “honor” (timēn), “glory” (doxan), “blessing” (eulogian). In Greek a single article governs all seven, joining them as one whole. Everything that kings and emperors claim belongs truly to the Lamb who was slain. The one who became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9) is worthy of all wealth.

What it does not mean. The Lamb does not receive these because he lacks them. As God, he has them eternally. As the slain Lamb, he is now acknowledged and honoured with them as the reward of his obedience (Philippians 2:8–11).

In a sentence. Then, as I looked, I heard the voices of angels beyond counting, thousands upon thousands and millions upon millions, surrounding the throne, the living beings and the elders, and they called out with a loud voice: The Lamb who was slaughtered is worthy to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and praise!

For worship. When you worship, you are joining a choir of millions. Add your voice.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

Setting and background. Philippians 2:10–11 says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them. Key words. “Every creature” (pan ktisma, all created things). The circle widens to the whole universe. Everything God made praises him. John sees ahead to the end, when all creation acknowledges God and the Lamb.

Saying, To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever! Key words. The climax: the one on the throne and the Lamb are praised together, in exactly the same words. Chapter 4 praised God as Creator; chapter 5 praises the Lamb as Redeemer; now both are worshipped as one. This is the clearest picture in Revelation of the Son’s full equality with the Father.

And the four living creatures said, Amen! and the elders fell down and worshiped. Key words. “Amen”: so be it, it is true. The worship ends where it began, with the living creatures and elders, falling down before God.

Where Christians differ: will every creature be saved? Universalists read this verse, with Philippians 2:10–11, as meaning that all creatures, including those now in rebellion, will finally be reconciled and saved. Verdict: universal acknowledgement is not universal salvation. Revelation clearly teaches that some will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (14:9–11; 20:10, 15; 21:8). Every creature will confess that God and the Lamb are worthy; for the redeemed it is joyful worship, and for the lost it is the forced admission of a truth they rejected. God’s glory will be acknowledged everywhere, in mercy and in justice.

What it does not mean. Worshipping the Lamb with the Father does not mean there are two Gods. Revelation is strictly monotheistic. The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3) and receive one worship.

In a sentence. Then I heard every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, everything in the whole creation, saying: To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be praise, honour, glory and power for ever and ever! And the four living beings said, Amen, and the elders fell down and worshipped.

For worship. Worship the Father and the Son together, with the same praise. And say Amen with all of heaven.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals, and with each seal a new dimension of history is revealed. The first four seals release the famous Four Horsemen — one of the most powerful images in Western literature. The fifth seal lifts the veil on the souls of the martyrs beneath the heavenly altar and their agonizing cry: “How long, O Lord?” The sixth seal unleashes cosmic convulsion on a terrified earth. The seventh seal — which will bring complete silence in heaven — is withheld until chapter 8.

Interpretive flag — Sequential or Recapitulatory? This is the second major structural decision point of Revelation. The sequential reading (predominant in dispensational premillennialism) understands the seals, trumpets, and bowls as three successive series of events: the seals run their course, then the trumpets begin, then the bowls pour out — covering the seven-year tribulation in ascending severity. The recapitulatory reading (predominant in amillennial/idealist interpretation) understands the three series as parallel sweeps, each covering the same period (the church age and/or the final tribulation) from different vantage points and with increasing intensity. Several features of the text favor recapitulation: (1) the sixth seal already appears to describe the final judgment (vv. 12–17), yet the narrative continues; (2) the sixth trumpet and sixth bowl also appear to describe the same climactic events; (3) the interludes (chapters 7, 10–11) break the sequential pattern; (4) the phrase “the great day of their wrath has come” (v. 17) sounds like a finale, yet much remains. The seals are read here as the first of three parallel sweeps, with the sequential reading noted respectfully.

The Four Horsemen are among the most theologically misread images in Revelation. They are not four distinct events in a future tribulation timeline. They are the recurring instruments of divine governance that have marked history since the fall: war, internecine conflict, famine, and death. They describe the ongoing reality of a fallen world under the Lord’s providential judgment — not unprecedented novelties but the intensified concentration of what the church has always known. The question the martyrs ask — “How long?” — is the question the church has been asking since Abel’s blood first cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and a white horse rides out whose rider has a bow and a crown that was given to him. Whether that rider is Christ, the gospel’s advance, or conquest itself is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse. Verses 3–4: a bright red horse, whose rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people should slay one another — mutual killing, the neighbour with the knife — and is given a great sword.

Verses 5–6: a black horse, its rider holding scales, and a voice from the midst of the living creatures quoting the price list. A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was one man’s daily ration. A labourer in full work can feed himself and nobody else. Do not harm the oil and wine sets a limit on the famine and also describes its injustice: bread is rationed while the luxury trade goes on undisturbed.

Verses 7–8: a pale horse — chlōros, the green of a corpse — and the only rider who is named. Death rides, and Hades follows to collect. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth, with the four instruments of Ezekiel 14:21. The fraction matters: the trumpets will touch a third, and only at the end does anything become total.

Verses 9–11 break the pattern: no horse, no rider. Under the altar, where the blood of every sacrifice was poured out (Lev. 4:7), are the souls of those slain — esphagmenōn, the word used of the Lamb at 5:6. They cry how long? like a third of the psalter. Verse 11 answers with a white robe each, permission to rest, and a reason for the delay that is very hard: until the number of their brothers who are to die in the same way is complete.

Verses 12–14: the sixth seal removes every fixed point in the universe — earthquake, sun black as sackcloth (goat hair, so the comparison is exact), moon like blood (Joel 2:31), stars falling like the winter figs a gale brings down, the sky rolled up (Isa. 34:4), every mountain and island moved. Verses 15–17: seven classes of people, from kings down to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them — choosing burial over being looked at — and the chapter ends on an unanswered question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.

Meaning first. Revelation 6 shows the Lamb opening the first six seals of the scroll, and what happens on earth as he does. Four horsemen ride out at the command of the four living creatures: a white horse whose rider conquers (vv. 1–2), a red horse that takes peace from the earth (vv. 3–4), a black horse bringing famine and high prices (vv. 5–6), and a pale horse named Death, followed by Hades, killing a quarter of the earth by sword, famine, plague and wild beasts (vv. 7–8). At the fifth seal, the souls of martyrs under the altar cry out, How long until you judge? They are given white robes and told to wait until the number of their fellow martyrs is complete (vv. 9–11). At the sixth seal, the universe itself comes apart: earthquake, a black sun, a blood moon, falling stars, the sky rolled up, mountains and islands moved (vv. 12–14). Everyone, from kings to slaves, hides and begs the mountains to fall on them, to hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand (vv. 15–17)? The chapter shows that the wars, famines and deaths of history are not out of control: they are released by the Lamb, limited by God, and leading to the final day of judgement.

Setting and background. Zechariah saw horses of different colours, red, black, white and dappled, sent out to patrol the earth (Zechariah 1:8–11; 6:1–8). Jesus, in his teaching about the end, spoke of wars, rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines and earthquakes as the beginning of birth pains, followed by persecution, and then the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, and the stars falling from heaven (Matthew 24:6–29; Luke 21:9–26). The seals follow the same order. In the first century, Rome feared the Parthians, an empire to the east whose mounted archers on white horses had defeated Roman armies.

Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals. Key words. The Lamb opens the seals. Everything that follows is under his authority. The disasters are not outside his control; they are part of his plan.

And I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, Come! Key words. “Come” (erchou). The command is to the horseman, summoning him out. The living creatures, representing creation, call for the judgements that will lead to creation’s renewal.

And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him. Key words. “Bow” (toxon), the weapon of the Parthian cavalry. “Crown” (stephanos, victor’s wreath). “Was given” (edothē): a phrase that recurs through Revelation for God’s permission. Even evil powers act only as God allows.

And he came out conquering, and to conquer. Key words. “Conquering” (nikōn). Military conquest, invasion, empire-building.

Where Christians differ: who is the rider on the white horse? Some identify him with Christ, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11, and they read the first seal as the gospel going out and conquering. Others see him as the antichrist or false messiahs, imitating Christ. Others take him as military conquest in general. Verdict: the rider is conquering war, aggression and empire, like the other three horsemen, who all bring disaster. The four belong together as a set of judgements, following Jesus’ teaching (wars, then famines and death). Christ in chapter 19 has many crowns and a sword from his mouth, not a bow; and Christ is the one opening the seals, not one released by them. The white colour may suggest a deceptive imitation of Christ, as conquerors always promise peace and glory, or the white horses of victorious generals.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Come and see”, as if the living creature were speaking to John. The best manuscripts read simply “Come!”, addressed to the horseman.

What it does not mean. The four horsemen are not one-time future events only. They describe what happens throughout the age between Christ’s comings: conquest, war, famine and death. They were real in John’s day and are real in ours. Nor does God’s permission make him the author of human evil. He limits it, uses it and will judge it.

In a sentence. Then I watched as the Lamb broke the first of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living beings call out in a voice like thunder, Come! and I saw a white horse, whose rider carried a bow; he was given a crown, and he rode out as a conqueror, bent on conquest.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of invasions and wars, remember that they are not outside Christ’s control. Pray for peace, and trust the Lamb who holds the scroll.
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!” And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.

Setting and background. In John’s day, the empire boasted of the Pax Romana, the peace of Rome, kept by its legions. Yet the first century saw civil war in AD 68–69 (the year of four emperors), the Jewish war that destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, and endless bloodshed on the frontiers.

And out came another horse, bright red. Key words. “Bright red” (pyrros, fiery red). The colour of blood and fire.

Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth. Key words. “Permitted” (edothē, it was given). Again, God’s sovereign permission. “Take peace”: the false peace of empire is fragile. Without the true peace that Christ gives (John 14:27), human peace does not last.

So that people should slay one another. Key words. “Slay” (sphaxousin, slaughter): the same verb used for the Lamb who was slain (5:6). Civil war, violence, people killing each other. Human sin, released and allowed to run, destroys itself.

And he was given a great sword. Key words. “Sword” (machaira, a short sword for close combat, used for killing).

What it does not mean. God does not cause people to hate and kill. The violence comes from human hearts (James 4:1–2). The judgement is that God removes the restraint and lets sin bear its own fruit, as Paul describes in Romans 1:24–28, where God gives people up to what they desire.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the second seal, I heard the second living being say, Come! and another horse came out, fiery red; its rider was allowed to take peace away from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another, and he was handed a huge sword.

On a Tuesday. Every outbreak of violence shows that human beings cannot make lasting peace on their own. Be a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9), and point people to the Prince of Peace.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”

Setting and background. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). A quart (a choinix, about a litre) of wheat was roughly one person’s daily ration. Normally a denarius would buy eight to sixteen times as much. So a whole day’s wage would buy only enough wheat for one person, or enough barley, a coarser grain, for a small family. Nothing would be left for anything else. In AD 92, there was a grain shortage in Asia, and the emperor Domitian ordered half the vineyards in the provinces to be cut down to grow more grain; the order provoked such protest that he withdrew it.

And I looked, and behold, a black horse! Key words. “Black” (melas): the colour of mourning, hunger and death (Lamentations 4:8; 5:10).

And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. Key words. “Scales” (zygon, a balance). Food being weighed out carefully, rationed. In Ezekiel 4:16, God says the people will eat bread by weight, with anxiety. Scarcity.

And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures. Key words. A voice from the very centre of heaven, near the throne. God himself sets the limits of the famine.

A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius. Key words. Famine prices: roughly ten times the normal cost. The poor would suffer most, spending everything just to eat.

And do not harm the oil and wine! Key words. “Oil” (elaion, olive oil) and “wine” (oinon). Olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive drought better than grain. The judgement is limited: severe, but not total. It is a warning, not yet the end. Some also see irony: the luxuries of the rich are untouched while the poor cannot afford bread.

What it does not mean. The scales are not a sign of justice here, but of scarcity. Nor is this a forecast of one particular famine. It describes the economic hardship that recurs throughout history, until Christ returns.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the third seal, I heard the third living being say, Come! and I saw a black horse whose rider held a pair of scales; and I heard what sounded like a voice from among the four living beings, saying, A day’s pay for a single ration of wheat, a day’s pay for three rations of barley, but do not damage the olive oil and the wine.

On a Tuesday. Hunger is still real for millions. Give generously to relieve it, and remember that God has set limits even on famine.
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 14:21, God speaks of his four severe judgements on Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. The fourth horseman brings all four.

And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! Key words. “Pale” (chlōros, pale green, greenish-grey). The colour of a corpse, of sickness and decay. The English word chlorine comes from it.

And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. Key words. “Death” (ho Thanatos), personified. “Hades” (ho Hadēs), the realm of the dead, following behind to swallow up those Death strikes down. But Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). They ride only at his word, and they will be thrown into the lake of fire (20:14).

And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth. Key words. “A fourth”: a limited judgement. The trumpets will affect a third (8:7–12), and the bowls will be complete (16:1). The judgements intensify as history moves toward the end, but God sets their limits.

To kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth. Key words. “Pestilence” (thanatō, literally death, a common Greek Old Testament word for plague). The fourth horseman sums up the first three and adds disease and wild animals. These are the great killers of human history.

What it does not mean. Every death in war, famine or plague is not a specific punishment for that person’s sin. The four horsemen show that the world as a whole lives under God’s judgement because of sin (Romans 8:20–22), and that these sufferings are warnings to repent (Luke 13:1–5). Believers suffer them too, but for believers, death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55).

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living being say, Come! and I saw a pale, sickly horse; its rider was named Death, and the grave came close behind him; they were given power over a quarter of the earth, to kill by war, famine, disease and wild animals.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of pandemics and disasters, let them remind you how short life is, and turn to the one who holds the keys of Death.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”

Setting and background. In the temple, the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Paul spoke of his coming death as being poured out like a drink offering (2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17). The cry “How long?” is the cry of suffering believers throughout the Psalms (Psalm 13:1–2; 79:5–10) and the prophets (Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12). The blood of Abel cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar. Key words. “Altar” (thysiastēriou, the place of sacrifice). The martyrs’ deaths are seen as sacrifices offered to God. Their lives were poured out like the blood of the offerings at the foot of the altar. What looked like defeat was worship.

The souls of those who had been slain. Key words. “Souls” (psychas, persons, lives). They have died, but they are alive and conscious in God’s presence, waiting for the resurrection. “Slain” (esphagmenōn): the same word used for the Lamb (5:6). They share his death.

For the word of God and for the witness they had borne. Key words. As John was on Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (1:9). They died because they would not stop believing and confessing Christ.

They cried out with a loud voice, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true. Key words. “Sovereign Lord” (despotēs, master, absolute ruler). “Holy and true”: because God is holy and true, he must judge evil. Their prayer appeals to his character.

How long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Key words. “How long” (heōs pote, until when). “Judge” (krineis) and “avenge” (ekdikeis, vindicate, see justice done). “Those who dwell on the earth”: in Revelation, unbelievers in rebellion against God (3:10). They do not ask for personal revenge, but for God to act as judge and put things right publicly. It is a prayer for justice, which God promises to answer (Luke 18:7–8; Romans 12:19).

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some groups teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, or that the soul does not exist apart from the body. Verdict: the martyrs are conscious, speaking, praying and comforted, while their bodies are in the grave. Scripture teaches an intermediate state in which believers are with Christ at once when they die (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not yet in their final state, which comes at the resurrection, but they are with the Lord, at rest (v. 11). Nor is there any purgatory; they are under the altar, in God’s presence, not being purified.

What it does not mean. Praying for God’s justice is not hatred or a lack of love. Jesus prayed for his enemies’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34), and so did Stephen (Acts 7:60). Both prayers belong together: we pray for our enemies to repent, and we pray for God to judge evil and vindicate his people if they do not. We leave vengeance to God.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed because of God’s word and the testimony they had held to, and they cried out loudly: Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how much longer before you judge the inhabitants of the earth and avenge our blood?

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians today, and pray with them for God’s justice. The prayers of the suffering church are heard (8:3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.

Then they were each given a white robe. Key words. “White robe” (stolē leukē): purity, victory, vindication. As promised to the conquerors (3:4–5). Before the final judgement, God gives them his verdict: they are righteous, and their cause is just. In this world they were condemned as criminals; in heaven they are honoured.

And told to rest a little longer. Key words. “Rest” (anapausontai). Not a rebuke of their prayer, but comfort while they wait. Their rest contrasts with the restless torment of those who worship the beast (14:11). “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord … that they may rest from their labors” (14:13).

Until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete. Key words. “Number … complete” (plērōthōsin, be filled up, fulfilled). God has a set number of martyrs, as he has a set number of the elect (Romans 11:25). The end will come when his purposes are complete, not before. History moves on God’s timetable. This also explains the delay: God is patient, giving time for more to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and his plan includes the faithful witness of the church through suffering.

Who were to be killed as they themselves had been. Key words. “Were to be” (mellontes, about to). More martyrdoms are coming. The church was not promised escape from suffering.

What it does not mean. The fixed number does not mean God enjoys the death of his people. Precious in his sight is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). It means that even martyrdom is not random; it is within his loving and wise plan, and each death matters to him.

In a sentence. Each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers and sisters who were going to be killed just as they had been, was complete.

For worship. Thank God that those who have died for Christ are at rest and honoured. Pray for courage for those still facing that cost.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.

Setting and background. The Old Testament prophets described the Day of the LORD in terms of cosmic collapse: the sun and moon darkened, the stars falling, the heavens rolled up like a scroll, the mountains shaking (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31; Haggai 2:6). Jesus used the same language for his coming (Matthew 24:29–30). Sometimes this language described the fall of earthly empires (Isaiah 13 is about Babylon), but here its universal scope points to the end of the age.

There was a great earthquake. Key words. “Earthquake” (seismos). In Scripture, earthquakes accompany God’s coming in power (Exodus 19:18; Hebrews 12:26–27). Asia was earthquake country, and every reader would have understood the terror.

And the sun became black as sackcloth. Key words. “Sackcloth” (sakkos): coarse cloth made from black goat hair, worn in mourning.

The full moon became like blood. As in Joel 2:31, quoted by Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

And the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. Key words. “Winter fruit” (olynthous, unripe late figs that drop off easily). As in Isaiah 34:4. The heavens, which seem the most stable things in the world, collapse.

The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up. Key words. “Vanished” (apechōristhē, was split apart, removed). Isaiah 34:4 speaks of the skies rolled up like a scroll. The created order as we know it passes away (2 Peter 3:10; 20:11).

And every mountain and island was removed from its place. Key words. The most solid things on earth are moved. Nothing is left to hide behind.

Where Christians differ: is this the end, or a stage on the way? Many futurist readers place the sixth seal early in a future tribulation, with many more judgements to follow in a strict sequence. Verdict: the sixth seal describes the final day of judgement itself, when Christ returns. The language is the language Jesus used for his coming, and the people cry that the great day of wrath has come (v. 17). This shows that Revelation is not one long timeline but a series of parallel visions, each ending at or near the end. The seals take us to the end; the trumpets and bowls go over the same ground again from other angles, with growing intensity. This is called recapitulation, and it fits the amillennial reading of the book.

What it does not mean. The cosmic language is not a scientific description of astronomical events. It is the prophets’ way of describing the shaking and passing away of the whole created order at God’s coming. It may be literal in part, and it is certainly real; but its main point is that nothing in creation can stand before its Creator.

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the sixth seal, I looked and saw a great earthquake: the sun went black like mourning cloth, the full moon turned red as blood, and the stars fell to earth like unripe figs shaken from a tree in a storm; the sky split open and rolled up like a scroll, and every mountain and island was moved out of its place.

On a Tuesday. Everything that seems permanent will be shaken. Build your life on the one kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:27–28).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

Setting and background. Isaiah 2:19–21 describes people fleeing into caves and holes in the ground from the terror of the LORD when he rises to terrify the earth. Hosea 10:8 says they will say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us. Jesus quoted Hosea on his way to the cross (Luke 23:30). Malachi 3:2 asks, who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? Nahum 1:6 asks, who can stand before his indignation?

Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful. Key words. Seven classes of people, complete humanity. “Kings” (basileis): the same kings over whom Christ is ruler (1:5). “Great ones” (megistanes, nobles, top officials). “Generals” (chiliarchoi, commanders of a thousand). “Rich” (plousioi). “Powerful” (ischyroi). Those who seemed untouchable, who persecuted the church, are the first to flee.

And everyone, slave and free. Key words. No one is exempt. Status means nothing on that day.

Hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. Key words. The mountains have just been moved (v. 14); there is nowhere to hide.

Calling to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us and hide us. Key words. They would rather be crushed than face God. Not repentance, but terror. They do not ask for mercy; they ask to be hidden.

From the face of him who is seated on the throne. Key words. “Face” (prosōpou). The face of God, which the redeemed long to see (22:4), is what the lost cannot bear to see.

And from the wrath of the Lamb. Key words. “Wrath” (orgēs, settled, righteous anger). An astonishing phrase. The Lamb is gentle, but he is not soft. Those who reject the Lamb’s sacrifice will face the Lamb’s anger. The one who died for sinners will judge those who refuse him (John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:31).

For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? Key words. “The great day” (hē hēmera hē megalē): the Day of the LORD, the final judgement (Joel 2:11, 31; Zephaniah 1:14). “Their wrath”: the wrath of God and the Lamb, one wrath. “Who can stand” (tis dynatai stathēnai): who is able to stand firm, survive and be acquitted? The answer comes in chapter 7: those sealed by God and washed in the Lamb’s blood stand before the throne (7:9).

What it does not mean. God’s wrath is not uncontrolled rage or a bad temper. It is his holy, just and settled opposition to evil, which he has delayed in patience. And it is not the whole picture of God. The same Lamb whose wrath is feared offers to bear wrath in our place (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

In a sentence. Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the military commanders, the rich and the powerful, and everyone else, slave or free, hid in caves and among the mountain rocks, calling out to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the anger of the Lamb, for the great day of their anger has come, and who can survive it?

On a Tuesday. No one can hide from God. The only safe place on that day is in Christ, under the blood of the Lamb. Run to him now, and urge others to do the same.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!”<sup>2</sup>And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.<sup>3</sup>When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”<sup>4</sup>And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.<sup>5</sup>When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.<sup>6</sup>And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”<sup>7</sup>When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”<sup>8</sup>And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.<sup>9</sup>When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.<sup>10</sup>They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”<sup>11</sup>Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.<sup>12</sup>When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood,<sup>13</sup>and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.<sup>14</sup>The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.<sup>15</sup>Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains,<sup>16</sup>calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,<sup>17</sup>for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the first great interlude of Revelation — a pause between the sixth and seventh seals that answers the question that ended chapter 6: “Who can stand?” The answer comes in two scenes that together present the whole people of God from two perspectives. The 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 1–8): the church as it endures on earth, the complete and protected people of God in the midst of judgment. The great multitude from every nation (vv. 9–17): the church as it will appear before the throne, the redeemed in their innumerable fullness, already standing where the kings of the earth could not.

The 144,000 has generated more interpretive controversy than almost any other passage in Revelation. A strictly literal reading — exactly 144,000 ethnic Jewish males from the twelve tribes of Israel — faces several difficulties: (1) Dan is missing from the list and Manasseh (Joseph’s son) substituted, while Levi (not a territorial tribe) is included, making this no straightforward census; (2) the twelve tribes as distinct ethnic communities had not existed since the Assyrian deportation of the northern tribes in 722 BC; (3) the number 12 × 12 × 1,000 is conspicuously mathematical — in a book where seven means completeness, twelve means the people of God, and 1,000 means an immense completeness, 144,000 is the fullness of the fullness of God’s people. The majority Reformed/amillennial reading understands the 144,000 as the complete church of both testaments, the spiritual Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 3:29; 6:16; Philippians 3:3), sealed for protection through the tribulation. The dispensational reading understands them as 144,000 literal Jewish evangelists who will be saved and minister during the tribulation.

The great multitude of verses 9–17 is most likely the same group seen from a different vantage point — not a second group that supplements the 144,000 but the 144,000 as they appear before the throne, their number now seen to be “a great multitude that no one could number.” The innumerable quality is not a contradiction of the 144,000 but its complement: both “complete” and “uncountable” describe the fullness of the redeemed. The scene before the throne anticipates the final state, giving the church a vision of its own destiny as it endures the trials of the present.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and a question hanging: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1, and everything here sits in that gap, answering the question before the last seal breaks.

Verse 1: four angels at the four corners of the earth hold back the four winds, so that no wind blows on earth or sea or against any tree. The stillness before a storm — destruction under restraint. Verse 2: a fifth angel ascends from the rising of the sun with the seal of the living God, and outranks the four. Verse 3 gives his order: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. Judgment is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9).

The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9:4, where a man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over what is being done in Jerusalem, and the executioners are told to touch nobody who carries the mark. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, and guaranteed authenticity; all three apply.

Verse 4 gives the number: 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Verses 5–8 list the twelve, twelve thousand each — Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin. The list matches no tribal register in the Old Testament: Judah heads it rather than Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; Levi, which had no territorial allotment, is counted; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his own father. Who the 144,000 are is set out at the verse, with the evidence on both sides.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sealed Before the Storm

The winds of judgement are held back until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9. Whether the 144,000 are ethnic Israel or the whole people of God, God knows the number exactly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The seal did not exempt them from the tribulation; it marked them as God’s within it.

Now: The text caps nobody’s hope: the next scene is a multitude no one could number.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”

Meaning first. Revelation 7 is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals, and it answers the question that ended chapter 6: who can stand? Four angels hold back the winds of judgement until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3). John hears the number of the sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 4–8). Then he looks and sees a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes, waving palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb (vv. 9–10). All the angels fall down and worship (vv. 11–12). An elder explains: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation, who have washed their robes white in the Lamb’s blood (vv. 13–14). So they are before God’s throne, serving him day and night; he shelters them with his presence; they will never again hunger, thirst or be scorched; the Lamb will shepherd them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes (vv. 15–17). The chapter shows the church twice: on earth, sealed and protected as God’s true Israel before the storm; and in heaven, a countless multitude safe for ever after it.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 9:4–6, before Jerusalem was judged, God told a man with a writing case to put a mark on the foreheads of those who grieved over the city’s sins, so that the executioners would spare them. At the first Passover, the blood on the doorposts marked the houses God would pass over (Exodus 12:13). In the ancient world, a seal on a document or object marked ownership and protection; slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded with their master’s or general’s mark.

After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth. Key words. “Four corners” and “four winds”: the whole earth, from every direction (Jeremiah 49:36; Zechariah 6:5). The winds are destructive forces of judgement, perhaps the four horsemen of chapter 6 under another image (Zechariah 6:1–5 links horses and winds). “Holding back” (kratountas, gripping firmly). Judgement is restrained by God’s angels until his purpose is done.

That no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. All creation waits.

Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun. Key words. “Rising of the sun” (anatolēs hēliou, the east). In Scripture, the east is often the direction from which God’s glory and salvation come (Ezekiel 43:2). Hope comes before judgement.

With the seal of the living God. Key words. “Seal” (sphragida, signet ring, stamp). The seal of the living God, in contrast to idols that are dead.

Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. Key words. “Sealed” (sphragisōmen). The seal marks God’s ownership and guarantees his protection. In 14:1, the 144,000 have the name of the Lamb and his Father written on their foreheads. The seal is God’s name, which means they belong to him. In the New Testament, believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13; 4:30). It contrasts with the mark of the beast on the foreheads or hands of his followers (13:16–17). Everyone bears one mark or the other.

What it does not mean. Sealing does not protect believers from all suffering or from death; many will be martyred (6:11; 13:7). It protects them from the wrath of God that falls on unbelievers (9:4), and above all from losing their faith and their place in God’s kingdom. Their bodies may suffer; their souls are safe.

In a sentence. After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the earth’s four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree; then I saw another angel coming up from the east with the seal of the living God, and he shouted to the four angels who had been given power to harm land and sea: Do not harm the land or the sea or the trees until we have put a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are sealed by his Spirit. Whatever storms come, God has marked you as his own, and he does not lose what he owns.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.

Setting and background. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob. The Old Testament lists them about twenty times, in many different orders. By John’s day, ten of the tribes had been scattered since the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC, and Jews looked forward to God gathering all twelve tribes in the last days (Isaiah 11:12; Ezekiel 37:15–28). Before a war, Israel took a census of the tribes to count its fighting men (Numbers 1). Jesus chose twelve apostles, who would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), signalling that he was reconstituting Israel around himself.

And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000. Key words. John hears a number. 144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000: twelve (the tribes of Israel) times twelve (the apostles), times a thousand (a vast, complete number). It is a symbolic number for the complete people of God, the whole of God’s true Israel.

Sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Key words. Organised like an army, counted by tribes as in the census of Numbers 1. In 14:1–4, the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion, follow him wherever he goes, and are called first fruits for God and the Lamb, redeemed from mankind. They are God’s army, which conquers not by fighting but by following the Lamb.

12,000 from the tribe of Judah. Key words. The list is unusual. Judah comes first, not Reuben the firstborn, because the Messiah, the Lion of Judah (5:5), comes from Judah. Dan is missing, perhaps because the tribe of Dan was the first to fall into idolatry (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29–30). Ephraim is also missing, replaced by Joseph. Levi, which normally received no land and was not counted among the tribes, is included, perhaps because all God’s people are now priests (1:6). The list has been reworked to show the new Israel, gathered around the Messiah.

Where Christians differ: who are the 144,000? Dispensationalists usually see them as literal ethnic Jews, converted during a future tribulation after the church has been raptured, who then evangelise the world. Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that exactly 144,000 people form a heavenly class, while other believers live on earth. Others take them as Jewish Christians in the church, distinct from Gentile believers. Verdict: the 144,000 are the whole church, the true Israel of God, Jew and Gentile together, seen on earth, sealed and protected. Four reasons. First, John hears a number (v. 4) and then sees a countless multitude from every nation (v. 9), just as in 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb: the two are the same reality, described first in Old Testament terms and then in its fulfilment. Second, the sealing is for all God’s servants (v. 3), and in 9:4 everyone without the seal is harmed, so the sealed must be all believers. Third, the New Testament calls the church the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16), the twelve tribes (James 1:1), and Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). Fourth, the tribe list itself has been deliberately altered, which signals a symbolic, not a literal, Israel. Nothing in the text supports a special class of 144,000 with a different destiny.

What it does not mean. This does not mean God has forgotten ethnic Israel. Jewish believers are part of the 144,000, as they were the first members of the church. And Paul looks forward to a great turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27). But in Christ, there is one people of God, not two.

In a sentence. Then I heard how many were sealed: 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel, twelve thousand each from Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin.

For worship. Thank God that his people are counted, every one, and none is missing. You are not lost in the crowd; you are numbered among God’s Israel.
verseByVerse.note: The tribe list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh appear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
