Verses 9–10: John looks and sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages — the fourfold phrase of 5:9, so that this chapter is the receipt for that purchase. They are standing, which answers 6:17 directly, in white robes and holding palm branches (Lev. 23:40–43; John 12:13), and they cry Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! Not a syllable of the song is about what they did.

Verses 11–12: all the angels stand in the outer ring — the redeemed are nearer the throne than the angelic host — and fall on their faces with a sevenfold doxology bracketed by Amen. It matches the ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving replacing wealth. Heaven falls down because a crowd of forgiven human beings has just sung.

Verses 13–14: an elder asks who they are and where they have come from, and John answers Sir, you know (cf. Ezek. 37:3). The answer has two halves: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation — a present, continuous participle, a stream still emerging — and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Blood does not whiten cloth; the image is deliberately impossible.

Verse 15: therefore they are before the throne, serving him day and night in his temple in priestly service (latreuō), and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence — literally, will spread his tent over them (cf. Ex. 40:34; John 1:14; Rev. 21:3). Verses 16–17 close with five promises quoted from Isaiah 49:10: no hunger, no thirst, no sun, no scorching heat; the Lamb in the midst of the throne as their shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water; and God wiping away every tear from their eyes.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and sings that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. They came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, and are sheltered by God’s presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hunger, thirst and scorching heat were the daily lot of many first hearers.

Now: God himself will wipe away every tear — every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”

Setting and background. God promised Abraham that his offspring would be as numerous as the stars of heaven, too many to count (Genesis 15:5; 22:17). At the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel waved palm branches and lived in shelters, remembering how God had sheltered them in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:40–43). When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds waved palm branches and shouted Hosanna, save us (John 12:13). Palm branches were also used to celebrate military victories (1 Maccabees 13:51).

After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number. Key words. “Great multitude” (ochlos polys). John heard a number (144,000); he looks and sees a crowd beyond counting. God’s promise to Abraham is fulfilled. Heaven will not be thinly populated.

From every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages. Key words. Four terms, as in 5:9: all humanity. The Lamb’s blood ransomed people from every group, and here they are.

Standing before the throne and before the Lamb. Key words. “Standing” (hestōtes). This answers the question of 6:17: who can stand? These can, because the Lamb stands for them.

Clothed in white robes. Purity, victory, washed in the Lamb’s blood (v. 14).

With palm branches in their hands. Key words. “Palm branches” (phoinikes). Victory and joyful celebration, like a heavenly Feast of Tabernacles. God will shelter them (v. 15), and the wilderness journey is over.

And crying out with a loud voice, Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! Key words. “Salvation” (hē sōtēria, deliverance, rescue). They give all the credit to God and the Lamb. Salvation is entirely his work: planned by the Father, accomplished by the Son. Not one of them says they saved themselves. As Jonah said, salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9).

What it does not mean. This is not a separate group from the 144,000, one Jewish and one Gentile. It is the same people of God, seen first as God’s Israel, sealed and counted on earth, and then as the countless multitude from all nations, safe in heaven.

In a sentence. After this I looked and saw an enormous crowd that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing in front of the throne and the Lamb, dressed in white robes and holding palm branches, and shouting loudly: Salvation comes from our God, who sits on the throne, and from the Lamb!

For worship. Join the great multitude in giving all the credit for your salvation to God and the Lamb. And let the diversity of heaven shape your love for believers of every nation now.
verseByVerse.note: John hears a number (v. 4) but sees a multitude no one can count — likely the same people seen from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. Key words. Circles of worship around the throne: living creatures, elders, the multitude, angels.

And they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God. Key words. The angels respond to the salvation of human beings with worship. Jesus said there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10); here is joy over a countless multitude.

Saying, Amen! Key words. They agree with the multitude’s cry.

Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen. Key words. Seven ascriptions, as in 5:12, complete praise. “Thanksgiving” (eucharistia) replaces “wealth” in the earlier list. The angels thank God for salvation, though they have not been redeemed themselves. Every item has the definite article in Greek: the blessing, the glory, all of it, belongs to God. The doxology begins and ends with Amen, wrapping the praise in agreement.

What it does not mean. Angels do not need salvation in the way humans do. The holy angels never fell, and Scripture offers no redemption for fallen angels (Hebrews 2:16). They worship God for his saving work among human beings, into which they long to look (1 Peter 1:12).

In a sentence. All the angels standing around the throne, the elders and the four living beings fell face down before the throne and worshipped God, saying: Amen! Praise and glory, wisdom and thanks, honour, power and strength belong to our God for ever and ever. Amen!

For worship. If angels rejoice over your salvation, how much more should you? Add your own Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

Setting and background. In Daniel 12:1, there will be a time of trouble such as never has been, and at that time God’s people will be delivered, everyone whose name is written in the book. Jesus spoke of great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world (Matthew 24:21). In Ezekiel 37:3, when God asked the prophet whether the dry bones could live, Ezekiel answered, O Lord GOD, you know.

Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? Key words. A teaching question, like a teacher’s question to a pupil. The elder wants John, and us, to understand.

I said to him, Sir, you know. Key words. “Sir” (kyrie, my lord, a title of respect). John admits he does not know, like Ezekiel. Revelation interprets itself here.

These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. Key words. “Coming out” (hoi erchomenoi, present tense: the ones who keep coming). Not a single group arriving at once, but a steady stream of believers coming out of tribulation, as each one dies or as the age ends. “The great tribulation” (tēs thlipseos tēs megalēs). John already shared the tribulation with the churches (1:9).

They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Key words. “Washed” (eplynan) and “made white” (eleukanan). A vivid paradox: robes made white by washing them in blood. The blood of the Lamb, his sacrificial death, cleanses from sin (1 John 1:7; Isaiah 1:18). Their white robes are not their own achievement but the result of Christ’s death applied to them by faith. They washed their robes by trusting in his blood. Exodus 19:10, 14 shows Israel washing their garments to meet God at Sinai.

Where Christians differ: what is the great tribulation? Dispensationalists understand it as a specific seven-year period at the end of history, after the church has been raptured, and see this multitude as those converted during that time. Verdict: the great tribulation describes the suffering of God’s people throughout the whole age between Christ’s comings, which John and his readers were already in (1:9; 2:9–10), and which will intensify toward the end in a final climax of persecution (Matthew 24:21–22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). The multitude is the whole number of the redeemed, from every nation, coming out of that tribulation through all history. The present tense, “coming out”, suits a continuing stream. The church is not removed from tribulation; it is brought through it.

What it does not mean. Washing their robes is not a work that earns salvation. It is faith, trusting in what the Lamb has done. Their robes are white because of his blood, not because of their sufferings.

In a sentence. Then one of the elders asked me, Who are these people dressed in white, and where have they come from? I answered, Sir, you are the one who knows; and he told me, These are the ones who are coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering for Christ, you are part of the stream coming out of the great tribulation. Your robe is white not because of what you endure but because of the blood of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.

Setting and background. In the wilderness, God’s glory dwelt in the tabernacle, a tent among his people, and he sheltered them with the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 40:34–38). Isaiah 4:5–6 promised that the LORD would create a cloud by day and fire by night over Zion as a canopy and shelter. John’s Gospel says the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us (John 1:14).

Therefore they are before the throne of God. Key words. “Therefore” (dia touto, for this reason). They are before God because they are washed in the Lamb’s blood. Their access to God rests on Christ’s sacrifice, not on their merit.

And serve him day and night in his temple. Key words. “Serve” (latreuousin, serve as priests, worship). They are priests (1:6; 5:10), serving God in his presence. “Day and night”: unceasing. Heaven is not idleness but joyful worship and service. “Temple” (naō, sanctuary, the inner shrine): they are in the very place where God dwells. In the new Jerusalem, God and the Lamb are the temple (21:22).

And he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence. Key words. “Shelter” (skēnōsei, will spread his tent over them, will tabernacle over them). God himself will be their shelter. The same word appears in 21:3: the dwelling place (skēnē) of God is with man, and he will dwell (skēnōsei) with them. The people who were driven out by persecution, who perhaps had no home, are given God himself as their home.

What it does not mean. Serving day and night does not mean heaven is exhausting or monotonous. There is no tiredness there (22:5), and the service is perfect freedom and delight.

In a sentence. That is why they stand before God’s throne and worship him day and night in his temple, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

For worship. Your worship on earth is a rehearsal for heaven. Serve God gladly now, and look forward to the day when he will shelter you with his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.

Setting and background. The words come almost directly from Isaiah 49:10, where God promises the exiles returning home that they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. John sees the final fulfilment of the promise of a new exodus.

They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore. Key words. “No more” (ou … eti, never again). Hunger and thirst, the daily fears of the poor, and the punishments of persecution (Smyrna’s poverty, 2:9), and the results of the black horse’s famine (6:5–6), are over for ever. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him will never hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst (John 6:35).

The sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. Key words. “Strike” (pesē, fall on). “Scorching heat” (kauma, burning heat). Exposure, exhaustion, suffering. In the Middle East, the sun was a real danger to travellers. Psalm 121:6 promises that the sun shall not strike you by day. In 16:8–9, the fourth bowl scorches the wicked with fire from the sun; the redeemed are spared.

What it does not mean. This is not only a promise for the future. Believers already taste it in Christ, the bread of life and the living water. But its full reality comes after the tribulation, in God’s presence.

In a sentence. They will never again be hungry or thirsty, and the sun and its burning heat will never beat down on them.

On a Tuesday. If you are weary, poor or suffering, this is God’s promise to you: one day it will be over for ever. Meanwhile, care for those who are hungry and thirsty now (Matthew 25:35).

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

Setting and background. Psalm 23 begins, The LORD is my shepherd. Ezekiel 34:23 promises that God will set over his people one shepherd, his servant David. Jesus said, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11). Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death for ever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces.

For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd. Key words. “In the midst of the throne” (ana meson tou thronou): at the centre, sharing God’s throne. “Shepherd” (poimanei, will shepherd them). A wonderful reversal: the Lamb becomes the Shepherd. The one who was led like a lamb to the slaughter leads his flock. He knows what they have suffered because he suffered it.

And he will guide them to springs of living water. Key words. “Guide” (hodēgēsei, lead on the way). “Living water” (zōēs pēgas hydatōn, springs of the waters of life). Eternal life, flowing from God himself (Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:14; 7:37–39). In the new Jerusalem, the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1).

And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Key words. “Wipe away” (exaleipsei, wipe out completely). “Every tear” (pan dakryon). Not that there will be nothing to weep over, but that God himself, personally and tenderly, will wipe away every tear. The image is of a parent drying a child’s eyes. Repeated in 21:4: death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain. Every sorrow of this life, every martyrdom, every loss, will be healed.

What it does not mean. Wiping away tears does not mean that the sufferings of this life did not matter or will be forgotten as if they had never happened. It means they will be fully comforted and healed. The Lamb still bears his wounds (5:6), and the suffering of his people is honoured, but tears will be no more.

In a sentence. For the Lamb at the centre of the throne will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, and God himself will wipe every tear from their eyes.

For worship. Read this verse at funerals and in times of grief. The Lamb is the Shepherd, and God himself will dry every tear.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea,<sup>3</sup>saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”<sup>4</sup>And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:<sup>5</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad,<sup>6</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh,<sup>7</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar,<sup>8</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.<sup>9</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,<sup>10</sup>and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”<sup>11</sup>And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,<sup>12</sup>saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”<sup>13</sup>Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?”<sup>14</sup>I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened and nothing happens. There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Everything the reader has heard for four chapters — the ceaseless holy, holy, holy of the living creatures (4:8), the myriads crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12), a multitude nobody could number (7:10) — stops. Scripture repeatedly commands exactly this silence before God acts in judgment (Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13), and the crowd outside the temple prayed in silence while the incense was offered (Luke 1:10). Both are probably in view.

Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets — the second of the book’s three sevens. A trumpet in Israel sounded at Sinai (Ex. 19:16), brought down Jericho (Josh. 6:16–20), raised the alarm (Joel 2:1), announced Jubilee (Lev. 25:9) and will sound at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52).

Verses 3–4: before a trumpet sounds, another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints, and the smoke rises before God. This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls which John identified as those prayers. Three details matter: all the saints; the incense is added from the other side, so the prayers do not go up on their own account; and they arrive.

Verse 5 turns everything over. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, followed by thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake — the Sinai signs of 4:5 with an earthquake added. The same censer that carried the prayers up now carries fire down. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

Meaning first. Revelation 8 opens the seventh seal and begins the seven trumpets. When the last seal is broken, heaven falls silent for half an hour (v. 1). Seven angels receive seven trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the prayers rise before God (vv. 2–4). Then the angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, with thunder, lightning and earthquake: the saints’ prayers are being answered in judgement (v. 5). The first four trumpets strike a third of creation: hail and fire burn a third of the land (vv. 6–7); a burning mountain turns a third of the sea to blood (vv. 8–9); a star called Wormwood makes a third of the fresh water bitter (vv. 10–11); and a third of the sun, moon and stars is darkened (v. 12). An eagle cries woe, woe, woe to the earth’s inhabitants because of the three trumpets still to come (v. 13). The trumpets are warning judgements, echoing the plagues on Egypt: partial, so that people may repent, and sent in answer to the prayers of God’s suffering people.

Setting and background. Trumpets in the Old Testament announced God’s presence (Exodus 19:16), summoned Israel to worship and war (Numbers 10:1–10), brought down the walls of Jericho after seven priests blew seven trumpets on the seventh day (Joshua 6), and warned of coming judgement (Joel 2:1; Ezekiel 33:3–6). The trumpets of Revelation recall the ten plagues on Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, locusts. As the plagues judged Pharaoh’s Egypt and freed Israel, so the trumpets judge the world that persecutes God’s people, while his sealed servants are protected (9:4).

When the Lamb opened the seventh seal. Key words. The last seal. The scroll is now fully open. What does it contain? The seventh seal seems to unfold into the seven trumpets, as the seventh trumpet unfolds into the seven bowls. Each series ends at the final judgement and then the next goes over the same ground with greater intensity.

There was silence in heaven. Key words. “Silence” (sigē). After the ceaseless praise of chapters 4–7, heaven falls silent. Three explanations fit together. Awe: the prophets call for silence before the LORD as he comes to judge (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:13). Prayer: in the temple, incense was offered in silence while the people prayed outside, and heaven falls silent so that the prayers of the saints may be heard (vv. 3–4). And the stillness before a storm: judgement is about to fall.

For about half an hour. Key words. A short but noticeable time, suspense before what follows. Half of an hour may also hint at incompleteness: this is not yet the end.

What it does not mean. The silence does not mean worship has stopped for good, or that God is absent. It is a deliberate pause, full of meaning, and the praise resumes (11:15–18).

In a sentence. When the Lamb broke the seventh seal, heaven went silent for about half an hour.

For worship. There is a time for silence before God. Make room in worship, and in your own prayer, to be still before him (Psalm 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.

Setting and background. In the tabernacle and temple, a golden altar of incense stood in the Holy Place, before the curtain of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 30:1–10). Twice a day, a priest burned incense on it while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:8–10). The rising smoke pictured prayer going up to God (Psalm 141:2). Jewish tradition named seven archangels who stand before God, among them Gabriel, who said, I am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God (Luke 1:19).

Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. Key words. “Stand before God” (enōpion tou theou hestēkasin): angels of the highest rank, ready to serve. “Were given”: the trumpets come from God.

And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer. Key words. “Censer” (libanōton, a firepan for carrying burning coals and incense).

And he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints. Key words. “Much incense” (thymiamata polla). “All the saints”: every believer, not only the martyrs. In 5:8, the elders held bowls of incense that were the saints’ prayers. Here the incense is added to the prayers, making them acceptable and fragrant before God.

On the golden altar before the throne. Key words. In heaven, the altar is right before the throne. The prayers of God’s people go straight into his presence.

And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel. Key words. “Rose” (anebē, went up). The prayers of persecuted believers in small churches across Asia rise to the throne of the universe. Not one is lost. The cry of the martyrs, How long? (6:10), is part of this.

Where Christians differ: should we pray to angels or saints, or through them? Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have used passages like this to support asking angels and departed saints to present our prayers to God. Verdict: the angel serves as part of the heavenly worship, offering the prayers before God, but he is not prayed to, and the saints on earth do not address him. Scripture teaches that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and that believers may come boldly to the throne of grace through him (Hebrews 4:14–16). The incense that makes our prayers acceptable is the intercession and merit of Christ, our great High Priest, who always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

What it does not mean. The angel does not make prayers acceptable by his own merit, or decide which prayers are heard. He serves God’s purposes. The scene shows how precious our prayers are, not that they need a heavenly middleman.

In a sentence. Then I saw the seven angels who stand in God’s presence, and they were given seven trumpets; another angel, holding a golden censer, came and stood at the altar, and he was given a large amount of incense to offer, together with the prayers of all God’s people, on the golden altar in front of the throne; and the smoke of the incense went up before God from the angel’s hand, along with the prayers of the saints.

On a Tuesday. Your prayers, however weak they feel, rise before God’s throne. Keep praying, especially for persecuted believers. Heaven falls silent to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 10:2, a man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem in judgement. The coal from the altar that touched Isaiah’s lips brought cleansing (Isaiah 6:6–7); here fire from the altar brings judgement.

Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar. Key words. The same censer that carried the prayers now carries fire. The same altar is the source of both.

And threw it on the earth. Key words. “Threw” (ebalen, cast). The answer to the saints’ prayers is God’s judgement on the earth. The prayers of the persecuted church are not ignored; they move heaven to act. Prayer is powerful in God’s government of the world (James 5:16).

And there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. Key words. As at 4:5, the signs of God’s throne and presence, now with an earthquake added. The same sequence comes again, more intensely, at 11:19 and 16:18–21. Each series of judgements ends with this sign, showing that each reaches the final judgement.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians should pray for the destruction of their enemies. We pray for God’s kingdom to come and his will to be done, which includes the defeat of evil, and we pray for our enemies’ repentance. God decides how to answer, and his judgements are always just.

In a sentence. Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar and hurled it down on the earth, and there came thunder, rumbling, lightning and an earthquake.

On a Tuesday. Pray, Your kingdom come, knowing that God hears and will answer. History is shaped not only by governments and armies but by the prayers of his people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6: the seven angels prepare to blow. Verse 7: the first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees and all green grass are burned. Verses 8–9: the second brings something like a great mountain, burning, thrown into the sea — the image Jeremiah used of Babylon as a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25) — and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of its creatures die, a third of the ships are destroyed. For seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was the economy, not the scenery.

Verses 10–11: the third trumpet drops a blazing star, Wormwood, on the fresh water, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Apsinthos is bitter rather than poisonous, and it is the prophets’ standing image for judgment that makes the sweet unswallowable (Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Lam. 3:19) — most pointedly in Amos, where men turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7) and here find their own wells undrinkable.

Verse 12: the fourth strikes a third of the sun, moon and stars, so that a third of the light is darkened — the ninth plague on Egypt (Ex. 10:21–23), aimed at a nation whose chief god was the sun and whose Pharaoh was his son.

Verse 13 closes with an eagle at the zenith, where everyone can see it, crying Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth — one woe for each trumpet still to come. Four trumpets have struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky, the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky — each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.

Setting and background. The seventh plague on Egypt was hail mixed with fire, which struck every plant and broke every tree in the field (Exodus 9:23–25). Joel 2:30 speaks of blood and fire and columns of smoke before the day of the LORD.

Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. Key words. “Prepared” (hētoimasan, made ready). Everything is ordered and deliberate.

The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood. Key words. Like the plague on Egypt, but worse: blood is added. A terrifying picture of destruction from the sky.

And these were thrown upon the earth. Key words. “Thrown” (eblēthē, a divine passive: God throws them).

And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up. Key words. “A third” (to triton). The seals struck a quarter (6:8); the trumpets strike a third; the bowls will strike everything (16). The judgements grow more severe, but they are still partial, leaving room for repentance (9:20–21). Ezekiel 5:2, 12 speaks of judgement on Jerusalem by thirds. “All green grass”: perhaps all the grass in the third that is burned.

Where Christians differ: are the trumpets literal events? Some read the trumpets as literal future events, perhaps nuclear war or asteroid strikes. Historicists match each trumpet to an event in church history (invasions of the Roman Empire by Goths, Vandals and others). Verdict: the trumpets are symbolic pictures of God’s judgements on a rebellious world throughout the age between Christ’s comings, drawn from the plagues of Egypt. They include natural disasters and ecological catastrophes, which are real and recur through history, as warnings to repent. Their purpose is stated in 9:20–21: to call people to turn from idols. They are not a timeline to be decoded, but they are real, and they may also intensify before the end.

What it does not mean. These judgements do not mean God does not care about his creation. The new creation will be its renewal (21:1–5). Creation suffers now because of human sin (Romans 8:20–22), and God uses even its suffering to warn the world.

In a sentence. Then the seven angels holding the seven trumpets got ready to blow them; the first angel blew his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood rained down on the earth, and a third of the land was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.

On a Tuesday. When you see wildfires, storms and disasters, let them be trumpets calling you and others to repent and turn to God (Luke 13:1–5).
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

Setting and background. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood, so that the fish died (Exodus 7:20–21). Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain that God will make a burnt mountain. In AD 79, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy buried Pompeii, and stories of a burning mountain falling into the sea would have been fresh in readers’ minds.

And something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea. Key words. “Something like” (hōs, as it were). John describes what he saw by comparison. The image may suggest a volcanic eruption, or a falling empire like Babylon (Jeremiah 51:25), but its main point is catastrophe on the sea.

And a third of the sea became blood. As in the plague on the Nile, on a greater scale.

A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed. Key words. The sea was the lifeline of the Roman economy: trade, food, transport. The destruction of ships strikes at the wealth of the empire, as the fall of Babylon will strike the merchants and sailors (18:17–19).

What it does not mean. This is not a prediction of a particular volcano or meteor. It is a picture of God’s judgement on the sea and on the commerce of a world that lives without him.

In a sentence. The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a huge mountain on fire was hurled into the sea; a third of the sea turned to blood, a third of the creatures living in the sea died, and a third of the ships were wrecked.

On a Tuesday. The world’s economy is not as secure as it seems. Do not trust in trade and wealth; trust in God, who holds even the seas in his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.

Setting and background. Wormwood (apsinthos) is a bitter plant, related to the plant used to make absinthe. In the Old Testament, it pictures bitterness, sorrow and God’s judgement: I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19). At Marah, God made bitter water sweet for Israel (Exodus 15:23–25); here, sweet water is made bitter. Isaiah 14:12 describes the king of Babylon as a day star fallen from heaven.

The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch. Key words. “Star” (astēr). In Revelation, stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This may be an angel carrying out God’s judgement, or simply a burning meteor-like object.

And it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. Fresh water, essential for life.

The name of the star is Wormwood. Key words. The name tells us its meaning: bitterness. Those who turn away from the living water of God, and drink the poisoned waters of idolatry, find life bitter (Jeremiah 2:13; 9:13–15).

A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Key words. Wormwood is not normally deadly; the image is intensified. The waters of life become the waters of death.

What it does not mean. Wormwood is not a code word for a specific modern disaster, such as the Chernobyl nuclear accident (some have pointed out that a Ukrainian word for a type of wormwood is close to Chernobyl). Revelation’s symbols draw on the Old Testament, not on modern place names.

In a sentence. The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star blazing like a torch fell from the sky onto a third of the rivers and springs; the star is called Wormwood, and a third of the waters turned bitter, and many people died from drinking the water because it had been made bitter.

On a Tuesday. Life without God turns bitter in the end. Drink from Christ, the spring of living water (John 4:14), and offer it to others.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

Setting and background. The ninth plague on Egypt was darkness over the land for three days, though the Israelites had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). God created the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day, to give light and to mark times (Genesis 1:14–18). The Egyptians worshipped the sun god, so the darkness was a judgement on their gods. Hosea 8:1 says, set the trumpet to your lips, for one like a vulture (or eagle) is over the house of the LORD.

The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars. Key words. “Struck” (eplēgē, smitten; the word for plague, plēgē, comes from it). God strikes the lights he created. The world that worships created things instead of the Creator (Romans 1:25) loses part of the light it takes for granted.

So that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Key words. Darkness pictures judgement, sorrow and the absence of God. Like the first four seals, the first four trumpets strike the natural world: land, sea, fresh water, sky.

Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead. Key words. “Eagle” (aetou, eagle or vulture). A bird of prey, circling over what is about to die (Matthew 24:28). “Directly overhead” (en mesouranēmati, in mid-heaven, the highest point of the sky, where everyone can see and hear).

Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth. Key words. “Woe” (ouai, alas, a cry of grief and doom). Three woes, for the three trumpets still to come (9:12; 11:14). “Those who dwell on the earth”: unbelievers in rebellion against God.

At the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow! Key words. The last three trumpets will be worse. The first four struck nature; the next will strike people directly, with demonic torment and death.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “an angel flying” instead of “an eagle flying”. The two Greek words (angelou and aetou) look somewhat alike. The best manuscripts read “eagle”.

What it does not mean. The darkening of a third is not a scientific description of how sunlight would be reduced. It is a picture: part of creation’s light withdrawn as a warning, before the deeper darkness of the bowls (16:10).

In a sentence. The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun, a third of the moon and a third of the stars were struck, so that a third of them went dark, and a third of the day and of the night were without light; then, as I watched, I heard an eagle flying high overhead and crying out loudly: Woe, woe, woe to the people of the earth, because of the trumpet blasts that the other three angels are about to sound!

On a Tuesday. God’s warnings grow louder. If you have been putting off turning to him, or speaking to others about him, do not delay.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.<sup>3</sup>And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,<sup>4</sup>and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.<sup>5</sup>Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.<sup>6</sup>Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them.<sup>7</sup>The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a star fallen from heaven — a perfect participle, an event already complete — who is immediately a he, and who was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opens it, and before anything comes out the light goes: smoke like the smoke of a great furnace darkens the sun and the air (cf. Gen. 19:28).

Verses 3–4: locusts come up out of the smoke with the power of scorpions — and are told not to touch grass, plant or tree, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Their only target is those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads: the first cash-out of chapter 7, and the doorpost of the Exodus Passover moved from the house to the person (cf. Ex. 8:22; 10:23).

Verses 5–6: they are allowed to torment for five months — about the life cycle of a locust swarm — but not to kill. And then the hardest sentence in the chapter: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (cf. Job 3:21; Jer. 8:3).

Verses 7–10 describe them in eight comparisons, each introduced by like: horses prepared for battle (Joel 2:4), what looked like crowns of gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth (Joel 1:6), iron breastplates, wings like many chariots, and scorpion tails in which their power to hurt resides.

Verses 11–12: Proverbs 30:27 says locusts have no king; these have one — the angel of the bottomless pit, named in both languages, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction, Job 26:6; 28:22; Prov. 15:11) and Apollyon (Greek for destroyer). Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer — a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation — tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.

Meaning first. Revelation 9 describes the fifth and sixth trumpets, the first two woes, in which judgement moves from nature to people, and from natural forces to demonic ones. At the fifth trumpet, a fallen star opens the bottomless pit, and smoke darkens the sky (vv. 1–2). Out of the smoke come locusts with the sting of scorpions, allowed to torment, but not kill, those without God’s seal for five months, so that people long to die (vv. 3–6). They are described as monstrous war horses with human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates and scorpion tails (vv. 7–10), and their king is the angel of the pit, Abaddon or Apollyon, the Destroyer (vv. 11–12). At the sixth trumpet, a voice from the altar releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for this very hour, to kill a third of mankind (vv. 13–15). An army of two hundred million cavalry appears, with fire-coloured breastplates and lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulphur, with tails like serpents (vv. 16–19). Yet the rest of mankind still does not repent of worshipping demons and idols, or of murder, sorcery, immorality and theft (vv. 20–21). The chapter shows the horror of a world given over to the demonic powers it has chosen, God’s protection of his sealed people, and the terrible hardness of the human heart.

Setting and background. The eighth plague on Egypt was locusts, which covered the land and darkened it (Exodus 10:12–15). The prophet Joel described a locust plague as an invading army: like horses, with a sound like chariots, with teeth like a lion’s, darkening the sun and moon, a picture of the Day of the LORD (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). In the ancient Near East, a locust swarm could strip a whole region bare in hours. In Jewish thought, the abyss was the prison of evil spirits (Luke 8:31; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6).

And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth. Key words. “Fallen” (peptōkota, perfect tense: having fallen, and lying there). John does not see it fall; he sees it already fallen. A star in Revelation can represent an angel (1:20), and this one is a person (“he was given”). Jesus said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18), and Isaiah 14:12 speaks of the fall of the day star. This is probably a fallen angel, possibly Satan himself, or perhaps one of God’s angels sent down with the key (as in 20:1). Either way, he can act only because he was given the key.

And he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. Key words. “Was given” (edothē): permission from God. Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18); any other key is borrowed. “Bottomless pit” (abyssou, the abyss, the deep). The prison of demonic powers, from which the beast also rises (11:7; 17:8) and in which Satan will be bound (20:1–3). “Shaft” (phreatos, well, pit).

He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace. Key words. Smoke like that of Sodom’s destruction (Genesis 19:28) and of Sinai (Exodus 19:18). Hell’s darkness rising into the world.

And the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft. Key words. Demonic deception darkens the mind and blots out the light (2 Corinthians 4:4).

What it does not mean. The abyss being opened does not mean evil has escaped God’s control. Every detail stresses that the key was given, the locusts were given power, they were told what to harm, and they were allowed only five months. God uses even demonic forces as instruments of judgement on those who have chosen them.

In a sentence. When the fifth angel blew his trumpet, I saw a star that had fallen from the sky to the earth, and it was given the key to the shaft of the abyss; when it opened the shaft, smoke poured up like smoke from a huge furnace, and the sun and the sky went dark with it.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual evil is real, but its key is borrowed. Do not be fascinated by the demonic, and do not fear it; fear and trust the one who holds all the keys.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth. Key words. “Locusts” (akrides). Not ordinary locusts: they come from the abyss and do not eat plants. They are demonic powers pictured as a locust plague.

And they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. Key words. “Scorpions” (skorpioi): their sting is agonising, though rarely fatal to adults. Jesus gave his disciples authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19), linking scorpions with demonic power.

They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree. Key words. “Were told” (errethē, it was said to them). Ordinary locusts eat plants; these are forbidden to. Their target is people.

But only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. Key words. The sealing of 7:3 now proves its purpose. God’s people are protected from this demonic torment, as Israel in Goshen was protected from the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:22; 9:4, 26; 10:23). The demonic powers cannot touch those who belong to God (1 John 5:18). Notice that this protection covers all who have God’s seal, which confirms that the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 are all believers.

What it does not mean. Protection from the locusts does not mean believers never face spiritual attack. Satan attacks them through temptation, accusation and persecution (12:10–17). But they cannot be possessed or destroyed by demonic power, and the judgement of the locusts is not for them.

In a sentence. Out of the smoke came locusts onto the earth, and they were given power like that of scorpions; they were told not to damage the grass or any plant or tree, but only the people who did not have God’s seal on their foreheads.

For worship. Thank God that you are sealed. The powers of the abyss cannot claim you.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.

Setting and background. The life cycle of a locust is about five months, and the locust season ran roughly from spring to late summer, about five months. Job 3:21 describes those who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures.

They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them. Key words. “Allowed” (edothē, it was given): permission again. “Torment” (basanisthēsontai, torture, intense pain). “Five months”: a limited period, perhaps the length of a locust season. God limits the time, and he does not allow them to kill. The purpose of the torment is to bring people to repentance (v. 20).

And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. Key words. Agonising but not fatal. What might this torment be? Perhaps the spiritual and psychological misery of life under demonic deception: despair, emptiness, fear, addiction, the inner torment of a life without God that has given itself to the powers of darkness.

And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them. Key words. “Seek” (zētēsousin). “Long” (epithymēsousin, desire intensely). “Flee” (pheugei). A terrible picture of despair. People would rather die than go on, but even death escapes them. Yet still they do not turn to God.

What it does not mean. This verse should never be used to suggest that a person in despair or with suicidal thoughts is under God’s judgement. Believers, too, can suffer deep depression and long for death, as Elijah did (1 Kings 19:4). The picture here is of judgement on those who reject God, and the right response to anyone in despair is compassion, care and the hope of the gospel.

In a sentence. They were permitted to torment those people for five months, but not to kill them, and the agony was like the pain of a scorpion’s sting; in those days people will look for death and not find it, they will long to die, but death will run away from them.

On a Tuesday. Many people around you live with quiet despair. Do not judge them; point them to the Christ who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.

Setting and background. Joel 2:4–5 says the locusts look like horses and run like war horses, with a noise like chariots. A locust’s head does look rather like a horse’s; the Italian and German words for locust mean little horse and hay horse. Joel 1:6 says the invader has teeth like a lion’s. The Parthians, Rome’s feared eastern enemy, were famous mounted archers who wore their hair long.

In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. Key words. “Like” (homoiōmata, likenesses). John piles up comparisons, each introduced with “like”. He is describing something beyond ordinary experience in the best images he has. Not a portrait to be drawn, but a series of impressions: unstoppable, terrifying, intelligent and cruel.

On their heads were what looked like crowns of gold. Key words. “What looked like”: not real crowns, but a show of authority and conquest. They seem victorious.

Their faces were like human faces. Key words. Intelligence. These are not mindless insects.

Their hair like women’s hair. Key words. Long, flowing hair, perhaps like the long-haired Parthian warriors, or the locusts’ long antennae. Seductive, perhaps, as well as wild.

And their teeth like lions’ teeth. Ferocious, destructive (Joel 1:6).

They had breastplates like breastplates of iron. Key words. Invulnerable, hard to resist. The locust’s armoured body.

And the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. Overwhelming, terrifying (Joel 2:5).

They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails. Key words. The sting is where the torment comes from. Limited again: five months.

Where Christians differ: what are the locusts? Some popular writers have identified them with modern weapons, such as attack helicopters with rotor blades, tail guns and armoured cockpits. Historicists have identified them with the Muslim Arab armies of the seventh century. Others take them as literal demonic creatures to be unleashed in a future tribulation. Verdict: the locusts are demonic powers, released by God’s permission to torment those who have rejected him, pictured with images drawn from Joel’s locust army. John uses “like” again and again, signalling symbols, not technical descriptions. Reading modern technology into them ignores how the first readers would have understood the book. The locusts describe demonic torment, real and terrible, wherever people give themselves over to evil, throughout the age and especially toward its end.

What it does not mean. The details are not to be decoded one by one, as though each feature were a separate clue. Together they build a single picture of overwhelming, intelligent, demonic hostility.

In a sentence. The locusts looked like horses equipped for battle; they wore what seemed to be gold crowns, their faces looked human, their hair was long like a woman’s, their teeth were like a lion’s, their chests were armoured as if with iron, and their wings roared like a mass of chariots and horses charging into battle; they had tails with stings like scorpions, and the power to hurt people for five months was in their tails.

On a Tuesday. Evil often looks impressive, crowned and armoured. Do not be taken in, and do not be afraid. It serves its time and is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.

Setting and background. Proverbs 30:27 says that the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank. These locusts do have a king. In the Old Testament, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction) is a name for the place of the dead, linked with Sheol and death (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11). The Greek god Apollo was sometimes symbolised by the locust, and the emperor Domitian liked to be seen as Apollo incarnate.

They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. Key words. “King” (basilea). The demonic powers are organised under a ruler. The angel of the abyss is either Satan himself or a high-ranking demonic spirit under him.

His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. Key words. “Abaddon” (destruction). “Apollyon” (Apollyōn, destroyer). The name sums up his nature: Satan comes only to steal, kill and destroy; Christ came that they may have life (John 10:10). The Greek name sounds very like Apollo, and may be a deliberate jab at Domitian and the emperor cult: the god the emperor imitates is the Destroyer.

The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come. Key words. The first of the three woes announced in 8:13. Worse is coming.

What it does not mean. Abaddon’s power, like the locusts’, is limited. He is a king, but not the King. Christ is King of kings (19:16), and Abaddon’s kingdom is the abyss into which Satan will finally be thrown (20:3, 10).

In a sentence. Their king was the angel who rules the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon, both meaning Destroyer; the first woe is past, but look, two more woes are still to come.

On a Tuesday. Satan’s name tells you what he does: he destroys. Whatever he promises, his end is destruction. Christ’s name is Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–14: the sixth trumpet, and a voice from the four horns of the golden altar — the incense altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered in 8:3–4 and from which fire was thrown down in 8:5. The order it gives is Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. They are bound; they must be released; the order comes from the altar where the church prays. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from.

Verse 15: the four had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year — one article in the Greek governs all four, so this is a fixed moment rather than a duration — and are released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction has moved from things to people. Verse 16 gives the number of mounted troops as twice ten thousand times ten thousand, with the telling clause I heard their number, exactly as at 7:4.

Verses 17–19: breastplates the colour of fire, sapphire and sulfur — the same three things the horses breathe. Lions’ heads; fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths, the substance of Sodom (Gen. 19:24) and of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10). A third of mankind killed by these three plagues. And the power is in mouths and in tails, the tails being like serpents with heads — the word John reserves for the dragon (12:9; 20:2).

Verses 20–21 give the verdict the whole sequence was building toward. The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent — not of the works of their hands, not of worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood which cannot see or hear or walk (Ps. 115:4–8), and not of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgement alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

Setting and background. The Euphrates was the great river of Mesopotamia, the northeastern boundary of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Israel’s great enemies, Assyria and Babylon, had come from beyond it. In John’s day, it was the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthians, Rome’s most feared enemy, whose cavalry had defeated Roman armies. The altar of incense had a horn at each corner (Exodus 30:2–3).

Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God. Key words. The golden altar where the prayers of the saints were offered (8:3). The voice from the altar links this judgement too to the prayers of God’s people. The horns of the altar were where atonement blood was applied (Leviticus 4:7); those who reject the atonement face judgement from the same altar.

Saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. Key words. “Bound” (dedemenous, perfect tense: having been bound and remaining bound). These are evil angels, held in check by God until now, as fallen angels are kept in chains (Jude 6). “Release” (lyson, loose). God holds back the forces of destruction, and releases them at his chosen time. The Euphrates, the ancient boundary from which invasion came, pictures the terror of foreign invasion and war.

Textual note. Some important manuscripts read “a voice from the horns of the golden altar”, without the word “four”. The meaning is unchanged.

What it does not mean. The Euphrates here is not necessarily a prediction of armies literally crossing that river in the future, though it may include that. In Revelation, place names often carry symbolic meaning: Babylon, Sodom, Egypt, Armageddon. The Euphrates stands for the frontier from which the terror of invasion comes.

In a sentence. Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice coming from the horns of the golden altar in God’s presence, telling the sixth angel with the trumpet, Set free the four angels who are bound at the great River Euphrates.

On a Tuesday. God restrains evil far more than we know. Thank him for every day of peace, and pray for those living under war.
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year. Key words. “Prepared” (hētoimasmenoi, made ready, perfect tense). God has appointed the exact moment. History is not random: even its catastrophes come at the hour, the day, the month and the year God has fixed.

Were released to kill a third of mankind. Key words. “A third”: a step beyond the fourth seal (a quarter, 6:8), but still partial. This is the first time the trumpets kill people directly. Under the fifth trumpet they longed for death; now it comes.

The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand. Key words. “Twice ten thousand times ten thousand” (dismyriades myriadōn, two myriads of myriads): two hundred million. In the ancient world, this was beyond imagination; the entire Roman army had perhaps three hundred thousand soldiers. The number means an army beyond counting, overwhelming.

I heard their number. Key words. As with the 144,000 (7:4), John hears a number. The two armies stand in contrast: God’s army, sealed and counted, and the demonic army, vast and destructive.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal army of two hundred million? Some popular writers have identified it with a future Chinese army, after China claimed it could field two hundred million soldiers. Verdict: the number is symbolic of an overwhelming, uncountable host, a demonic army more than a human one, as the description of the horses that follows makes clear. Its point is the terror of war and destruction let loose, not a prediction about any particular nation. Readings that tie it to modern nations have repeatedly had to be revised as world politics changed.

What it does not mean. The fixed hour does not mean God takes pleasure in death. He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather that they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). The fixed hour means that even judgement is under his wise and just control.

In a sentence. So the four angels, who had been kept ready for that very hour, day, month and year, were set free to kill a third of humanity; the number of their cavalry was two hundred million; I heard the number.

On a Tuesday. No disaster in the news happens outside God’s appointed hour. That does not make it less terrible, but it means it is not meaningless.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.
