By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.

Setting and background. Fire and sulphur (brimstone) rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24). In Revelation, they are the elements of the lake of fire (14:10; 19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The Parthian cavalry were famous for shooting arrows backwards as they rode away, so that their power seemed to be in their tails.

And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them. Key words. “In my vision” (en tē horasei). John reminds us that he is describing a vision.

They wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur. Key words. Red (fire), dark blue (hyakinthinous, the colour of smoke, hyacinth) and yellow (sulphur). The colours match the fire, smoke and sulphur that come from the horses’ mouths.

And the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. Key words. Monstrous, demonic horses, like dragons. Lions’ heads speak of ferocity. Fire, smoke and sulphur speak of hell itself breaking out into the world.

By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed. Key words. “Plagues” (plēgōn, blows, strokes). Fire, smoke and sulphur.

For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound. Key words. “Serpents” (ophesin): the serpent is the image of Satan (12:9). These horses kill from the front and wound from behind. Demonic power is deadly in every direction.

What it does not mean. This is not a description of modern tanks or military aircraft, as some have suggested. It is a vision of demonic destruction, drawing on the images of Sodom’s judgement and the lake of fire.

In a sentence. This is how the horses and their riders looked in my vision: the riders wore breastplates that were fiery red, smoky blue and sulphur yellow, the horses had heads like lions, and fire, smoke and sulphur came out of their mouths; these three plagues, the fire, smoke and sulphur pouring from their mouths, killed a third of humanity; for the horses’ power was in their mouths and in their tails, which were like snakes with heads that they used to wound people.

On a Tuesday. War and violence are not only human; they are also demonic. Pray against the spiritual powers behind them (Ephesians 6:12).

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

Setting and background. Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again under the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34). The Old Testament mocks idols that have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear (Psalm 115:4–7; 135:15–17; Daniel 5:23). Paul taught that behind idols are demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent. Key words. “Did not repent” (ou metenoēsan). This is the purpose of the trumpets: they were warnings, calling people to repent. And this is the tragedy: they did not. The same words return in 16:9, 11. Suffering by itself does not change the heart.

Of the works of their hands. Key words. Idols made by human hands.

Nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk. Key words. “Demons” (daimonia). Idolatry is not harmless; behind the idols are demons. The very powers that tormented them are the ones they keep worshipping. Gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood: idols for the rich and the poor alike. Idols include anything people trust and serve in place of God: money, power, pleasure, status (Colossians 3:5).

Nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts. Key words. Four sins, breaking the commandments of the second table: murder (sixth commandment), sexual immorality (seventh), theft (eighth). “Sorceries” (pharmakōn, from pharmakeia, the use of drugs and potions in magic and the occult; our word pharmacy comes from it). Idolatry, breaking the first table of the law, always leads to breaking the second (Romans 1:21–32).

Where Christians differ: can people repent whenever they choose? Many hold that people always have the natural ability to repent and believe if they choose to. Verdict: this verse shows the terrible bondage of the human will apart from grace. Even under overwhelming judgement, people do not repent, because their hearts are enslaved to sin and they love darkness (John 3:19). Scripture teaches that sinners are dead in sin (Ephesians 2:1) and unable to come to Christ unless the Father draws them (John 6:44). Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). This does not excuse unbelievers; they are responsible for refusing. But it shows why we pray for God to give new hearts, and why we preach the gospel, which is God’s power to save (Romans 1:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one ever repents through suffering. Many do (11:13). But suffering alone does not save; only God’s grace through the gospel does.

In a sentence. Yet the rest of humanity, those who were not killed by these plagues, still did not turn away from what they had made with their own hands; they did not stop worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood, which cannot see, hear or walk, and they did not turn from their murders, their magic arts, their sexual immorality or their stealing.

On a Tuesday. Pray for unbelieving friends and family, asking God to do what suffering alone cannot: give them new hearts. And keep sharing the gospel with them.

They will long to die, but death will flee from them.<sup>7</sup>In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces,<sup>8</sup>their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth;<sup>9</sup>they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle.<sup>10</sup>They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.<sup>11</sup>They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.<sup>12</sup>The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.<sup>13</sup>Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God,<sup>14</sup>saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”<sup>15</sup>So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.<sup>16</sup>The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.<sup>17</sup>And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.<sup>18</sup>By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths.<sup>19</sup>For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.<sup>20</sup>The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,<sup>21</sup>nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six trumpets have sounded; the seventh does not sound until 11:15. Everything between is an interlude, exactly as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals — a repetition that is itself an argument about how John builds his sevens.

Verses 1–2: another mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire — every detail borrowed from the descriptions of God and of Christ (1:7, 15, 16; 4:3; Ex. 13:21). He holds a little scroll, and it is already open, unlike the sealed scroll of chapter 5. He sets his right foot on the sea and his left on the land: the conqueror’s posture (Josh. 1:3), with one foot on each of the two places the beasts of chapter 13 will rise from.

Verse 3: he calls out like a lion roaring — the prophets’ image for God speaking (Amos 3:8; Hos. 11:10; Joel 3:16) — and the seven thunders sound, the definite article suggesting a known set, most likely the sevenfold voice of the LORD in Psalm 29. Verse 4: John, pen in hand and about to write, is stopped: Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.

Verses 5–7: the angel raises his right hand and swears — the posture of Daniel 12:6–7 — by the one who lives for ever and who made heaven, earth and sea, that there would be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

Verses 8–10: John is sent to take the open scroll and told Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey — Ezekiel’s commission exactly (Ezek. 2:9–3:3; cf. Jer. 15:16). He eats, and reports the tastes in the order he met them: sweet first, bitter after. Verse 11 sends him back to work: You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed — the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,

Meaning first. Revelation 10 is a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as chapter 7 was between the sixth and seventh seals. A mighty angel comes down from heaven, robed in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, shining like the sun, with a little open scroll in his hand, and plants his feet on sea and land (vv. 1–2). He roars like a lion, and seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said and not write it (vv. 3–4). The angel raises his hand and swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay: when the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God announced by the prophets will be fulfilled (vv. 5–7). John is told to take the little scroll and eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach (vv. 8–10). Then he is told that he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings (v. 11). The chapter renews John’s commission as a prophet, like Ezekiel’s, and prepares for chapter 11. God’s word is sweet to receive, and bitter to carry, because it brings both salvation and judgement, and the church that proclaims it must suffer.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, God gives Ezekiel a scroll written on front and back with lamentation, mourning and woe, and tells him to eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth, and then he is sent to prophesy to Israel. In Daniel 12:4–9, Daniel is told to seal up his vision until the end, and an angel raises both hands to heaven and swears by him who lives for ever that it will be for a time, times and half a time. Revelation 10 echoes both.

Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven. Key words. “Another mighty angel” (allon angelon ischyron). The first mighty angel asked who was worthy to open the scroll (5:2).

Wrapped in a cloud. Key words. Clouds accompany God’s presence (Exodus 13:21) and Christ’s coming (1:7).

With a rainbow over his head. Key words. The rainbow of God’s covenant faithfulness (4:3).

And his face was like the sun. Key words. Like Christ’s face in 1:16.

And his legs like pillars of fire. Key words. Recalling the pillar of fire that led Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), and Christ’s feet like burnished bronze (1:15).

He had a little scroll open in his hand. Key words. “Little scroll” (biblaridion). Open, not sealed. Probably closely connected with the scroll of chapter 5, which the Lamb has now opened: God’s revealed purpose, now to be given to John to proclaim.

And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land. Key words. A gigantic figure, astride the world. His message concerns the whole earth. Sea and land are also where the two beasts arise (13:1, 11); God’s authority over both is asserted before they appear.

Where Christians differ: is the mighty angel Christ? Some identify him with Christ himself, because of the cloud, the rainbow, the sun-like face and the fiery legs. Verdict: he is most likely a powerful angel who reflects Christ’s glory and represents him. Revelation never calls Christ an angel; he is the one the angels worship (5:11–12). This angel swears by God (v. 6), which Christ, who is God, would not need to do in this way. He is called another mighty angel, linking him to the angel of 5:2. Angels who come from God’s presence share something of his glory, as Moses’ face shone after he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

What it does not mean. The angel’s glory does not make him an object of worship. When John later falls at an angel’s feet, he is told not to: worship God (19:10; 22:9).

In a sentence. Then I saw another powerful angel coming down from heaven, clothed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face shining like the sun and legs like pillars of fire; he held a small scroll lying open in his hand, and he planted his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is for the whole world, sea and land. Your part of the world is included, and your part in passing it on matters.

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”

Setting and background. Amos 3:8 says the lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy? Hosea 11:10 says the LORD will roar like a lion. Psalm 29 describes the voice of the LORD seven times as thunder over the waters. Paul was caught up into paradise and heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter (2 Corinthians 12:4).

And called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. Key words. “Roaring” (mykatai, roars, bellows). A voice of power that demands attention, like the voice of God himself.

When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. Key words. “Seven thunders” (hai hepta brontai, the seven thunders, with the article, as if well known). Probably the voice of God, as in Psalm 29, where the voice of the LORD is sevenfold thunder. They spoke words, which John understood.

And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write. John was faithful to the command to write what he saw (1:11, 19).

But I heard a voice from heaven saying, Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down. Key words. “Seal up” (sphragison). Unlike the rest of Revelation, which is unsealed (22:10), these words are kept secret. Why? Perhaps because they were further judgements that God has chosen to cancel or cut short, so that the end comes without more warnings (the next verse says there will be no more delay). Or simply to teach that God has not told us everything. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29).

What it does not mean. The sealed thunders do not invite speculation, or claims by later teachers to have discovered what they said. Some groups have claimed that their founders revealed the seven thunders. But what God has sealed, no one may unseal, and the canon is closed (22:18–19). We have everything we need for life and godliness in what is written (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

In a sentence. He shouted with a loud voice like a lion roaring, and when he shouted, the seven thunders spoke; when they had spoken, I was about to write it down, but I heard a voice from heaven say, Keep secret what the seven thunders said; do not write it.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to know everything about the future. Be content with what God has revealed, and trust him with what he has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

Setting and background. In Daniel 12:7, an angel raised his hands to heaven and swore by him who lives for ever that it would be for a time, times and half a time, and when the shattering of the power of the holy people came to an end, all these things would be finished. Raising the hand was the gesture of a solemn oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40). The martyrs had asked, How long? (6:10), and were told to wait a little longer (6:11).

And the angel … raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever. Key words. “Swore” (ōmosen, took an oath). The most solemn guarantee. He swears by the eternal God, the highest authority.

Who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it. Key words. The Creator of everything, every realm. Because he made it all, he has the right and the power to bring it to its end.

That there would be no more delay. Key words. “No more delay” (chronos ouketi estai, time will no longer be). Not that time itself will end, but that there will be no more waiting. The answer to the martyrs’ How long? is: no longer. God’s patience, which delayed judgement to give time for repentance, will come to an end.

But that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel. Key words. The seventh trumpet (11:15) announces the coming of God’s kingdom in full.

The mystery of God would be fulfilled. Key words. “Mystery” (mystērion): God’s plan, once hidden, now revealed. In the New Testament, the mystery is God’s plan of salvation in Christ, including the gathering of Gentiles with Jews into one people (Ephesians 3:3–6; Colossians 1:26–27), and its completion at the end, when all things are united in Christ (Ephesians 1:9–10). “Fulfilled” (etelesthē, completed, brought to its goal).

Just as he announced to his servants the prophets. Key words. “Announced” (euēngelisen, preached as good news; the verb from which evangelise comes). God’s final victory is good news, proclaimed through all the prophets (Amos 3:7).

Textual note. The King James Version translates “that there should be time no longer”, which some have taken to mean the end of time itself. The Greek word chronos can mean delay, and the context, answering the martyrs’ How long?, shows that this is the meaning here.

What it does not mean. “No more delay” does not mean the end came in John’s lifetime. It means that when the seventh trumpet sounds, the end will come without further postponement. Until then, God’s patience continues, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9).

In a sentence. Then the angel I had seen standing on sea and land lifted his right hand to heaven and swore by the one who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven, earth and sea and everything in them, that there would be no more waiting: when the seventh angel blows his trumpet, God’s hidden plan will be completed, just as he announced it as good news to his servants the prophets.

For worship. God has sworn that his plan will be completed. Worship him as the Creator who will bring all things to their good end, just as he promised.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.” So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.” And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.

Setting and background. Ezekiel ate a scroll full of lamentation and woe, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 3:1–3); afterwards he went in bitterness, in the heat of his spirit (Ezekiel 3:14). Jeremiah said, your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (Jeremiah 15:16), and yet his ministry brought him great suffering. Psalm 19:10 and 119:103 call God’s words sweeter than honey.

Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, Go, take the scroll. Key words. John is not just to look at the scroll but to take it. God’s word must be received personally.

Take and eat it. Key words. “Eat” (kataphage, devour). To eat a scroll means to take God’s word inside, to absorb it, make it part of oneself, before speaking it to others. A prophet cannot pass on what he has not first taken in.

It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. Key words. “Bitter” (pikranei). “Sweet” (glyky). God’s word is sweet: it is his word, full of grace, and it tells of his victory and the salvation of his people. It is also bitter: it brings judgement on the unrepentant, and those who proclaim it will suffer, as chapter 11 is about to show. Both are true of the gospel at once.

And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter. Key words. John obeys, and experiences both. The order is reversed in the telling: sweet first in experience, then bitter.

What it does not mean. The bitterness does not mean God’s word is harmful. It means that taking God’s word seriously brings grief as well as joy: grief over sin and judgement, and the cost of faithful witness. A preacher or Christian who only ever finds the word sweet may not have digested all of it.

In a sentence. Then the voice I had heard from heaven spoke to me again: Go and take the open scroll from the hand of the angel standing on the sea and the land; so I went to the angel and asked him for the little scroll, and he said, Take it and eat it; it will turn your stomach sour, but in your mouth it will taste as sweet as honey; I took the little scroll from his hand and ate it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had swallowed it, my stomach turned bitter.

On a Tuesday. Read the Bible not just for information but to take it in, slowly, prayerfully, until it becomes part of you. Expect it to bring both delight and grief, and let both shape how you speak to others.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

And I was told. Key words. “I was told” (legousin moi, they say to me): an indefinite plural, probably meaning the heavenly voice and the angel together.

You must again prophesy. Key words. “Must” (dei): it is necessary, a divine command. “Again” (palin): John’s commission is renewed. He has already prophesied; now he must go on, with the second half of the book. “Prophesy” (prophēteusai).

About many peoples and nations and languages and kings. Key words. “About” (epi, concerning, or against). The whole world, and its rulers, are the subject of what follows. A fourfold list, as in 5:9 and 7:9, with “kings” in place of “tribes”, pointing ahead to the kings of the earth in chapters 13–19. The message concerns the fate of the nations and their rulers, for judgement and for salvation.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that John will literally travel and preach to all nations. His prophecy, written in this book, goes to them. And the church, taking up his commission, prophesies to the nations through the gospel (11:3–6).

In a sentence. Then I was told, You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings.

On a Tuesday. The gospel concerns every nation and every ruler. Pray for kings and those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and support the spread of the gospel to all peoples.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire.<sup>2</sup>He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,<sup>3</sup>and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded.<sup>4</sup>And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”<sup>5</sup>And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven<sup>6</sup>and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay,<sup>7</sup>but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.<sup>8</sup>Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”<sup>9</sup>So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”<sup>10</sup>And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.<sup>11</sup>And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers — but expressly not the outer court, which is given over to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Measuring in the prophets is a legal owner marking out what is his (Ezek. 40–42; Zech. 2:1–5). Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–4: two witnesses are granted authority to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth — the coarse black goat hair of mourning, not the uniform of a triumphant movement. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands of Zechariah 4, where two olive trees feed oil straight into a lampstand and the governing word is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:6).

Verses 5–6 give their powers, and they are two men’s résumés side by side: fire from the mouth (cf. Jer. 5:14), shutting the sky so that no rain falls — Elijah, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25) — and turning water to blood and striking with plagues, which is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

Verses 7–8: when they have finished their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. John supplies the interpretive key himself: pneumatikōs, symbolically. Verses 9–10: for three and a half days the world gazes at the bodies, refuses them burial, and throws the only party in the book — making merry and exchanging presents, because these two prophets had been a torment.

Verses 11–12: a breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Ezek. 37:10), and a loud voice says Come up here! — the words spoken to John at 4:1 — and they go up in a cloud and their enemies watched them. Verse 13: an earthquake takes a tenth of the city and seven thousand people, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Verse 14 closes the section: the second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

Meaning first. Revelation 11 shows the church’s life and witness in this age, and then the sounding of the seventh trumpet. John is told to measure God’s temple, its altar and its worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months (vv. 1–2): God’s people are protected in their inner life, while exposed outwardly to persecution. Two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth, prophesy for 1,260 days; they are the two olive trees and two lampstands, and like Elijah and Moses they have power to devour enemies with fire, shut the sky and strike the earth with plagues (vv. 3–6). When their testimony is finished, the beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie unburied in the great city, spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified, while the world celebrates (vv. 7–10). After three and a half days, God’s breath enters them, they stand up, and they are taken up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watch (vv. 11–12). An earthquake strikes, seven thousand die, and the rest give glory to God (vv. 13–14). Then the seventh trumpet sounds: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ; the elders give thanks that God has begun to reign, judged the dead, rewarded his servants and destroyed the destroyers; and God’s temple in heaven opens to show the ark of the covenant (vv. 15–19). The chapter pictures the whole church age: a witnessing church, protected yet suffering, apparently defeated, finally vindicated, and the kingdom of Christ coming in full.

Setting and background. Ezekiel 40–48 describes an angel measuring a new temple, a vision of God’s restored dwelling among his people. Zechariah 2:1–5 describes a man measuring Jerusalem, which God will protect as a wall of fire. Measuring in the Old Testament can mean protecting and preserving what belongs to God (Zechariah 2), or marking out for judgement (2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Daniel spoke of a period of a time, times and half a time (three and a half years) during which a hostile king would persecute God’s holy people (Daniel 7:25; 12:7). Jesus said that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24).

Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff. Key words. “Measuring rod” (kalamos, a reed, a measuring stick about three metres long).

Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there. Key words. “Temple” (naon, sanctuary, the inner shrine). “Those who worship there”: people, not just a building. In the New Testament, the temple of God is the church, God’s people in whom he dwells (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:19–22; 1 Peter 2:5). Measuring the temple means God marks out his people as his own and guarantees their protection, as the sealing did in chapter 7.

But do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations. Key words. “Leave that out” (ekbale exōthen, throw it outside). The outer court was where Gentiles could come in Herod’s temple. Here it stands for the church’s outward, visible life in the world, which is exposed to attack. The church is safe in its inner relationship with God, but outwardly vulnerable to persecution.

And they will trample the holy city for forty-two months. Key words. “Trample” (patēsousin, tread under foot). “Holy city”: God’s people, the church, as the new Jerusalem (21:2). “Forty-two months”: three and a half years, the same period as 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, times and half a time (12:14). It recalls Daniel’s period of persecution, and the three and a half years of drought in Elijah’s day (Luke 4:25; James 5:17). Half of seven: a limited time, cut short, of trouble for God’s people. In Revelation, it is the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings, when the church witnesses and suffers.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal temple in Jerusalem? Dispensationalists hold that a third temple will be rebuilt in Jerusalem before Christ returns, with sacrifices restored, and that this passage describes it during a literal three-and-a-half-year period. Verdict: the temple is the church, the people of God. The New Testament never anticipates a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices; Hebrews teaches that Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice has made the temple and its sacrifices obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:11–18). Revelation itself shows no temple in the new Jerusalem, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The worshippers are measured with the temple, showing that people are in view. And the number forty-two months is drawn from Daniel’s symbolic times, used in Revelation for the whole church age.

What it does not mean. The trampling does not mean that God has abandoned his people or lost control. He measures and protects; he sets the time limit. The outer court is given over by his permission, for a set time.

In a sentence. Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and told: Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count those who worship there; but leave out the courtyard outside the temple and do not measure it, because it has been handed over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

On a Tuesday. The world may trample on the church outwardly, mocking, marginalising and persecuting it. But God has measured you as his own. Your inner life with him is safe.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.” These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

Setting and background. In Zechariah 4, the prophet sees a golden lampstand with two olive trees beside it, supplying oil; they are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, a king and a priest who rebuilt the temple, not by might nor by power, but by God’s Spirit. In the law, two witnesses were required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus sent his disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Sackcloth was worn in mourning and repentance, as by the prophets (Isaiah 20:2; Jonah 3:5–6).

And I will grant authority to my two witnesses. Key words. “Witnesses” (martysin). Witness is the church’s calling throughout Revelation (1:2, 9; 2:13; 6:9; 12:11, 17). “Two”: the legal number for valid testimony. Their witness is true and will stand in God’s court.

And they will prophesy for 1,260 days. Key words. 1,260 days is forty-two months, the same period as the trampling of the holy city (v. 2). The church witnesses through the whole time of its suffering.

Clothed in sackcloth. Key words. Their message is a call to repentance, and they mourn over the world’s sin.

These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. Key words. “Lampstands”: in 1:20, the lampstands are the churches. So the two witnesses are the church, in its role of witness. “Olive trees”: from Zechariah 4, a king and a priest, empowered by the Spirit; the church is a kingdom of priests (1:6), and its witness depends on the Spirit, not on might or power. In Zechariah there is one lampstand; here there are two, perhaps for the two witnesses required by law, or for the church drawn from Jews and Gentiles. Of the seven churches, two (Smyrna and Philadelphia) received only praise, faithful witnesses.

Where Christians differ: who are the two witnesses? Many futurists see them as two individual prophets in a future tribulation, often Moses and Elijah returned, or Enoch and Elijah (who did not die). Others suggest Peter and Paul, martyred in Rome. Verdict: the two witnesses symbolise the witnessing church throughout this age. Revelation tells us the lampstands are churches (1:20). Their ministry lasts for the same period as the church’s trampling, the whole age. The whole world sees their deaths (v. 9), which suits a worldwide church better than two individuals. And the beast makes war on them (v. 7), as it makes war on the saints (13:7). They are pictured with the powers of Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, because the church carries on the prophetic witness of the Old Testament, in the power of the Spirit.

What it does not mean. The two witnesses are not a special class of Christians while others are spectators. All believers are called to be faithful witnesses to Christ, in word and life (Acts 1:8).

In a sentence. And I will give my two witnesses authority to prophesy for 1,260 days, dressed in sackcloth; these witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand in the presence of the Lord of the earth.

On a Tuesday. You are part of the witnessing church. Not by might nor by power, but by God’s Spirit, your words and life point people to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.

Setting and background. Elijah called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent to arrest him (2 Kings 1:10–12), and announced a drought that lasted three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17). Moses turned the Nile into blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). God told Jeremiah, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them (Jeremiah 5:14).

And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. Key words. “From their mouth” (ek tou stomatos autōn). Not from heaven, as in Elijah’s case, but from their mouth: their words. As Christ’s sword comes from his mouth (1:16), the witnesses’ fire is the word of God they speak. The word of judgement they proclaim will finally consume those who reject it.

If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. Key words. “Doomed” (dei, must). Those who oppose God’s witnesses are opposing God, and will be judged by the word they rejected (John 12:48).

They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying. Key words. Like Elijah. The church’s prayers and witness have real power in the world (James 5:16–18).

And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire. Key words. Like Moses. The plagues of the trumpets are linked to the church’s witness and prayers (8:3–5). The witnesses’ word announces God’s judgements, and their prayers call them down.

Where Christians differ: should the church expect such miracles today? Some read these verses as promising that end-time believers will perform Elijah-like and Moses-like miracles, and some charismatic groups expect such signs as normal. Verdict: the images are symbolic of the power of the church’s witness, which comes through the word of God and prayer. The miraculous signs of Moses, Elijah and the apostles served to confirm new revelation at key moments in redemptive history (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). This app holds, charitably, that such sign gifts have ceased with the completion of the canon. God still answers prayer powerfully, and still judges the world; but the church’s fire is the word it speaks, not miracles performed at will.

What it does not mean. This does not authorise Christians to call down judgement on their enemies. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is God’s, through the word; we preach and pray, and leave judgement to God.

In a sentence. If anyone tries to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and burns up their enemies; anyone who wants to hurt them must die like this; they have power to shut up the sky so that no rain falls while they are prophesying, and power to turn water into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague whenever they want.

On a Tuesday. The word of God is powerful. When you speak it faithfully and pray, you are doing more than you know.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.

Setting and background. In Daniel 7:21, the horn of the fourth beast made war with the saints and prevailed over them. To leave a body unburied was the greatest dishonour in the ancient world (Psalm 79:2–3). Sodom was the Old Testament’s symbol of wickedness (Genesis 19; Isaiah 1:10); Egypt was the land of slavery and oppression of God’s people.

And when they have finished their testimony. Key words. “Finished” (telesōsin, completed). Until then, nothing could harm them. God’s witnesses are immortal until their work is done. Only when God allows it can the beast touch them.

The beast that rises from the bottomless pit. Key words. “Beast” (thērion, wild animal). The first mention of the beast, introduced as if already known (Daniel 7), and described fully in chapter 13. It rises from the abyss, the realm of demons (9:1–2), and represents the power of the state, or of any human system, when it sets itself against God and persecutes his people.

Will make war on them and conquer them and kill them. Key words. “Conquer” (nikēsei). The beast seems to conquer, as in 13:7. But the church conquers by being faithful unto death, as the Lamb did (12:11). Apparent defeat is real victory.

And their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city. Key words. “Great city” (tēs poleōs tēs megalēs). In Revelation, the great city is always Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10), the world system opposed to God. The holy city (v. 2) and the great city stand opposed.

That symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt. Key words. “Symbolically” (pneumatikōs, spiritually). John tells us directly that the city is to be understood symbolically. It is Sodom in its wickedness, Egypt in its oppression of God’s people.

Where their Lord was crucified. Key words. This points to Jerusalem, where Jesus died. But Jerusalem in rejecting him became like Sodom and Egypt (Isaiah 1:9–10). And the great city is wherever the world rejects Christ and persecutes his witnesses. Jerusalem crucified the Lord; the world system kills his witnesses. As their Lord was treated, so are they (John 15:18–20).

What it does not mean. The great city is not just one city on a map. It is the world in its rebellion against God, which showed its true face by crucifying Christ, and which shows it again whenever it persecutes his people.

In a sentence. When they have finished giving their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will wage war on them, overpower them and kill them, and their corpses will lie in the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, the city where their Lord was also crucified.

On a Tuesday. You cannot be stopped until your work is done. And if faithfulness costs you, you are walking where your Lord walked.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.

For three and a half days. Key words. A short time compared with their 1,260 days of witness. Three and a half again: limited, cut short. The world’s triumph over the church is brief.

Some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies. Key words. “Gaze” (blepousin, look at). The four terms for all humanity (5:9; 7:9). People from every nation see. This points to a worldwide reality: the church’s suffering is seen by the whole world, not just one city.

And refuse to let them be placed in a tomb. Key words. Denial of burial: total contempt, the final insult.

And those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents. Key words. “Rejoice” (chairousin) and “make merry” (euphrainontai). “Exchange presents” (dōra pempsousin, send gifts), as at a festival (Esther 9:19, 22). A grotesque parody of a holiday: the world celebrates the silencing of God’s witnesses. Compare the joy of heaven when Babylon falls (18:20; 19:1–3).

Because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth. Key words. “Torment” (ebasanisan). The witnesses’ message, calling people to repent, and warning them of judgement, tormented the consciences of the world. People hate the light, because it exposes their deeds (John 3:20).

What it does not mean. The world’s rejoicing does not mean the church has failed. Its witness was so powerful that its silence brought relief to its enemies. The world rejoiced over Jesus’ death too, but only for three days.

In a sentence. For three and a half days, people from every people, tribe, language and nation will stare at their bodies and will not allow them to be buried; the inhabitants of the earth will gloat over them, celebrate and send each other gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them.

On a Tuesday. If the world celebrates when Christians are silenced or disgraced, do not be surprised. The truth always troubles a guilty conscience. Hold on: the world’s party is short.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 37:5, 10, God says to the dry bones that he will cause breath to enter them and they will live, and breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Jesus ascended in a cloud while his disciples watched (Acts 1:9).

But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them. Key words. “Breath of life” (pneuma zōēs, spirit of life). The same word means breath and spirit. As in Ezekiel 37 and Genesis 2:7, God gives life by his breath. The witnesses are raised by God, as their Lord was.

And they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Key words. “Great fear” (phobos megas). The celebration turns to terror. The resurrection of God’s people is their vindication, and their enemies’ dismay.

Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, Come up here! Key words. The same call John heard in 4:1. They are summoned into God’s presence.

And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them. Key words. Like Christ’s ascension. Their enemies see it publicly. God vindicates his witnesses openly.

Where Christians differ: is this the rapture? Some read this as a mid-tribulation rapture of two individual prophets, or of the church. Verdict: if the two witnesses are the church, their resurrection and ascension picture the resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ rise and the church is caught up to meet the Lord in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). It is public, seen by their enemies, not secret. It follows the church’s whole period of witness and suffering, and it is followed at once by the final judgement and the seventh trumpet (v. 15), which Paul also links with the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52). There is one visible return, with one resurrection of the righteous and the gathering of the church at that time.

What it does not mean. The church is not raised to escape the world’s judgement before it suffers. It is raised after it has finished its witness, after its death. Vindication comes through suffering, not instead of it.

In a sentence. But after three and a half days, the breath of life from God came into them, and they stood up, and terror gripped everyone who saw them; then they heard a loud voice from heaven calling to them, Come up here! and they went up to heaven in a cloud while their enemies looked on.

On a Tuesday. Whatever happens to you for Christ’s sake, God will have the last word, and it will be resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.

Setting and background. In Elijah’s day, God kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Here the number is reversed: seven thousand die. In the Old Testament, giving glory to God sometimes means confessing the truth and turning to him in repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16).

And at that hour there was a great earthquake. Key words. Earthquakes accompany God’s coming in judgement (6:12; 8:5; 16:18).

And a tenth of the city fell. Key words. “A tenth”: a further step beyond the quarter (seals) and third (trumpets), but still partial. A tithe, perhaps: a portion offered up in judgement, while the rest is spared to repent.

Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake. Key words. Literally, seven thousand names of men. A tenth of the city, perhaps symbolic of a city of seventy thousand. Seven: completeness.

And the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Key words. “Gave glory” (edōkan doxan). Unlike the response to the trumpets (9:20–21), where people did not repent, here they do. What judgements alone could not do, the church’s witness, death and vindication achieve. This is the purpose of the church’s suffering witness: the conversion of the nations. Most of the city, nine-tenths, turns to God. Compare the reversal of Elijah’s seven thousand: then only a remnant was saved; here only a remnant is judged, and most are saved.

Where Christians differ: is this genuine repentance? Some take “gave glory” as a terrified, forced acknowledgement of God, not true conversion. Verdict: the phrase in Revelation is used for true worship and repentance: in 14:7 the angel calls the nations to fear God and give him glory, and in 16:9 those who did not repent refused to give him glory. Here, unlike 9:20–21, the response is positive. It points to the fruit of the church’s faithful witness: many from the nations turning to God. This fits the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24).

The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come. Key words. The second woe is the sixth trumpet with its interlude (9:13–11:14). The third woe is the seventh trumpet, the final judgement.

What it does not mean. The conversion of many does not mean everyone will be saved. Seven thousand died under judgement. But it shows that the gospel will triumph among the nations.

In a sentence. At that very moment there was a violent earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed; seven thousand people died in the earthquake, and the survivors were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven; the second woe has passed, and look, the third woe is coming quickly.

On a Tuesday. The church’s faithful witness, even through suffering, bears fruit. Do not lose heart: many will yet turn to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 15: the seventh trumpet sounds and brings no plague at all, only an announcement — The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Singular kingdom, not plural: one worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands. And the verb is aorist, a completed act: not will become but has become.

Verses 16–17: the twenty-four elders come off their own thrones onto their faces, giving thanks to Lord God Almighty, who is and who was — and the threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8 has lost its third term. The one who is to come has come, and the future tense drops out of the name of God. You have taken your great power and begun to reign: not been given, but taken. He was always sovereign; what changes is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed.

Verse 18 quotes Psalm 2:1 in the past tense — the nations raged, and it is over — and lists what the moment contains: wrath; the dead judged; the servants rewarded, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great; and destroying the destroyers of the earth, an exact reciprocity using the same root twice.

Verse 19 opens the temple in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple — the object that stood behind the veil, seen by one man once a year, and lost when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Then the storm signs, now five of them: lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was — the one to come has come — and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

Setting and background. Psalm 2:2 speaks of the kings of the earth setting themselves against the LORD and against his Anointed (Christ). Daniel 2:44 and 7:14, 27 foretell a kingdom that God will set up that will never be destroyed, given to the Son of Man and to the saints of the Most High, an everlasting kingdom. Exodus 15:18, the song of Moses, ends: The LORD will reign for ever and ever.

Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet. Key words. The last trumpet, the third woe (11:14), announced in 10:7 as the moment when the mystery of God would be fulfilled. Paul speaks of the last trumpet at which the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The seventh trumpet does not describe new plagues; it announces the end.

And there were loud voices in heaven, saying, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Key words. “Kingdom of the world” (hē basileia tou kosmou, singular): the whole world system, under the rule of Satan and the beast, now becomes the kingdom of God and his Messiah. “Has become” (egeneto, past tense): so certain it is described as done. “Christ” (Christou, Anointed One, Messiah), as in Psalm 2.

And he shall reign forever and ever. Key words. “He” (singular). God and his Christ reign as one. Handel’s Hallelujah Chorus sets these words. The reign is eternal: no thousand-year limit, no end.

And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God. The representatives of God’s people respond with worship.

Saying, We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was. Key words. “Who is and who was”: notice that “and who is to come” (1:4, 8; 4:8) is missing. He has now come. The future has arrived.

For you have taken your great power and begun to reign. Key words. “Taken” (eilēphas, perfect tense, decisively taken). “Begun to reign” (ebasileusas, entered on your reign). God has always been sovereign, but now his reign is openly established over all opposition. What was hidden is revealed; what was contested is settled.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “and art to come” after “who is and who was”. The best manuscripts do not have it, and its absence is deliberate: at this point in the vision, God has come.

Where Christians differ: does Christ’s kingdom come gradually or suddenly? Postmillennialists believe that the gospel will gradually transform the world until most of humanity is Christian, and then Christ will return. Premillennialists believe Christ will return to set up a thousand-year earthly kingdom. Verdict: Christ already reigns now, at the Father’s right hand (1:5; Ephesians 1:20–22), and his kingdom grows through the gospel. But the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ in full only at his return, at the last trumpet, when he judges the living and the dead. There is no thousand-year interval between the last trumpet and the eternal reign; he will reign for ever and ever from the moment of his return.

What it does not mean. God did not lack power before. The words describe the open, public, final display of the reign he always had.

In a sentence. Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven proclaimed: The rule over the world now belongs to our Lord and to his Messiah, and he will reign for ever and ever; and the twenty-four elders, seated on their thrones before God, fell face down and worshipped God, saying: We thank you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, because you have taken up your great power and begun your reign.

For worship. Sing the Hallelujah Chorus with understanding. One day, every kingdom of this world will belong to Christ, and he will reign for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.” Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

Setting and background. Psalm 2:1, 5 says the nations rage, but God speaks to them in his wrath. The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, stood in the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s throne on earth, where the high priest sprinkled atoning blood once a year (Exodus 25:10–22; Leviticus 16). It disappeared when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid it, and it would reappear when God gathered his people again (2 Maccabees 2:4–8).

The nations raged, but your wrath came. Key words. “Raged” (ōrgisthēsan, were angry) and “wrath” (orgē): the same root. The nations’ anger against God is met by God’s anger against them. Their rage is futile; his is just and final.

And the time for the dead to be judged. Key words. “Time” (kairos, the appointed moment). The final judgement of all the dead (20:11–15).

And for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great. Key words. “Rewarding” (dounai ton misthon, giving the wages). God rewards his people: the prophets, and all the saints, small and great. No one is too insignificant to be noticed and rewarded (Matthew 10:42). The reward is grace, not wages earned (22:12).

And for destroying the destroyers of the earth. Key words. “Destroying” (diaphtheirai, ruining, corrupting). A fitting justice: those who ruin the earth, morally and physically, by violence, idolatry and corruption, will be ruined. Babylon is said to have corrupted the earth (19:2). God made the earth good, and he will judge those who destroy it, and renew it.

Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. Key words. “Opened” (ēnoigē). The Most Holy Place, once closed to all but the high priest once a year, is opened. God’s presence is accessible. The ark, lost for centuries, is seen in heaven: God has not forgotten his covenant. The covenant promises, sealed with blood, are kept.

There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail. Key words. The same sign that ended the seals (8:5), now intensified with hail. The final judgement. The same sign, intensified again, ends the bowls (16:18–21).

What it does not mean. The seventh trumpet does not end the book because Revelation is not a straight timeline. Chapter 12 will go back to the birth of Christ and show the same age again, from the angle of the spiritual war behind it.

In a sentence. The nations were furious, but now your anger has come, and the time has come to judge the dead, to reward your servants the prophets, your people and all who fear your name, the unimportant and the important alike, and to destroy those who destroy the earth; then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant could be seen inside it, and there came lightning, rumbling, thunder, an earthquake and a great hailstorm.

For worship. Worship the God who keeps his covenant. The ark is in heaven, and the way into God’s presence is open through Christ’s blood.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.
