verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman — the covenant people, Israel and the church — bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.

Meaning first. Revelation 12 goes behind the scenes of history to show the spiritual war that explains why the church suffers. A woman clothed with the sun, crowned with twelve stars, cries out in labour (vv. 1–2). A great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, whose tail sweeps down a third of the stars, waits to devour her child (vv. 3–4). She gives birth to a son who will rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God’s throne, and she flees to the wilderness, where God nourishes her for 1,260 days (vv. 5–6). War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, and he is thrown down to earth with his angels (vv. 7–9). A voice in heaven rejoices: the accuser has been thrown down, and believers have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives even unto death; but woe to the earth, for the devil has come down in great fury, knowing his time is short (vv. 10–12). The dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings to escape to the wilderness, and the earth swallows the flood he sends after her (vv. 13–16). Furious, he goes to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus (v. 17). The chapter explains the church’s situation: Satan is a defeated enemy, beaten at the cross, enraged because his time is short, and taking out his fury on God’s people, who are protected by God and who conquer him through Christ’s blood and their faithful witness.

Setting and background. In Joseph’s dream, the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his father, mother and brothers, the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9–10). The prophets picture Israel, or Zion, as a woman in labour, longing for deliverance (Isaiah 26:17–18; 66:7–9; Micah 4:10; 5:3). In Genesis 3:15, God told the serpent that the offspring of the woman would crush his head, and that he would strike his heel. Ancient myths told similar stories: in the Greek myth, the dragon Python pursued the goddess Leto, pregnant with Apollo, who later killed the dragon. The emperors identified themselves with Apollo. Revelation tells the true story behind the myths: the real child is Christ, and the real dragon is Satan.

And a great sign appeared in heaven. Key words. “Sign” (sēmeion). John tells us directly that this is a symbol. The first time Revelation uses the word.

A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. Key words. Glory, authority and heavenly identity. Twelve stars: the twelve tribes of Israel, and also the twelve apostles. She is the people of God, the messianic community from which the Messiah comes and which continues as the church.

She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth. Key words. “Birth pains” (ōdinousa). The suffering of God’s people in the Old Testament as they waited for the Messiah. The long years of Israel’s history, under oppression, longing for the promised offspring.

Where Christians differ: is the woman Mary? Roman Catholic tradition has long identified the woman with the Virgin Mary, and has used this passage in support of Marian devotion and of her bodily assumption into heaven. Verdict: the woman is the people of God, Israel and then the church. There is a secondary allusion to Mary, who literally gave birth to the Messiah, and she belongs to the people of God. But the woman’s experiences cannot be Mary’s: she is persecuted in the wilderness for 1,260 days after her child ascends (v. 6), and she has other offspring who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (v. 17), who are believers. The twelve stars point to the twelve tribes. Nothing here supports praying to Mary, or her being given a special role in salvation.

What it does not mean. The woman is not the church only in the New Testament sense, as if the Messiah were born from the church. She is the one people of God across both covenants, from whom Christ came, and who continues in the church.

In a sentence. Then a great sign appeared in the sky: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head; she was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth.

On a Tuesday. You belong to a people with a long story, stretching back through Israel to Eve. God’s promise of a Saviour was carried through centuries of pain, and it was kept.
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.

Setting and background. In the Old Testament, the sea monster or dragon (Leviathan, Rahab) is a symbol of chaos and of evil powers opposed to God, and of empires such as Egypt (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13–14; Ezekiel 29:3). Daniel 7 describes four beasts, the fourth with ten horns, representing world empires. Daniel 8:10 describes a horn that grew great and threw down some of the stars to the ground and trampled them. At Christ’s birth, King Herod tried to kill him by slaughtering the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:13–18).

And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon. Key words. “Dragon” (drakōn, a great serpent). Identified in v. 9 as the devil, Satan. “Red” (pyrros, fiery red): the colour of bloodshed, like the second horseman (6:4). He was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).

With seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. Key words. “Seven heads”: complete cunning or power. “Ten horns”: great strength, as in Daniel’s fourth beast. “Diadems” (diadēmata, royal crowns, not victors’ wreaths). Satan claims royal authority over the world (Luke 4:5–6; John 12:31). The beast of chapter 13 will look like him, because the beast is his agent.

His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. Key words. Stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This probably refers to the angels who fell with Satan, the demons (v. 9). Or it pictures his destructive power and his attack on God’s people, like the horn in Daniel 8:10.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it. Key words. “Devour” (kataphagē, eat up). Satan’s great aim throughout history was to destroy the promised offspring: through Pharaoh’s murder of the Hebrew boys (Exodus 1), through attempts to wipe out the line of David (2 Kings 11:1–3), through Haman (Esther 3), through Herod, and finally through the cross.

What it does not mean. The dragon’s crowns do not mean his rule is legitimate or unlimited. He is a usurper, and his crowns are claims, not rights. Christ wears many diadems (19:12).

In a sentence. Then another sign appeared in the sky: a huge red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, with a royal crown on each head; his tail dragged a third of the stars out of the sky and flung them down to earth; and the dragon stood in front of the woman as she was about to give birth, ready to devour her child the moment it was born.

On a Tuesday. Behind the evil you see in the world is a real enemy with a real strategy. Do not be naive about him, but do not be afraid either: he failed to devour the child.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.

Setting and background. Psalm 2:9 says that God’s Son, his anointed King, will break the nations with a rod of iron. After the exodus, God led Israel into the wilderness, where he fed them with manna and protected them for forty years (Exodus 16; Deuteronomy 8:2–4). Elijah fled into the wilderness and was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:2–6; 19:4–8). The holy family fled into Egypt to escape Herod (Matthew 2:13–15).

She gave birth to a male child. Key words. “Male child” (huion arsen, a son, a male). Echoing Isaiah 66:7, where Zion gives birth to a son before her labour pains. The child is clearly Christ.

One who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. Key words. From Psalm 2:9, as in 2:27 and 19:15. Christ is the Messiah-King.

But her child was caught up to God and to his throne. Key words. “Caught up” (hērpasthē, snatched up, the same word used for believers caught up to meet the Lord in 1 Thessalonians 4:17). The whole life of Jesus, his ministry, death and resurrection, is compressed into a single moment between birth and ascension. The point is that the dragon failed. Christ was not devoured; he was exalted to God’s throne. The cross, which seemed to be Satan’s victory, led to Christ’s enthronement.

And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God. Key words. “Wilderness” (erēmon, desert). In Scripture, the wilderness is a place of testing but also of God’s protection and provision. “Prepared by God” (hētoimasmenon apo tou theou). The church, after Christ’s ascension, lives as in the wilderness: not yet in the promised land, exposed to hardship, but protected and provided for by God.

In which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days. Key words. “Nourished” (trephōsin, fed, sustained). As God fed Israel with manna, he sustains his church by his word and Spirit. 1,260 days: the same period as the witnesses’ prophesying and the trampling of the holy city (11:2–3). The whole age between Christ’s ascension and return.

What it does not mean. The church in the wilderness does not mean the church is hidden or withdrawn from the world. It means the church lives as pilgrims and exiles (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11), protected by God in the midst of hostility.

In a sentence. She gave birth to a son, a boy who is to rule all the nations with an iron rod, but her child was snatched up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the desert to a place God had prepared for her, where she would be cared for during 1,260 days.

On a Tuesday. The church is in the wilderness, between Egypt and the promised land. Expect hardship, and expect God’s daily provision. He feeds his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.

Setting and background. In Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1, Michael is the great prince who protects God’s people. In Jude 9 he is called the archangel. In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1, Satan appears before God to accuse God’s people. Jesus said, when the seventy-two returned from their mission, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18), and, as the cross approached, now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31).

Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. Key words. “Michael” (Hebrew: who is like God?). The protector of God’s people. Notice that it is Michael, not God or Christ, who fights the dragon: Satan is not God’s equal rival but a creature defeated by another creature. The real victory has already been won by the Lamb (v. 11); Michael’s victory in heaven reflects Christ’s victory on earth.

And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated. Key words. “Defeated” (ouk ischysen, was not strong enough). Satan is powerful, but not powerful enough.

And there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Key words. Satan lost his position as accuser before God (v. 10). After the cross, his accusations have no standing.

And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent. Key words. “Ancient serpent” (ho ophis ho archaios): the serpent of Eden (Genesis 3:1), who deceived Eve. The one whose head the woman’s offspring would crush (Genesis 3:15).

Who is called the devil and Satan. Key words. “Devil” (diabolos, slanderer, accuser). “Satan” (Hebrew satan, adversary, accuser). Four names: dragon, serpent, devil, Satan. All his identities are exposed.

The deceiver of the whole world. Key words. “Deceiver” (ho planōn, the one who leads astray). Deception is his main weapon, from Eden onwards (2 Corinthians 4:4; 11:3, 14). He deceives the nations through the beast and false prophet (13:14; 20:3, 8).

He was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him. Key words. “Thrown down” (eblēthē, three times). Decisive defeat. His sphere is now the earth, where he rages against the church (v. 12).

Where Christians differ: when was Satan thrown down? Some place this at Satan’s original fall before creation; others at a future point in the last days, at the midpoint of a seven-year tribulation. Verdict: the context places it at Christ’s death, resurrection and ascension. The child has just been caught up to God’s throne (v. 5), and the voice in heaven says that salvation and the kingdom have now come, because the accuser has been thrown down, and that believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). The cross is where Satan was defeated (John 12:31–32; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). His original rebellion lies behind this, and his final destruction lies ahead (20:10), but his decisive defeat happened at Calvary.

What it does not mean. Being thrown down does not mean Satan is powerless now. He is defeated but still dangerous, like a wounded animal, and the next verses show his fury. But he is a beaten foe.

In a sentence. Then war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back, but they were not strong enough and lost their place in heaven; the great dragon was thrown down, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, who leads the whole world astray; he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels with him.

On a Tuesday. When you face temptation or accusation, remember that the devil is a defeated enemy. He lies, and his greatest lie is that he is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”

Setting and background. In Zechariah 3:1–5, Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him; the LORD rebukes Satan and removes Joshua’s filthy garments, clothing him in pure clothes. Paul asks, who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come. Key words. “Now” (arti, at this moment). With Christ’s victory, the kingdom of God has come. Not only future: it arrived at the cross and resurrection, and Christ now has authority (Matthew 28:18).

For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Key words. “Accuser” (katēgōr, prosecutor). Satan accuses believers before God, pointing to their sins and arguing that they deserve condemnation. And he accuses them in their own consciences. But he has lost his case: Christ has paid for every sin, and there is now no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1).

And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb. Key words. “Conquered” (enikēsan). How do believers defeat Satan? First, by the blood of the Lamb. Satan’s accusations are answered by Christ’s death in our place. His blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). This is the heart of the gospel, and the foundation of every victory over Satan.

And by the word of their testimony. Key words. “Testimony” (martyrias, witness). Second, by holding to and speaking the truth about Jesus. The deceiver is defeated when the truth is told.

For they loved not their lives even unto death. Key words. “Loved not” (ouk ēgapēsan). Third, by being willing to die rather than deny Christ. Satan’s last weapon is the threat of death, and it has no power over those who do not cling to their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). Jesus said that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it (Matthew 16:25).

Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! Key words. “You who dwell” (hoi … skēnountes, who tabernacle). Heaven rejoices because the accuser is gone. Believers, whose real home is in heaven, share this joy.

But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath. Key words. “Great wrath” (thymon megan, fury, rage). His defeat makes him more furious, not less.

Because he knows that his time is short! Key words. “Short” (oligon kairon, a little time). The whole age between Christ’s ascension and return is Satan’s short time, the same as the 1,260 days. He knows he is doomed. The persecution of the church is the rage of a defeated enemy.

What it does not mean. Conquering by the blood of the Lamb does not mean using the phrase as a magic formula, as in some deliverance practices. It means trusting in Christ’s finished work as the answer to every accusation.

In a sentence. Then I heard a loud voice in heaven say: Now God’s salvation, power and kingdom have come, and the authority of his Messiah, because the one who accused our brothers and sisters before our God day and night has been thrown down; they defeated him through the blood of the Lamb and the testimony they gave, because they did not cling to their lives even when faced with death; so celebrate, you heavens and all who live there; but how terrible for the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, full of fury, knowing that his time is short.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you, or the devil reminds you of your sins, answer with the blood of the Lamb. Christ has paid; the case is closed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.

Setting and background. God told Israel at Sinai, you have seen how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Exodus 19:4). Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle carrying its young on its wings. Isaiah 40:31 says those who wait on the LORD shall mount up with wings like eagles. Daniel 7:25 speaks of the saints given into the hand of the persecuting king for a time, times and half a time.

And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman. Key words. “Pursued” (ediōxen, persecuted, chased). Having failed to destroy the child, Satan turns on the child’s people, the church. Persecution of the church is Satan’s revenge on Christ.

But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle. Key words. “Was given”: God’s provision. As God carried Israel out of Egypt on eagles’ wings, he carries his church through the wilderness of this age.

So that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished. As in v. 6. God protects and feeds his people.

For a time, and times, and half a time. Key words. From Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: one year, two years and half a year, three and a half years. The same period as 1,260 days (v. 6) and forty-two months (11:2): the whole church age, a time of persecution limited by God.

What it does not mean. Protection in the wilderness does not mean individual believers will never suffer or die. The rest of her offspring are attacked (v. 17), and some are killed (13:7). It means the church as a whole will never be destroyed. The gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

In a sentence. When the dragon realised he had been thrown down to the earth, he went after the woman who had given birth to the boy; but the woman was given the two wings of a great eagle, so that she could fly away from the serpent to her place in the desert, where she would be cared for, out of his reach, for a time, times and half a time.

For worship. Thank God that he carries his people on eagles’ wings. However fierce the attack, the church will not be destroyed.

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

Setting and background. In the Psalms, floods and many waters picture overwhelming danger and the attacks of enemies (Psalm 18:4, 16; 32:6; 124:4–5). At the Red Sea, God opened a path through the waters for Israel, and the waters swept away Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14–15). When Korah rebelled against Moses, the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the rebels (Numbers 16:30–32). In the song of Moses, Israel sang, you stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them (Exodus 15:12).

The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. Key words. “Out of his mouth” (ek tou stomatos autou). The flood comes from his mouth: lies, deception, false teaching, slander and propaganda. As the witnesses’ fire is their word (11:5), so Satan’s flood is his. He tries to drown the church in falsehood.

But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river. Key words. God uses even his creation to protect his people. As at the Red Sea and with Korah, God intervenes. The flood of lies does not succeed. Throughout history, persecutions and heresies have risen and been swallowed up, while the church has survived.

Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring. Key words. “Furious” (ōrgisthē). “The rest of her offspring” (tōn loipōn tou spermatos autēs, the rest of her seed): the seed of the woman, as in Genesis 3:15. Christ is her first offspring; believers are her other children, Christ’s brothers and sisters (Romans 8:29; Hebrews 2:11–13). If the church as a whole is protected, individual believers are still attacked.

On those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. Key words. The definition of a true believer in Revelation: obedience to God and loyalty to Jesus (14:12). These are Satan’s targets.

And he stood on the sand of the sea. Key words. The dragon takes his stand at the seashore, ready to call up his ally from the sea (13:1). Satan works through human agents and systems.

Textual note. The last sentence is numbered 12:18 in some Bibles and 13:1 in others. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “I stood on the sand of the sea”, making John the subject. The best manuscripts read “he stood”, referring to the dragon.

What it does not mean. Satan’s war on believers does not mean God has abandoned them. They are her offspring, and God protects the woman. But they are on the front line, and they must keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.

In a sentence. Then the serpent spewed water like a river from his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away in the flood; but the earth helped the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing the river the dragon had spewed out; then the dragon was enraged with the woman and went off to wage war against the rest of her children, those who obey God’s commandments and hold firmly to their testimony about Jesus; and he stood on the seashore.

On a Tuesday. Satan floods the world with lies. Hold to the truth, keep God’s commandments, and hold the testimony of Jesus. That is what makes you his target, and that is how you overcome.

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the political theology chapter of Revelation. The dragon, standing on the seashore, summons two beasts — one from the sea, one from the land — and delegates to them his authority, his throne, and great power. Together the dragon and the two beasts form a Satanic trinity that parodies the Holy Trinity: the dragon parodies the Father, the beast from the sea parodies the Son (including a parody death and resurrection), and the beast from the land parodies the Spirit (pointing away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit points away from himself to the Son). The unholy trinity is the political and religious power structure of every totalitarian system that demands ultimate allegiance.

Interpretive flag — The Beast from the Sea: This is the third major structural decision point. The preterist reading identifies the beast as Nero Caesar — and the gematria (numerical value of letters) of “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew adds up to 666. The mortal wound that was healed (v. 3) refers to the Nero redivivus myth: rumors after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he had survived and would return from the east with the Parthian army. The historicist reading has identified the beast with various historical powers including the papacy. The futurist/dispensational reading sees a still-future individual world ruler, a literal Antichrist who will arise in the last days, be given global political power, and demand global worship. The idealist/amillennial reading understands the beast as the pattern of totalitarian political power that demands ultimate allegiance in every age — with Rome as the first-century embodiment and every subsequent empire that makes similar demands as its successor. The idealist position is followed here, while the specific Nero/Rome referent is fully acknowledged as the primary first-century layer.

Interpretive flag — 666: Three readings predominate. (1) Gematria: “Neron Kaisar” in Hebrew letters (nun-resh-vav-nun / qoph-samek-resh) adds to 666; the spelling without the final n adds to 616, which is the reading of some early manuscripts. The specific first-century referent. (2) The number of incompleteness: six is one less than seven (the number of divine completeness); 666 is the triple intensification of falling short of the divine — the beast is humanity at its most grandiose, still falling short of the glory of God. (3) The number of humanity: six was associated with humanity in some traditions (created on the sixth day). The beast is the ultimate expression of humanity’s totalitarian self-divinization. All three readings illuminate the symbol; none is exhaustive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a beast rises out of the sea with the dragon’s own features — seven heads, ten horns, royal diadems — and blasphemous names on its heads, which is what Roman coins and inscriptions actually gave the emperors. It is like a leopard, with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth: Daniel’s four beasts (Dan. 7:2–7) compressed into one. And the dragon gave it his power, his throne and great authority — the offer Christ refused in the desert (Luke 4:6).

Verses 3–4: one head has a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth marvels. The Greek uses the same participle used of the Lamb at 5:6, so the parody is deliberate. The world worships dragon and beast together, chanting Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? — the song of the exodus (Ex. 15:11) with a different object, and the meaning of the name Michael turned to the wrong address.

Verses 5–6: the beast was given a mouth of haughty and blasphemous words and was allowed authority for forty-two months (cf. Dan. 7:8, 25). It blasphemes God’s name and his dwelling — and John glosses the dwelling himself: that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Verses 7–8: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them, with authority over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all the earth-dwellers worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: If anyone has an ear, let him hear — captivity to captivity, sword to sword (cf. Jer. 15:2) — Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.

Meaning first. Revelation 13 introduces the dragon’s two allies, the instruments through which Satan makes war on the saints. A beast rises from the sea, with ten horns and seven heads like the dragon, combining features of Daniel’s four beasts, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority (vv. 1–2). One of its heads seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole world marvels and worships both the dragon and the beast: who is like the beast? (vv. 3–4). It speaks blasphemies against God for forty-two months, makes war on the saints and conquers them, and everyone whose name is not written in the Lamb’s book of life worships it (vv. 5–8). The saints are called to endure: captivity and death may come, and they must not resist with the sword (vv. 9–10). A second beast rises from the earth, with horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon; it promotes the worship of the first beast, performs deceptive signs, sets up a speaking image of the beast, and has those who refuse to worship it killed (vv. 11–15). It forces everyone to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell (vv. 16–17). The number of the beast is 666, the number of a man (v. 18). The chapter unmasks the political and religious powers that demand total loyalty in place of God. In John’s day that was Rome and its emperor cult; through the age it takes many forms; and it will reach a final climax before Christ returns.

Setting and background. In Daniel 7, four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a terrifying fourth beast with ten horns, representing four world empires, usually understood as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. A little horn on the fourth beast speaks great things, makes war on the saints and prevails for a time, times and half a time, until the Ancient of Days judges it and gives the kingdom to the saints. For John’s readers, Rome came from across the sea, and Roman governors arrived in Asia by ship. The emperors claimed divine titles: the coins called Augustus son of god and Domitian lord and god.

And I saw a beast rising out of the sea. Key words. “Beast” (thērion, wild animal, monster). “Sea”: the realm of chaos and evil (Daniel 7:2–3), and the abyss (11:7). The beast is a power from below, given human form.

With ten horns and seven heads. Key words. The same as the dragon (12:3). The beast is the dragon’s image. In 17:9–12, the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, and the ten horns ten kings.

With ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. Key words. “Diadems” (royal crowns). “Blasphemous names” (onomata blasphēmias): titles that belong only to God, such as lord, god, son of god and saviour, all claimed by the emperors.

And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. Key words. It combines Daniel’s first three beasts, in reverse order. It sums up all the godless empires of history in one. It is not just one empire but the spirit of every empire that sets itself against God.

And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority. Key words. “Gave” (edōken). The beast’s power comes from Satan. A grim parody of how the Father gives authority to the Son (2:27). Satan offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him (Luke 4:5–7); Jesus refused, but the beast accepts.

Where Christians differ: who is the beast? Preterists identify the beast with the Roman Empire and the emperor Nero. Historicists, including many Reformers, identified it with the papacy. Futurists see a single future world dictator, the Antichrist, at the end of history. Verdict: the beast is the persecuting power of the state, or any human system, that claims divine authority and demands worship, empowered by Satan. In John’s day it was clearly the Roman Empire and its emperor cult; through history it has reappeared in many forms, whenever a power demands the total loyalty that belongs to God alone; and Scripture expects a final, intensified manifestation before Christ returns, the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3–10). Many Reformers were right to see beastly features in the persecuting medieval church, but the beast is wider than any one institution. This combined view honours the first readers, every generation, and the end.

What it does not mean. Not all government is beastly. Paul teaches that governing authorities are instituted by God for good (Romans 13:1–7). The state becomes the beast when it oversteps its role, claims divine authority and demands worship, and persecutes those who refuse.

In a sentence. Then I saw a beast coming up out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, a royal crown on each horn and blasphemous names on its heads; it looked like a leopard, with feet like a bear’s and a mouth like a lion’s, and the dragon handed over to it his own power, his throne and great authority.

On a Tuesday. Respect the authorities God has placed over you, and pray for them. But give your ultimate loyalty only to Christ. When any power demands what belongs to God, the Christian must refuse.
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”

Setting and background. After Nero’s suicide in AD 68, the empire fell into civil war, with four emperors in one year, and seemed about to collapse, until Vespasian restored order. Rumours spread that Nero had not really died and would return from the east with a Parthian army (the Nero redivivus myth). In the Old Testament, Who is like you, O LORD? is a cry of praise to God (Exodus 15:11; Psalm 35:10; Micah 7:18); the name Michael means Who is like God?

One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound. Key words. “Seemed” (hōs, as though). “Mortal wound” (esphagmenēn eis thanaton, slain to death). The same word used of the Lamb who was slain (5:6). The beast imitates Christ’s death.

But its mortal wound was healed. Key words. “Healed” (etherapeuthē). A parody of Christ’s resurrection. The beast’s power seems to be destroyed, then revives. Godless powers often seem to fall, only to reappear in new forms.

And the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. Key words. “Marveled” (ethaumasthē, was amazed). “Followed” (opisō, after): as disciples follow a master. The world follows the beast as the church follows the Lamb (14:4).

And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast. Key words. Worshipping the beast is really worshipping Satan. All idolatry has a demonic source (1 Corinthians 10:20).

And they worshiped the beast, saying, Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? Key words. A parody of Israel’s praise of God. The world admires and fears power. The beast seems invincible. But the answer is Michael, Who is like God, who has already defeated the dragon (12:7–9), and the Lamb, who will conquer the beast (17:14).

What it does not mean. The healed wound is not a prediction that a particular leader will be assassinated and then come back to life. It is a parody of Christ’s death and resurrection, showing that the beast is a counterfeit Christ, and that evil powers revive after apparent defeat.

In a sentence. One of the beast’s heads looked as if it had been fatally wounded, but the deadly wound had healed, and the whole world was astonished and went after the beast; people worshipped the dragon, because he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast too, saying, Who can compare with the beast? Who can fight against it?

On a Tuesday. Watch what amazes you. The world is dazzled by power, success and strength. Be amazed instead by the Lamb who was slain and rose again.

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Setting and background. In Daniel 7:8, 11, 20, 25, the little horn has a mouth speaking great things, and speaks words against the Most High. Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Greek king who persecuted the Jews in 167–164 BC, called himself God manifest, desecrated the temple, and is often seen as a forerunner of the antichrist (Daniel 11:36; 1 Maccabees 1).

And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words. Key words. “Was given” (edothē): four times in vv. 5–7. The beast does nothing except by permission. God sets its limits. “Haughty” (megala, great things, arrogant boasts).

And it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. Key words. The same period as the trampling of the holy city (11:2), the witnesses’ prophesying (11:3), and the woman’s protection in the wilderness (12:6, 14). The whole church age, between Christ’s comings. The beast’s rule and the church’s witness run side by side, for the same limited time.

It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven. Key words. “Blaspheming” (blasphēmēsai, slandering, insulting). Against God’s name (his character), his dwelling (skēnēn, tabernacle), and those who dwell in heaven. God’s tabernacle is his people (21:3), and those who dwell in heaven are believers, whose citizenship is there (12:12; Ephesians 2:6). So the beast mocks and slanders the church.

What it does not mean. Forty-two months is not a literal three and a half years at the end of history. It is Daniel’s symbolic period of persecution, which Revelation applies to the whole time of the church’s witness.

In a sentence. The beast was allowed to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and was permitted to exercise its authority for forty-two months; it opened its mouth to blaspheme God, insulting his name and his dwelling place, those who live in heaven.

On a Tuesday. When the culture mocks God and his people, remember that its time is limited. Do not answer mockery with mockery; answer with faithful witness.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.

Setting and background. Daniel 7:21 says the horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and judgement was given for the saints.

Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. Key words. “Conquer” (nikēsai). The beast seems to win: it kills believers (11:7). But in Revelation, those killed for their faith are the true conquerors (12:11; 15:2). The beast wins the battle of bodies; the saints win the battle of faithfulness.

And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation. Key words. A parody of the Lamb’s redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation (5:9). The beast’s rule seems universal.

And all who dwell on earth will worship it. Key words. “Those who dwell on earth”: the unbelieving world. Everyone worships something. Those who do not worship God will worship the beast.

Everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Key words. “Written” (gegraptai, perfect tense: has been written and stands written). “From the foundation of the world” (apo katabolēs kosmou). “Book of life of the Lamb”: the Lamb’s register of his people. The only ones who resist the beast are those written in the Lamb’s book. Their names were written before creation, by God’s eternal choice. Their perseverance rests not on their own strength but on God’s election.

Where Christians differ: what does “from the foundation of the world” go with? The Greek word order allows “the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (as in the King James Version) or “written from the foundation of the world in the book of life” (as in the ESV). Verdict: the second is more likely, because 17:8 uses the same phrase clearly of names written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. Both truths are biblical: Christ was foreknown as the sacrifice before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), and God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). The verse teaches unconditional election: God wrote the names of his people in the Lamb’s book before they were born, not because of anything they would do, and he keeps them from worshipping the beast.

What it does not mean. Election does not make anyone’s worship of the beast excusable; people are responsible for their idolatry. Nor does it make faithfulness unimportant; the elect are precisely those who refuse to worship the beast. God’s choice is the root, and faithful endurance is the fruit.

In a sentence. It was also allowed to wage war against God’s people and to overcome them, and it was given authority over every tribe, people, language and nation; all the earth’s inhabitants will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written, since the world was founded, in the book of life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.

For worship. Thank God that your name was written in the Lamb’s book before the world began. That is why you belong to him, and why you will not be lost.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.

Setting and background. Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11 say: those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword, and those who are for captivity, to captivity. When Peter drew his sword to defend Jesus, Jesus said, put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52).

If anyone has an ear, let him hear. Key words. The call of the seven letters (2:7). A direct application to the church.

If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes. Key words. Some believers will be imprisoned. This is under God’s sovereign plan. Accept it; do not try to escape by compromise.

If anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Key words. Some will be executed. This, too, is within God’s purpose.

Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints. Key words. “Endurance” (hypomonē, steadfastness, staying power). “Faith” (pistis, faith, faithfulness). The church’s response to the beast is not rebellion, revolution or violence, but patient endurance and faithful trust. This is how the saints conquer.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the second line. Some read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a warning against taking up the sword, as in Matthew 26:52 and the King James Version. Others read “if anyone is to be killed with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a call to accept martyrdom. Either way, the lesson is the same: believers must not resist the beast by violence, but endure in faith.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians may never defend themselves or others, or that believers should seek martyrdom. It means that the church does not advance its cause by force, and that when persecution comes because of faith, believers accept suffering rather than deny Christ or take up arms for the gospel.

In a sentence. Whoever can hear should listen: anyone destined for captivity will go into captivity, and anyone destined to be killed by the sword will be killed by the sword; this is why God’s people need endurance and faithfulness.

On a Tuesday. When you face hostility for your faith, do not retaliate. Endure, trust God and stay faithful. That is how the church wins.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–12: a second beast rises out of the earth — the opposite element, so that between them the dragon has the whole world covered. It has two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. Named three times later as the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), its entire function is to make the world worship the first beast.

Verses 13–15: it performs great signs, including fire from heaven — Elijah’s credential on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) — and by the signs it is allowed to work it deceives the earth-dwellers, telling them to make an image for the beast. It is allowed to give the image breath so that it speaks and orders the death of anyone who will not worship it. Behind this stands Daniel 3: an image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, and a furnace — and three men who said But if not (Dan. 3:17–18).

Verses 16–17: it marks all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Verse 18 sets the puzzle: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark — the beast’s name — without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.

Setting and background. Jesus warned of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15), and of false christs and false prophets who would perform great signs to deceive, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24). In the province of Asia, the emperor cult was promoted by local elites: priests of the imperial temples, city councils and the provincial council (the koinon), who organised festivals, sacrifices and games in the emperor’s honour.

Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. Key words. “Earth” (gē, land). The first beast came from the sea, from far away; the second comes from the land, local and familiar. Later called the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10).

It had two horns like a lamb. Key words. “Like a lamb” (homoia arniō). It looks harmless, even Christlike: a parody of the Lamb. Religious deception often looks gentle and attractive.

And it spoke like a dragon. Key words. Its message is Satan’s. It looks like a lamb but sounds like the serpent, deceiving as he did in Eden.

It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence. Key words. It serves the first beast, as the Holy Spirit glorifies Christ (John 16:14). Dragon, beast and false prophet form an unholy trinity, a counterfeit of Father, Son and Spirit.

And makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed. Key words. The false prophet’s role is religious: to promote the worship of the political power. Religion in service of the state; ideology that makes people worship power.

What it does not mean. The second beast is not only one future individual. It is the religious and ideological propaganda that supports godless power in every age: the imperial priesthood in John’s day, and every religion, philosophy, media or education system that persuades people to give the state, or any human power, the devotion that belongs to God.

In a sentence. Then I saw another beast, coming up out of the earth; it had two horns like a lamb’s, but it spoke like a dragon; it exercises all the authority of the first beast on its behalf, and it makes the earth and all who live on it worship the first beast, whose deadly wound had been healed.

On a Tuesday. Not everything that looks like a lamb is the Lamb. Test every message, especially gentle-sounding religious ones, by whether it leads you to worship Christ or something else.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.

Setting and background. In Daniel 3, King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image and commanded everyone to worship it, on pain of death; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused. Elijah called down fire from heaven to prove that the LORD is God (1 Kings 18:38). Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ miracles (Exodus 7:11, 22). In the ancient world, statues in temples were sometimes made to appear to speak or move by priests using hidden devices or ventriloquism. In the province of Asia, statues of the emperor stood in temples and public squares, and Christians were sometimes required to offer incense before them to prove their loyalty, as Pliny the governor of Bithynia reported around AD 112.

It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people. Key words. “Signs” (sēmeia). Counterfeit miracles, imitating Elijah and the two witnesses (11:5). Paul warned that the coming of the lawless one would be with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

And by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth. Key words. “Deceives” (plana, leads astray). Deception is its main weapon, as it is Satan’s (12:9). “Allowed” (edothē): again, God’s permission and limits.

Telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. Key words. “Image” (eikona, statue, likeness). Idolatry of the state, of its leader or its ideology.

And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak. Key words. “Breath” (pneuma, spirit, breath). A parody of God giving breath to the witnesses (11:11). Idols have mouths but cannot speak (Psalm 115:5), but this one seems to.

And might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain. Key words. As in Daniel 3. The demand for worship is enforced with death. The choice is stark: worship the beast or die.

What it does not mean. Miracles alone do not prove that a message is from God. Scripture warns that false prophets can perform signs (Deuteronomy 13:1–3; Matthew 24:24). The test is whether a message leads people to worship the true God revealed in Christ and agrees with his word.

In a sentence. It performs impressive signs, even making fire come down from the sky to the earth in full view of people; by the signs it is permitted to do on behalf of the first beast, it deceives the earth’s inhabitants, telling them to set up an image in honour of the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived; it was permitted to give breath to the beast’s image so that it could speak, and to have everyone who refused to worship the image put to death.

On a Tuesday. Do not be impressed by signs and wonders alone. Hold to the word of God, and worship Christ alone, whatever the pressure.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.

Setting and background. In Deuteronomy 6:8, Israel was told to bind God’s commandments as a sign on their hand and as frontlets between their eyes, so that their actions and thoughts would be shaped by his word. In the ancient world, slaves were sometimes branded or tattooed with their owner’s mark, and soldiers with their general’s name. Trade guilds in the cities of Asia required members to honour patron gods and the emperor; refusing could exclude a Christian from work and trade (2:9, 14, 20). Roman coins bore the emperor’s image and divine titles.

Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave. Key words. Everyone, at every level of society. No one is exempt from the pressure.

To be marked on the right hand or the forehead. Key words. “Mark” (charagma, stamp, brand, the impression of a seal on a document or coin). A counterfeit of God’s seal on the foreheads of his servants (7:3; 14:1). Everyone bears one mark or the other: God’s name or the beast’s. The forehead represents the mind and identity; the right hand represents action and work. The mark means belonging to the beast and serving it, in thought and deed.

So that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark. Key words. Economic pressure. Those who refuse to give their loyalty to the beast are shut out of the economy. In John’s day, Christians who refused guild idolatry lost their livelihood (Smyrna’s poverty, 2:9).

That is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Key words. The mark is the beast’s name, or its number. To bear someone’s name is to belong to them.

Where Christians differ: what is the mark of the beast? Over the centuries, many things have been identified as the mark: barcodes, credit cards, identity cards, microchips implanted in the hand, even vaccines. Verdict: the mark is not a physical device that someone might take by accident. It is a symbol of allegiance, the counterpart of God’s seal, which is also invisible (God’s name, 14:1, and his Spirit, Ephesians 1:13). To receive the mark is to give one’s worship and loyalty to the beast: to think and act as its servant. No one receives it without choosing to worship the beast (14:9–11). Christians should not live in fear of new technologies as though they might accidentally take the mark. They should watch their loyalty, and refuse to compromise their worship of Christ, whatever the economic cost.

What it does not mean. Taking part in the economy is not the mark of the beast. Christians may buy and sell, work and trade. What they may not do is give to any power, economic or political, the worship and loyalty that belong to God.

In a sentence. It also forces everyone, unimportant and important, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, so that no one could buy or sell anything without the mark, which is the beast’s name or the number that stands for its name.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness to Christ may cost you a promotion, a client or your job. Be willing to pay that price. Ask whose mark is on your thinking and your work.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

Setting and background. In Hebrew and Greek, letters of the alphabet also served as numbers, so every name had a numerical value. The practice of adding up the letters of a name was called gematria. A graffito at Pompeii reads: I love her whose number is 545. Nero Caesar, written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr), adds up to 666. Spelled without the final n, as in the Latin form Nero, it adds up to 616, and some manuscripts of Revelation read 616.

This calls for wisdom. Key words. “Wisdom” (sophia). Not cleverness, but spiritual discernment, to recognise the beast for what it is (17:9).

Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. Key words. “Calculate” (psēphisatō, count up, reckon, from the word for a pebble used in counting). John expects his first readers to be able to work it out.

For it is the number of a man. Key words. “Of a man” (anthrōpou, of a human being). It may mean a particular man, or a human number, the number of humanity. The beast, for all its claims to divinity, is merely human.

And his number is 666. Key words. Six is one short of seven, the number of completeness and perfection. Three sixes: falling short again and again, a counterfeit trinity that never reaches the divine. Jesus’ name in Greek (Iēsous) adds up to 888, one beyond seven, the number of resurrection and new creation. The beast is the ultimate human pretender to deity, always falling short. The number also very likely pointed John’s first readers to Nero, the persecuting emperor, as the model of the beast.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts read 616 instead of 666, as the early church father Irenaeus noted around AD 180. He defended 666 as the original, which the best manuscripts support. The variant may have arisen because 616 matches the Latin spelling of Nero Caesar, which shows that early readers connected the number with Nero.

Where Christians differ: who is 666? The number has been applied to countless figures: popes, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, various modern politicians, and titles such as the papal title Vicarius Filii Dei. Verdict: the number pointed first to Nero, the emperor who began the persecution of Christians and became the pattern of the persecuting beast; and its symbolism, six falling short of seven, describes every human power that claims to be divine. Attempts to fit it to modern figures have repeatedly failed and discredited the church. The right response is not number-crunching names in the news, but the wisdom to recognise and resist any power that demands worship.

What it does not mean. The number 666 is not unlucky or dangerous in itself. Christians need not fear house numbers, phone numbers or dates containing it. Its meaning lies in what it symbolises.

In a sentence. This is where wisdom is needed: let anyone with insight work out the number of the beast, for it is a human number, and the number is six hundred and sixty-six.

On a Tuesday. Pray for wisdom to see through the claims of power. Every human pretender to god falls short. Only Christ is Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads.<sup>2</sup>And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation,<sup>8</sup>and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.<sup>9</sup>If anyone has an ear, let him hear:<sup>10</sup>If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is a triptych of three visions, each answering the terror of chapter 13 with a counter-vision of divine certainty. First: the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000 — the redeemed in their completeness, standing where the beast could not reach them. Second: three angels flying in midheaven, each with a message that together constitute the gospel, the judgment, and the warning. Third: the great harvest of the earth — the grain harvest of the redeemed and the grape harvest of the wicked, two harvests that together depict the final judgment in all its terrible binary clarity.

The chapter is the hinge of Revelation. Behind it lies the cosmic backstory (chapters 12–13) and the long unfolding of the seals and trumpets (chapters 6–11). Before it lies the bowl judgments, Babylon's fall, the Rider on the white horse, and the new creation. Chapter 14 stands at the center and declares: the outcome is certain. The Lamb is on Mount Zion. The harvest is coming. The one who endures to the end will be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the hand or forehead and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Verse 1: on Mount Zion stands the Lamb, and with him the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7, complete, wearing his name and his Father’s. Everyone in this book is marked; the alternative to the beast’s mark is not an unmarked crowd.

Verses 2–3: a voice like the roar of many waters and loud thunder — and, in the same breath, like harpists playing on harps. They sing a new song before the throne, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. Not because the words are difficult, but because a song about being ransomed cannot be sung truly by someone who has not been.

Verses 4–5 describe them: they have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they are firstfruits (aparchē, the first sheaf that both belongs to God and guarantees more is coming); and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless — language taken from the servant of Isaiah 53:9 and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13, and amōmos, the word for a sacrificial animal without defect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: Ask whether the song of the cross is a statement you admire or your own account.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.

Meaning first. Revelation 14 answers the terror of chapter 13 with a series of visions of hope and judgement. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear his and his Father’s name, not the beast’s mark, and sing a new song only the redeemed can learn (vv. 1–3). They are pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, are firstfruits redeemed from humanity, and no lie is in their mouths (vv. 4–5). Three angels then fly overhead. The first proclaims an eternal gospel to every nation: fear God, give him glory and worship the Creator, for the hour of judgement has come (vv. 6–7). The second announces that Babylon the great has fallen (v. 8).
