The third warns that anyone who worships the beast and receives its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath and be tormented for ever, with no rest day or night (vv. 9–11). So the saints must endure, and a voice from heaven blesses those who die in the Lord: they rest from their labours, and their deeds follow them (vv. 12–13). Finally, two harvests: one like a son of man on a white cloud reaps the earth with a sickle (vv. 14–16), and an angel gathers the grapes of the earth into the great winepress of God’s wrath, from which blood flows for 1,600 stadia (vv. 17–20). The chapter sets the two destinies side by side: the Lamb’s people, safe and singing; the beast’s worshippers, judged; and it calls everyone to choose now whom they will worship.

Setting and background. Mount Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where David’s city and the temple stood, and it became a name for God’s dwelling and his people. Psalm 2:6 says God has set his King on Zion, his holy hill. Joel 2:32 says that in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and among the survivors those whom the LORD calls. Hebrews 12:22 tells believers that they have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb. Key words. “Stood” (hestos), firm and victorious, in contrast to the dragon standing on the sand of the sea (12:17). The beasts rose from the sea and earth; the Lamb stands on Zion, the place of God’s King (Psalm 2:6). Zion here is the heavenly Zion, where the church already belongs (Hebrews 12:22).

And with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. Key words. The same 144,000 as in 7:4, the whole people of God, sealed. Not one is missing: after all the beast’s war on the saints, the full number stands with the Lamb. Their seal is now revealed: the name of the Lamb and the Father, in contrast to the beast’s name on its followers (13:17).

And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. Key words. Overwhelming, like Christ’s voice (1:15) and God’s.

The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps. Key words. Powerful and also beautiful, music rather than noise.

And they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. Key words. “New song” (ōdēn kainēn), as in 5:9: the song of redemption.

No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. Key words. “Learn” (mathein). Only the redeemed can sing the song of redemption, because only they have experienced it. Angels can praise God for salvation (7:11–12), but they cannot sing as those who have been bought with the Lamb’s blood. “Redeemed” (ēgorasmenoi, bought, purchased), as in 5:9.

What it does not mean. The 144,000 here are not a special elite separate from other believers. They are the whole church, sealed in chapter 7, now seen safe with the Lamb after the beast’s persecution.

In a sentence. Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him 144,000 people who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads; and I heard a sound from heaven like the roar of a great waterfall and like loud thunder, yet like harpists playing their harps; they were singing a new song in front of the throne, the four living beings and the elders, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been bought out of the earth.

For worship. You have a song that angels cannot sing: the song of the redeemed. Sing it with all your heart.

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.

Setting and background. Israel’s soldiers had to abstain from sexual relations during holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5). The 144,000 were counted like an army (7:4–8). The prophets picture God’s people as his virgin bride (Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4), and idolatry as adultery or prostitution (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16). Paul told the Corinthians he had betrothed them to Christ, to present them as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). Firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, offered to God as belonging to him, and a pledge of the full harvest to come (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:10). Zephaniah 3:13 says that the remnant of Israel shall speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue.

It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. Key words. “Defiled” (emolynthēsan, stained). “Virgins” (parthenoi, a word that can be used of men as well as women). In the context of Revelation, where Babylon is the great prostitute (17:1–5) and idolatry is spiritual immorality (2:14, 20), this means they kept themselves pure from the idolatry of the beast. They are the faithful bride of the Lamb (19:7–8; 21:2). They are also like holy warriors, set apart for the Lamb’s war.

It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Key words. “Follow” (akolouthountes, the word for discipleship). Wherever he goes, including to suffering and death. In contrast, the world follows the beast (13:3).

These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb. Key words. “Firstfruits” (aparchē). They belong wholly to God, offered to him. And they are the first part of a harvest, which suggests that the harvest of v. 15 is the gathering of the redeemed. James calls believers a kind of firstfruits of God’s creatures (James 1:18). Here the whole church is the firstfruits offered from all humanity.

And in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless. Key words. “Lie” (pseudos). The beast and false prophet deceive (13:14); the Lamb’s people tell the truth. They did not say Caesar is Lord or deny Christ. “Blameless” (amōmoi, without blemish, the word for an unblemished sacrifice). Like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19). Their blamelessness comes from his blood (7:14) and shows in their faithful lives.

Where Christians differ: does this praise celibacy? Some, from the early church onwards, have read this verse as praising literal virginity and celibacy as a higher form of Christian life, and used it to support celibate monks, nuns and clergy. Verdict: the virginity here is spiritual purity from idolatry, the faithfulness of the Lamb’s bride. Scripture honours marriage (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24), calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and says that marriage is not defiling. Celibacy is a good gift for some (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), but it is not a higher state of holiness. The 144,000 are the whole church, married and single, who refused to commit spiritual adultery with the beast.

What it does not mean. Blameless does not mean sinless perfection in this life. It means forgiven, washed and faithful, without the stain of compromise with the beast.

In a sentence. These are the ones who have kept themselves pure and not been defiled with women; they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they were bought from among humanity as the first part of the harvest offered to God and the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouths; they are without blemish.

On a Tuesday. Follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Keep yourself from the idols of the age, and speak the truth, even when a lie would be easier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: an angel flies directly overhead — at the zenith, where everyone can see — with an eternal gospel for every nation and tribe and language and people, and calls out three imperatives: fear God, give him glory, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water, because the hour of his judgment has come. The list is deliberate: those are the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12).

Verse 8: a second angel announces Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great — Isaiah’s watchman’s cry (Isa. 21:9; cf. Jer. 51:8) — she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Babylon is announced as finished three chapters before she is even described.

Verses 9–11: a third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torment goes up for ever, and they have no rest, day or night.

Verse 12 turns to the reader with the sentence already used at 13:10: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. Verse 13 gives the second of the book’s seven beatitudes, and one of the few sentences John is specifically commanded to write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on — with the Spirit adding a comment of his own: that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, “Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water.”

Setting and background. The eagle flew overhead crying woe (8:13); now an angel flies overhead with good news. Paul preached to pagans at Lystra and Athens that they should turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth and the sea (Acts 14:15; 17:24–31), and that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world. Jesus said that this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come (Matthew 24:14).

Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead. Key words. “Directly overhead” (en mesouranēmati, in mid-heaven): where all can see and hear.

With an eternal gospel to proclaim. Key words. “Eternal gospel” (euangelion aiōnion, everlasting good news). The only time Revelation uses the noun gospel. It is eternal because it never changes and its effects last for ever. Even in the midst of judgement, God proclaims good news.

To those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. Key words. To the same people who worship the beast (13:8). God offers them the gospel. The fourfold list of all humanity again.

And he said with a loud voice, Fear God and give him glory. Key words. “Fear” (phobēthēte, reverence, awe). “Give him glory”: worship him, and repent (11:13; 16:9). The call is to turn from the beast to the true God.

Because the hour of his judgment has come. Key words. “Hour” (hōra). The good news includes the warning. Judgement is near, so turn now.

And worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water. Key words. The Creator, who alone deserves worship (4:11). Echoing the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:11). Heaven, earth, sea and fresh water: the four realms struck by the first four trumpets (8:7–12). The one who made them all is the one to worship, not the beast who rose from the sea and earth.

Where Christians differ: is this a last chance after death, or a different gospel? Some have read the eternal gospel as a final chance for salvation given after the church’s age, or even as a gospel different from that of Christ, without the cross. Verdict: the eternal gospel is the same gospel of Jesus Christ preached throughout this age, summed up here in the call to turn from idols to the living God, which was the first step of the apostles’ preaching to pagans (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul says there is no other gospel (Galatians 1:6–9). It is proclaimed to the living, before the hour of judgement, not after death (Hebrews 9:27). The angel pictures the worldwide preaching of the gospel by the church before the end.

What it does not mean. Angels do not replace the church’s task of preaching the gospel. The angel symbolises the gospel going to all nations, which Christ has entrusted to his people (Matthew 28:18–20).

In a sentence. Then I saw another angel flying high overhead with an eternal gospel to announce to the people who live on the earth, every nation, tribe, language and people; he shouted: Fear God and give him glory, because the time has come for him to judge; worship the one who made heaven, earth, sea and springs of water.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is still for everyone, even those who seem most committed to the beast. Share it with urgency: the hour of judgement is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.”

Setting and background. Babylon was the great empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC and took God’s people into exile. It became the Bible’s symbol of human pride and rebellion against God, from the tower of Babel (Genesis 11) onwards. Isaiah 21:9 cries, fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground. Jeremiah 51:7–8 says Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank her wine, therefore they went mad; suddenly Babylon has fallen. Peter calls Rome Babylon (1 Peter 5:13).

Another angel, a second, followed, saying, Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great. Key words. “Fallen” (epesen, past tense, twice). So certain that it is announced as done. The first mention of Babylon in Revelation, anticipating chapters 17–18. In John’s day, Babylon was Rome, the great city built on seven hills (17:9, 18), but it stands for every proud human civilisation organised without God: its economics, culture, pleasures and power.

She who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Key words. “Passion” (thymou, which can mean passion or wrath). “Sexual immorality” (porneias, prostitution). Babylon seduces the nations into idolatry and immorality, like a prostitute offering wine to intoxicate her clients. The same wine she makes them drink becomes the wine of God’s wrath (v. 10; 16:19). Those who drink her passion will drink God’s anger.

What it does not mean. Babylon is not only ancient Rome, or one future rebuilt city in Iraq. It is the spirit of the world in every age: the seductive, proud, self-indulgent civilisation that turns people away from God. It falls in every empire’s fall, and finally at Christ’s return.

In a sentence. A second angel followed, saying: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the great, who made all the nations drink the intoxicating wine of her sexual immorality.

On a Tuesday. The world’s pleasures and power look permanent, but Babylon is already fallen in God’s sight. Do not drink her wine.

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.”

Setting and background. In the Old Testament, the cup of God’s wrath is a picture of judgement (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16). Wine in the ancient world was usually mixed with water; to pour it full strength, unmixed, was to make it at its most powerful. Fire and sulphur destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28). Isaiah 34:9–10 describes Edom’s judgement: its smoke shall go up for ever. In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him (Matthew 26:39); he drank the cup of God’s wrath for his people.

And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand. Key words. The warning is aimed at those who choose to worship the beast. Receiving the mark means giving allegiance to the beast. No one takes it by accident.

He also will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger. Key words. “Wrath” (thymou, passion, fury) and “anger” (orgēs, settled wrath). “Full strength” (akratou, unmixed, undiluted). The judgements of the seals and trumpets were mixed with mercy, partial and limited. This is God’s wrath unmixed, with no mercy left.

And he will be tormented with fire and sulfur. Key words. “Tormented” (basanisthēsetai, tortured, in pain). Fire and sulphur: the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The worst images Scripture has, to describe the worst reality.

In the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. Key words. Not that the angels and the Lamb watch with pleasure, but that the judgement is carried out under their authority, and is just. The one who refused the Lamb’s mercy faces the Lamb as judge.

And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever. Key words. “Forever and ever” (eis aiōnas aiōnōn, to the ages of the ages): the same phrase used for God’s eternal life (4:9; 15:7) and for the saints’ reign (22:5). The torment does not end.

And they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name. Key words. “No rest” (ouk echousin anapausin). In contrast with the living creatures, who have no rest from praise (4:8), and with the dead in the Lord, who rest from their labours (v. 13). The worshippers of the beast have endless unrest.

Where Christians differ: is hell eternal conscious punishment? Annihilationists (or conditionalists) believe the wicked are punished and then cease to exist, and read “the smoke goes up forever” as the lasting result of a destruction that is complete. Universalists believe all will finally be saved. Verdict: this passage teaches eternal, conscious punishment. The wicked are tormented, they have no rest day or night, and this continues for ever and ever. Revelation 20:10 uses the same language of the devil, beast and false prophet: tormented day and night for ever and ever, which plainly cannot mean annihilation. Jesus spoke of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46). This is terrible, and it should be spoken of with tears, not glee. But it is what Scripture says, and it shows both the seriousness of sin against an infinitely holy God and the greatness of Christ’s love in bearing God’s wrath for all who trust in him.

What it does not mean. This warning is not meant to make Christians afraid that they might lose their salvation. It is meant to make them refuse the beast at any cost, and to warn the world. Those who belong to the Lamb will never drink this cup, because he drank it for them.

In a sentence. A third angel followed them, shouting: If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on the forehead or the hand, that person will also drink the wine of God’s fury, poured undiluted into the cup of his anger, and will be tormented with fire and sulphur in front of the holy angels and the Lamb; the smoke of their torment rises for ever and ever, and there is no rest day or night for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s warnings seriously, for yourself and for those you love. And thank Christ, who drank the cup of wrath so that you never will.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Blessed indeed,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!”

Setting and background. This is the second of Revelation’s seven beatitudes (1:3). Isaiah 57:1–2 says the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart, but he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness. Hebrews 4:9–11 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God.

Here is a call for the endurance of the saints. Key words. “Endurance” (hypomonē). Because the stakes are eternal, believers must endure, refusing the beast, whatever it costs. The warning of vv. 9–11 is a reason to stay faithful.

Those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. Key words. “Faith in Jesus” (tēn pistin Iēsou, faith in Jesus, or the faithfulness of Jesus). As in 12:17. Obedience and faith together mark the true believer.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying, Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. Key words. “In the Lord” (en kyriō): united to Christ by faith. “From now on” (ap’ arti): from this point in history, as persecution intensifies, or from the moment of death. Those who die faithful, perhaps as martyrs, are not to be pitied. They are blessed. The world calls them losers; heaven calls them blessed.

Blessed indeed, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors. Key words. “Indeed” (nai, yes). The Spirit adds his confirmation. “Rest” (anapaēsontai). “Labors” (kopōn, toil, hard work, the exhaustion of service and suffering). In contrast with the restless torment of the beast’s worshippers (v. 11), the dead in Christ rest.

For their deeds follow them! Key words. “Deeds” (erga, works). “Follow” (akolouthei, accompany). Their faithful works are not lost; they go with them into God’s presence, as evidence of their faith and as the basis of their reward (22:12). Nothing done for Christ is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Where Christians differ: do believers go to purgatory, or rest? Roman Catholic teaching holds that many who die in God’s grace must still be purified in purgatory before entering heaven. Others hold that the soul sleeps until the resurrection. Verdict: the dead in the Lord are blessed from the moment of death, and they rest. There is no purging of sin after death; Christ’s blood has cleansed them completely (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 10:14), and to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their rest is conscious enjoyment of Christ (6:9–11), not unconscious sleep. They wait for the resurrection of the body, but they are already with him.

What it does not mean. Their deeds following them does not mean they are saved by their works. They died in the Lord, which means united to Christ by faith. Their works follow them; they do not go before them to buy them entry.

In a sentence. This is why God’s people, who keep his commandments and hold on to their faith in Jesus, must endure; and I heard a voice from heaven say: Write this down: from now on, how happy are those who die belonging to the Lord! Yes, says the Spirit, they will rest from their hard work, for what they have done goes with them.

For worship. Read this verse at Christian funerals. Those who die in the Lord are blessed and at rest, and nothing they did for him is lost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14–16: one like a son of man (Dan. 7:13; cf. Rev. 1:13) is seated on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle. An angel comes out of the temple with word that the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe, and he swings his sickle and the earth is reaped — in a single sentence, with no resistance recorded.

Verses 17–19: a second angel with a sharp sickle comes out of the temple, and a third comes from the altar, having authority over the fire, and orders the vintage: gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. The grapes are thrown into the great winepress of the wrath of God (cf. Isa. 63:3; Joel 3:13).

Verse 20: the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia — about a hundred and eighty miles, roughly the length of Palestine, and four times four times a hundred, four being the number of the earth in this book. The figure means the whole world, completely.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, “Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe.” So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.

Setting and background. Joel 3:13 says: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; go in, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for their evil is great. Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. Jesus told parables of harvest at the end of the age: the wheat gathered into the barn and the weeds burned (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43), and the angels sent to gather his elect from the four winds (Matthew 24:31). He said, the harvest is plentiful (Matthew 9:37–38), and that the fields are white for harvest (John 4:35).

Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man. Key words. Christ, as in 1:13 and Daniel 7:13, coming on the clouds (1:7).

With a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. Key words. “Crown” (stephanon, victor’s crown): he has conquered. “Sickle” (drepanon), the curved blade for harvesting grain.

And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, Put in your sickle, and reap. Key words. The angel brings the message from God’s presence (the temple): the Father has fixed the hour (Mark 13:32; Acts 1:7). The angel does not command Christ; he conveys the Father’s timing.

For the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe. Key words. “Fully ripe” (exēranthē, has become dry, ready). The time has come.

So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped. Key words. A single, decisive act. The end of the age.

Where Christians differ: is the grain harvest salvation or judgement? Some see both harvests in vv. 14–20 as judgement, following Joel 3:13. Others see the grain harvest as the gathering of the redeemed and the grape harvest as the judgement of the wicked. Verdict: the grain harvest is most likely the gathering of God’s people at Christ’s return. Christ himself reaps it, as he sends his angels to gather his elect (Matthew 24:31); in the Gospels, the grain harvest is regularly the harvest of salvation (Matthew 9:37–38; 13:30; John 4:35–38); and the 144,000 have just been called firstfruits (v. 4), the beginning of this harvest. Nothing is said about destroying the grain. The grape harvest, by contrast, is explicitly thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath. Together they picture the two outcomes of the last day.

What it does not mean. The harvest does not mean God waits passively until humanity ripens by itself. He sets the hour, and Christ acts. History ripens under his hand.

In a sentence. Then I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on it someone like a son of man, with a gold crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand; another angel came out of the temple and called loudly to the one on the cloud, Take your sickle and reap, because the time to reap has come and the earth’s harvest is ripe; so the one seated on the cloud swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested.

On a Tuesday. Christ will gather his people home. Meanwhile, pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, and be one yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, “Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.” So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia.

Setting and background. Grapes were trodden in a winepress, a stone vat in which people trampled the grapes, and the juice ran down a channel into a lower vat. The red juice looked like blood. Isaiah 63:1–6 shows the LORD coming from Edom with garments stained crimson, saying, I have trodden the winepress alone; I trod them in my anger, and their lifeblood spattered on my garments. Joel 3:13 says, tread, for the winepress is full. Executions were carried out outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Hebrews 13:12). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (184 miles), roughly the length of the land of Israel from north to south.

Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. Key words. This time an angel holds the sickle, carrying out the judgement.

And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire. Key words. The altar where the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5), and under which the martyrs cried, How long? (6:9–10). This harvest answers their prayers.

Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. Key words. “Vine of the earth”: in contrast with Christ, the true vine (John 15:1), and Israel, God’s vine (Isaiah 5:1–7). The earth’s vine is humanity in rebellion, ripe in its sin.

So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. Key words. “Winepress” (lēnon). “Wrath” (thymou). The judgement is described in terms of the crushing of grapes. Christ himself treads the winepress in 19:15.

And the winepress was trodden outside the city. Key words. “The city”: God’s city, the holy city where his people are (20:9). Judgement falls outside, where his enemies are. And Jesus himself suffered outside the gate, bearing the judgement his people deserved (Hebrews 13:12).

And blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia. Key words. Horrific, deliberately exaggerated imagery. 1,600 is 4 × 4 × 100 (or 40 × 40): four, the number of the earth, squared and multiplied. A judgement covering the whole earth. Jewish writings used similar language: 1 Enoch 100:3 says the horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal river of blood three hundred kilometres long, to be measured. It is a vivid, terrible symbol of the completeness and severity of God’s final judgement on unrepentant evil. Nor does it portray God as cruel. It is the just answer to the blood of the martyrs (6:10; 16:6; 19:2), and it falls only on those who refused his eternal gospel (v. 6).

In a sentence. Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, also holding a sharp sickle, and yet another angel, who has authority over fire, came from the altar and called loudly to the one with the sharp sickle: Take your sharp sickle and gather the bunches of grapes from the earth’s vine, because they are ripe; so the angel swung his sickle over the earth, gathered its grapes and threw them into the great winepress of God’s anger; the winepress was trampled outside the city, and blood poured out of it, rising as high as a horse’s bridle for about three hundred kilometres.

On a Tuesday. Do not take sin lightly, yours or the world’s. God will judge it fully. And do not take the cross lightly, where Christ was trodden outside the city for all who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles; a stadion was about 607 feet — roughly the length of the land of Israel.

The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps,<sup>3</sup>and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.<sup>4</sup>It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. 21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the destination toward which every page of Revelation has been moving. Every sealed scroll, every trumpet, every suffering saint, every martyr’s cry of ‘How long?’ — all of it was moving toward this: “Behold, I am making all things new.” The new creation is not the consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed. It is the goal, the telos, the end for which the whole story was told.

The chapter falls into two great movements. The first (vv. 1–8) describes the new heaven and new earth from a distance — the cosmic renewal, the descent of the holy city, the voice from the throne declaring the end of tears and death, and the character of those who will inherit and those who will not. The second (vv. 9–27) zooms in: the angel takes John in the Spirit to a high mountain and shows him the new Jerusalem in breathtaking architectural detail — dimensions, gates, foundations, materials, light, temple, nations.

The key to the chapter is understanding what the new Jerusalem is. It is not primarily a city in the architectural sense; it is a person — “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” The new Jerusalem is the church, the bride of Christ, dwelling with God in the fullness of the covenant relationship that all of redemptive history has been building toward. The city and the bride are the same reality: the people of God in their final, perfected, glorified state, living in the presence of God as his dwelling place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea was no more; and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The word for new is kainos, which usually means new in kind, renewed. And the direction is downward.

Verses 3–4: the dwelling place of God is with man — skēnē, a tent — with the covenant formula complete: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. Then four abolitions: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore (cf. Isa. 25:8).

Verses 5–6: God the Father speaks in the first person for the second and last time in the book — Behold, I am making all things new; Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true; It is done!; I am the Alpha and the Omega; and the offer, to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14).

Verses 7–8: the last promise to the conqueror — I will be his God and he will be my son, the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 handed to anyone who holds on — and then the eight excluded categories, beginning startlingly with the cowardly and ending with all liars, whose portion is the second death.
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth — renewed, not replaced — and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

Meaning first. Revelation 21 shows the goal of all history: the new creation, where God lives with his people for ever. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride (vv. 1–2). A voice from the throne announces that God’s dwelling is now with humanity: he will be their God, wipe away every tear, and end death, mourning, crying and pain (vv. 3–4). God says, I am making all things new; it is done; I am the Alpha and the Omega; he gives the water of life freely to the thirsty; the one who conquers will inherit all this and be his child, but the cowardly, faithless and wicked will have their part in the lake of fire (vv. 5–8). Then an angel shows John the bride, the new Jerusalem, shining with God’s glory (vv. 9–11). It has twelve gates bearing the names of the twelve tribes, and twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (vv. 12–14). It is a perfect cube, twelve thousand stadia on each side (vv. 15–17), built of jasper and pure gold, its foundations adorned with twelve precious stones, its gates of pearl (vv. 18–21). It has no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, no sun or moon, because God’s glory is its light and the Lamb its lamp; the nations walk by its light and bring their glory into it; its gates are never shut; and nothing unclean enters, only those written in the Lamb’s book of life (vv. 22–27). The chapter is the answer to every fear and sorrow in the book: Babylon has fallen, and the bride has come; the world’s glory passes away, and God’s glory fills everything.

Setting and background. Isaiah 65:17–25 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth, where the former things shall not be remembered, and there will be no more weeping. Isaiah 54:11–12 promises a city built with sapphires, rubies and jewels. Ezekiel 40–48 describes a restored city and temple, ending with the name of the city: The LORD is there (Ezekiel 48:35). Abraham looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10). Peter says we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–23).

Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth. Key words. “New” (kainon, new in quality, renewed, not merely new in time). Not a different world replacing this one, but this world made new. God does not abandon what he made; he restores and transforms it. The Bible begins with God creating the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1) and ends with him making them new.

For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away. Key words. “Passed away” (apēlthan, gone away). The first creation, under the curse of sin, has gone (20:11). Its old order, marked by sin, death and decay, is over.

And the sea was no more. Key words. In Revelation, the sea is the source of chaos and evil, from which the beast rose (13:1), the place of the dead (20:13), and the barrier that separated John on Patmos from the churches. In the new creation, all that it stood for is gone: no more chaos, danger, evil or separation.

And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. Key words. “Holy city” (tēn polin tēn hagian). “New Jerusalem”: the fulfilment of all God’s promises to Zion. “Coming down” (katabainousan): it comes from God; it is his gift, not human achievement. Babel tried to build up to heaven (Genesis 11:4); the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven. And heaven comes to earth: the final destiny of God’s people is not to float away to heaven, but to live with God on a renewed earth.

Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. Key words. “Prepared” (hētoimasmenēn). “Adorned” (kekosmēmenēn, beautifully dressed; our word cosmetics comes from it). The city is the bride (v. 9), the people of God. The new Jerusalem is not only a place; it is a people, God’s people in their perfected community, in contrast to Babylon the prostitute.

Where Christians differ: will this earth be destroyed and replaced, or renewed? Some Christians, reading 2 Peter 3:10 (the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the earth and the works on it will be burned up), believe the present creation will be annihilated and replaced with something entirely new. Others think of eternity as a purely spiritual existence in heaven. Verdict: Scripture teaches that this creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Paul says creation will be set free from bondage (Romans 8:21); Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things (Matthew 19:28); Peter speaks of the restoration of all things (Acts 3:21). The fire of 2 Peter 3 purifies, as metal is refined, and the earth is laid bare to judgement. Just as our bodies will be raised and transformed, not replaced, so creation will be raised and transformed. The final hope of believers is not disembodied existence but resurrection life on a new earth, with God.

What it does not mean. The new Jerusalem is not a literal city of particular dimensions to be mapped. It is a vision, full of symbols, of the perfect, eternal dwelling of God with his people. But what it describes is real: a real new creation, with real resurrected people, and God truly present.

In a sentence. Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and the first earth had gone, and there was no longer any sea; and I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared and dressed like a bride beautifully adorned for her husband.

On a Tuesday. Your future is not an endless cloud, but a renewed earth. Care for God’s creation now, and live in hope of its renewal.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”

Setting and background. The heart of God’s covenant promise throughout Scripture is: I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and I will dwell among you (Leviticus 26:11–12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27). God walked with Adam in the garden (Genesis 3:8), dwelt in the tabernacle and temple, and became flesh and tabernacled among us in Christ (John 1:14). Now his presence is complete. Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death for ever and wipe away tears from all faces. Isaiah 35:10 and 65:19 promise that sorrow and sighing shall flee away, and no more shall be heard the sound of weeping.

And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. Key words. “Dwelling place” (hē skēnē, tent, tabernacle). God’s tabernacle, his presence, is now permanently with humanity. What Eden had, and sin lost, is restored and surpassed.

He will dwell with them. Key words. “Dwell” (skēnōsei, tabernacle, pitch his tent). As in 7:15.

And they will be his people. Key words. “People” (laoi, plural, peoples, in the best manuscripts). The many nations of the redeemed, now one people of God. The promise once made to Israel now includes all nations.

And God himself will be with them as their God. Key words. “God himself” (autos ho theos). Not merely his gifts, but God himself. Immanuel, God with us, in full.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Key words. As in 7:17. God personally comforts his people.

And death shall be no more. Key words. The last enemy destroyed (20:14; 1 Corinthians 15:26).

Neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore. Key words. Every result of sin and the curse is gone.

For the former things have passed away. Key words. “The former things” (ta prōta, the first things). The old order of sin and suffering is gone for ever.

What it does not mean. No more tears does not mean we will forget everything about this life, or that our relationships and history will be erased. It means every sorrow will be healed and every loss made up, so that nothing will cause pain any more.

In a sentence. And I heard a loud voice from the throne say: Look, God’s home is now among people; he will live with them, they will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God; he will wipe every tear from their eyes; there will be no more death, no more grief, no more crying and no more pain, because the old order of things has gone.

For worship. Read this at funerals, in hospitals and in grief. This is the end of the story: God with us, and every tear wiped away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.” And he said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.

Setting and background. This is only the second time in Revelation that God himself speaks directly (the first was 1:8). Isaiah 43:19 says, behold, I am doing a new thing. Isaiah 55:1 calls: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat; buy wine and milk without money and without price. Jesus offered living water to the Samaritan woman (John 4:10–14) and cried out at the feast, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

And he who was seated on the throne said, Behold, I am making all things new. Key words. “I am making” (poiō, present tense: I am doing it). Not all new things, but all things new: renewal, not replacement. God’s work of renewal has already begun in Christ, in whom anyone is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and it will be completed.

Also he said, Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true. Key words. “Trustworthy” (pistoi, faithful) and “true” (alēthinoi). A guarantee. The new creation is certain.

And he said to me, It is done! Key words. “It is done” (gegonan, they have happened). As in 16:17. The whole plan of God is complete.

I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. Key words. As in 1:8. God began everything and brings everything to its goal.

To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. Key words. “Thirsty” (tō dipsōnti, the one who is thirsting). “Water of life” (tou hydatos tēs zōēs): eternal life, God himself. “Without payment” (dōrean, as a gift, freely). Salvation is free. No one can buy it or earn it. The only qualification is thirst: knowing that you need it.

What it does not mean. “Without payment” does not mean salvation is cheap. It cost the Lamb his blood. It is free to us because Christ paid in full.

In a sentence. Then the one seated on the throne said, Look, I am making everything new! and he told me, Write this down, because these words are reliable and true; then he said to me, It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end; to anyone who is thirsty I will give water from the spring of the water of life as a free gift.

On a Tuesday. If you are thirsty for meaning, forgiveness or life, come to Christ. The water is free. And offer it freely to others.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

Setting and background. God promised David that his son would be God’s son: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:14). Paul applies this to all believers: I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18). The seven letters each ended with a promise to the one who conquers (chapters 2–3); here is the sum of them all.

The one who conquers will have this heritage. Key words. “Heritage” (klēronomēsei, will inherit). All the promises of the seven letters come together. The meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

And I will be his God and he will be my son. Key words. “Son” (huios): an heir, with full rights. The most intimate relationship. Through Christ, the Son, believers become sons and daughters of God by adoption (Galatians 4:4–7).

But as for the cowardly. Key words. “Cowardly” (deilois, timid, fearful). Heading the list: those who, out of fear, deny Christ under persecution. The opposite of the one who conquers. Not the fearful who still trust Christ, but those whose fear leads them to abandon him.

The faithless. Key words. “Faithless” (apistois, unbelieving, unfaithful). Those who refuse to trust and obey Christ.

The detestable. Key words. “Detestable” (ebdelygmenois, polluted with abominations), linked with Babylon’s abominations (17:4).

As for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars. Key words. The sins of Babylon and the beast’s worshippers (9:21; 22:15). “All liars”: those who belong to the father of lies (John 8:44) and the false prophet.

Their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death. Key words. “Portion” (meros, share, part). As in 20:14–15.

What it does not mean. This list does not mean that anyone who has ever committed these sins is beyond salvation. Paul lists similar sins and then says, and such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The list describes those who persist in these sins without repentance, refusing the free water of life (v. 6). Even a murderer or an idolater who comes thirsty to Christ will be given the water of life.

In a sentence. The one who conquers will inherit all this, and I will be his God and he will be my son; but the cowards, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practise magic, the idolaters and all liars will have their place in the lake that burns with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.

On a Tuesday. Take courage: God calls you his child and heir. And if any sin on this list still grips you, bring it to Christ today, who washes and makes new.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–11: one of the seven bowl angels — the same rank, and almost the same words, as 17:1 — says Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, and carries John to a great high mountain (17:3 was a wilderness). He promised a Bride and shows a city: the people are the place. It has the glory of God, radiant like jasper, clear as crystal — the description of the one on the throne at 4:3.

Verses 12–14: twelve gates, three on each side, bearing the names of the twelve tribes (cf. Num. 2; Ezek. 48:30–35); twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (cf. Eph. 2:19–20). Verses 15–17: the city is measured with a golden rod — 12,000 stadia, about fourteen hundred miles, its length and width and height are equal — and its wall 144 cubits, twelve times twelve.

Verses 18–21: a wall of jasper and a city of gold like clear glass; twelve foundation stones named one by one, most of them from the high priest’s breastpiece (Ex. 28:17–21); twelve gates each made of a single pearl; and a street of gold like transparent glass.

Verse 22: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Verses 23–25: no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light and its lamp is the Lamb (cf. Isa. 60:19); the nations walk by that light and the kings bring their glory in; the gates never shut, and there is no night. Verses 26–27: they will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations — and nothing unclean, detestable or false enters, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube — the Most Holy Place enlarged — with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart once a year is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.” And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.

Setting and background. In 17:1–3, one of the seven bowl angels said, come, I will show you the judgement of the great prostitute, and carried John in the Spirit into a wilderness. The parallel is exact and deliberate: two women, two cities, two destinies. Ezekiel was brought in visions of God to a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city (Ezekiel 40:2). Isaiah 2:2 says the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be lifted up above the hills. Moses saw the promised land from a mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1–4). Satan showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world from a very high mountain (Matthew 4:8).

Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues. Key words. The same kind of angel that showed John Babylon. Those who carried out judgement now reveal glory.

And spoke to me, saying, Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb. Key words. “Bride” (nymphē) and “wife” (gynaika). The marriage of 19:7 has happened. The church is now the Lamb’s wife.

And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain. Key words. The fourth “in the Spirit” (1:10; 4:2; 17:3). Babylon was seen from a wilderness; the bride from a high mountain, the place of revelation and of God’s dwelling.

And showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God. Key words. The city is the bride. A people and a place together.

Having the glory of God. Key words. “Glory” (doxan). The city shines with God’s own glory, the shekinah glory that filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11; Ezekiel 43:2–5). God’s presence makes it what it is.

Its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal. Key words. “Radiance” (phōstēr, light, brilliance). “Jasper”: as in 4:3, the appearance of God on the throne. The city reflects God’s own glory. “Clear as crystal”: pure, transparent, nothing hidden.

What it does not mean. The bride is not a separate entity from the city, or from the believers who make it up. All the descriptions of the city describe the glorified people of God, and the place where they live with him.

In a sentence. Then one of the seven angels who had held the seven bowls filled with the seven last plagues came and said to me, Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb; and he carried me away in the Spirit to a huge, high mountain and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, shining with God’s glory, its brilliance like a rare jewel, like jasper, as clear as crystal.

For worship. The church, which now seems weak and flawed, will shine with the glory of God. Love her now as Christ does.

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed—on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

Setting and background. Ezekiel 48:30–35 describes the restored Jerusalem with twelve gates, three on each side, named after the twelve tribes. Israel camped around the tabernacle in the wilderness, three tribes on each side (Numbers 2). Paul says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20).

It had a great, high wall. Key words. “Wall” (teichos). Security, protection, belonging. In ancient cities, walls kept enemies out. Here there are no enemies left; the wall marks the city as safe and distinct.

With twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels. Key words. “Gates” (pylōnas). Angels as gatekeepers, as cherubim guarded Eden (Genesis 3:24). But now the gates are open (v. 25).

And on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed. Key words. Old Testament Israel is part of the city. God’s promises to Israel are fulfilled.

On the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. Key words. Access from every direction. People come from east, west, north and south (Luke 13:29).

And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. Key words. “Foundations” (themelious). The apostles, who laid the foundation of the church by their witness to Christ. Together, the twelve tribes and twelve apostles form one city: the one people of God across both covenants. This is the clearest confirmation that the twenty-four elders (4:4) represent Israel and the church together.

What it does not mean. Israel’s names on the gates and the apostles’ names on the foundations do not mean there are two peoples of God, one Jewish and one Christian, with different destinies. There is one city, one bride, one people, built on Christ.

In a sentence. It had a massive, high wall with twelve gates, with twelve angels at the gates, and the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were written on the gates, three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south and three on the west; the city wall had twelve foundation stones, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

For worship. Thank God for the whole people of God through history, Israel and the church. You belong to a city built on the apostles’ witness.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.

Setting and background. The Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple was a perfect cube, twenty cubits long, wide and high, overlaid with pure gold (1 Kings 6:20). Ezekiel saw an angel measuring the new temple and city (Ezekiel 40–48). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 12,000 stadia is about 2,220 kilometres (1,380 miles), roughly the distance from London to Athens, or the width of the known Greek world. A cubit was about 45 centimetres (18 inches), so 144 cubits is about 65 metres (216 feet).

And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. Key words. In 11:1, John measured the temple to show its protection. Here the angel measures the whole city with a gold rod, fitting for a golden city. Measuring shows that the city is complete, secure and belongs to God.

The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. Key words. “Foursquare” (tetragōnos, square). Perfect, complete.

And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. Key words. A perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place. The whole city is the Most Holy Place: God’s presence fills it all, and all God’s people dwell where once only the high priest could enter once a year. 12,000 is 12 × 1,000: the people of God (twelve) in fullness (a thousand). The size, vast beyond imagining, shows there is room for the great multitude no one can count.

He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement. Key words. 144 is 12 × 12, the number of God’s people, as in the 144,000 (7:4). The wall, compared with the city, is small: protection is no longer needed. “By human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement”: the angel uses ordinary units, but their meaning is symbolic.

What it does not mean. The dimensions are not a blueprint for a literal cube-shaped city 2,220 kilometres high. They are symbols of perfection, completeness and the holiness of God’s presence, drawn from the Most Holy Place and from the numbers of God’s people.

In a sentence. The angel who talked with me had a gold measuring rod to measure the city, its gates and its wall; the city was laid out as a square, as long as it was wide; he measured the city with the rod, and it was twelve thousand stadia, about 2,200 kilometres, in length, width and height alike; he measured its wall too, and it was 144 cubits thick, by the human measure the angel was using.

For worship. In the new creation, all God’s people will live in the Most Holy Place, in his presence. Worship now as one who will one day dwell there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.

Setting and background. The high priest’s breastplate held twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of one of the tribes of Israel, worn over his heart when he entered God’s presence (Exodus 28:15–21). Isaiah 54:11–12 promises Jerusalem foundations of sapphires, battlements of agate, gates of carbuncles and walls of precious stones. The king of Tyre, in Eden, was covered with every precious stone (Ezekiel 28:13). The prostitute Babylon was adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (17:4).

The wall was built of jasper. Key words. Jasper: the appearance of God (4:3). The wall reflects God’s glory.

While the city was pure gold, like clear glass. Key words. “Pure gold” (chrysion katharon). Like the gold-covered Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20). Gold so pure it is transparent, a kind of gold unknown on earth. Purity and glory together.

The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. Key words. Twelve stones on twelve foundations, as twelve stones on the high priest’s breastplate. The whole people of God, precious to him, now in his presence for ever. Most of the stones correspond, as far as ancient names can be matched, to those on the breastplate.

The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. Key words. A rainbow of colour: clear, blue, green, red, golden, purple. The exact identity of ancient gem names is uncertain. The point is overwhelming beauty and variety, reflecting God’s glory in many colours, like the many nations of the redeemed.

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl. Key words. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world (Matthew 13:45–46). Gates made of a single pearl are beyond imagination. The source of the phrase pearly gates.

And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass. Key words. “Street” (plateia, main street, broad way). What people most prize on earth is the pavement of the city of God.

What it does not mean. The gold and jewels do not mean heaven is about wealth. They are symbols of beauty, glory, permanence and preciousness. What Babylon used to seduce and adorn herself is, in God’s city, given freely as the setting for his people’s life with him. The greatest treasure in the city is God himself (22:4).

In a sentence. The wall was made of jasper, and the city of pure gold, as clear as glass; the foundation stones of the city wall were decorated with every kind of precious stone: the first jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth and the twelfth amethyst; the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate made from a single pearl, and the main street of the city was pure gold, transparent as glass.

On a Tuesday. Hold the things of this world loosely. In God’s city, gold is pavement. Set your heart on the treasure that lasts.
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.

Setting and background. For Israel, the temple was the centre of life: the place where God dwelt and where sacrifices were offered. Ezekiel’s vision of the restored city centred on a new temple (Ezekiel 40–48). Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on a particular mountain (John 4:21–24). He called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21).

And I saw no temple in the city. Key words. “Temple” (naon, sanctuary). A startling statement for a Jewish reader. Everyone would expect the new Jerusalem to have a glorious temple. But there is none.

For its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Key words. A temple was needed because God’s presence was limited to one place, and sin kept people at a distance. Now God’s presence fills the whole city, and nothing separates his people from him. The temple was always a pointer to this: God himself living with his people. God and the Lamb together are the temple: the Son shares the Father’s presence and glory.

What it does not mean. No temple does not mean no worship. The whole city is a temple, and all of life is worship. It also confirms that there will be no rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices in God’s final plan; Christ’s sacrifice has fulfilled them all.

In a sentence. I did not see any temple in the city, because its temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb.

For worship. Through Christ, you can come into God’s presence now, anywhere. One day, there will be nowhere that is not his temple.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.

Setting and background. Isaiah 60:1–3, 11, 19–20 promises Jerusalem: arise, shine, for your light has come; nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising; your gates shall be open continually, day and night they shall not be shut; the sun shall be no more your light by day, but the LORD will be your everlasting light. Jesus said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12). In ancient cities, gates were shut at night for protection.

And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it. Key words. Not that the sun and moon no longer exist, but that they are not needed. A greater light outshines them.

For the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. Key words. “Glory” (doxa). “Lamp” (lychnos). God’s glory is the light, and the Lamb is the lamp through which it shines. We see God’s glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

By its light will the nations walk. Key words. “Nations” (ethnē). The redeemed from every nation, living in God’s light. Their national and cultural diversity is preserved in the new creation.

And the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. Key words. “Kings of the earth”: the same phrase used of those who committed immorality with Babylon (17:2; 18:9). Some kings, who once rebelled, are redeemed. The good things of human culture, its achievements, beauty and treasures, cleansed of sin, are brought into the new creation.

And its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there. Key words. Gates open because there is no danger. No night, because God is the light. Perfect safety and perfect welcome.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it”, adding “of them which are saved”. The best manuscripts simply read “the nations”. The addition explains correctly who the nations are.

Where Christians differ: does this mean the nations outside are finally saved? Some read the nations and kings coming into the city as unbelievers being saved after the final judgement, so that all will eventually enter. Verdict: the nations here are the redeemed nations, the great multitude from every nation (7:9), who come into the city because their names are written in the Lamb’s book (v. 27). The lake of fire is final (20:15; 21:8), and outside the city are those who practise wickedness (22:15). The passage shows that the redeemed include people from every nation, and that the best of human culture is brought in, purified. It does not teach a second chance after death.

What it does not mean. No night does not mean no rest. It means no darkness, no danger, no fear, no evil.

In a sentence. The city does not need the sun or the moon to shine on it, because the glory of God gives it light, and the Lamb is its lamp; the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their splendour into it; its gates will never be shut during the day, and there will be no night there.

On a Tuesday. The good work you do in your culture, art, science and service, done for God’s glory, is not wasted. Its glory, purified, may yet be brought into the city.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

Setting and background. Isaiah 52:1 says that the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more come into Jerusalem. Isaiah 60:5, 11 says the wealth of the nations shall come to Zion. Haggai 2:7 says the treasures of all nations shall come in and God will fill his house with glory.

They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. Key words. “Glory” (doxan) and “honor” (timēn). As in v. 24. All that is good and beautiful in the world’s peoples is gathered into God’s city.

But nothing unclean will ever enter it. Key words. “Unclean” (koinon, common, defiled, profane). The city is wholly holy. Nothing that defiles can enter.
