Come, Lord Jesus!<sup>21</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished — it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.

Meaning first. Revelation 15 is the shortest chapter in the book. It prepares for the seven bowls of chapter 16, the last plagues, which complete God’s wrath (v. 1). Before the plagues fall, John sees those who conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps (v. 2). Like Israel beside the Red Sea, they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, praising God’s great deeds, his just and true ways, his holiness, and the coming worship of all nations (vv. 3–4). Then the heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, opens, and seven angels come out dressed as priests (vv. 5–6). One of the living creatures gives them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and the sanctuary fills with smoke from God’s glory, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished (vv. 7–8). The chapter places the final judgements in the context of worship: the redeemed praise God’s justice before it is displayed, and the judgements come from his holy presence.

Setting and background. The bowl judgements follow the pattern of the plagues on Egypt even more closely than the trumpets: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs, hail. And the scene by the sea of glass recalls Israel singing beside the Red Sea after God destroyed Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 15). The new exodus is complete.

Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing. Key words. “Sign” (sēmeion), as in 12:1, 3: the third great sign. “Amazing” (thaumaston, marvellous).

Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last. Key words. “Plagues” (plēgas, blows). “Last” (eschatas): the final series of judgements. The seals struck a quarter, the trumpets a third; the bowls strike everything.

For with them the wrath of God is finished. Key words. “Finished” (etelesthē, completed, brought to its end). God’s wrath is not endless rage in history; it has a goal and an end. When the bowls are poured out, God’s judgement on this age is complete. The same verb Jesus used on the cross: It is finished (John 19:30, tetelestai). There, God’s wrath against his people’s sin was finished, borne by Christ; here, his wrath against the unrepentant world is completed.

What it does not mean. “Last” does not necessarily mean the bowls happen after the seals and trumpets in strict time. They are the last in John’s sequence of visions and in their intensity, describing the final outpouring of God’s judgement, which the earlier series also reached in their own way (6:12–17; 11:15–19).

In a sentence. Then I saw another great and astonishing sign in heaven: seven angels holding the seven last plagues, the last because with them God’s anger is brought to completion.

For worship. God’s judgement has an end. Thank him that for his people it was finished at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.

Setting and background. Israel crossed the Red Sea, and stood on the far shore, safe, while the waters closed over Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14:26–31). Then Moses and Israel sang (Exodus 15:1–18), and Miriam led the women with tambourines (Exodus 15:20–21). The sea of glass first appeared before God’s throne (4:6).

And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire. Key words. “Mingled with fire” (memigmenēn pyri). The calm sea of 4:6, now glowing with fire: the fire of God’s judgement about to fall, or the reflection of his blazing holiness. The sea, symbol of chaos and the beast’s origin (13:1), has been passed through and subdued.

And also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. Key words. “Conquered” (nikōntas, the conquering ones). Those killed by the beast (13:7, 15) are here called its conquerors. They refused its worship, image and mark, and so they won. Victory by faithfulness, even unto death (12:11).

Standing beside the sea of glass. Key words. “Beside” (epi, by, on). Like Israel standing beside the sea after crossing it. They have come through the great tribulation (7:14), and stand safe.

With harps of God in their hands. Key words. “Harps of God”: instruments given by God for his worship (5:8; 14:2).

What it does not mean. The conquerors are not a special group of martyrs only. All who refuse the beast’s worship and remain faithful to Christ, whether or not they are killed, are conquerors.

In a sentence. And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and standing beside it, holding harps given by God, were those who had won the victory over the beast, its image and the number of its name.

For worship. If you have refused the idols of this age, you are counted among the conquerors. You will stand beside the sea and sing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

Setting and background. The song of Moses in Exodus 15 celebrated God’s victory over Pharaoh: who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness? (Exodus 15:11). Deuteronomy 32, another song of Moses, says: his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice; a God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he (Deuteronomy 32:4). The words of this new song are drawn almost entirely from Old Testament praise: Psalm 86:9 (all the nations shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name), Psalm 98:1–2, 111:2, 139:14, 145:17, Jeremiah 10:6–7 (who would not fear you, O King of the nations?), and Malachi 1:11.

And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Key words. One song, not two: the song of Moses, fulfilled in the song of the Lamb. As Moses led Israel out of Egypt through the sea, the Lamb has led his people out of the world’s bondage through his blood. The first exodus and the final exodus are celebrated together.

Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Key words. “Deeds” (erga, works). God’s works in creation, redemption and judgement. “Almighty” (pantokratōr), as in 1:8.

Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Key words. “Just” (dikaiai, righteous) and “true” (alēthinai, faithful, genuine). Before the bowls are poured out, the redeemed declare that God’s ways are just. His judgements are not arbitrary or cruel; they are right. “King of the nations”: not Caesar, but God.

Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? Key words. A rhetorical question: everyone ought to fear and glorify him.

For you alone are holy. Key words. “Holy” (hosios, devout, pure, holy; a word used of God only here and in 16:5 in Revelation). God alone, not the beast with its blasphemous claims.

All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed. Key words. “Righteous acts” (dikaiōmata, just deeds, judgements). From Psalm 86:9. Seeing God’s righteous acts, the nations will come and worship. This looks to the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and to the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24–26).

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on God’s title in v. 3. The best manuscripts read “King of the nations”; others read “King of the ages”; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “King of saints”. All three are true of God; “nations” fits the song’s theme of all nations coming to worship.

Where Christians differ: will all nations, and so all people, be saved? Universalists sometimes cite “all nations will come and worship you” as proof that everyone will finally be saved. Verdict: “all nations” means people from every nation, not every individual in every nation. The great multitude comes from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9), but Revelation is clear that those who worship the beast and refuse to repent are judged for ever (14:9–11; 21:8). The song celebrates the worldwide scope of God’s salvation, fulfilling his promise to Abraham, and the universal acknowledgement of his justice.

What it does not mean. The redeemed do not praise God’s justice because they are hard-hearted toward the lost. They praise it because they see clearly, as we often cannot, that every one of his ways is right.

In a sentence. They sing the song of God’s servant Moses and the song of the Lamb: Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the nations; who will not fear you, Lord, and give glory to your name? You alone are holy; all nations will come and bow down before you, because your just acts have been made plain for all to see.

For worship. Sing this song. When you cannot understand what God is doing, confess with the redeemed that his ways are just and true.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it — pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.

Setting and background. The tabernacle in the wilderness was called the tent of witness (or testimony, Numbers 17:7; 18:2), because it held the ark containing the tablets of the law, the testimony of God’s covenant (Exodus 25:16; 31:18). The priests wore white linen (Leviticus 16:4). Christ in 1:13 wore a golden sash around his chest.

After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. Key words. “Sanctuary” (naos, inner shrine). “Tent of witness” (tēs skēnēs tou martyriou). The heavenly reality of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy (Hebrews 8:5). The law of God, his covenant testimony, is kept there. The judgements that follow come from God’s holy law, which the world has broken. The ark of the covenant was seen there in 11:19.

And out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues. Key words. They come from God’s very presence. The judgements are holy acts, carried out by those who stand before God.

Clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests. Key words. “Linen” (linon). Priestly dress: purity and holiness. The angels carry out God’s judgement as a priestly service. Like Christ’s golden sash (1:13), the sashes show their dignity and their connection with him.

What it does not mean. The angels are not acting on their own initiative. They come out of the sanctuary; they serve God’s will.

In a sentence. After this I looked, and the inner shrine of the tent of the testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels holding the seven plagues came out of it, dressed in pure, shining linen, with gold sashes around their chests.

On a Tuesday. God’s law is not a dead letter. It stands at the centre of heaven, and its testimony will be upheld. Take it seriously in your own life.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

Setting and background. Golden bowls were used in the temple for carrying incense and the blood of sacrifices (1 Kings 7:50; 2 Chronicles 4:22). The golden bowls of 5:8 were full of incense, the prayers of the saints. When the tabernacle and the temple were dedicated, God’s glory filled them as a cloud, so that Moses and the priests could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). In Isaiah’s vision, the house was filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4).

And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls. Key words. “Bowls” (phialas, shallow bowls). The same golden bowls that held the saints’ prayers (5:8) now hold God’s wrath. God’s judgement is the answer to his people’s prayers. A living creature, representing creation, hands them over: creation itself longs for its liberation (Romans 8:19–22).

Full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever. Key words. “Full” (gemousas, filled to the brim). The eternal God’s wrath is not a passing temper. It is his settled, holy opposition to evil.

And the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power. Key words. “Smoke” (kapnou). God’s glory and power, in overwhelming holiness, as at Sinai and the temple dedication.

And no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished. Key words. No one can intercede now. The time for mediation is past; judgement must run its course. This is the most solemn moment in the book: the door of intercession closes.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that today it is too late to pray or to turn to God. The scene describes the final judgement at the end of history. Today is still the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and Christ still intercedes for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

In a sentence. Then one of the four living beings gave the seven angels seven gold bowls filled with the anger of God, who lives for ever and ever, and the temple was filled with smoke from God’s glory and power, so that no one could go into it until the seven plagues of the seven angels were over.

On a Tuesday. There will come a day when it is too late. Today it is not. Pray for those who do not yet know Christ, and urge them to come while the door is open.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five draw on the Egyptian plagues, though not in their order: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne — the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, “Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God.” So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.

Meaning first. Revelation 16 pours out the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the last and fullest judgements on a world that has chosen the beast. The first bowl brings painful sores on the beast’s worshippers (vv. 1–2); the second turns the sea to blood (v. 3); the third turns the rivers and springs to blood, and the angel of the waters and the altar declare God just, for those who shed the saints’ blood are given blood to drink (vv. 4–7). The fourth scorches people with the sun, and they curse God and do not repent (vv. 8–9). The fifth plunges the beast’s kingdom into darkness, and still they curse God and do not repent (vv. 10–11). The sixth dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east, and three frog-like demonic spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings of the whole world for battle on the great day of God, at the place called Armageddon; in the middle, Christ warns that he comes like a thief, and blesses those who stay awake (vv. 12–16). The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, with the greatest earthquake ever known: Babylon splits apart and drains the cup of God’s wrath, islands and mountains vanish, and huge hailstones fall, and still people curse God (vv. 17–21). Like the seals and trumpets, the bowls reach the end of history; unlike them, they are complete, not partial. They show God’s justice against those who persecute his people, and the terrible hardness of hearts that will not repent.

Setting and background. The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores (the sixth plague, Exodus 9:8–12), water turned to blood (the first, Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (the ninth, Exodus 10:21–23), frogs (the second, Exodus 8:1–15), and hail (the seventh, Exodus 9:22–26). As Pharaoh hardened his heart, so do the beast’s worshippers. And the trumpets and bowls run in parallel: both strike earth, sea, rivers, sun, the realm of darkness and the Euphrates, and both end with the final judgement. But the trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike all.

Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels. Key words. From the temple, where no one could enter (15:8): the voice of God himself.

Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God. Key words. “Pour out” (ekcheete), as drink offerings and blood were poured out at the altar. Psalm 79:6 prays, pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you.

So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth. The land.

And harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Key words. “Sores” (helkos, ulcer, festering wound), the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the boils on the Egyptians. “Harmful and painful” (kakon kai ponēron, bad and evil). Those who took the beast’s mark now bear another mark on their bodies. The judgement falls specifically on the beast’s worshippers, not on God’s people.

What it does not mean. The bowls are not aimed at believers. As in Egypt, where the plagues did not touch Israel in Goshen, God’s people are not the targets of his wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). They may still suffer from the beast, but not from God’s anger.

In a sentence. Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, Go and pour out the seven bowls of God’s anger on the earth; so the first angel went and poured his bowl on the land, and ugly, painful sores broke out on the people who had the beast’s mark and worshipped its image.

On a Tuesday. Whatever mark people choose, they will bear its consequences. Choose today to belong to the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.

Setting and background. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile and all Egypt’s waters to blood, so that the fish died and the river stank (Exodus 7:17–21). The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (8:8–9) and the third made a third of the rivers bitter (8:10–11).

The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse. Key words. “Blood of a corpse” (haima hōs nekrou, blood like that of a dead man): thick, congealed, rotting. A horrifying image of death.

And every living thing died that was in the sea. Key words. “Every” (pasa). Not a third, as with the trumpets, but all. The bowls are complete.

The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood. Key words. Fresh water, essential for life, is gone. The world that rejected the living water (7:17; 21:6) loses even ordinary water.

What it does not mean. These are not predictions of a particular ecological disaster, though disasters in nature are real and serve as warnings. They are pictures of God’s final judgement on a world that has turned its back on the Creator, in which the creation that sustained it turns against it.

In a sentence. The second angel poured his bowl into the sea, and it turned into blood like that of a dead body, and every living creature in the sea died; the third angel poured his bowl into the rivers and springs, and they turned to blood.

On a Tuesday. Every glass of clean water is a gift from God. Thank him for it, and do not take his goodness in creation for granted.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, “Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!” And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!”

Setting and background. Jewish writings spoke of angels with charge over different parts of creation, such as fire (14:18), winds (7:1) and waters. The principle of fitting judgement runs through Scripture: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Genesis 9:6). Isaiah 49:26 says God will make the oppressors drunk with their own blood. Psalm 19:9 says the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether. Pharaoh had the Hebrew boys thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22); God turned the Nile to blood.

And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, Just are you, O Holy One. Key words. “Just” (dikaios, righteous). “Holy One” (hosios, as in 15:4). The angel whose realm has been struck does not complain; he declares God just.

Who is and who was. Key words. As in 11:17: “and is to come” is missing, because now he has come in judgement.

For you brought these judgments. Key words. “Brought” (ekrinas, judged). God is the judge.

For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. Key words. The punishment fits the crime. Those who poured out the blood of God’s people now have only blood to drink. This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry (6:10).

It is what they deserve! Key words. “Deserve” (axioi eisin, they are worthy). A grim echo of the praise of the Lamb as worthy (5:9, 12). The Lamb is worthy of glory; the persecutors are worthy of judgement.

And I heard the altar saying, Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments! Key words. “The altar” speaks: the altar under which the martyrs’ souls cried out for justice (6:9–10), and from which the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5). The answer to their prayers has come, and the altar says, Yes. “True and just” (alētheinai kai dikaiai), as the redeemed sang (15:3).

Textual note. In v. 5 the King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”, following a late reading; the best manuscripts read “who is and who was, the Holy One”. In v. 7, the King James Version reads “I heard another out of the altar say”, but the best manuscripts read simply “I heard the altar saying”.

What it does not mean. Praising God’s judgement is not rejoicing in suffering for its own sake. It is the recognition that God has put things right, that evil has not had the last word, and that the blood of the innocent has not been forgotten. Without God’s justice, the world’s victims would have no hope.

In a sentence. Then I heard the angel who has charge of the waters say: You are just, Holy One, who is and who was, in judging like this; they poured out the blood of your people and your prophets, and you have given them blood to drink, which is what they deserve; and I heard the altar answer: Yes, Lord God Almighty, your judgements are true and just.

For worship. When you see injustice that is never put right in this life, bring it to God in prayer, and trust that his judgements will be true and just. The altar will one day say, Yes.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.

Setting and background. The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12). The redeemed are promised that the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat (7:16).

The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. Key words. “Allowed” (edothē, it was given). “Scorch” (kaumatisai, burn). The sun, which God made to give light and life, becomes an instrument of judgement. What the redeemed are spared, the beast’s worshippers suffer.

They were scorched by the fierce heat. Key words. “Fierce heat” (kauma mega, great heat).

And they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. Key words. “Cursed” (eblasphēmēsan, blasphemed, slandered). They know God is behind the plagues; they acknowledge his power. But instead of turning to him, they curse him. They have become like the beast, whose mouth utters blasphemies (13:6).

They did not repent and give him glory. Key words. “Did not repent” (ou metenoēsan), as in 9:20–21. “Give him glory”: the response called for by the eternal gospel (14:7), and given by some in 11:13. Here it is refused.

What it does not mean. The plagues are not the reason they refuse to repent; their hard hearts are. Judgement reveals what is already in the heart. Pharaoh, too, hardened his heart under the plagues, and God also hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12).

In a sentence. The fourth angel poured his bowl on the sun, and the sun was allowed to burn people with fire; they were seared by the intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had power over these plagues, but they refused to repent and give him glory.

On a Tuesday. Suffering can soften or harden a heart. When hardship comes, turn toward God, not away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.

Setting and background. The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23). Jesus spoke of the outer darkness where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12; 22:13).

The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast. Key words. “Throne of the beast” (ton thronon tou thēriou): the seat of its power, given by the dragon (13:2). The judgement strikes at the heart of the beast’s rule.

And its kingdom was plunged into darkness. Key words. “Plunged into darkness” (eskotōmenē, darkened). The beast’s kingdom, which seemed so dazzling and powerful, collapses into darkness. All human empires that defy God end this way.

People gnawed their tongues in anguish. Key words. “Gnawed” (emasōnto, chewed). “Anguish” (ponou, pain). Extreme agony.

And cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. Key words. The sores of the first bowl remain. The plagues accumulate.

They did not repent of their deeds. The third time this refusal is mentioned (9:20–21; 16:9). Their hearts are set.

What it does not mean. The darkness does not mean God is unable to reach them. It means he gives them what they chose: they loved darkness rather than light (John 3:19), and now they have it.

In a sentence. The fifth angel poured his bowl on the beast’s throne, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness; people bit their tongues in agony and cursed the God of heaven because of their pains and sores, but they did not turn from what they had done.

On a Tuesday. Every kingdom built against God ends in darkness. Invest your life in the kingdom of light.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

Setting and background. God dried up the Red Sea and the Jordan for Israel (Exodus 14:21; Joshua 3:14–17). Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC by diverting the Euphrates and marching his army along the riverbed into the city (Herodotus; compare Isaiah 44:27–28; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). The second plague on Egypt was frogs (Exodus 8:1–15). In the Old Testament, frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:9–12). The prophets foretold a final gathering of the nations against God and his people, which God would defeat (Joel 3:2; Zechariah 12:3; 14:2; Ezekiel 38–39).

The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up. Key words. The same river as the sixth trumpet (9:14). The barrier that held back invasion is removed.

To prepare the way for the kings from the east. Key words. “From the east” (apo anatolēs hēliou, from the rising of the sun). In John’s day, the Parthians beyond the Euphrates. Here, the forces of the world gathering against God. The drying of the river recalls both the exodus and Cyrus’s capture of Babylon: Babylon is about to fall.

And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. Key words. The unholy trinity (12:3; 13:1, 11). From their mouths: their words, lies and propaganda. “Unclean spirits” (pneumata tria akatharta). “Like frogs”: croaking, ugly and unclean. Deception, loud and persistent but worthless.

For they are demonic spirits, performing signs. Key words. “Demonic” (daimoniōn). “Signs”: deceptive wonders, as in 13:13–14.

Who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty. Key words. “Assemble” (synagagein, gather together). “Battle” (polemon, war, with the article in Greek: the battle, the final one). “The great day of God the Almighty”: the day of judgement. The demonic spirits deceive the rulers of the world into a final war against God. They think they are gathering to fight; in fact, God is gathering them to be judged. The same battle is described in 19:19 and 20:8.

What it does not mean. The kings from the east are not a coded prediction about any modern nation, such as China. The Euphrates and the east are symbols drawn from Israel’s history and the Roman world’s fears.

In a sentence. The sixth angel poured his bowl on the great River Euphrates, and its water dried up to open the way for the kings from the east; then I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet; they are demonic spirits that perform signs, and they go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for the battle on the great day of God Almighty.

On a Tuesday. Demonic deception often comes through words and propaganda. Measure what you hear by God’s word, and refuse lies, however loud.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
(“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”) And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.

Setting and background. Megiddo was a fortified city overlooking the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon) in northern Israel, on the main route between Egypt and Mesopotamia, and the site of many decisive battles. There Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 5:19), and King Josiah was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29–30; Zechariah 12:11). Nearby Mount Carmel was where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). Jesus said he would come like a thief (Matthew 24:43–44), as he warned Sardis (3:3), and he told Laodicea to buy white garments to cover the shame of its nakedness (3:18).

Behold, I am coming like a thief! Key words. Christ suddenly interrupts the vision. In the middle of the gathering for the final battle, he speaks directly to his church: be ready. His coming will be unexpected for those who are not watching.

Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on. Key words. The third beatitude in Revelation. “Stays awake” (grēgorōn, keeps watch). “Keeping his garments on” (tērōn ta himatia autou, guarding his clothes). Temple guards were said to be beaten and stripped if found asleep on duty. The garments are the white robes of Christ’s righteousness and a faithful life (3:4–5, 18; 19:8).

That he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! Key words. “Exposed” (tēn aschēmosynēn, shame, disgrace). To be found unprepared at Christ’s coming is to be shamed.

And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon. Key words. “Armageddon” (Harmagedōn). Probably from the Hebrew har Megiddo, mountain of Megiddo. But there is no mountain of Megiddo, only a plain and a hill (tel). The name is symbolic: the place of decisive battle, where God’s enemies are defeated. Some connect it with Mount Carmel nearby, or with the mountain of assembly (Isaiah 14:13). John says it is called this “in Hebrew”, a signal to look for its meaning.

Where Christians differ: is Armageddon a literal battle in northern Israel? Many futurists expect the armies of the world to gather literally in the valley of Megiddo for a final war in the Middle East, before Christ returns. Verdict: Armageddon is a symbolic name for the final conflict between the powers of the world and God, drawn from Israel’s history of decisive battles at Megiddo. The battle is described three times in Revelation (16:14–16; 19:17–21; 20:7–10), and each time no battle is actually fought: the enemies are gathered and then destroyed instantly by Christ at his coming. It is the same final event, seen from different angles. It may involve a literal gathering of hostile powers, but its location and form are not the point; its outcome is. Christ wins without a fight.

What it does not mean. “Armageddon” in Revelation does not mean nuclear war or a global catastrophe caused by human beings, as the word is often used today. It means the day when God judges the world’s rebellion.

In a sentence. (Look, I am coming like a thief! How blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not have to walk around naked and be seen in his shame!) And the spirits gathered the kings together at the place called in Hebrew Armageddon.

On a Tuesday. Do not speculate about Armageddon; prepare for Christ’s coming. Stay awake, keep your garments clean, and live as one who will meet him.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!” And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.

Setting and background. On the cross, Jesus said, It is finished (John 19:30). The same signs of lightning, thunder and earthquake ended the seals (8:5) and the trumpets (11:19), and here they reach their climax. Daniel 12:1 speaks of a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation.

The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air. Key words. “Air” (aera). The realm of the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2), where demonic powers operate. The last bowl strikes the whole environment of human life.

And a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, It is done! Key words. “It is done” (gegonen, it has happened, it has come to pass, perfect tense). God’s own voice from his throne. The judgement of this age is complete. Christ’s It is finished on the cross accomplished salvation; God’s It is done completes judgement. The same word is spoken again at the making of all things new (21:6).

And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder. As at 4:5, 8:5 and 11:19.

And a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake. Key words. The greatest earthquake in history. The final shaking of the created order, so that only what cannot be shaken remains (Hebrews 12:26–28).

What it does not mean. “It is done” does not mean that nothing more happens in Revelation. Chapters 17–20 go back and describe the fall of Babylon and the final defeat of the beast and Satan in detail. It means that God’s judgement on this age has reached its end.

In a sentence. The seventh angel poured his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, It is done! and there came lightning, rumbling, thunder and a massive earthquake, greater than any since human beings have been on earth.

For worship. Worship the God whose word is final. What Christ finished on the cross and what God completes at the end are both sure.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.

Setting and background. The seventh plague on Egypt was the worst hailstorm the country had ever seen (Exodus 9:18–26). God threw great hailstones from heaven on the Amorite kings fleeing from Joshua (Joshua 10:11). Ezekiel 38:22 promises hailstones, fire and sulphur against Gog. A talent (talantiaia) weighed about 45 kilograms (100 pounds).

The great city was split into three parts. Key words. “The great city”: Babylon (v. 19; 17:18). Split into three: completely shattered.

And the cities of the nations fell. Key words. Every human city and civilisation built without God collapses with Babylon.

And God remembered Babylon the great. Key words. “Remembered” (emnēsthē). God had not forgotten her sins (18:5). Delayed judgement is not cancelled judgement.

To make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Key words. Babylon made the nations drink her wine (14:8); now she drinks God’s (14:10). Chapters 17–18 describe her fall in detail.

And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. Key words. As at the sixth seal (6:14), and at the final judgement (20:11), when earth and sky flee from God’s presence. The old creation passes away.

And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people. Key words. Enormous, crushing, deadly. The final blow.

And they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe. Key words. To the very end, they curse God rather than repent. The last word of the bowls is not repentance but blasphemy. This is the true horror of sin: it hardens until it cannot turn.

What it does not mean. The persistent cursing does not mean God failed to give them opportunity. He sent warnings, judgements, witnesses and the eternal gospel. They chose, again and again, to refuse. God gave them what they chose.

In a sentence. The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed; God remembered Babylon the great and made her drink the cup filled with the wine of his furious anger; every island disappeared and the mountains could no longer be found; huge hailstones, each weighing about forty-five kilograms, fell from the sky on people, and they cursed God because of the hail, because the plague was so terrible.

On a Tuesday. Do not harden your heart today. If God is calling you to repent of something, turn now, while your heart can still be softened.
