17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Chapter 17 introduces one of Revelation’s two great female figures: the great prostitute who sits on many waters, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations. She is the counterpart to the bride of the Lamb (chapters 19 and 21) — two women, two cities, two ways of organising human life. The bride is pure, faithful, clothed in the righteousness of the Lamb. Babylon is seductive, unfaithful, clothed in the luxury of empire. Every human being in history has been drawn toward one or the other.

The identity of Babylon is both specific and universal. In the first century, every reader knew who she was: Rome. The seven hills (v. 9), the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, the city that rules over the kings of the earth (v. 18) — all of this pointed unmistakably to the imperial city on the Tiber. Preterists and idealists agree on this much. Where they differ is on what Rome represents: preterists see primarily the historical Rome of Nero and Domitian; idealists see Rome as the type of every civilisation that organises itself around wealth, power, and the seduction of the nations away from the living God. The idealist position is followed here: Babylon is Rome, and Babylon is every Rome.

The chapter falls into two movements: the vision of the woman on the beast (vv. 1–6) and the angel’s interpretation (vv. 7–18). The interpretation is deliberately cryptic — ‘this calls for a mind that has wisdom’ (v. 9) — and the details about the seven kings and the eighth king have generated more interpretive proposals than almost any other passage in Revelation. The main options are presented honestly here rather than forcing a specific identification that the text itself refuses to make definitive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: one of the bowl angels — tying this chapter to 16:19, where God remembered Babylon — invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters (cf. Jer. 51:13). The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk on her wine. The same invitation will come from the same rank of angel at 21:9: Come, I will show you the Bride.

Verses 3–4: carried in the Spirit into a wilderness (the Bride is shown from a high mountain, 21:10), John sees a woman riding the scarlet beast of chapter 13 — seven heads, ten horns, blasphemous names. She is arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding a golden cup full of abominations (cf. Jer. 51:7; Matt. 23:25).

Verse 5: a name on her forehead, in a book where that is never incidental (7:3; 13:16; 14:1) — Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations, which the ESV prints in capitals. Verse 6: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus — and John, seeing her, marveled greatly, using the verb this book twice uses of the world’s reaction to the beast (13:3; 17:8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome for the first readers, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents — and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”

Meaning first. Revelation 17 zooms in on Babylon, whose fall was announced in 14:8 and 16:19, and shows her as a great prostitute. An angel invites John to see her judgement: she sits on many waters, the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the world is drunk on her wine (vv. 1–2). In the wilderness John sees her riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple, scarlet and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations, with her name on her forehead: Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes; and she is drunk with the blood of the saints (vv. 3–6). The angel explains: the beast was, is not, and will come up from the abyss and go to destruction, and the world will marvel at it (vv. 7–8). Its seven heads are seven hills where the woman sits and seven kings; the beast is an eighth king, belonging to the seven (vv. 9–11). Its ten horns are ten kings who rule briefly with the beast and make war on the Lamb, but the Lamb conquers them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and his people are called, chosen and faithful (vv. 12–14). The waters are the peoples of the world, and in the end the beast and the kings will turn on the prostitute and destroy her, because God put it in their hearts to fulfil his purpose (vv. 15–17). The woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth (v. 18). The chapter exposes the seductive glamour of the world system, the economic, cultural and religious power of Rome in John’s day and of every godless civilisation since, and shows that evil turns on itself, while the Lamb wins.

Setting and background. The prophets called cities that lured others into idolatry and greed prostitutes: Nineveh (Nahum 3:4), Tyre (Isaiah 23:15–17), and even Jerusalem when unfaithful (Ezekiel 16; 23). Ancient Babylon was built on the Euphrates with canals around it, and Jeremiah addressed it as you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures (Jeremiah 51:13). In John’s day, Rome was the centre of a vast trading empire, rich, luxurious, and the seat of the emperor cult; Roman writers themselves called it a city of vice. The goddess Roma was worshipped in Asia, and a coin of Vespasian showed her seated on Rome’s seven hills.

Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me. Key words. One of the bowl angels: chapters 17–18 expand on the seventh bowl, the fall of Babylon (16:19).

Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute. Key words. “Judgment” (krima, verdict, sentence). “Prostitute” (pornēs, harlot). The opposite of the bride of the Lamb, whom another bowl angel will show John in exactly the same words (21:9). Two women, two cities: Babylon and the new Jerusalem.

Who is seated on many waters. Key words. Explained in v. 15: peoples, multitudes, nations and languages. She rules over the world.

With whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality. Key words. The kings have joined her in idolatry and in the pursuit of wealth and power. Political and economic alliances with the godless world system.

And with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk. Key words. “Drunk” (emethysthēsan). Intoxicated by her luxury, pleasures and values, unable to think clearly about God.

What it does not mean. The prostitute is not a picture of women or of sexuality as such. It is a prophetic image for seductive unfaithfulness to God, as the Old Testament used it for cities and nations.

In a sentence. Then one of the seven angels who held the seven bowls came and said to me, Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute who sits enthroned over many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and with whose immoral wine the people of the earth got drunk.

On a Tuesday. The world’s seductions are attractive. Ask what intoxicates you, and whether it draws you away from Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.

Setting and background. Purple dye was extremely expensive, made from shellfish, and was worn by royalty and the very rich. Scarlet was also costly. Jeremiah 51:7 calls Babylon a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunk. Jeremiah 4:30 pictures unfaithful Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and adorning herself with gold to attract lovers.

And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness. Key words. “In the Spirit” (en pneumati), as in 1:10 and 4:2. The third such phrase, marking a new section. “Wilderness”: the place where the woman of chapter 12 was protected. From the wilderness, the place of the faithful church, John sees Babylon clearly for what she is. Later he is carried to a high mountain to see the bride (21:10).

And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast. Key words. “Sitting on” (kathēmenēn epi): riding, supported by, controlling. The prostitute depends on the beast’s power. The beast is the same as in chapter 13: political power empowered by Satan. Babylon, the world’s culture and economy, rides on the back of political power.

That was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. As in 13:1.

The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls. Key words. Luxury, wealth and seduction. A parody of the bride, who wears fine linen, bright and pure (19:8), and of the new Jerusalem, adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (21:18–21). Babylon offers a counterfeit glory.

Holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality. Key words. “Abominations” (bdelygmatōn, detestable things, especially idolatry). “Impurities” (akatharta, unclean things). Outwardly golden, inwardly filthy. Jesus said of the Pharisees that they cleaned the outside of the cup while inside it was full of greed and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:25).

What it does not mean. Beauty, wealth and fine clothes are not evil in themselves; the new Jerusalem is glorious. Babylon’s sin is using them to seduce people away from God and to serve herself.

In a sentence. Then the angel carried me away in the Spirit to a desert, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast covered with blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns; the woman was dressed in purple and scarlet and glittered with gold, precious stones and pearls, and she held a gold cup filled with detestable things and the filth of her immorality.

On a Tuesday. Do not be dazzled by the glitter of the world. Look at what is in the cup.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.” And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.

Setting and background. Roman writers mention that prostitutes in Rome sometimes wore a headband bearing their name. Jeremiah 3:3 tells unfaithful Israel, you have the forehead of a prostitute; you refuse to be ashamed.

And on her forehead was written a name of mystery. Key words. “Forehead”: her identity, as with the seal of God (7:3) and the mark of the beast (13:16). “Mystery” (mystērion): a name with a hidden meaning that must be understood spiritually. Babylon is not literally the ancient city on the Euphrates, which was in ruins in John’s day.

BABYLON THE GREAT. Key words. The city of pride and rebellion, from Babel (Genesis 11) onward, the destroyer of Jerusalem. In John’s day, Rome (1 Peter 5:13), and in every age, the human city organised against God.

MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS. Key words. “Mother”: the source, the origin. All the world’s idolatries and corruptions flow from her.

And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. Key words. “Drunk with blood”: she has killed God’s people in great numbers, and revels in it. “Martyrs” (martyrōn, witnesses). Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many killed horribly; Peter and Paul died in Rome.

When I saw her, I marveled greatly. Key words. “Marveled” (ethaumasa … thauma mega, I wondered with great wonder). John is astonished, perhaps even impressed. The world’s glamour can fascinate even believers. The angel will correct him (v. 7).

Where Christians differ: who is the prostitute? Many Reformers and later Protestants identified the prostitute with the Roman Catholic Church and the papacy, seeing in her purple and scarlet the robes of cardinals, and in her drunkenness the blood of the persecuted Reformers. Others see her as apostate Christianity in general, or a future one-world religion. Preterists see first-century Jerusalem. Verdict: the prostitute is Rome, the great city of John’s day (v. 18), seen as the centre of a seductive world system of wealth, idolatry and persecution; and she stands for the godless world system in every age, the culture, commerce and false religion that seduce people from God and persecute his people. Wherever a church becomes rich, worldly and persecuting, as the Reformers saw in their day, it takes on Babylon’s features. But the image is wider than any one church: she is the whole seductive world, which Christians are called to come out of (18:4).

What it does not mean. Seeing Babylon in the world does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, hate their cities, or treat individuals as enemies. They are called to seek the welfare of the city where they live (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its idols.

In a sentence. On her forehead was written a name with a hidden meaning: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF ALL THE EARTH’S DETESTABLE THINGS; and I saw that the woman was drunk with the blood of God’s people, the blood of those who bore witness to Jesus; and when I saw her, I was utterly astonished.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the persecuted church. And beware of being fascinated by the culture that persecutes it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: the angel rebukes the marvelling and explains — and vv. 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in the book, saying this is or these are six times. The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction, and those who marvel at it are those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

Verses 9–11: this calls for a mind with wisdom — the seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings, five fallen, one is, one still to come who must remain only a little while; and the beast is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

Verses 12–14: ten horns are ten kings (cf. Dan. 7:24) who receive authority for one hour and hand their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.

Verses 15–16: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages; and the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire (cf. 2 Kings 9:36; Lev. 21:9). Verse 17: they do it because God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose… until the words of God are fulfilled. Verse 18 closes: the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not — a parody of God’s name — and goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty, but their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful — in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.

Setting and background. God is the one who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8). The beast has a counterfeit title. The Nero redivivus legend held that Nero, who died in AD 68, would return.

But the angel said to me, Why do you marvel? Key words. A gentle rebuke. The world’s power and glamour should not impress the people of God. They should see through it.

I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. Key words. “Mystery”: the hidden meaning, which the angel will explain.

The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. Key words. “Was, and is not, and is about to rise”: a parody of God’s eternal title. God was, is and is to come; the beast was, is not, and will come up only to go to destruction. It is a counterfeit of Christ’s death and resurrection (13:3). Its comings and goings, its apparent defeats and revivals, all end in destruction (apōleian, perdition). The beast appears in one empire, falls, reappears in another, and finally rises for a last time before its end.

And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast. Key words. As in 13:8. Those not written in the Lamb’s book are fascinated by the beast. Those whose names are written are protected from its deception. Election protects.

Because it was and is not and is to come. Key words. Its ability to revive after apparent death astonishes the world.

What it does not mean. The beast’s revival does not mean that a specific dead person, such as Nero, will literally return. It means the beastly power that persecuted the church in Rome will rise again in other forms, and finally in a last great form before Christ’s return.

In a sentence. But the angel said to me, Why are you so amazed? I will explain to you the secret meaning of the woman and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her: the beast you saw once was, now is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to its destruction; and the people of the earth whose names have not been written in the book of life since the creation of the world will be amazed when they see the beast, because it once was, now is not, and yet will come.

On a Tuesday. When evil seems to revive after defeat, do not be amazed or afraid. It is heading for destruction. Christ alone was dead and is alive for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

Setting and background. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills (the Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian and Aventine). Roman writers such as Virgil, Horace and Cicero refer to it this way, and an annual festival, the Septimontium, celebrated the seven hills. Emperors from Augustus to Domitian included Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, then Galba, Otho and Vitellius (in AD 68–69), then Vespasian, Titus and Domitian.

This calls for a mind with wisdom. Key words. As in 13:18. Spiritual discernment is needed.

The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated. Key words. A clear reference to Rome, the city on seven hills. The first readers could not have missed it.

They are also seven kings. Key words. The symbols have more than one meaning: the heads are both hills and kings. Seven: completeness. The full line of rulers of the beastly empire.

Five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. Key words. Many attempts have been made to match these to specific emperors, but they depend on where one starts counting and whether one includes the three short-lived emperors of AD 68–69, and no scheme fits perfectly. More likely, John’s point is that most of the beast’s rule is already past, the present ruler is in power now, and only a short time remains. Seven: the complete series of rulers. History is nearer its end than its beginning.

As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction. Key words. “An eighth”: one beyond the seven, a final ruler, yet belonging to the same line and spirit. Possibly a reference to the expectation of Nero returning in a new form; possibly Domitian, often seen as a second Nero. In biblical symbolism, eight is the number of new beginning; the beast’s eighth is a counterfeit resurrection, heading only for destruction.

What it does not mean. The seven kings are not a code for predicting modern political leaders or nations, as many have tried. The symbolism shows the beast’s line of rulers, its limited time, and its sure end.

In a sentence. This needs a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven hills on which the woman sits; they are also seven kings: five have fallen, one is reigning now, and the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must stay only a short time; the beast that once was and now is not is an eighth king, yet it is one of the seven, and it is going to its destruction.

On a Tuesday. Rulers come and go, and the beast’s time is short. Do not put your hope in any political leader, and do not despair over any either.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

Setting and background. Daniel 7:24 says that the ten horns of the fourth beast are ten kings. Deuteronomy 10:17 calls the LORD God of gods and Lord of lords. Daniel 2:47 calls him God of gods and Lord of kings. The title King of kings was used by Babylonian and Persian emperors.

And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power. Key words. “Ten”: a large, complete number. They are future from John’s point of view: rulers who will arise.

But they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. Key words. “One hour” (mian hōran): a very short time. Their power is brief.

These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. Key words. “One mind” (mian gnōmēn, one purpose). They unite with the beast against God. The nations of the world, united in rebellion (Psalm 2:2).

They will make war on the Lamb. Key words. “Make war” (polemēsousin). The final battle of 16:14 and 19:19.

And the Lamb will conquer them. Key words. “Conquer” (nikēsei). The Lamb, who conquered by his death (5:5–6), conquers his enemies at his return. No battle is described: they are simply defeated.

For he is Lord of lords and King of kings. Key words. The highest titles, belonging to God (Deuteronomy 10:17), now given to the Lamb. Reversed in 19:16. Every emperor’s claim is answered.

And those with him are called and chosen and faithful. Key words. Three words describing believers. “Called” (klētoi): summoned by God’s effective call (Romans 8:30). “Chosen” (eklektoi, elect): chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). “Faithful” (pistoi): trusting and loyal to the end. The order matters: God calls and chooses, and those he calls and chooses prove faithful. Jesus said many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:14), using call there for the outward invitation; here it is the inward, effectual call.

What it does not mean. Those with the Lamb do not fight with weapons. They share his victory, won by his word (19:15). Their part is to be faithful.

In a sentence. The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet begun to reign, but they will receive royal authority for one hour, together with the beast; they have one purpose, and they will hand over their power and authority to the beast; they will wage war against the Lamb, but the Lamb will defeat them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are his called, chosen and faithful followers.

For worship. If you are with the Lamb, you are called, chosen and faithful by his grace. Worship him as King of kings and Lord of lords.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,

Setting and background. Ezekiel 23:25–29 describes how the lovers of unfaithful Jerusalem would turn on her, strip her naked and leave her bare. Jezebel’s flesh was eaten by dogs (2 Kings 9:36). In AD 68–69, Rome itself was torn apart in civil war, and the Capitol was burned by rival Roman armies. The fire of AD 64 had already destroyed much of the city.

And the angel said to me, The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. Key words. Fourfold: all humanity (5:9; 7:9). Babylon’s influence is worldwide.

And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. Key words. “Hate” (misēsousin). A shock: the beast and its allies turn against the woman who rode on them. Evil has no loyalty. Political power eventually destroys the culture and economy that supported it. The godless world system is self-destructive.

They will make her desolate and naked. Key words. “Desolate” (ērēmōmenēn, laid waste, made a wilderness). “Naked”: stripped of her finery and exposed.

And devour her flesh and burn her up with fire. Key words. Like Jezebel, eaten; like a city sacked and burned. The punishment for a priest’s daughter who became a prostitute was burning (Leviticus 21:9).

What it does not mean. The beast destroying Babylon does not make the beast good. It shows that evil destroys evil, and that God uses even the wicked to judge the wicked.

In a sentence. Then the angel said to me, The waters you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, crowds, nations and languages; and the ten horns you saw and the beast will come to hate the prostitute; they will strip her bare and leave her ruined, eat her flesh and burn her up with fire.

On a Tuesday. The world’s alliances and pleasures do not last; those who serve them are eventually devoured by them. Find your security in Christ alone.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

Setting and background. Scripture often shows God using the free actions of wicked people to accomplish his purposes: Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20), Assyria (Isaiah 10:5–7), Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1–4), and above all those who crucified Jesus, who did what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Proverbs 21:1 says the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.

For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose. Key words. “Put it into their hearts” (edōken eis tas kardias autōn, gave into their hearts). “Purpose” (gnōmēn, mind, plan). God is sovereign even over the evil intentions of the beast and its kings. They act freely and wickedly, and they are responsible for what they do; yet God directs it to his own ends.

By being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast. Key words. Even their alliance with the beast serves God’s plan.

Until the words of God are fulfilled. Key words. “Fulfilled” (telesthēsontai, completed). God’s word sets the limit. Nothing happens apart from it.

And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth. Key words. “Has dominion” (echousa basileian, has a kingdom, rules). In John’s day, there was only one city that ruled the kings of the earth: Rome. The angel makes the identification as clear as it could safely be made in a letter that might fall into Roman hands.

Where Christians differ: is God the author of evil? Some worry that saying God put it into their hearts makes God responsible for their sin, and so they soften the verse to mean only that God permits it. Verdict: Scripture teaches that God ordains all that comes to pass, including the evil acts of creatures, without himself being the author of sin, and without taking away their responsibility (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). He does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13), nor infuse wickedness into their hearts; but he directs their evil desires to fulfil his good purpose. This mystery is not a reason for fear but for comfort: even the beast’s schemes serve God’s plan.

What it does not mean. God’s sovereignty does not excuse the beast and the kings. They are judged for what they do (19:19–21).

In a sentence. For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, by agreeing together to hand their royal authority over to the beast until God’s words are fulfilled; and the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.

On a Tuesday. When world events seem out of control, remember that God directs even the plans of the wicked. Trust him, and pray.

When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is Revelation’s sustained lament over the fall of the great city. It is one of the longest chapters in the book, and it is deliberately literary in character — structured like the great prophetic dirges of the Old Testament (Isaiah 13–14 over Babylon; Ezekiel 26–28 over Tyre; Ezekiel 27 especially, whose cargo list John adapts in vv. 12–13). The chapter uses the Old Testament’s own poetic forms to announce the end of the Old Testament’s great enemy.

The chapter moves through three distinct movements. First (vv. 1–8): the angelic announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her. Second (vv. 9–20): the threefold lament of the kings, merchants, and seafarers — three groups whose wealth depended on Babylon, each mourning from a safe distance as the city burns. Third (vv. 21–24): the millstone sign and the sixfold silence — the total, irreversible end of the city that made the nations drunk with her wine.

The economic detail of chapter 18 is one of its most striking features. The cargo list of vv. 12–13 is specific, comprehensive, and damning — ending with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Babylon’s economy is built on everything, including people. The city that offered the nations luxury and culture and wealth was also the city that traded in human beings as commodities. This is Revelation’s most direct indictment of the economics of empire, and it is not limited to the Roman slave trade: every economic system that treats human beings as means rather than ends falls under the same indictment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: an angel with great authority comes down and the earth was made bright with his glory (cf. Ezek. 43:2). Verses 2–3: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! — the announcement of 14:8 now given twenty-four verses instead of one. She becomes a haunt of demons and unclean birds, which is exactly what the prophets said of the first Babylon (Isa. 13:21–22; Jer. 50:39). And three groups are named who will structure the chapter: the nations who drank, the kings who traded, and — new here — the merchants, who grew rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Verses 4–5: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Jer. 51:45; Isa. 52:11; cf. 2 Cor. 6:17), for her sins are heaped high as heaven — a tower again (Gen. 11:4) — and God has remembered her iniquities.

Verses 6–8: repay her double in the cup she mixed; and Babylon speaks in her own voice, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isa. 47:7–8): I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The three things she says she will never see are the three that arrive: death and mourning and famine, all in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her — not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”

Meaning first. Revelation 18 is a funeral song over Babylon, the world city of wealth, luxury and persecution, written in the style of the Old Testament prophets’ laments over Babylon and Tyre. A glorious angel announces that Babylon has fallen and become a haunt of demons, because she seduced the nations, kings and merchants with her wealth and immorality (vv. 1–3). A voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her, so as not to share her sins or plagues, and calls for her to be repaid double for her pride and self-glorification, for she said, I sit as a queen, and her plagues will come in a single day (vv. 4–8). Then three groups lament from a distance: the kings who shared her luxury (vv. 9–10), the merchants who grew rich from her trade in every luxury, and even in human beings (vv. 11–17a), and the sailors whose wealth came from her shipping (vv. 17b–19). Each cries, alas, in a single hour she is ruined. But heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are told to rejoice, because God has judged her for them (v. 20). Finally, a mighty angel throws a great millstone into the sea: so Babylon will be thrown down, and music, craft, the mill, lamplight and the voices of bride and groom will be heard in her no more, because her merchants were the world’s great ones, she deceived the nations by sorcery, and in her was found the blood of the prophets and saints (vv. 21–24). The chapter exposes the hollow glory of a civilisation built on greed, luxury and exploitation, warns the church not to be entangled in it, and assures the suffering that God will judge it completely.

Setting and background. The chapter draws heavily on Isaiah 13, 21 and 47, Jeremiah 50–51 (oracles against Babylon) and Ezekiel 26–28 (the laments over Tyre, the great trading city of the ancient world). In John’s day, Rome imported vast quantities of goods from across the empire, by sea through its port at Ostia, to supply the luxury of its elite, and the wealth of the provinces flowed to it. Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder complained about the extravagance of Roman luxury and its drain on the empire.

After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority. Key words. “Great authority” (exousian megalēn). Babylon claimed great authority; this angel’s is greater.

And the earth was made bright with his glory. Key words. As in Ezekiel 43:2, where the earth shone with God’s glory. In contrast with Babylon, whose lights go out (v. 23).

And he called out with a mighty voice, Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! Key words. As in 14:8 and Isaiah 21:9. Past tense: so certain it is as good as done.

She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. Key words. “Haunt” (phylakē, prison, lair). Isaiah 13:21–22 and 34:11–14 describe ruined Babylon and Edom inhabited by wild animals, owls, jackals and goat-demons. The glittering city becomes a desolate ruin. Her true nature, demonic all along, is revealed.

For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. As in 14:8 and 17:2.

And the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living. Key words. “Merchants” (emporoi, wholesale traders). “Luxurious living” (strēnous, arrogant luxury, excess). Three groups shared her sin and will lament her fall: kings, merchants and sailors (vv. 9–19). Political power and economic profit were bound up with her idolatry.

What it does not mean. Trade and commerce are not evil in themselves. Babylon’s sin is luxury pursued in pride, at the expense of others, as a substitute for God, and built on idolatry and exploitation.

In a sentence. After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven with great authority, and the earth was lit up by his splendour; he shouted with a powerful voice: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a home for demons, a lair for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird and every unclean and hated animal, because all the nations have drunk the wine of her passionate immorality, the kings of the earth committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from her extravagant luxury.

On a Tuesday. Ask how much of your life is shaped by the pursuit of luxury. Babylon’s glory ends in ruins.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.

Setting and background. The prophets called the Jewish exiles to flee from Babylon before its fall: go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! (Jeremiah 51:45; also 50:8; 51:6; Isaiah 48:20; 52:11). Lot was urged to flee Sodom before its destruction (Genesis 19:12–22). Paul quoted Isaiah 52:11 to the Corinthians: go out from their midst, and be separate from them (2 Corinthians 6:17). The tower of Babel was built to reach the heavens (Genesis 11:4); Babylon’s sins now pile up to heaven.

Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, Come out of her, my people. Key words. “Come out” (exelthate). “My people”: God’s people are still in Babylon, in the world system, living among its temptations. They are called to come out.

Lest you take part in her sins. Key words. “Take part” (synkoinōnēsēte, share, have fellowship with). The danger is not just living in Babylon, but sharing her sins: idolatry, greed, luxury, immorality, injustice.

Lest you share in her plagues. Key words. Those who share her sins will share her judgement.

For her sins are heaped high as heaven. Key words. “Heaped high” (ekollēthēsan, glued together, piled up). Like the tower of Babel, but made of sins. God’s patience has an end.

And God has remembered her iniquities. Key words. As in 16:19. God’s delay is not forgetfulness.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christians should withdraw from society? Some groups, such as some Anabaptists and monastic movements, have taken such passages to call for physical separation from the world, forming separate communities. Others have used the verse to call believers out of particular churches they regard as Babylon. Verdict: coming out of Babylon is mainly spiritual and moral: refusing to share the world’s idolatry, greed and sin, while still living in the world as salt and light. Jesus prayed not that his disciples would be taken out of the world, but that they would be kept from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians not to leave the world, but not to share the sins of professing believers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Sometimes faithfulness will require leaving a particular job, relationship or even church that demands compromise. But the call is to holiness, not withdrawal.

What it does not mean. Coming out of Babylon does not mean God’s people can lose their salvation if they are found in the city when it falls. It is a call to be what they are: God’s holy people, not Babylon’s.

In a sentence. Then I heard another voice from heaven say: Come out of her, my people, so that you will not share in her sins or suffer any of her plagues; for her sins are piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.

On a Tuesday. Where are you being drawn into the world’s sins, at work, online or in your spending? Come out of her, not by leaving the world, but by refusing her ways.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’ For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

Setting and background. Jeremiah 50:15, 29 says of Babylon: repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done. In Isaiah 47:7–9, Babylon says, I shall be mistress for ever; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children; but God replies that these two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day: the loss of children and widowhood. Double repayment was a principle of restitution in the law (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9), and Isaiah 40:2 and Jeremiah 16:18 speak of double punishment.

Pay her back as she herself has paid back others. Key words. “Pay back” (apodote, render, give back). Addressed perhaps to the agents of God’s judgement. The principle of just retribution: what she did to God’s people will be done to her.

And repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. Key words. “Double” (diplōsate ta dipla, double the double). Possibly meaning a full equivalent, a matching copy, rather than twice as much. Her judgement fits her sin precisely and completely.

As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning. Key words. “Glorified herself” (edoxasen hautēn): the root sin is pride, taking the glory that belongs to God. “Lived in luxury” (estrēniasen). Self-glorification and self-indulgence go together.

Since in her heart she says, I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. Key words. Pride and false security. She thinks she is untouchable and permanent: the city that called itself eternal (Roma aeterna). Every proud civilisation thinks the same.

For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine. Key words. “In a single day” (en mia hēmera). Sudden collapse. The three-part list echoes the horsemen (6:8).

And she will be burned up with fire. As in 17:16.

For mighty is the Lord God who has judged her. Key words. “Mighty” (ischyros). Babylon was called the mighty city (v. 10), but the Lord God is mightier.

What it does not mean. The call for repayment is not a call for Christians to take revenge. It is God’s own sentence on Babylon, carried out by his agents. Believers are forbidden to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19); they leave vengeance to God, who will repay.

In a sentence. Give back to her as she has given, and pay her back double for what she has done; in the cup she mixed for others, mix her a double portion; give her as much torment and grief as the glory and luxury she gave herself, because in her heart she boasts, I sit enthroned as a queen; I am not a widow; I will never mourn; so her plagues will overtake her in a single day, death, mourning and famine, and she will be burned with fire, for the Lord God who judges her is mighty.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the thought, I am secure, nothing can touch me. Pride goes before a fall. Find your security in God, not in wealth or status.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three sets of mourners in descending rank, modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre (Ezek. 26–28). Verses 9–11: the kings weep and wail, stand far off, in fear of her torment, and cry Alas! Alas! You great city… For in a single hour your judgment has come; and the merchants mourn since no one buys their cargo anymore.

Verses 12–13 give the manifest: twenty-eight items in seven groups, running downward from precious metals and stones through fabrics, fine furniture, spices, food and livestock — and ending and slaves, that is, human souls. Verse 14 speaks to the city directly: the fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you… never to be found again.

Verses 15–16: the merchants stand far off and describe her as a dressed body — linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls, nearly the wording of 17:4. Verses 17–19: shipmasters, seafaring men and sailors stand far off, throw dust on their heads (cf. Ezek. 27:29–32), and cry What city was like the great city? and in a single hour she has been laid waste.

Verse 20 opens a window in the middle of the funeral: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!
verseByVerse.theology:
The Threefold Lament

Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and weep — for their trade, not for her. The cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls. Heaven and the saints are called to rejoice because God has given judgement for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole Roman world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: Ask whose hands made what you hold, and whether your deepest grief would be for a person or for a market.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.” And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,

Setting and background. Ezekiel 26:16–18 and 27:29–36 describe the princes of the sea, merchants and sailors lamenting the fall of Tyre, the great trading city, standing on the shore, crying bitterly, throwing dust on their heads. Revelation 18 follows the same pattern with three groups of mourners.

And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her. Key words. The first group of mourners: political rulers who shared her idolatry and luxury.

Will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. Key words. “Weep” (klausousin) and “wail” (kopsontai, beat their breasts). Their grief is for themselves, for what they have lost. Not one of them grieves for her victims or repents.

They will stand far off, in fear of her torment. Key words. “Far off” (apo makrothen). They do not come to help her. They keep their distance, afraid of sharing her fate. Their loyalty was only to what she could give them.

And say, Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! Key words. “Alas” (ouai, the same word as woe). The double cry of lament.

For in a single hour your judgment has come. Key words. “Single hour” (mia hōra). Repeated three times (vv. 10, 17, 19). The suddenness of her collapse is astonishing. Centuries of power undone in an hour.

And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore. Key words. The second group: the traders. Their grief is openly economic. They mourn the end of the market, not the city.

What it does not mean. The mourners’ distance does not mean they were innocent. They shared her sin. They are simply trying to escape her punishment.

In a sentence. When the kings of the earth who committed immorality with her and shared her luxury see the smoke rising from her burning, they will weep and mourn over her; terrified by her torment, they will stand at a distance and cry: How terrible, how terrible for you, great city, mighty city of Babylon! In one hour your judgement has come; and the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her because nobody buys their goods any more.

On a Tuesday. Notice who mourns Babylon: those who profited from her. Ask what you would grieve if the world’s economy collapsed tomorrow, and whether your treasure is in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21).
verseByVerse.note: The laments echo Ezekiel’s dirge over the trading city of Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.

Setting and background. This list closely matches the luxury imports of first-century Rome, which drew goods from across the known world: gold and silver from Spain, pearls from the Indian Ocean, silk from China, citron wood from North Africa (prized for expensive tables), ivory from Africa and India, marble from Greece, cinnamon and spices from India and Arabia, wine from Italy and Greece, wheat from Egypt (Rome depended on Egyptian grain), horses and chariots from many provinces. Rome had an enormous slave population, perhaps a third of the city, bought and sold in markets across the empire. Ezekiel 27:12–24 contains a similar list of Tyre’s trade, which also included human beings (Ezekiel 27:13).

Cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls. Key words. Precious metals and stones, the adornments of the prostitute (17:4). In the new Jerusalem, gold, jewels and pearls are the building materials (21:18–21), freely given.

Fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth. Key words. Luxury fabrics. Silk came from China along the Silk Road and was enormously expensive.

All kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble. Key words. Materials for luxurious furniture and buildings. “Scented wood” (xylon thyinon, citron wood), used for expensive tables.

Cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense. Key words. Exotic spices and perfumes, some used in worship. Frankincense and myrrh were among the gifts brought to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11).

Wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep. Key words. Food, from luxury (fine flour) to staples (wheat).

Horses and chariots. Key words. “Chariots” (rhedōn, four-wheeled carriages, a Latin word). Transport and luxury.

And slaves, that is, human souls. Key words. “Slaves” (sōmatōn, bodies, the trade term for slaves). “Human souls” (psychas anthrōpōn, lives of human beings). The climax of the list, and its deepest condemnation. Babylon’s economy treated human beings as commodities, listed alongside cattle and horses. John deliberately adds “that is, human souls”, insisting that these bodies are people, made in God’s image. Babylon’s wealth was built on the exploitation of persons.

What it does not mean. The list does not condemn trade in these goods as such. God gives food, wine and oil to gladden human hearts (Psalm 104:15). It condemns an economy driven by greed and luxury, that devours people and puts profit above persons.

In a sentence. No one buys their cargoes of gold, silver, precious stones and pearls; fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet; every kind of fragrant wood and articles of ivory, expensive wood, bronze, iron and marble; cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense; wine and olive oil, fine flour and wheat; cattle and sheep; horses and carriages; and human bodies and souls sold as slaves.

On a Tuesday. Ask where the things you buy come from, and whether people were exploited to make them. Babylon’s economy treats people as cargo; God’s people must not.
verseByVerse.note: The cargo list ends with human beings — the slave trade on which Rome’s economy depended.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!” The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, “Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!

The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you. Key words. “Fruit” (opōra, ripe fruit, late summer harvest). “Longed” (epithymias, craving, lust). What she craved most is gone.

And all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again! Key words. “Delicacies” (ta lipara, rich, fat things, luxuries). “Splendors” (ta lampra, bright, glittering things). “Never” (ouketi ou mē, never again, the strongest negative). Everything the world prizes is temporary.

The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment. As the kings did (v. 10).

Weeping and mourning aloud, Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls! Key words. They describe her as she appeared in 17:4. Their lament is for her appearance and wealth, the surface glitter, and for their lost profits.

What it does not mean. Enjoying good things is not sin. The problem is a soul that longs for them above God, so that when they are gone, nothing is left.

In a sentence. The fruit you longed for is gone from you; all your luxury and splendour have vanished, and you will never find them again; the merchants who sold these things and grew rich from her will stand far away, terrified by her torment, weeping and mourning: How terrible, how terrible for the great city, dressed in fine linen, purple and scarlet, glittering with gold, precious stones and pearls!

On a Tuesday. What does your soul long for? If it is anything this world offers, one day it will be gone. Long for Christ, who is never lost.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?” And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.

Setting and background. Throwing dust on the head was a sign of grief and mourning (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; Ezekiel 27:30, where the sailors throw dust on their heads over Tyre). Rome’s grain and luxury goods came by sea, through the port of Ostia and the Bay of Naples.

For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste. Key words. “Laid waste” (ērēmōthē, made desolate, a wilderness). The second “single hour”.

And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea. Key words. The third group of mourners: the shipping industry. The whole economy of the sea was bound up with Babylon.

Stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, What city was like the great city? Key words. A parody of the world’s cry, Who is like the beast? (13:4), and of Israel’s praise, Who is like you, O LORD? (Exodus 15:11). They had made the city their god.

And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned. As the sailors mourned Tyre.

Crying out, Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! Key words. “Grew rich” (eploutēsan). Again, their grief is for their own losses.

For in a single hour she has been laid waste. The third and final “single hour”.

What it does not mean. Sailors and traders are not singled out as especially wicked. They represent everyone whose livelihood and identity were wrapped up in Babylon’s economy.

In a sentence. In a single hour all this wealth has been wiped out! And every ship’s captain, every seafarer, all the sailors and everyone who makes a living from the sea stood far off, and when they saw the smoke of her burning they cried out, Was there ever a city like this great city? They threw dust on their heads and shouted, weeping and mourning: How terrible, how terrible for the great city, where everyone with ships at sea grew rich from her wealth! In one hour she has been ruined!

On a Tuesday. If your whole identity is tied to your work, your income or the economy, you will be devastated when they fail. Build your life on Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”

Setting and background. Jeremiah 51:48 says: then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon. Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the nations to rejoice with God’s people, for he avenges the blood of his children. This verse leads into the great hallelujahs of 19:1–5.

Rejoice over her, O heaven. Key words. “Rejoice” (euphrainou, be glad, celebrate). In contrast to the earth’s mourners, heaven rejoices. The kings, merchants and sailors weep; God’s people celebrate.

And you saints and apostles and prophets. Key words. All God’s people, and especially those who led and suffered: apostles (such as Peter and Paul, killed in Rome) and prophets. Their blood was found in her (v. 24).

For God has given judgment for you against her! Key words. “Given judgment for you against her” (ekrinen ho theos to krima hymōn ex autēs, God has judged your case against her). A legal image: the saints brought their case to God’s court (6:10), and he has ruled in their favour. Babylon condemned them; now God has condemned her and vindicated them.

Where Christians differ: is it right to rejoice over judgement? Many Christians are uneasy with this verse, feeling that rejoicing over anyone’s destruction contradicts Christ’s command to love our enemies. Verdict: the joy here is not delight in suffering, nor personal revenge. It is joy that God has kept his promise, that justice has been done, that evil has been defeated, and that the persecuted have been vindicated. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and neither should we. But when the judgement is final, his people will see clearly that it was right, and rejoice in God’s justice. Now, before that day, we love our enemies, pray for them and seek their salvation, leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21).

What it does not mean. Christians should not rejoice now at the misfortunes of unbelievers, or wish for their destruction. The rejoicing is over the final, completed judgement of an unrepentant world system.

In a sentence. Celebrate over her, heaven, and you saints, apostles and prophets, because God has judged her for the way she treated you.

For worship. Thank God that he hears the cries of his persecuted people, and that he will vindicate them. Pray for them now, and for their persecutors to repent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sixfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21: a mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea — the act Jeremiah commanded of Seraiah, who tied a stone to the scroll of Babylon’s doom and threw it into the Euphrates saying Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more (Jer. 51:59–64). A millstone is the heaviest ordinary object in an ancient town and the last thing in the world that floats.

Verses 21–23 toll a sixfold silence, six things heard or found no more: Babylon herself; the sound of harpists and musicians, flute players and trumpeters; a craftsman of any craft; the sound of the mill; the light of a lamp; and the voice of bridegroom and bride. Jeremiah listed the same three — millstones, lamp, bridegroom and bride — as the sum of what a judged city loses (Jer. 25:10). Two reasons are given: your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery (pharmakeia, as at 9:21).

Verse 24 gives the indictment: And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Millstone and the Silence

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon sinks. Music, craft, the mill, the lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom are heard in her no more — and in her is found the blood of the prophets and saints.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jeremiah had sunk Babylon’s doom in the Euphrates; John’s angel repeats the sign.

Now: The ordinary goods of life — bread, lamplight, weddings — were always worth more than the cargo. Nothing hidden stays unlooked-for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

Setting and background. In Jeremiah 51:59–64, Jeremiah had his prophecy against Babylon written on a scroll, and told his messenger to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, saying: thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more. A great millstone could weigh several tonnes and was turned by a donkey. Jesus said it would be better to have a great millstone fastened around one’s neck and be drowned in the sea than to cause one of his little ones to sin (Matthew 18:6). Jeremiah 25:10 says God will banish from Judah the voice of mirth, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.

Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea. Key words. “Millstone” (mylinon megan, a great millstone). A dramatic acted prophecy. A millstone thrown into the sea sinks instantly and is never recovered.

Saying, So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more. Key words. “Violence” (hormēmati, with sudden force). “Found no more” (ou mē heurethē eti). Her destruction is total and permanent.

And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more. Key words. The first of six “no more”s (ou mē … eti). Music and celebration silenced. The city of entertainment is quiet.

And a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more. Key words. Work and skill ended.

And the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more. Key words. The daily grinding of grain for bread: ordinary life ended.

And the light of a lamp will shine in you no more. Key words. Darkness. No home is lived in. In the new Jerusalem, God is the light (21:23; 22:5).

And the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more. Key words. No more weddings, no more joy, no future. In contrast, the marriage of the Lamb is about to be announced (19:7).

For your merchants were the great ones of the earth. Key words. The first reason for her judgement: her merchants were exalted, wealth was worshipped. Isaiah 23:8 says of Tyre that her merchants were princes.

And all nations were deceived by your sorcery. Key words. “Sorcery” (pharmakeia, magic, drugs, enchantment). The second reason: she bewitched the nations, intoxicating them with her seductive power so that they could not see the truth.

And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth. Key words. The third and deepest reason: murder. She is responsible for the blood of God’s people, and, as the embodiment of the godless world in every age, for all the innocent blood shed on earth (Matthew 23:35).

What it does not mean. The end of music, work, food, light and marriage in Babylon does not mean that God hates these good things. They are his gifts, and they will be restored and perfected in the new creation. Babylon loses them because she abused them and rejected the Giver.

In a sentence. Then a powerful angel picked up a boulder the size of a huge millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: With this kind of violence Babylon the great city will be hurled down, never to be found again; the music of harpists, musicians, flute players and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any trade will ever be found in you again; the sound of a millstone will never be heard in you again; the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voices of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again; your merchants were the world’s great men, and your magic spells led all the nations astray; and in her was found the blood of prophets and of God’s people, and of all who have been killed on the earth.

On a Tuesday. Enjoy God’s gifts of music, work, food, light and love, and thank him for them. Give him the glory, so that what you enjoy is never Babylon’s, but his.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah had a scroll against Babylon tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.<sup>2</sup>And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”<sup>11</sup>And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,<sup>12</sup>cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble,<sup>13</sup>cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.<sup>14</sup>“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”<sup>15</sup>The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud,<sup>16</sup>“Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!<sup>17</sup>For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off<sup>18</sup>and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”<sup>19</sup>And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the great pivot of Revelation — the hinge between Babylon’s fall and the new creation. It opens with the loudest sound in the book: the fourfold Hallelujah chorus of heaven celebrating the justice of God and the arrival of the marriage supper of the Lamb. It closes with the appearance of the Rider on the white horse, whose name is Word of God, whose robe is dipped in blood, who strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth, and who is named King of kings and Lord of lords.

The chapter falls into two movements that mirror each other. The first (vv. 1–10) is pure celebration: heaven erupts in praise, the twenty-four elders and four living creatures worship, the great multitude shouts like the roar of many waters, and the Bride has made herself ready in fine linen bright and pure — the righteous deeds of the saints. The second (vv. 11–21) is the appearing of the Rider: heaven opened, white horse, faithful and true, eyes of flame, many diadems, name unknown, Word of God, armies following, sharp sword from his mouth, King of kings. The beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire.
