The relationship between the two movements is crucial. The praise precedes the appearing; the wedding supper is announced before the battle is described. This is Revelation’s consistent pattern: the outcome is declared before the outworking. Heaven celebrates the marriage of the Lamb while the final confrontation with the beast is still being described. The sequence is not chronological; it is theological. The Lamb has already conquered. What the Rider on the white horse depicts is the visible manifestation of a victory already secured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a great multitude cries Hallelujah! — Hebrew, untranslated, the great word of the psalter, and used in the New Testament only in these six verses, four times. The grounds are given: his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute… and has avenged on her the blood of his servants — the two verbs the martyrs asked for at 6:10, now in the past tense. And the smoke from her goes up forever and ever (cf. Isa. 34:10).

Verses 4–5: the elders and living creatures, in their last appearance in the book, fall down and say two Hebrew words — Amen. Hallelujah! (cf. Ps. 106:48). Then a voice from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.

Verses 6–8: the last hallelujah, in a voice like many waters and thunder — the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (cf. Ps. 93:1; 97:1) — and the announcement the book has been travelling toward: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure — for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Verses 9–10: the fourth beatitude, and one of the few sentences John is told to write down (cf. 14:13; 21:5) — Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John falls down to worship the angel and is stopped: You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you… Worship God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited — and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.” Once more they cried out, “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever.”

Meaning first. Revelation 19 moves from Babylon’s fall to the Lamb’s wedding and Christ’s return. Heaven bursts into hallelujahs: God’s judgements are true and just, for he has judged the prostitute and avenged his servants’ blood (vv. 1–3). The elders and living creatures say Amen, Hallelujah, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants to praise him (vv. 4–5). A great multitude, like thunder, sings: the Lord our God the Almighty reigns; the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints (vv. 6–8). The angel blesses those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb; John falls to worship him and is told: do not, worship God (vv. 9–10). Then heaven opens, and Christ rides out on a white horse, Faithful and True, with eyes like fire, many crowns, a robe dipped in blood, named the Word of God, followed by the armies of heaven (vv. 11–14). From his mouth comes a sword to strike the nations; he treads the winepress of God’s wrath; and on his robe and thigh is written King of kings and Lord of lords (vv. 15–16). An angel summons the birds to the great supper of God (vv. 17–18). The beast and the kings gather to make war on him, but the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from his mouth (vv. 19–21). The chapter shows the two suppers at the end of history: the marriage supper of the Lamb for his bride, and the great supper of God for his enemies, and Christ’s single, glorious, victorious return.

Setting and background. “Hallelujah” is a Hebrew word meaning praise the LORD (hallelu, praise; Yah, the short form of God’s name). In the New Testament it occurs only in this chapter, four times. In the Psalms it often begins or ends a psalm, especially Psalms 104–106, 111–117 and 146–150. Psalms 113–118, the Hallel, were sung at Passover, and Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn, probably from these psalms, after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). Psalm 104:35 is the first Hallelujah in the Psalter: let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!

After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven. Key words. “Great multitude” (ochlou pollou), as in 7:9: the redeemed.

Crying out, Hallelujah! Key words. Praise the LORD. In contrast with the earth’s Alas, alas (18:10, 16, 19), heaven sings Hallelujah.

Salvation and glory and power belong to our God. Key words. As in 7:10 and 12:10. All credit belongs to God.

For his judgments are true and just. Key words. As the redeemed (15:3) and the altar (16:7) declared. God’s justice is the ground of their praise.

For he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. Key words. “Corrupted” (ephtheiren, ruined, destroyed). She destroyed the earth (11:18).

And has avenged on her the blood of his servants. Key words. “Avenged” (exedikēsen). The answer to the martyrs’ prayer, How long before you avenge our blood? (6:10). The same verb. Prayer answered.

Once more they cried out, Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever. Key words. As with Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and Edom (Isaiah 34:10). Her judgement is final and permanent. She will never rise again.

What it does not mean. The hallelujahs are not gloating. They praise God because his justice has been done, and evil will never again corrupt the earth or kill his people.

In a sentence. After this I heard what sounded like the roar of a huge crowd in heaven, shouting: Hallelujah! Salvation, glory and power belong to our God, because his judgements are true and just; he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and he has avenged the blood of his servants that she shed; and again they shouted: Hallelujah! The smoke from her rises for ever and ever.

For worship. Sing Hallelujah with understanding: praise the LORD, because he is just and true, and he hears his people’s cries.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!” And from the throne came a voice saying, “Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.”

Setting and background. Psalm 106:48 ends: and let all the people say, Amen! Praise the LORD! Psalm 115:13 says the LORD will bless those who fear him, both the small and the great. Psalm 135:1, 20 calls all the servants of the LORD to praise him.

And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne. Key words. The last appearance of the elders and living creatures in Revelation. They have been there from the first throne vision (4:4–11), and they close the worship of this age.

Saying, Amen. Hallelujah! Key words. “Amen”: it is true, so be it. “Hallelujah”: praise the LORD. They confirm the multitude’s song.

And from the throne came a voice saying, Praise our God, all you his servants. Key words. “From the throne”: possibly Christ, or an angel near the throne, since the speaker says “our God”. “Servants” (douloi): all believers.

You who fear him, small and great. Key words. “Fear” (phoboumenoi, revere). “Small and great”: everyone, whatever their status. In God’s presence, distinctions of rank disappear; all praise him together.

What it does not mean. Fearing God does not mean being terrified of him. It means reverent awe, the humble worship of those who know who he is.

In a sentence. The twenty-four elders and the four living beings fell down and worshipped God, who sits on the throne, saying, Amen! Hallelujah! Then a voice came from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, all who fear him, from the least to the greatest!

For worship. Whoever you are, small or great, God calls you to praise him. Say Amen and Hallelujah today.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure”—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Setting and background. In the Old Testament, God is Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5–6; Hosea 2:16–20). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20) and told parables of wedding feasts (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13). Paul says Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). A Jewish wedding had two stages: betrothal, a binding commitment, and then, after a period of preparation, the wedding itself, when the groom came to take his bride to his home, followed by a feast. Isaiah 61:10 says, he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder. Key words. Overwhelming sound, like Christ’s own voice (1:15) and the 144,000 (14:2).

Crying out, Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Key words. “Reigns” (ebasileusen, has begun to reign, has taken up his reign). As in 11:17. God’s reign is now openly established. The great words of Handel’s Hallelujah Chorus.

Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory. Key words. “Rejoice” (chairōmen) and “exult” (agalliōmen, be overjoyed). As Jesus told the persecuted, rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven (Matthew 5:12).

For the marriage of the Lamb has come. Key words. “Marriage” (ho gamos, the wedding). The goal of all history: the union of Christ with his people, perfect and permanent. Betrothed now by faith (2 Corinthians 11:2), the church will be united with Christ at his return.

And his Bride has made herself ready. Key words. “Bride” (gynē, wife, woman). In contrast with the prostitute. “Made herself ready” (hētoimasen heautēn). The church prepares for Christ by faithful living, holiness and perseverance.

It was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure. Key words. “It was granted” (edothē, it was given). The bride’s dress is a gift. She clothes herself, but only with what is given her. “Fine linen” (byssinon). In contrast with the prostitute’s purple and scarlet, gold and jewels (17:4). The bride’s beauty is purity.

For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints. Key words. “Righteous deeds” (dikaiōmata, righteous acts). The faithful lives of believers, their works of obedience and love. Their deeds follow them (14:13).

Where Christians differ: is the bride’s righteousness her own deeds or Christ’s? Some read “righteous deeds of the saints” as meaning that believers are made acceptable to Christ by their own good works. Others, emphasising imputed righteousness, are uneasy with the phrase. Verdict: both grace and works are in the verse. The linen was given to her (granted), and her robes were washed white in the Lamb’s blood (7:14): her standing before God rests wholly on Christ’s righteousness credited to her by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). And the linen is her righteous deeds, the fruit of that grace, the good works God prepared beforehand for her to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). Justification by faith alone is the root; sanctification is the fruit, and both are gifts. The bride is dressed by her bridegroom.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “the Lord God omnipotent reigneth”, following later manuscripts. The best manuscripts read “the Lord our God the Almighty reigns”. The meaning is the same.

What it does not mean. The marriage does not mean that individual believers are each married to Christ in a romantic sense. The bride is the church together, the whole people of God.

In a sentence. Then I heard what sounded like a great crowd, like the roar of rushing waters and like loud thunder, shouting: Hallelujah! For our Lord God Almighty has begun to reign; let us celebrate and be glad and give him the glory, because the wedding of the Lamb has come and his bride has got herself ready; she has been given fine linen, shining and clean, to wear; for the fine linen stands for the righteous acts of God’s people.

On a Tuesday. The church is preparing for her wedding. Every act of faithfulness and love today is part of the bride’s dress. Live in a way that gets her ready.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.” Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.” For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

Setting and background. Isaiah 25:6–8 promises that the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever. Jesus said many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11), and at the Last Supper said he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). Colossians 2:18 warns against the worship of angels.

And the angel said to me, Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. Key words. The fourth beatitude (1:3; 14:13; 16:15). “Invited” (keklēmenoi, called, the same word as in 17:14: the called). “Marriage supper” (deipnon tou gamou, wedding feast). The bride and the guests are the same people seen from two angles: the church is both the bride and the invited guests. The feast pictures the joy of the new creation, fellowship with Christ, and the fulfilment of the Lord’s Supper, which looks forward to it (1 Corinthians 11:26).

And he said to me, These are the true words of God. Key words. “True” (alēthinoi, genuine, reliable). A guarantee: this promise will happen.

Then I fell down at his feet to worship him. Key words. Overwhelmed, John makes a mistake, which he records honestly. He does it again in 22:8.

But he said to me, You must not do that! Key words. “You must not” (hora mē, see that you do not). An urgent warning.

I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Key words. “Fellow servant” (syndoulos). Angels, however glorious, are servants like us (Hebrews 1:14).

Worship God. Key words. Worship belongs to God alone. This is crucial evidence for Christ’s deity: the angel refuses worship, but the Lamb receives it (5:8–14).

For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. Key words. “Testimony of Jesus” (hē martyria Iēsou): the testimony that Jesus gave, and the testimony about Jesus. “Spirit of prophecy”: the essence, the heart of prophecy. All true prophecy bears witness to Jesus. The angel, John and the church share one task: witnessing to Christ.

Where Christians differ: does this mean prophecy continues in the church? Some read “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” as meaning that every witnessing believer has a gift of prophecy, so that new revelations continue today. Verdict: the verse teaches that the heart of all prophecy is witness to Jesus, and that every believer who bears that witness shares in the prophetic calling of the church (11:3). It does not promise new revelation. The prophetic word that John received is now written and closed (22:18–19). Today, the church bears the testimony of Jesus by proclaiming the completed Scriptures, which this app holds, with charity, is how the prophetic gift functions now.

What it does not mean. The angel’s refusal of worship is not false modesty. Worshipping anyone or anything other than God, whether angels, saints or images, is idolatry.

In a sentence. The angel said to me, Write this: How blessed are those who are invited to the wedding banquet of the Lamb! And he added, These are the true words of God; I fell at his feet to worship him, but he said, Do not do that! I am a servant just like you and your brothers and sisters who hold to the testimony about Jesus; worship God! For the testimony about Jesus is the heart of all prophecy.

For worship. At the Lord’s Supper, look forward to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And worship God alone, giving no creature the honour that belongs to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–13: heaven opens — not a door this time — and a rider comes out on a white horse, called Faithful and True (cf. 1:5; 3:14), and in righteousness he judges and makes war (cf. Isa. 11:3–4). His eyes are a flame of fire (1:14); on his head are many diadems, against the dragon’s seven and the beast’s ten; he has a name written that no one knows but himself; he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood; and he is called The Word of God — John’s own title for him (John 1:1).

Verses 14–16: the armies of heaven follow, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure — the Bride’s dress from v. 8, in the same words. From his mouth comes a sharp sword (1:16; Isa. 11:4); he will rule with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9); he treads the winepress (Isa. 63:3). And on his robe and thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords (cf. Deut. 10:17; Rev. 17:14).

Verses 17–18: an angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God (Ezek. 39:17–20), to eat the flesh of kings, captains, mighty men, horses and riders, both free and slave, both small and great. Verses 19–21: the beast and the kings gather to make war — and the beast was captured, with the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire; and the rest are slain by the sword from the rider’s mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.

Setting and background. Roman generals celebrated victory in a triumph, riding into Rome on a white horse, followed by their army, displaying captives and spoil. Isaiah 63:1–3 describes the LORD coming from Edom in crimson garments, stained from treading the winepress of his wrath. Psalm 45:3–6 describes the king riding out victoriously for the cause of truth and righteousness. John’s Gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1).

Then I saw heaven opened. Key words. In 4:1, a door was opened in heaven for John; now heaven itself is opened for Christ to come out. This is his return.

And behold, a white horse! Key words. The horse of victory. Not the same as the white horse of the first seal (6:2), which was a counterfeit conqueror.

The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True. Key words. As in 3:14. Christ keeps every promise and speaks only truth. His coming is the fulfilment of God’s word.

And in righteousness he judges and makes war. Key words. “Righteousness” (dikaiosynē). Unlike human wars, his war is perfectly just. Isaiah 11:4 says the Messiah will judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth.

His eyes are like a flame of fire. As in 1:14 and 2:18. He sees through everything.

And on his head are many diadems. Key words. “Many diadems” (diadēmata polla). The dragon had seven (12:3), the beast ten (13:1). Christ has many: his authority surpasses all. He is King of kings.

And he has a name written that no one knows but himself. Key words. There is a depth in Christ that no creature fully comprehends (Matthew 11:27). He is more than all his titles.

He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood. Key words. “Dipped” (bebammenon, dipped, soaked). Whose blood? Either the blood of his enemies, as in Isaiah 63:3, before the battle has even begun, pointing to his certain victory; or his own blood, shed on the cross, by which he conquered (5:9; 12:11). Revelation regularly reinterprets Old Testament war imagery in the light of the cross, and the robe is mentioned before any battle, so his own blood is most likely, with a hint of judgement as well.

And the name by which he is called is The Word of God. Key words. “The Word of God” (ho logos tou theou). The title of Christ in John 1:1, 14. He is God’s final self-revelation and speech. He conquers by speaking (v. 15).

Where Christians differ: is this Christ’s return before a millennium, or his final coming? Premillennialists read 19:11–21 as Christ’s return to defeat the antichrist, followed in chapter 20 by a thousand-year reign on earth before the final judgement. Verdict: this is Christ’s one, final, visible return, which brings the last battle, the final judgement and the new creation. Revelation is a series of parallel visions, and chapter 20 goes back to describe the whole church age again from another angle. The same final battle appears in 16:14–16, 19:19–21 and 20:7–10, described in the same words, drawn from Ezekiel 38–39 (the birds’ feast here, the fire there). There is one return, one battle, one final judgement.

What it does not mean. Christ’s warfare is not a call for Christians to wage holy war. He fights alone, with his word, and the victory is entirely his.

In a sentence. Then I saw heaven standing open, and there was a white horse, whose rider is called Faithful and True; he judges and wages war with justice; his eyes are like blazing fire, on his head are many royal crowns, and he has a name written on him that no one knows except himself; he wears a robe soaked in blood, and his name is the Word of God.

For worship. Worship Christ as the Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of many crowns. The one who was crucified will return in triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.

Setting and background. Zechariah 14:5 says the LORD will come, and all the holy ones with him. Jesus said the Son of Man will come in his glory, and all the angels with him (Matthew 25:31). Paul says Christ will come with his saints (1 Thessalonians 3:13) and with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7). Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2 speak of the Messiah’s mouth like a sharp sword, striking the earth with the rod of his mouth. In the ancient world, a name or title might be written on a statue’s thigh, or on the part of a rider’s robe that covered the thigh, where it would be seen as he rode.

And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. Key words. “Armies” (strateumata). Dressed in fine linen like the bride (v. 8), and those with the Lamb are the called, chosen and faithful (17:14). They include his saints and his angels. Notice: they carry no weapons and do not fight. They simply follow.

From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations. Key words. “Sword” (rhomphaia), as in 1:16 and 2:16. His word. He conquers by speaking, as God created by speaking (Genesis 1). One word from him, and his enemies fall (2 Thessalonians 2:8: the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth).

And he will rule them with a rod of iron. As in Psalm 2:9; 2:27; 12:5.

He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. Key words. As in 14:19–20 and Isaiah 63:3. Christ himself carries out God’s final judgement.

On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords. Key words. The supreme title, as in 17:14 (reversed). Written where all can see. Every emperor, king and lord is under him. Domitian’s claims are answered once and for all.

What it does not mean. The armies of heaven do not fight. The battle belongs to Christ alone. The church does not establish Christ’s kingdom by force. Its weapons now are the word and prayer, and at his coming he alone wins the victory.

In a sentence. The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and clean, were following him on white horses; out of his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod; he treads the winepress of the furious anger of God Almighty; and on his robe and on his thigh he has this name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.

On a Tuesday. Whoever has power over you, Christ has more. Live under his lordship today, whatever any lesser lord demands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great.”

Setting and background. Ezekiel 39:17–20 describes God summoning the birds and wild beasts to a great sacrificial feast on the bodies of Gog’s defeated armies: you shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. In the ancient world, to be left unburied, eaten by birds, was the ultimate disgrace (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Kings 14:11). Jesus said, wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matthew 24:28).

Then I saw an angel standing in the sun. Key words. Blazing, visible to all, at the highest point.

And with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead. Key words. “Directly overhead” (en mesouranēmati, in mid-heaven), as in 8:13 and 14:6. Birds of prey, vultures.

Come, gather for the great supper of God. Key words. “Great supper of God” (to deipnon to mega tou theou). A terrible contrast with the marriage supper of the Lamb (v. 9). There are two suppers at the end of history: one where the redeemed feast with Christ, and one where his enemies become the feast. Everyone will be at one supper or the other.

To eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great. Key words. Every class of people who opposed Christ, as at the sixth seal (6:15). “Small and great”: as the redeemed include small and great (v. 5), so do the lost. Rank gives no protection.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal description of birds eating corpses at the end of the world, to be imagined in detail. It is a vivid, shocking symbol, drawn from Ezekiel, of total and shameful defeat for those who fight against God.

In a sentence. Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he called out loudly to all the birds flying high overhead: Come, gather for God’s great supper, to eat the flesh of kings, military commanders and powerful men, of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all people, free and slave, unimportant and important.

On a Tuesday. There are two suppers. Make sure you have accepted the invitation to the Lamb’s, and urge others to accept it too (Luke 14:16–24).

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

Setting and background. Psalm 2:2 says the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed. The gathering was announced in 16:14–16 (Armageddon) and 17:14. Daniel 7:11 says the beast was killed and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. Korah, Dathan and Abiram went down alive into Sheol (Numbers 16:33).

And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. Key words. “Gathered” (synēgmena), as in 16:14, 16 and 20:8. The final battle. All the forces of evil gathered in one place.

And the beast was captured. Key words. “Captured” (epiasthē, seized). No battle is described. There is no fight, no struggle, no contest. The beast, which seemed so invincible (13:4), is simply taken.

And with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. Key words. The second beast of 13:11–17. Its deceptions are recalled, and its judgement shown.

These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. Key words. “Alive” (zōntes). “Lake of fire” (tēn limnēn tou pyros): the place of final, eternal punishment, first mentioned here. Later the devil is thrown there (20:10), then death and Hades, and all whose names are not in the book of life (20:14–15). It was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41).

And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse. Key words. By his word alone. The armies of heaven do nothing; Christ speaks, and it is over.

And all the birds were gorged with their flesh. Key words. “Gorged” (echortasthēsan, filled, satisfied). The great supper of God (v. 17).

Where Christians differ: are the beast and false prophet persons, and is the lake of fire eternal? Some say that since the beast and false prophet are symbols of systems, not individuals, the lake of fire may mean only their abolition, not eternal punishment. Verdict: the beast and false prophet represent systems of persecuting power and deception, and also, finally, the persons who lead them. Their being thrown into the lake of fire shows the total end of those systems, and the eternal punishment of the persons who embody them, together with all who follow them. Revelation 20:10 says the devil, the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night for ever and ever: the punishment is conscious and endless. Christ’s victory over every evil power is complete and permanent.

What it does not mean. The final battle is not a long war in which the outcome is uncertain. It is over the moment Christ appears. Evil is no match for him.

In a sentence. Then I saw the beast, the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to wage war against the rider on the horse and his army; but the beast was captured, along with the false prophet who had performed signs on its behalf, by which he had deceived those who received the beast’s mark and worshipped its image; the two of them were thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with sulphur, and the rest were killed by the sword that came from the mouth of the rider on the horse, and all the birds ate their fill of their flesh.

On a Tuesday. The powers that seem invincible today will be taken without a fight. Stay with the Lamb; he has already won.

19.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,<sup>2</sup>for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.”<sup>3</sup>Once more they cried out, “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever.”<sup>4</sup>And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!”<sup>5</sup>And from the throne came a voice saying, “Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.”<sup>6</sup>Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.<sup>7</sup>Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready;<sup>8</sup>it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure”—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”<sup>10</sup>Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.” For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war.<sup>12</sup>His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself.<sup>13</sup>He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.<sup>14</sup>And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses.<sup>15</sup>From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.<sup>16</sup>On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.<sup>17</sup>Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God,<sup>18</sup>to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great.”<sup>19</sup>And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army.<sup>20</sup>And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.<sup>21</sup>And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Chapter 20 contains the most debated passage in the most debated book of the Bible: the millennium. The thousand-year reign of Christ with his saints (vv. 1–6) has divided serious, Scripture-loving Christians for two thousand years and continues to do so. The amillennial position is followed here as the Reformed mainstream, with all four major views presented with genuine respect and fairness. The stakes in this debate are high — but the non-negotiables that all four views share are higher: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, the righteous will be glorified, and God will be all in all.

The Four Positions — Stated Fairly: Dispensational Premillennialism (MacArthur, Walvoord, Ryrie, Swindoll): After the pre-tribulation Rapture and the seven-year tribulation, Christ returns bodily to earth and establishes a literal thousand-year kingdom centred in Jerusalem, with a rebuilt temple and a restored national Israel fulfilling the Old Testament covenants. Satan is literally bound in the abyss. The martyred saints and tribulation believers are resurrected to reign with Christ. At the end of the millennium, Satan is released, defeated, and cast into the lake of fire. Then the Great White Throne judgment and the eternal state. Historic Premillennialism (Ladd, Grudem): Similar to dispensational, but without the pre-trib Rapture — the church goes through the tribulation. Christ returns, binds Satan, raises the martyrs (the first resurrection), and reigns on earth for a literal thousand years. Postmillennialism (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Warfield in some respects): The thousand years represents the gospel era of expanding Christian influence, gradually Christianising the world through the preaching of the gospel, before Christ returns to a world largely won for the kingdom. The binding of Satan is the progressive restriction of his power through the gospel. Amillennialism (Augustine, Calvin, Vos, Berkhof, Hoekema, Beale — the position followed here): The thousand years is the entire period between the first and second comings of Christ — the church age. The binding of Satan (vv. 1–3) was accomplished at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15; Luke 10:18) and restricts his ability to deceive the nations so the gospel can go to all peoples. The first resurrection (vv. 4–6) is the spiritual resurrection of souls reigning with Christ in heaven now, or the new birth through which believers participate in Christ’s resurrection life. The thousand years is a symbolic number (10 x 10 x 10 = complete fullness) for the complete church age. Satan’s release at the end (vv. 7–9) represents the brief intensification of opposition immediately before Christ’s return. The Great White Throne (vv. 11–15) is the final universal judgment of all the dead.

The chapter divides into two sections: the millennium and Satan’s career (vv. 1–10) and the Great White Throne (vv. 11–15). Both sections are eschatologically essential and both are theologically clear on the matters that count: no one escapes the final judgment, no name not written in the book of life survives it, and the last enemies — Death and Hades themselves — are thrown into the lake of fire. Whatever one believes about the millennium, these outcomes are certain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: one angel with a key and a chain seizes, binds, throws, shuts and seals the dragon — named with the four names of 12:9 — for a thousand years, and the binding is given a stated purpose: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. After that he must be released for a little while, using the word of divine necessity.

Verse 4: thrones, with authority to judge committed to those on them; the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and those who had not worshipped the beast or taken its mark; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Verses 5–6: the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Then the fifth beatitude: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him.

Verses 7–8: Satan is released, deceives the nations at the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog (Ezek. 38–39) — and gathers a host like the sand of the sea. Verses 9–10: they surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, fire comes down and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power — on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.

Meaning first. Revelation 20 is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of a thousand years, and it shows Satan’s defeat and the final judgement. An angel binds Satan with a chain and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years, so that he can no longer deceive the nations, after which he must be released for a little while (vv. 1–3). John sees thrones and those given authority to judge, and the souls of those beheaded for Jesus and those who refused the beast; they come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years (v. 4). This is the first resurrection; those who share in it are blessed, the second death has no power over them, and they are priests reigning with Christ (vv. 5–6). When the thousand years end, Satan is released and gathers the nations, Gog and Magog, as numerous as the sand, to surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city; but fire from heaven consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet, to be tormented for ever (vv. 7–10). Then John sees a great white throne, from which earth and sky flee; the dead, great and small, are judged according to their works recorded in the books; the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead; Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death; and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown in too (vv. 11–15). In the amillennial reading this app follows, the chapter goes back to the beginning of the church age once more: Satan was bound at Christ’s first coming so that the gospel could go to the nations; the martyrs and faithful dead now reign with Christ in heaven; at the end Satan is released briefly for a final assault; and then Christ returns to judge all people.

Setting and background. Jesus said no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (Matthew 12:29), and he did this by casting out demons through the Spirit of God, showing that the kingdom of God had come. He said, now will the ruler of this world be cast out, and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:31–32). Through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, the devil (Hebrews 2:14), and disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15). Jude 6 speaks of angels kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgement.

Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven. Key words. “Then I saw” (kai eidon): John’s regular formula for a new vision. It marks the order of visions, not necessarily the order of events. Chapter 12 already went back to Christ’s birth, after the seventh trumpet had announced the end.

Holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. Key words. “Key” (kleida) and “chain” (halysin). Symbols of authority and restraint. A spiritual being cannot literally be chained; the images show that Satan’s power is restricted by God.

And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan. Key words. All four names from 12:9. The same enemy.

And bound him for a thousand years. Key words. “Bound” (edēsen), the same word Jesus used of binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29). “A thousand years” (chilia etē, from which the word millennium comes, Latin for a thousand years). In Revelation, numbers are symbolic: a thousand is ten cubed, the number of completeness raised to its fullest. A long, complete period, determined by God.

And threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him. Key words. “Sealed” (esphragisen). Thoroughly restrained.

So that he might not deceive the nations any longer. Key words. The binding has a specific purpose: to stop him deceiving the nations. It does not mean Satan is inactive in every way; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), tempts and persecutes. It means he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the nations, or gather the nations for the final assault on the church until God permits. Before Christ, the nations were in darkness, with only Israel knowing God; since Christ, the gospel has gone to all nations, and people from every nation have been freed from Satan’s deception (Acts 26:18).

Until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while. Key words. “Must” (dei): part of God’s plan. “A little while” (mikron chronon): a short time at the end of history, a final outburst of deception and persecution before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

Where Christians differ: what is the thousand years? Premillennialists, including dispensationalists, hold that Christ will return before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth, during which Satan is bound and Christ rules from Jerusalem; then Satan is released, defeated, and the final judgement follows. Postmillennialists hold that the gospel will gradually triumph in the world, bringing a long golden age of Christian influence, after (post-) which Christ returns. Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a symbol for the present church age, between Christ’s first and second comings: Satan is now bound so that he cannot stop the gospel; believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven; and Christ’s return brings the end, with no separate earthly millennium. Verdict: the amillennial view fits Revelation best. Revelation repeatedly goes back over the same period in parallel visions, and chapter 20 does so again. The binding of Satan is what Jesus and the apostles say happened at the cross. The reign is with Christ, who already reigns from heaven. The final battle of 20:7–10 is the same as 16:14–16 and 19:19–21, all drawn from Ezekiel 38–39, and gathered in the same words. And the rest of the New Testament teaches one return of Christ, bringing the resurrection of both righteous and wicked together (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), the final judgement and the new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13), with no interval of a thousand years. Premillennial and postmillennial believers are brothers and sisters in Christ, and this is a matter where Christians may charitably differ; but the amillennial reading is the most faithful to the text.

What it does not mean. Satan’s binding does not mean evil has disappeared. Evil is everywhere, and Satan still tempts and attacks. It means his power to keep the nations in darkness has been broken, and the gospel advances in spite of him.

In a sentence. Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a huge chain in his hand; he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; he threw him into the abyss, locked it and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations any more until the thousand years were over; after that he must be set free for a short time.

On a Tuesday. Share the gospel with confidence. Satan cannot stop it reaching the nations; he has been bound. The people around you can be set free from his deception.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

Setting and background. Daniel 7:9, 22 says thrones were placed, and judgement was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), and the overcomer that he would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21). Paul says the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). Beheading with a sword was the Roman method of executing citizens, as Paul was executed.

Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Key words. “Thrones” (thronous). In Revelation, thrones are almost always in heaven (47 times). “Authority to judge” (krima edothē autois, judgement was given to them): either they were given authority to judge, or judgement was given in their favour (as in Daniel 7:22), vindicating them.

Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God. Key words. “Souls” (psychas): as in 6:9, the souls under the altar. These are believers who have died, now alive in God’s presence. They were killed on earth; now they reign in heaven.

And those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. Key words. Possibly a separate group, all faithful believers who did not compromise, whether martyred or not. All who conquered the beast (15:2).

They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Key words. “Came to life” (ezēsan, lived). Not their bodily resurrection, which comes at the end (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52), but their entry into life with Christ when they died. Though their bodies were killed, they live and reign with him (Luke 20:38; John 11:25–26). “Reigned with Christ” (ebasileusan meta tou Christou): sharing his rule from heaven, where he reigns now (Ephesians 1:20–22). The answer to 6:9–11: the martyrs who waited under the altar are now seen on thrones.

Where Christians differ: is this a bodily resurrection to rule on earth? Premillennialists read “came to life” as a bodily resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, followed by a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Verdict: John sees souls, not bodies, on thrones, which in Revelation are in heaven. The scene is the heavenly reign of believers who have died, during the present age, while Satan is bound on earth. The same word for living is used of the beast who was and is not (13:14), and of Christ who was dead and is alive (1:18; 2:8); life after death is meant. The bodily resurrection of all believers comes at Christ’s single return at the end (1 Thessalonians 4:16). This is the great comfort of the passage for persecuted believers: those who die for Christ are not defeated; they reign with him now.

What it does not mean. Reigning with Christ does not mean that the dead in Christ rule the earth now in a political sense, or that we should pray to them. They share his heavenly reign and await the resurrection.

In a sentence. Then I saw thrones, and those seated on them were given authority to judge; I also saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of their testimony about Jesus and because of the word of God, those who had not worshipped the beast or its image or received its mark on their foreheads or hands; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

For worship. Thank God for believers who have died in faith: they are alive with Christ and reign with him. Death has not defeated them.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

Setting and background. Jesus said that an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28–29). He also said, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Paul says believers have been raised with Christ and seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1).

The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. Key words. “The rest of the dead”: unbelievers. They do not share the life and reign with Christ during the present age; they come to life only to be judged, at the end (vv. 12–13).

This is the first resurrection. Key words. “First resurrection” (hē anastasis hē prōtē). The phrase occurs only here. If there is a first resurrection, there is implicitly a second: the bodily resurrection at the end. Just as there is a first death (physical) and a second death (eternal), so there is a first resurrection (spiritual, entering life with Christ, at conversion and at death) and a second (bodily, at Christ’s return). Believers share both resurrections and only the first death; unbelievers share both deaths and only the second resurrection, to judgement.

Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Key words. The fifth beatitude. “Holy” (hagios): set apart for God.

Over such the second death has no power. Key words. “Second death”: the lake of fire (v. 14). As promised to Smyrna (2:11). Those who belong to Christ will never face eternal judgement.

But they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years. Key words. “Priests” (hiereis) and “reign” (basileusousin). The kingdom of priests of 1:6 and 5:10, fulfilled. “Of God and of Christ”: Christ is served with the same priestly service as God.

Textual note. One important early manuscript (Codex Sinaiticus) and some others omit the first sentence, “The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended”. Most manuscripts include it, and it is probably original.

Where Christians differ: are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart? Premillennialists read the first resurrection as a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, and the second as a bodily resurrection of unbelievers after it. Verdict: the rest of the New Testament teaches one bodily resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous at the same time, on the last day (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Daniel 12:2). Jesus says he will raise up believers on the last day (John 6:39–40, 44, 54), which leaves no room for a thousand years after their resurrection. The first resurrection is the believer’s sharing in Christ’s resurrection life, beginning at new birth and carried into heaven at death, while the body awaits the last day.

What it does not mean. The first resurrection is not a special reward for martyrs only. All believers share in it (Ephesians 2:5–6).

In a sentence. The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were over; this is the first resurrection; how blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them; they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him for a thousand years.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you have already passed from death to life, and the second death has no power over you. Live today as a priest and king with him.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.

Setting and background. In Ezekiel 38–39, Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast coalition of nations from the far north against God’s restored people Israel, living securely; God destroys them with fire and brimstone, and the birds and beasts feast on their bodies (Ezekiel 39:4, 17–20). In Jewish tradition, Gog and Magog became symbols of the final enemies of God’s people. Revelation 19:17–21 used the birds’ feast from Ezekiel 39; 20:7–10 uses the fire from Ezekiel 38:22. Both describe the same final battle.

And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison. Key words. “Released” (lythēsetai). As announced in v. 3. God allows a final, brief period of satanic deception and persecution at the end of the age, which Jesus and Paul also foretold (Matthew 24:21–24; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

And will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth. Key words. “Deceive” (planēsai). Released from restraint, he immediately returns to his old work. “Four corners”: the whole world.

Gog and Magog. Key words. In Ezekiel, Gog is a ruler and Magog his land. Here both are names for the nations. Symbols of all the world’s forces opposed to God.

To gather them for battle. Key words. “The battle” (ton polemon, with the definite article): the battle already described in 16:14 and 19:19, in nearly identical words. The same event.

Their number is like the sand of the sea. Key words. Countless. The church will seem overwhelmed.

Where Christians differ: is Gog and Magog a specific nation, such as Russia? Some popular prophecy teachers identified Gog and Magog with Russia, linking Rosh (Ezekiel 38:2, in some translations) with Russia and Meshech with Moscow. Verdict: those connections are based on sound-alike words, not on language or history; Rosh is a Hebrew word meaning chief, and Meshech and Tubal were peoples in what is now Turkey. In Revelation, Gog and Magog are explicitly the nations at the four corners of the earth: not one nation but the whole world in rebellion. The point is not geography but the final, worldwide assault on God’s people, and its sure defeat.

What it does not mean. Satan’s release does not mean God has lost control. He is released by God’s permission, for God’s purpose: to expose the persistence of human rebellion and to bring all evil into the open for final judgement.

In a sentence. When the thousand years are over, Satan will be let out of his prison and will go out to deceive the nations in every corner of the earth, Gog and Magog, and gather them for battle, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

On a Tuesday. If you see opposition to the gospel growing, do not panic. The final assault was foretold, and its end is certain.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

Setting and background. Ezekiel 38:22 says God will rain upon Gog torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulphur. Fire came down from heaven on Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and at Elijah’s word on soldiers sent against him (2 Kings 1:10–12). Psalm 87:2 says the LORD loves the gates of Zion. Israel camped around the tabernacle in the wilderness (Numbers 2).

And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth. Key words. “Broad plain” (to platos tēs gēs, the breadth of the earth). Spreading over the whole world.

And surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Key words. “Camp” (parembolēn): the people of God as an army or as pilgrims in the wilderness, like Israel’s camp. “The beloved city”: the people of God, the new Jerusalem in its present form, the church. Not a literal city in one location, since the nations come from all over the world; the church throughout the world is surrounded and threatened.

But fire came down from heaven and consumed them. Key words. Instant destruction, as in 19:20–21. No battle; God acts alone. This is Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8: the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire).

And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were. Key words. The beast and false prophet were thrown there in 19:20, the same final event. Now their master joins them. The unholy trinity is finished.

And they will be tormented day and night forever and ever. Key words. “Tormented” (basanisthēsontai). “Day and night forever and ever” (hēmeras kai nyktos eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn). Conscious and endless. The devil’s defeat, begun at the cross, is completed.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fire came down from God out of heaven”. The meaning is the same.

What it does not mean. The saints do not defend themselves in this battle. They are surrounded and helpless, and God delivers them. The church’s safety at the end, as always, is God himself.

In a sentence. They marched across the whole breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of God’s people, the city he loves; but fire came down from heaven and burned them up, and the devil, who had deceived them, was thrown into the lake of burning sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown, and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

For worship. Thank God that Satan’s end is certain. The accuser, deceiver and destroyer will trouble God’s people no more.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 11: a great white throne, and one seated on it whom John does not describe — as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

Verse 12: the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (cf. Dan. 7:10).

Verse 13: the sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades give up theirs, and they were judged, each one of them. Verse 14: Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. Verse 15: And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book — and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.

Setting and background. Daniel 7:9–10 says thrones were placed, the Ancient of Days took his seat, his throne was fiery flames, the court sat in judgement, and the books were opened. Psalm 62:12 says God will render to a man according to his work. Jesus said the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and that he will sit on his glorious throne and all the nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 25:31–32). Paul says we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. Key words. “Great” (megan): majesty. “White” (leukon): purity, holiness and perfect justice. “Him who was seated on it”: God, who judges through Christ (Acts 17:31; Romans 2:16). The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3).

From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. Key words. “Fled away” (ephygen). The old creation passes away before God’s holiness (2 Peter 3:10; 21:1). Nowhere to hide (6:14–16). Everyone stands alone before God.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. Key words. “The dead”: all humanity, raised for judgement. “Great and small”: no one is too important to be judged or too insignificant to be overlooked.

And books were opened. Key words. “Books” (biblia): records of every person’s deeds. God knows everything people have done, said and thought (Ecclesiastes 12:14; Matthew 12:36).

Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. Key words. The Lamb’s book (13:8; 21:27), with the names of those chosen before the foundation of the world (17:8). Two kinds of books: the books of deeds, and the book of life. The first shows what each person deserves; the second shows who belongs to the Lamb.

And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done. Key words. “According to what they had done” (kata ta erga autōn, according to their works). The judgement is perfectly just, based on the evidence. No one will be condemned unfairly.

Where Christians differ: if judgement is by works, how is salvation by grace? Some take judgement according to works as meaning that final salvation depends on our works. Others think that believers are not judged at all. Verdict: everyone is judged according to works, because works reveal what is in the heart. For unbelievers, their works condemn them, because all have sinned (Romans 3:23). For believers, their names are in the book of life; they are saved by grace through faith alone, because Christ has borne their condemnation (Romans 8:1; John 5:24), and their works are the evidence of their faith and the basis of their rewards (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). No one is saved by works; but no one is saved without the works that true faith produces (James 2:14–26). The book of life is what finally decides (v. 15).

What it does not mean. The books of deeds do not mean believers will be shamed by a public display of their forgiven sins. Their sins are removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12), blotted out (Isaiah 43:25). They stand clothed in Christ’s righteousness.

In a sentence. Then I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it; earth and sky fled from his presence and there was no place for them to go; and I saw the dead, important and unimportant, standing before the throne, and books were opened; then another book was opened, the book of life, and the dead were judged by what was recorded in the books, according to what they had done.

On a Tuesday. You will stand before this throne. Make sure your name is in the Lamb’s book, by trusting him now; and live today knowing that every deed is recorded.

verseByVerse.quote: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.

Setting and background. In the ancient world, people feared being lost at sea, because the body could not be buried and they thought the dead might be lost. Isaiah 25:8 says God will swallow up death for ever. Paul says the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26), and death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18).

And the sea gave up the dead who were in it. Key words. No one is lost. Even those whose bodies vanished in the sea are raised. All will be judged.

Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them. Key words. “Death and Hades”: personified, as in 6:8. Death and the realm of the dead must release everyone they hold. The general resurrection.

And they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Key words. “Each one” (hekastos). Individual, personal judgement. Every person answers for himself or herself.

Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. Key words. Death itself is destroyed. The last enemy is gone. In the new creation, death shall be no more (21:4).

This is the second death, the lake of fire. Key words. Revelation defines the second death plainly (as in 2:11; 20:6; 21:8). The first death separates soul from body; the second is the final, eternal punishment of the whole person, separated from God’s goodness and under his wrath.

And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire. Key words. “Not found written” (ouch heurethē … gegrammenos). This is the decisive question. Not whether a person’s good deeds outweigh their bad, but whether their name is in the Lamb’s book. Only those who belong to Christ are saved.

Where Christians differ: is anyone saved apart from faith in Christ? Inclusivists hold that some may be saved through Christ’s work without consciously knowing or believing in him, by responding to the light they have; pluralists hold that many religions lead to God. Verdict: the book of life is the Lamb’s book (21:27), and salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Those who are saved are those who hold the testimony of Jesus and are washed in his blood (7:14; 12:11). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation, tribe and language (14:6; Romans 10:13–15). God will judge every person justly, according to the light they had (Romans 2:12–16), and no one will be condemned unfairly; but salvation is through Christ alone, received by faith.

What it does not mean. The lake of fire is not annihilation. Those thrown in join the devil, the beast and the false prophet, who are tormented day and night for ever (v. 10). It is terrible, and it should move us to tears, to prayer, and to proclaim Christ.

In a sentence. The sea gave up the dead in it, and Death and the grave gave up the dead in them, and each person was judged according to what they had done; then Death and the grave were thrown into the lake of fire; the lake of fire is the second death; and anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.

On a Tuesday. Everything comes down to one question: is your name in the Lamb’s book of life? If you are trusting Christ, it is. Tell others how theirs can be.
